"The Unpopular “Hostess” of the once great Meet the Press, now considered Meet the Fake Press, just stated that Donald Trump has 'mixed results' on his Endorsements of Candidates," Trump wrote in a post on his Truth Social account.
"Recent WINS of Darline Graham and Mike Mazzei, stand at 100% for the U.S. Senate, and 98% for the U.S. House, recently and over the longterm," he continued, adding: "How can anyone be allowed to say this, working for freely given Public Airwaves?"

Reusable rocket milestone opens a door for Hong Kong’s space ambitions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:30:05 UTC
06:30:05 KST

Reusable rocket milestone opens a door for Hong Kong’s space ambitions
Flurry of commercial activity offers opportunities for Hong Kong’s financial markets, research universities and the Northern Metropolis
On the morning of August 19, LandSpace’s Zhuque-3 Y2 rocket lifted off from the Dongfeng Commercial Space Innovation Test Area. After deploying its second stage and payload into orbit, the rocket’s first stage touched down softly at a recovery site in Gansu province using deployable landing legs.
It was China’s first successful land-based recovery of an orbital-class rocket booster that had just completed an orbital mission – a feat previously achieved only by SpaceX.
The benchmark for reusable rockets remains SpaceX’s Falcon 9, which pioneered vertical landing after launches of this kind and has conducted hundreds of recoveries. Through first-stage reuse, Falcon 9 has driven its launch price down to about US$2,700 per kg (US$1,225 per lb) – a reduction of 85 per cent from an average of US$18,500 in the pre-reusable era. In contrast, China’s commercial launch prices hover at between US$8,000 and US$14,000 per kg, depending on rocket type and mission profile.
The Zhuque-3 is explicitly designed to close that gap. Standing 66 metres tall with a lift-off mass of roughly 570 tonnes, its first stage is powered by nine methane-liquid oxygen engines. Its stainless-steel structure – a deliberate departure from Falcon 9’s aluminium alloy – offers better heat resistance at a lower manufacturing cost. The booster is designed to be reused at least 20 times.

Algeria moves to impose death penalty for setting forest fires after 12 killed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:27:12 UTC
06:27:12 KST

Tarek Chouiref
31 August 2026•Update: 31 August 2026
Algeria’s president on Sunday ordered the introduction of the death penalty for deliberately setting forest fires after recent blazes across the country killed 12 people.
Abdelmadjid Tebboune issued the directive during a high-level meeting on measures to deal with the aftermath of the fires, attended by senior civilian and military officials, state TV reported.
He instructed the justice minister to submit an amendment to the penal code by Sept. 15 providing for capital punishment for anyone convicted of intentionally setting fire to forested areas.
State television said the sentence would be carried out only after all legal avenues of appeal had been exhausted.
The death penalty remains in Algeria’s criminal code for several offenses, but the country has maintained a de facto moratorium on executions since 1993.
Under current law, deliberately setting forest fires is punishable by up to 30 years in prison or life in prison in certain cases.

Analysis: Why One Nation victory in Western Australian state by-election is a big deal

The so-called "orange tsunami" — the One Nation blitzkrieg raging across the country — feels like it is doing just that.
Once seen as mainly a threat to the Coalition, this weekend One Nation proved it could take seats off the Labor Party.
The damage it inflicts will not just involve shifting votes from one political column to the next on the right-wing side of politics. The damage is coming for the establishment — blue and red.

Marles to meet Hegseth, Streeting and tech giants
Defence Minister Richard Marles is travelling to the Untied States today to meet with top tech companies about Australia's AI ambitions.
He's expected to meet Anthropic, Google, Amazon, Open AI and Microsoft to discuss the federal government's proposed standards for data centres and the water and energy that powers them. The government isn't expecting to sign a deal with any of the companies on the trip, though.
Marles is also scheduled to meet with US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth and the UK's new Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting.
Assistant Minister for Technology Andrew Charlton, who's been one of the leading government figures in the AI discussions, is also travelling to North Carolina for a meeting with G20 countries on how technologies can drive productivity and economic growth.
Government to unveil proposed changes to Australia's privacy laws
Sticking with the issue of smart glasses, the federal government will today unveil proposed changes to Australia's privacy laws.
Attorney-General Michelle Rowland is unveiling a new identity protection service, IDLock, and protections to "keep pace" with the rapid development of AI and smart glasses.
The reforms will include a right to erasure, allowing individuals to request large digital platforms like social media and search platforms destroy their personal information.
Speaking with Nine, Labor frontbencher Murray Watt says it's about trying to "put Australians more in control of their private information".
"When it comes to smart glasses, we think that there are real privacy risks with people having photos of themselves, images of themselves taken by these glasses without their consent and when they don't even know it's happening," he says.
"So we're going to make sure that we keep changing the law to keep pace with technological change."
eSafety commissioner wants smart glasses to blur faces
The eSafety commissioner wants "smart glasses" to automatically blur the faces of people being filmed without their consent.
In a note published to industry, the watchdog warned of the harm people can experience after being unknowingly filmed.
"Used in this way, smart glasses can reinforce and normalise watching, recording and controlling women in public without their knowledge," the note said.
"This contributes to harmful gendered stereotypes and undermines women's agency in public spaces".
The eSafety commissioner outlined "critical steps" companies could take, including ensuring glasses have clear recording lights that can't be switched off or covered up.
"If we do not act now to prevent design elements from being weaponised to cause harm, we risk unsafe features becoming entrenched".
The federal Greens and some independents want the federal government to impose a 12-month ban on the import of "smart glasses" while Australia's privacy laws catch up.
Yesterday on Insiders, Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek said the government was considering it "very closely", but no plans have been announced.

"I had a conversation with him merely a day or so ago and that was completely the opposite of what he said to me. I mean this is in every party. You have to go through the discussion, the process, and you know, David's an incredibly important part of that," he says.
Asked if the discussion with Farley was prompted by the reports, Joyce insists the pair "talk all the time".

This year's Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) leaders meeting could be particularly politically charged and has already got off to a slightly tumultuous start.
Palau is famous for its stunning karst landscape — with hundreds of rainforest-covered limestone islands — and for its powerful international advocacy on climate change.
It is also one of Taiwan's three remaining Pacific allies and a key link in the US military's second island chain, which means that debates over Taipei's role in the Pacific and China's growing military might will take on more urgency this year.
That does not mean that a diplomatic bust-up is inevitable.
But when Anthony Albanese flies into Palau's largest city Koror this evening, he will know there is a real chance that — at some point — he will find himself in the middle of one.

NATO driving the Arctic toward ‘militarization’ – Lavrov (FULL ARTICLE)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:24:30 UTC
06:24:30 KST

NATO driving the Arctic toward ‘militarization’ – Lavrov (FULL ARTICLE)
NATO is driving the militarization of the Arctic through intense military preparations that pose a direct threat to Russia’s security and increase the risk of direct armed confrontation, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov has said.
However, other than the members of the US-led military bloc, the overwhelming majority of countries are willing to engage with Moscow on equal and mutually beneficial terms, the top diplomat wrote in an article for Arctic.ru published on Monday.
The sweeping article touched on Moscow’s plans to develop Arctic shipping and maritime logistics along its Northern Sea Route, upcoming international cooperation, and the steady erosion of previous guardrails for multilateral collaboration in the region.
Read the full text below:
On August 19, a landmark event took place in Arctic shipping. For the first time, a container ship from China arrived at the port of Murmansk via the Northern Sea Route, a vital part of the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor. In collaboration with our international partners, this represents the start of a new phase in the development of Russia’s Arctic region, which accounts for at least 10% of the country’s GDP and is home to more than 2.5 million of our citizens. In this regard, I would like to share a number of considerations on how we assess the current state of affairs in the Arctic and how we plan to develop international cooperation there.
Russia and international partners in the Arctic
The Foundations of the Russian State Policy in the Arctic for the Period up to 2035, approved by President Vladimir Putin, focus the efforts of all government bodies on improving the quality of life for the population of the Arctic zone of the Russian Federation, promoting economic growth in its territories, protecting the environment, and fostering mutually beneficial international cooperation. The latter is of particular importance to the Foreign Ministry, which is entrusted with coordinating functions in relations with foreign countries and intergovernmental organizations. And, I would like to emphasize, the whole range of issues relating to the development of the Arctic zone, maritime logistics and the Northern Sea Route plays an important role in the activities of the Maritime Board of the Russian Federation.
Foreign policy priorities at high latitudes have been enshrined in the currently effective Concept of the Foreign Policy of the Russian Federation of March 31, 2023. In the Arctic, Russia is seeking to preserve peace and stability, reduce the level of threats to national security, and create favorable external conditions for the country’s socio-economic development. We are open to interaction with all constructively minded foreign countries displaying reciprocal readiness to put these ideas into practice. There are quite a few such countries. The vast resource, transport, and logistics potential of the Far North, its unique natural and climatic features, long-standing traditions of regional cooperation, and the rich cultural heritage of its indigenous peoples offer broad opportunities for advantageous partnership.
The countries that cooperate closely with us in the Arctic include, first and foremost, China and India. Substantive discussions on Arctic issues take place with Beijing during regular meetings between the heads of government. The specialized bilateral sub-commission on the Northern Sea Route is operational, as are mechanisms for interministerial consultations and scientific exchanges. The results speak for themselves: they include the launch of regular container shipments across Russia’s northern seas, with plans to increase their frequency, and other achievements, including in polar research.
We are engaged in an active dialogue with New Delhi on issues related to high latitudes. In late August, it was discussed at a meeting of the Russian-Indian Intergovernmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technical, and Cultural Cooperation. Indian corporations are involved in developing the resource potential of Russia’s Arctic region. According to some experts, the Arctic could become a major area of cooperation between Russia and India over the next 20 years.
There are prospects for interaction in the Far North with Brazil, Indonesia, Iran and other BRICS countries. We are also ready to develop cooperation with Belarus and other partners and allies in the CIS. South Korea and Singapore should also be mentioned as showing an interest in joint work with Russia in some Arctic projects, notwithstanding their participation in the unfriendly sanction campaign launched by the collective West against our country.
The interest of non-Arctic countries in establishing cooperation with Russia in the High North is reflected in the active participation of foreign guests in symposia and conferences devoted to Arctic issues. Numerous foreign delegations will take part in discussions during special sessions at the 11th Eastern Economic Forum, which opens on September 1 in Vladivostok. Next March, we look forward to welcoming distinguished guests from abroad to the next major international forum of the Russian Arctic, The Arctic – Territory of Dialogue, which will take place in Murmansk.
Challenges affecting international cooperation in the Arctic
Preserving the Arctic as an area of peace and cooperation meets the interests of the entire international community, and Russia is undoubtedly interested in this as well. However, there are those who do not share this point of view. How else can one explain the fact that NATO countries, as well as the Alliance as a whole, are driving the region towards militarization and creating hotbeds of international tension there?
In February 2026, NATO launched its Arctic Sentry operation, designed to expand its military presence in the High North. Intensive military preparations are underway in close proximity to our northern borders. NATO is conducting large-scale military exercises involving non-regional countries and introducing new components of its command-and-control system.
Such military activity in the Far North poses a direct threat to Russia’s security. It also increases the risk of incidents that could trigger an armed confrontation with potentially disastrous consequences.
This deliberate and systematic effort to foster an atmosphere of mistrust in the military sphere is taking place alongside Western attempts to undermine Russia’s legitimate rights in international cooperation through illegitimate financial and economic sanctions targeting legal entities and individuals from countries of the Global Majority involved in joint projects in the Arctic region.
NATO members and other Western countries make no secret of their true motives, openly declaring their intention to turn the Arctic into a new front for opposing the development of Russia and its like-minded partners.
One manifestation of the West’s anti-Russian policy has been the disruption of previously effective mechanisms of multilateral cooperation in the Far North. Some have ceased to exist altogether, while others have largely lost their relevance without Russia’s participation, after Moscow was forced to suspend its engagement with them in response to hostile actions. The Arctic Council, established almost 30 years ago, on September 19, 1996, remains the only functioning intergovernmental organization.
The Council is approaching its anniversary in a shape that is far from ideal. Since March 2022, as a result of actions by its Western member states, its work has effectively been frozen, leaving the organization in a severe crisis. Ministerial meetings and sessions of its key coordinating body, the Senior Arctic Officials, have been suspended, while its capacity to implement projects has been significantly curtailed. The Council’s activities are now largely confined to expert-level contacts and remote meetings of its working bodies.
Russia is ready to resume the full-fledged work of the Arctic Council, provided that all parties engage in good faith and take into account the legitimate interests of every participant. At the same time, we are prepared for the scenario currently being pursued by NATO countries within the organization as they attempt to discuss Arctic issues among themselves, without Russia, thereby effectively discrediting and marginalizing the Arctic Council. Should this scenario materialize, Russia has the territory, logistics, technology, and reliable partners needed to carry out mutually beneficial projects and confidently implement its plans in the Arctic.
The future of international cooperation in the Arctic
A glance at the world map makes it clear that Russia has been, is, and will remain a leading Arctic state. As climate change continues and the polar ice cover recedes, experts predict that the Arctic will become increasingly accessible for transportation and resource development. The region is already playing an increasingly important role in maintaining stable trade links amid more frequent disruptions to global supply chains, particularly in the straits of the world’s oceans that are of systemic importance to the global economy.
The strategic importance of the Arctic to our country’s national interests and security will also continue to grow. We will pursue the comprehensive development of the High North and further expand the infrastructure of Russia’s Arctic zone in accordance with Russian law and the country’s development priorities.
In our economic activities, we will continue to proceed from the understanding that the Arctic maritime areas form an integral part of the World Ocean. The provisions of the 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea, which establish special rights and responsibilities for coastal states in the Arctic, apply there in full. Commitment to these rights and responsibilities was reaffirmed in the Ilulissat Declaration, adopted in 2008 by the five Arctic coastal states – Russia, Denmark, Canada, Norway, and the United States. At this stage, we see no need to develop new international legal instruments governing economic and other activities in the High North.
Russia’s foreign policy in the Arctic will remain comprehensive and pragmatic. We support the Arctic’s development as an integral part of the broader Eurasian space of security and cooperation.
Our current opponents should have learned the many lessons of history by now and understood that attempts to speak to Russia in the language of sanctions and threats are futile. Unfriendly and hostile actions have been and will continue to be met with an appropriate response, including asymmetric measures. Russia favors constructive dialogue in all regions of the world, but, when necessary, we will defend our national interests by all available means.
As President of Russia Vladimir Putin has repeatedly emphasized, extensive work is underway in the Arctic, and we are open to cooperation with all partners willing to engage on the basis of equality and mutual benefit. Such partners, beyond the circle of NATO countries pursuing Russophobic policies, constitute the overwhelming majority.Promising areas of cooperation include the development of natural resources and the Trans-Arctic Transport Corridor, including its key component, the Northern Sea Route. Priorities also include the development of industrial, transport, and tourism infrastructure.Improving the well-being of people living in the Far North, preserving the Arctic environment, and advancing scientific research will also remain key priorities. In all these areas, we see international cooperation as playing a major role.

The Icelandic parliament will discuss the results of the referendum on joining the EU
Kyiv • UNN
52.8% of Icelanders opposed resuming negotiations with the EU. Parliament will discuss the further fate of the application, which has not been officially withdrawn.
The Icelandic Parliament will discuss the future of the country's application to join the European Union after the majority of citizens opposed resuming negotiations with Brussels. Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir said this, Politico reports, writes UNN.
Details
According to the referendum results, 52.8% of voters opposed resuming EU accession negotiations, while 47.2% supported the proposal. Turnout was 82.5%.
Frostadóttir said that the government would discuss with the parliamentary Foreign Affairs Committee what to do with Iceland's application, which has still not been officially withdrawn.
There will be no EU accession negotiations for now
We will discuss with the parliamentary Foreign Affairs Committee how best to close this chapter. We do not intend to make any final decisions on this matter
Frostadóttir stressed that the referendum results would be respected, meaning that under the current government, negotiations on Iceland's accession to the EU will not resume. At the same time, she said, the issue of membership is likely to become a topic again in the next parliamentary elections.
Iceland began negotiations to join the EU in 2009, but they were suspended in 2013. However, the country has never officially withdrawn its membership application.

Flash floods hit Grand Canyon, at least 20 hikers missing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:17:52 UTC
06:17:52 KST

More than 20 hikers who visited the Grand Canyon in Arizona are missing after flash floods struck the area beginning at around 2:30 p.m. local time, the Daily Mail reported Sunday evening. Authorities are searching for the missing hikers and are asking the public to help identify those who were on the trails they had been hiking.
More than 62 people were evacuated from the area Saturday because of the flooding. All pedestrian bridges crossing Bright Angel Creek were destroyed by the unusual weather after the creek overflowed its banks.
The U.S. National Park Service said in a statement: “Grand Canyon National Park crews, in coordination with the Arizona Department of Public Safety, continue evacuation and incident response efforts and are working to locate individuals who may have been in the affected area.” 
Videos from the scene showed mudslides sweeping through the area as hikers filmed them from a suspension bridge.
There is currently no estimated timetable for reopening the blocked roads, and additional areas in the inner canyon may also have to be closed.
More than 60 people were evacuated from Phantom Ranch, which has a historic canteen and dorms, and is a common spot for rafters to get off and on the river. More evacuations were planned during Sunday, the park said. No injuries have been reported.
Erica Viola said she was at Bright Angel Campground when the rain started Saturday afternoon, and she and about 50 other hikers watched the creek rise and then debris start to flow by, including what looked like a bunkhouse. The group was taken by helicopter to safety, ending her adventure two days early, she said.
About half an inch to 1 inch (1 centimeter to 2.5 centimeters) of rain fell within about 30 minutes in the rocky area where there's a steep drop in elevation, said National Weather Service meteorologist Justin Johndrow in Flagstaff.
"Most of it ran off instantly," Johndrow said.
He said the flooding happened on the north side of the Grand Canyon, where Bright Angel Creek comes from the North Rim down to the Colorado River, dropping around 6,000 feet (1,828 meters).
More rain and thunderstorms were possible for the area into Monday.

US strikes Iranian launchers on Larak Island, marking first attacks in weeks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:12:00 UTC
06:12:00 KST

Yasin Gungor
31 August 2026•Update: 31 August 2026
US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island on Sunday, marking the first strikes on Iranian territory since late July, an official told Axios.
The operation, which followed a month-long period of relative stagnation in direct military engagements, targeted systems allegedly being prepared to launch rockets carrying sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz, a critical oil transit point.
According to the US official, American forces are “monitoring the area closely and remain prepared to protect the free flow of commerce” through the strategic waterway. The Strait of Hormuz narrows to just 39 kilometers (24 miles) between Larak Island and Oman’s Great Quoin Island.
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said several fighters and civilians were killed and injured in the strike and vowed to respond. Iran's Tasnim news agency reported that preliminary information suggested it was a drone attack.
Further details regarding the outcome of the strike were not immediately available.
US President Donald Trump recently said that all mines had been removed from the Strait of Hormuz, and warned of a “zero tolerance policy” on new mine placement. He said Washington was utilizing "Space Force" technology to monitor the area with extreme precision.
Iranian officials have asserted that "no one except Iran knows the location" of the mines in the strategic waterway.
Tensions between Tehran and Washington have remained high since the war began with strikes on Iran in late February. Although a memorandum of understanding was signed in June through Pakistani and Qatari mediation, the US began a two-week bombing campaign and reimposed a naval blockade in July after differences over navigation in the strait.
It has yet to be seen whether the latest strike represents a one-time operation or the start of a sustained new bombing campaign.

Right to question not defiance, every dissent not a threat: SC judge
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:10:44 UTC
06:10:44 KST

'In a democracy, the right to question is not an act of defiance.': Justice Bhuyan
NEW DELHI: In a constitutional democracy like India, govt must listen to citizens, give space for dissent, and have institutions that are accountable to society and do not treat every dissent as a threat, Supreme Court judge Ujjal Bhuyan said on Sunday."In a democracy, the right to question is not an act of defiance. It is an essential expression of citizenship, liberty and constitutional responsibility," Justice Bhuyan said at a convocation ceremony at National Law University, Delhi."If we want a democratic society that respects liberty and difference, that culture has to begin somewhere. It can only begin in our universities. A university... should be one of the first places where the habit of thinking freely begins," he said.A university should be a space where an idea is not accepted merely because it is familiar and where students do not hesitate to ask difficult questions simply because the answer may be uncomfortable,” Justice Bhuyan said.He said India’s Constitution guarantees free speech, thinking and believing differently. “Intolerance begins to undermine that framework when disagreement or dissent is no longer treated as a legitimate difference of opinion but as something that must be silenced, rejected or punished.
The ability to live with disagreement is not merely a social virtue. It is the very essence of a liberal constitutional democracy.”Justice Bhuyan said maturity of a democracy is reflected not merely in how it treated opinions that are popular, having the majoritarian mandate, but also in how it responds to opinions that are difficult, unpopular or inconvenient. “The freedom to express an opinion, to disagree with the prevailing view and to participate in public life would be meaningful only when there is space for dissent,” he added.
He quoted Justice O Chinnappa Reddy’s 1986 judgment in Bijoe Emmanuel case, in which the judge had said, “Our tradition teaches tolerance; our philosophy preaches tolerance; our constitution practises tolerance; let us not dilute it.”He pointed out that tolerance under our Constitution does not ask us to surrender our individuality. “It recognises that a free society would contain different opinions, beliefs and ways of looking at the world,” he said.

Key Event
Monash IVF profit slumps, new chair announced
Troubled fertility business Monash IVF has reported a 41% drop net profit to $16 million.
The result was below management's revised FY26 NPAT guidance of $17m-$18m, with the miss attributable to a post-tax $1.4m write-off of prepaid assets.
Revenue slipped by 1%, roughly in line with consensus expectations, while the final dividend of 1.3 cents per share beat expectations.
The company also announced a renewal of its board with experience director and former Nine Entertainment chair Catherine West replacing current chair Richard Davis.
Two other long serving directors will also be replaced.
Monash IVF has suffered recent reputational damage with two embryo mix ups coming to light last year.
Earlier this year, the company rebuffed a $350 million takeover offer from a consortium of ASX listed investment vehicle Washington H. Soul Pattinson and private equity group Genesis Capital.
Key Event
Austal's profit scuttled by 'onerous' US defence contracts
Shipbuilder Austral has seen its profits torpedoed by what it says are the "onerous contracts" it has with the US Department of War.
The non-cash provision relating to the US contracts saw last year's $90 million net profit swing to a $54 million loss in FY26.
This was despite an 11% increase in revenues to more than $2 billion.
Austal CEO Peter Gregg the result was dragged down by the US Department of War rejecting a request for relief from contracts he described as "onerous".
"We have commenced the longer, formal process to recover the value on these contracts and our position is supported by a documented factual and contractual record," Mr Gregg said in a statement to the ASX.
Austal's Australian operations did better with pre-tax earnings more than doubling to $85 million.
Austal currently has a record $5+ billion order book stretching out over 12 years.
The company won't pay a final dividend.
Key Event
CBA, Colonial First State and Avanteos to pay $249m in banking RC settlement
It's now eight years since the Royal Commission into Misconduct in the Banking, Superannuation and Financial Services Industry started examining some of the the sector's more dubious/illegal operations, but the process of remediation is still slowly rolling along.
In its action against Colonial First State Investments, Avanteos Investments and the Commonwealth Bank, Slater and Gordon Lawyers has finally landed a $249 million in principle settlement of a class action.
The proceedings commenced in 2018 as part of Slater and Gordon's "Get Your Super Back" series of class actions in the wake of the 2018 banking royal commission.
The settlement is still subject to Federal Court approval and was reached without Colonial First State, Avanteos or CBA admitting liability.
Here's more from Slater and Gordon's statement this morning.
"At its heart this case was about the alleged conflict between CFSIL, AIL and CBA's interests in profiting from members' savings, and CFSIL and AIL's duties as trustees to do the best they could for their members. The case alleged CFSIL and AIL failed to properly manage that conflict," said Nathan Rapoport, class actions practice group leader at Slater and Gordon Lawyers.
"Superannuation trustees must prioritise their members' interests over their own. If any superannuation trustees might be at risk of forgetting the lessons from the banking royal commission, the settlement in this case should serve as a reminder."
The case alleged that group members' retirement savings were reduced through the payment of low interest rates on certain cash and deposit investments with CBA offered through Colonial First State superannuation and wrap products, CFS FirstChoice and FirstWrap and Commonwealth Essential Super, between November 2008 and September 2021.
It was alleged that CFSIL and AIL did not act in the best interests of their superannuation fund members when they invested members' retirement savings with their parent bank CBA without trying to obtain the best interest rates available for their members.
It also alleged that CFSIL and AIL received undisclosed payments from CBA which incentivised them to invest members' savings with CBA at lower rates, and that CBA benefited by obtaining access to members' savings at low interest rates.
Slater and Gordon's case alleged that the cash and deposit investments at the centre of the proceeding did not provide members with the returns they were reasonably entitled to expect, and that in total members lost millions in aggregate retirement funding.

Key Event
Liontown posts maiden profit
WA-based lithium miner Liontown has posted its first profit thanks to higher prices and increasing production and sales.
Liontown swung from a $193 million loss last year to $93 million net profit after tax in FY26.
Its underlying profit, stripping out exceptional items, was $14 million.
Production and sales rose by about a third, while the realised price of its lithium concentrate jumped by around 60% in Australian dollar terms.
Liontown's cash balance at the end of the year was 260% higher at $561 million.
Gift card scam hits supermarket customers
An ABC investigation has discovered gift cards that have been tampered with are being sold by Australia's biggest supermarkets, with charges even being laid over the issue.
It is leaving shoppers confused and stressed, and raising questions about whether this is linked to a multi-billion-dollar criminal scam.
The investigation by Emilia Terzon and Eric Hao Zheng is well worth your time to read.

It's a busy week on the local macro front with second quarter GDP set to be published on Wednesday.
But before we get there, there are a couple of GDP partials that need to be fed into the equation.
Later this morning we will get Q2 Business indicators — company profits and inventories.
Company profits are expected to rebound after a Q1 decline as mining exports are expected to be higher after Q1's weather impacted results.
Inventories are likely to be a positive for GDP growth with imports of consumer goods, particularly cars, increasing across the quarter.
The final piece of the GDP puzzle, the Q2 Current Account Balance, is released on Tuesday.
The deficit is expected to have widened around $3 billion to $30 billion, but there should be a positive contribution from the primary income balance.
The overall Current Account/Balance of Payments contribution is expected to around zero.
For GDP itself, the market is expecting 0.4% growth in Q2, delivering an annual rate of a modest 1.9%. However, the picks vary from flat over the quarter to 0.6%.
CBA is forecasting the average of 0.4% growth.
"This would provide evidence that the economy is slowing which is required to bring the economy back to balance over time," CBA said.
Here are CBA's key component forecasts
- Household consumption: +0.6%/qtr
- Dwelling investment: 1.3%/qtr
- Business investment: -1.3%/qtr
- Public demand: +0.9%/qtr
- Net exports contribution: 0.0pp
Also, this week, we get the latest reading on home prices via Cotality's Home Value Index (Tuesday).
National home prices are forecast to fall another 1.2%, which would be the largest monthly decline in the current downturn, although it could equally be said that home affordability will increase by 1.2%.
Dwelling approvals for July will also be released on Tuesday.
It's a volatile series, driven by apartment approvals, so the market is forecasting a decline in July given the jump June approvals.
Across the ditch, the RBNZ is expected to raise rates for the second consecutive meeting, up 25 bps to 2.75% with inflation there now above 4%.
The Bank of Canada also holds a rates meeting on Wednesday but is likely to remain on hold at 2.25%.
ASX set to follow Wall Street lower as rate hike odds shorten
Wall Street's key indices closed lower after Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh reiterated the central bank's focus on fighting inflation, increasing prospects for a rate hike.
Without confidence that inflation is heading clearly and with sufficient speed to the Fed's 2% goal, the central bank would have "more work to do," Mr Warsh said in his first Jackson Hole speech to fellow central bankers.
That saw early gains in US equities fade, while European markets had already closed and finished the session with handy gains.
- S&P 500: -0.25%
- Dow: -0.02%
- Nasdaq: -0.5%
- Eurostoxx 600: +0.5%
ASX 200 futures trading closed on Saturday morning (AEST) pointing to a 0.4% decline today.
However, the S&P 500 still gained 0.5% over the week, while the ASX 200 picked up 0.4% snapping a two-week losing streak.
The Nasdaq was hit by a 4.3% drop in Nvidia shares and Marvel Technology fell more than 10%, however the megacaps Alphabet (+1.7%) and Apple (+1.6%) made solid gains.
Traders added to bets on a September rate hike after Mr Warsh also said he felt recent inflation data did not suggest a change in trend.
After the comments, bets that rates would be raised at the September meeting rose to a 56% probability from 35% on Thursday, according to CME Group's FedWatch tool.
Three Fed officials have already warned about sticky inflation, but Mr Warsh had previously resisted giving forward guidance on the path of interest rates.
"The crisp mountain air of the Grand Tetons may have helped bring clarity of speech to Fed Chair Warsh, who marked his 100th day in the job by offering seven principles to navigate by," NAB's Head of Rates Strategy Ken Crompton wrote in a note this morning.
"He gave no undertaking as to where the path ends — but left no doubt that underlying inflation trends are bringing him no comfort: the Fed must be confident inflation is heading to target 'clearly and at sufficient speed. Otherwise, we have work to do.'"
Traders are now split between a rate hike and a hold in September, as they were before inflation data this month painted a mixed picture.
"Why the market is modestly reacting is he (Warsh) is very adamant that the 2% inflation target is going to remain. He is reiterating the hawkishness, but in a more of a consistent way than an incremental way," chief market strategist for Nationwide, Mark Hackett told Reuters
"There's been somewhat misguided thoughts among investors that this would soften a little bit. Clearly, that's not the case."
MSCI's gauge of stocks across the globe slipped 0.1% on Friday, while the pan-European STOXX 600 index gained 0.5%.
In the bond market, the 2-year note, which typically moves in step with Fed interest rate expectations, rose sharply 12.79 basis points to 4.36%.
The yield on benchmark U.S. 10-year notes rose 5.6 basis points to 4.728%, while the 30-year bond yield rose 2.19 basis points to 5.2129%.
In foreign exchange markets, the US dollar jumped against other major currencies and was on track for its biggest daily climb in more than 2 months on the prospect of rising rates.
The dollar index, which measures the greenback against a basket of currencies including the yen and the euro, rose 0.6% to 99.71, although the Aussie dollar remained relatively unmoved at 71.58 US cents, just below its four-month high.
The Aussie was the best performing of all G10 currencies against the US dollar last week.
Oil slipped a tad on rumours that the Strait of Hormuz would soon reopen to shipping.
Gold fell more than 3% as the US rate-hike expectations spread. Silver fell 4%.

US strikes Iranian launchers on Larak island amid strait of Hormuz tensions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:05:43 UTC
06:05:43 KST

US forces have struck two Iranian launchers on Iran’s Larak island, a US official said, marking the first known American strikes since late July.
“I can confirm that earlier today US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak island. Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait of Hormuz,” the official said on Sunday.
The IRGC said the attack killed and wounded several soldiers and citizens and would be met with a “response and punishment” from Tehran, Iranian state media reported.
A spokesperson said the US would pay for the attack economically and militarily, according to the semi-official news agency Fars.
Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency reported the US had carried out a drone strike on the island.
On Sunday night, Reuters reported a US source as saying Iran had launched an attack on US forces in Jordan in apparent retaliation, with the source adding that all incoming missiles had been intercepted with no significant impact so far.
Donald Trump said last week that all mines had been detonated or removed from the international waters of the strait of Hormuz and Iran had been told that any ship or boat placing new mines would be destroyed.
The last known US strikes on Iran were in late July and the war has reached a stalemate in recent weeks, with Washington threatening to impose costly sanctions on countries that support Iran.
The US and Israel attacked Iran on 28 February and Iran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases. The Iran war has now crossed its six-month mark.
US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed thousands and displaced millions. Eighteen US service members have been killed in the conflict.
The war has led to the blockade of the strait of Hormuz, which before the conflict accounted for the transit of about a fifth of the world’s oil barrels consumed.

File photo: PM Modi being accorded a ceremonial welcome, in Tashkent. Uzbekistan President Shavkat Mirziyoyev is also seen.
India and Uzbekistan upgraded their relations to a comprehensive strategic partnership, set an annual trade target of $5 billion and closed in on an agreement for uranium supply to India, as PM Narendra Modi held talks with President Shavkat Mirziyoyev in Tashkent.Modi announced that India would get into a long-term arrangement for supply of uranium from Uzbekistan, a major regional producer and exporter. Both sides agreed to establish a foreign minister-level coordination council to guide all aspects of cooperation under the elevated partnership.Following the talks that focused on expanding cooperation in defence and security, trade and investment, critical minerals, AI, agriculture and health, the two sides signed 11 MoUs. The areas covered included culture, education, mining, Ayurveda, tourism and restoration of Buddhist sites.PM Modi also underscored the need for zero tolerance against terrorism and extremism, saying a stronger India-Uzbekistan partnership will be a powerful force for peace, progress and prosperity in Central Asia.PM Modi and Mirziyoyev endorsed growing defence cooperation between the two countries, including through regular exchanges, capacity-building and joint activities, and expressed in a joint statement their commitment to address common security challenges by further strengthening such cooperation.
Going forward, Modi said, both sides will promote direct linkages, co-production and co-development by the defence industries of both nations. “Close defence and security cooperation between our two countries reflects our deep mutual trust,” said the PM.Outlining an ambitious agenda for moving forward with “speed and tangible results” in this new phase of their partnership, the PM said both sides will also work systematically on market access, connectivity, banking and payment systems to achieve the target of $5 billion of trade by 2030.“We will work together to boost win-win cooperation in infrastructure development. Cooperation in DPI, AI, critical minerals, clean energy, space and nuclear energy is making our relationship future-ready,” said Modi, adding that Uzbekistan is at the heart of Central Asia and at the heart of India’s engagement with the region.
Both sides believe that while India is one of Uzbekistan’s top 10 trading partners, their annual trade of $1.32 billion remains significantly below its true potential. In the meeting, the two agreed to undertake joint measures to broaden the range of goods traded between the two countries, remove non-tariff barriers and promote industrial cooperation with a view to further increasing bilateral trade turnover. They also decided to create a joint working group to address non-tariff issues and investment barriers.There was also focus on Global South cooperation with PM Modi saying that Uzbekistan’s highest honour for a foreign leader that was conferred on him by the president had left India with the added responsibility of working with Uzbekistan as “Global South partners for the betterment of humanity”.

IRGC attacks US air bases in Jordan, Iranian state media reports
Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it retaliated for earlier American strikes on Larak Island by firing ballistic missiles at American positions in Jordan.
The IRGC said it caused "heavy damage" on what it referredto as the King Hussein base and the Al-Azraq base, both in Jordan.
The Jordanian army said it intercepted eight missiles that entered its airspace.
US sources also said that nearly all of the missiles had been intercepted, according to Fox News' chief international correspondent Trey Yingst.
US redirected dozens of ships to enforce Iran blockade
US forces have redirected dozens of ships as part of efforts to enforce a maritime blockade against Iran, the US Central Command said on Sunday night.
The US imposed a naval blockade on Iran in April, after Iran blocked most international shipping in the Strait of Hormuz in late February.
"As of August 30, CENTCOM forces have redirected 83 commercial vessels, disabled 3 and boarded 2 to ensure compliance with the blockade," CENTCOM said on social media.
US forces attack Iran for first time in weeks
US forces reportedly stuck Iranian military sites in the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday night — the first US strikes on Iran in over a month.
"Earlier today, US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Larak Island," US Navy Captain Tim Hawkins said in a message to the AFP news agency.
"Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps forces were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the Strait of Hormuz."
Iranian media reported explosions near Larak Island.
The US said last week that it had finished clearing Iranian sea mines from the strait's international shipping routes.
The IRGC said in a statement that the attack on Sunday night "will be answered by the sons of Iran and will result in the punishment of the aggressor."

Ukraine’s war didn’t go to plan. Its former defense minister’s career did
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
20:58:48 UTC
05:58:48 KST

Ukraine’s war didn’t go to plan. Its former defense minister’s career did
Former Ukrainian Defense Minister Mikhail Fedorov has suddenly – and rather unexpectedly – become an adviser to Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto. The news caught many conservative military analysts off guard. Why would Italy want him, and what does Rome hope to gain? Let’s try to make sense of the move without getting carried away.
A manager in khaki, not a marshal
It should be obvious that Fedorov is no military genius, nor does he possess any particular talent as a battlefield commander. That is simply not who he is. He was never a career officer, and he never made his name drawing thick red arrows across maps of future operations. First and foremost, Mikhail Fedorov is an effective IT executive – and a knowledgeable chief customer for the entire defense industry.
His path to that role began as the top digital strategist for Vladimir Zelensky’s presidential campaign, where he built an online campaign network and bet heavily on internet marketing. From there, he went on to create Ukraine’s Ministry of Digital Transformation and roll out the Diia digital ecosystem, which changed everyday life across the country. In 2026, Fedorov took over the Defense Ministry amid an urgent need to impose order and bring sweeping digitalization to the armed forces. The timing, it seems, could hardly have been better.
Several major changes in the Ukrainian military were introduced with Fedorov’s involvement:
- Drone procurement for military units was radically overhauled through the launch of a dedicated marketplace designed to minimize red tape. It was a highly unconventional move that significantly shortened the path from manufacturer to frontline unit while opening up a market for many small and relatively young companies. After drones, the same digital approach began spreading to other parts of the defense industry.
- Agile management methods were effectively brought into military life, breaking down long-established systems of multistage approval and allowing new ideas to be tested quickly under real battlefield conditions – directly in the trenches.
- The military opened its doors to software developed by civilian companies. The emphasis shifted toward finding new and unconventional solutions that could be deployed quickly and deliver results immediately, rather than waiting for lengthy testing reports and reviews by specialized military institutes.
Of course, Fedorov’s role in these changes should not be overstated. Many of the initiatives that reshaped the Ukrainian military began before he arrived at the Defense Ministry. What he brought was a fresh, digital perspective that helped cut some corners and speed up the adoption of new ideas.
There were no combat operations or battlefield triumphs involved. He was a digital-solutions manager who put on a military uniform – focused exclusively on digital systems and a project-based approach to reform. And naturally the process was not without its rough edges. Digitalization remains the only clear success he can point to.
Why Rome wants the “Ukraine playbook”
Perhaps that is precisely what Rome needs: not military victories or battlefield credentials, but a fresh, modern approach. That, presumably, is where Italy is placing its hopes. Modern European militaries, including Italy’s, are weighed down by bureaucracy. Decisions on the procurement of new weapons systems and software take years. By the time they are finally approved, technology has already moved on, leaving armed forces to adopt systems that were obsolete before they ever entered service.
Fedorov may well be useful to Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto as a new battering ram against his own conservative military establishment. Rome wants to borrow Ukraine’s experience of rapidly digitalizing military logistics and integrating unmanned systems in real time.
To understand exactly which processes Fedorov may seek to adapt for the Italian military, one need only look inside his “digital briefcase.” It contains no secret missile technology – only commercial software and civilian IT solutions adapted to the needs of a defense ministry.
The Italian military is eager to introduce new digital battle-management systems that combine geospatial tools with hundreds of information sources and a distributed network of users, extending from the General Staff all the way to a frontline commander’s tablet in the trenches. Italy is also naturally interested in digitalizing weapons and military-equipment procurement – and even more so in applying artificial intelligence to military command and control.
It is difficult to judge the results, but on paper Fedorov’s résumé looks highly impressive: experience introducing cutting-edge digital solutions in Europe’s only army currently fighting a major war. That is certainly one way to present it – and why be shy when listing your strengths on a résumé?
What Rome is really buying
A modern army increasingly resembles an IT corporation. Rome does not need Fedorov’s advice on how to defend its coastline or plan an armored offensive. It needs his ability to turn the military into a functioning digital platform.
But let’s take an honest look at the former defense minister’s record. Yes, there was digitalization and digital transformation. It may still be too early to assess the final results, but there have been no major successes on the battlefield – and that, one would think, is what an army is ultimately for and how its performance should be measured.
Then there is the less flattering part of the picture: the image of a petulant child who could not find common ground with career officers and began playing political games in the middle of an ongoing war to increase his own value back home. That hardly seems consistent with the image of a gifted digital manager. Wars, after all, are not won through digitalization alone, but through the coordinated action of different branches and types of forces.
It will be fascinating to see what Fedorov ‘achieves’ in his new job – and whether the spirit of Silicon Valley can take root in the austere offices of the Italian Defense Ministry.
As for the man with the polished résumé and the reputation of a ‘digitalization expert’, a position like this – especially in Rome – offers a splendid opportunity to make a graceful exit from Kiev and trade Ukraine’s brutal political reality for the warm, easygoing comforts of Europe.

For every 100 laundered, only 1 recovered by authorities: CJI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
20:57:29 UTC
05:57:29 KST

Economic crimes move faster than treaties; global cooperation key to recovery: CJI Surya Kant
NEW DELHI: Chief Justice of India Surya Kant said for every Rs 100 laundered, authorities and law enforcement agencies recovered only Re 1, mainly because of the ingenuity of economic offenders, and lack of global cooperation on extraditing fugitives.Money laundered globally in a year was more than enough to buy every single person on earth a modest laptop, CJI said at the 43rd International Symposium on Economic Crime in Cambridge Saturday. "...For every hundred parts of that wealth, ninety-nine are simply referred to in speeches and reports, while only one part is ever actually put right."CJI Surya Kant quoted ancient Indian statesman Kautilya’s Arthashastra, which had recorded that it was impossible for an official to handle the king’s revenue and take nothing from it, and provided for an antidote through audits, cross-verification and confiscation of ill-gotten gain.Referring to India’s layered legislations against economic crimes and its balancing by judicial interventions, the CJI said though India had signed extradition and mutual legal assistance treaties with foreign jurisdictions, “the property we actually recover remains, frankly, underwhelming”.
The CJI said that illicit wealth and economic crimes moved faster than the pace of ratification of treaties and, hence, no jurisdiction, however well resourced or determined, could pursue them alone, despite the existence of provisions for non-conviction based forfeitures, unexplained wealth orders, beneficial ownership registers and financial intelligence sharing.
“None of these tools is missing from our shelves. What is missing, and what each jurisdiction owes the other, is the willingness to use them together rather than one at a time: a forfeiture order in one country acted upon promptly by a registry in another, an intelligence tip followed through to an actual freeze rather than left to gather dust,” he further added.India had initiated processes for extraditions of Vijay Mallya with the UK authorities in 2017 and Nirav Modi with the US in 2018.None of them has fructified in extradition of the two, accused of misappropriating huge sums and fleeing the country.

Diabetes impacts men, women differently: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
20:40:49 UTC
05:40:49 KST

Study finds type 2 diabetes complications differ by gender: men face higher heart and kidney risks, women more likely to develop mental health conditions.
NEW DELHI: For men, type 2 diabetes more often sets the stage for heart and kidney disease; for women, the greater threat appears to be mental health problems, a new study tracking nearly 29,000 patients has found.The study, published in PLOS Medicine, followed 28,720 people newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes between 2010 and 2020 using linked primary and secondary healthcare records in the UK. Researchers used a multi-state analysis to track the order and timing of hypertension, cardiovascular disease, end-stage renal disease and mental health conditions over a median follow-up of 6.8 years. Women were more likely than men to be diagnosed with a mental health condition.Women were more likely than men to be diagnosed with a mental health condition, including anxiety, depression or somatoform disorders, after developing diabetes. Such conditions were recorded in 8.1% of women compared with 5.3% of men.Men, meanwhile, were more likely to develop cardiovascular disease or end-stage renal disease, with 8.4% following this trajectory compared with 5.3% of women.
Mental health risks are higher for women with diabetes as compared to men
Senior endocrinologist Prof Ravinder Goswami of All India Institutes of Medical Sciences (AIIMS) said diabetes can affect men and women differently.
Men may develop diabetes at a younger age, while women with diabetes lose the natural protection against heart disease that is usually seen before menopause. The study also found that women with diabetes may have a higher risk of problems related to memory, thinking and mental health.However, he cautioned that these problems may not be caused by diabetes alone, as cognitive and neuropsychiatric problems are generally more common in women. He said doctors should, therefore, watch for these issues while managing diabetes.Hypertension was the most common complication after type-2 diabetes across all age groups and in both sexes. It affected 21.1% of men and 20.2% of women. Men also experienced most complications earlier than women, while women generally had a later onset of events.The study linked diabetes, mental health and mortality, finding that people who developed a mental health condition after diabetes died earlier. Among those with the same disease trajectory, men died on average nine years younger than women.Despite this, women had higher average healthcare utilisation and long-term prescribing than men. The researchers said the lower healthcare use among men in the high-risk mental health trajectory could point to gaps in engagement with healthcare services.
The findings point to the need for sex-specific diabetes care, including routine mental health screening, particularly for younger women, and earlier cardiovascular and kidney monitoring for men.The researchers further added that tracking the sequence and timing of complications could help identify patients at higher risk and enable earlier intervention. However, as an observational study, the findings cannot establish cause and effect, and differences in mental health diagnoses may partly reflect healthcare-seeking behaviour.
Anuja Jaiswal is a Senior Assistant Editor at The Times of India, with an impressive 18-year career in narrative journalism. She specializes in health and heritage reporting, expertly simplifying complex health information to make it engaging and understandable for readers. Her deep dives into heritage topics are well-researched, resulting in captivating narratives that resonate with her audience. Over the years, she has worked in Chandigarh, Chhattisgarh and West UP, gaining diverse on-ground experience that shapes her storytelling.

Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency reported the US carried out a drone strike on the island.
US President Donald Trump said last week that all mines had been detonated or removed from the international waters of the Strait of Hormuz and Iran has been told that any ship or boat placing new mines will be destroyed.
The last known US strikes on Iran were in late July as the war has reached a stalemate in recent weeks with Washington threatening to impose costly sanctions on countries that support Iran.
The US and Israel attacked Iran on Feb 28 and Iran responded with its own strikes on Israel and Gulf states that host US bases. The Iran war has now crossed its six-month mark.
US-Israeli strikes on Iran and Israeli attacks on Lebanon have killed thousands and displaced millions. Eighteen US service members have been killed in the conflict.
The war has led to the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz, which before the conflict used to see a transit of about a fifth of the world’s oil supply.
The Iranian weapons launched at the US base on Aug 30 were ballistic missiles, Axios reported. REUTERS

‘Opening a new chapter’: Syria reopens embassy in Libya after talks
Syrian foreign minister and Libyan PM agree to cooperation committee and reopening of diplomatic missions closed for 14 years.
Syria and Libya have agreed to reopen Syria’s embassy in Tripoli, which has been closed for 14 years, and reactivate a committee for coordinating bilateral ties during talks between Prime Minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibah of Libya’s internationally recognised government and Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad Hassan al-Shaibani.
Al-Shaibani arrived in Tripoli on Sunday to meet with Libyan officials, according to a statement from Libya’s Government of National Unity (GNU).
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Can international diplomacy find a way forward in Libya?
- list 2 of 3Rival Libya factions sign deal to hold national elections within two years
- list 3 of 3Libya factions draft initial election pact amid lingering mistrust
Libya has been split since 2014 between the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity, led by Dbeibah, and an eastern administration, led by Osama Hammad and backed by renegade military commander Khalifa Haftar. Representatives of Libya’s rival governments signed a deal on Sunday to hold national elections within two years.
Cooperation agreement
Damascus and Tripoli signed an agreement to reactivate the Libyan-Syrian Joint Higher Committee, a committee at the prime ministerial level tasked with coordinating political, economic and social ties between the two countries.
Dbeibah and al-Shaibani also agreed to open a Syrian consulate in Benghazi, raising the level of diplomatic representation between the two states.
The talks covered security cooperation and counterterrorism, according to the GNU statement. The two sides also discussed consular services and the status of prisoners, detainees and refugees from both countries.
Economically, they addressed unresolved financial dues between Libyan and Syrian institutions. The Syrian foreign minister also met with Libya’s oil and gas minister and the country’s investment authority chief to discuss energy and investment cooperation.
‘A new chapter’
The Syrian embassy in Libya has been closed since 2012 after Libya’s then-Transitional National Council recognised the Syrian opposition and diplomatic relations between the two countries were severed during then-Syrian President Bashar al-Assad’s rule.
Syrian opposition forces ousted al-Assad in December 2024, ending 61 years of Baath Party rule.
In August 2025, a Syrian delegation raised the post-Assad Syrian flag over the Tripoli embassy, signalling that its reopening was imminent.
Dbeibah called Sunday’s meeting the start of “a new chapter” in their relations, saying it should be “based on shared interests, practical cooperation and addressing outstanding issues”.

manifesta 16 and the past, present, and future of ruhr’s churches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
20:35:29 UTC
05:35:29 KST

Manifest 16, the ‘European Nomadic Biennial,’ found its home in Germany’s Ruhr area. More specifically, it activated twelve churches across the cities of Essen, Gelsenkirchen, Duisburg, and Bochum, transforming them into hybrid exhibition and community places that cheekily spoke to the title of its 30th edition: ‘This is not a church.’ Through contemporary art, walks through these cities, architectural interventions (and a bit of basketball), the event proposes new ways to inhabit the numerous churches in the region that have fallen out of use.
The Ruhr region has a complex history within the European framework because of its natural resources. It sits at the meeting of the Ruhr and the Rhine, making it logistically advantageous as an inland port. To get around from city to city, the Manifesta Guide recommends biking, as the Erzbahntrasse, a former freight line turned bike path, not only exemplifies the infrastructural evolution but is also lined with the foliage of the region and offers a glimpse at the Rhine-Herne Canal.
Each of the twelve churches that make up Manifesta’s program opens with a bit of history that explains how the structure came to be. Bochum’s Gethsemane-Kirche has written that the modest structure, whose entrance is reached only after passing through a small path lined by a dense garden, was designed by architect Otto Bartning for Protestants after World War II. The goal was not to have a grand structure, but a simple place for worship. Because of this, these churches were built close to their parish, earning them the title of ‘pantoffelkirchen,’ or slipper churches, as in the place is so close, you could reach it in your slippers.
Gethsemane-Kirche was shaped by Anda Rottenberg & Krzysztof Kosciuczuk, two of Manifesta 16’s eight ‘creative mediators,’ the term the institution uses to refer to their curator-like organizers who guide the formation of the event. This church was still in use as a place of worship, which was not a given for all of the event’s sites. With that in mind, they decided to create interventions in the space that reflected the active community around the church.
One was the installation of Marina Naprushkina’s inflatable bell-shaped bouncy house that sits in the front lawn of the space. The bell is the ‘advertising symbol of the Bochumer Verein company,’ which had produced rail wheels in the area, with the playful sculpture both inviting people to interact with the work while also opening a dialogue about labor in the region. Inside, Mehtap Baydu’s work, Anali Kazli – With Mothers with Daughters, is a performance-based work that works with eleven women from the city to cook meals for a large audience. In it, she reflects on the pattern within the Turkish language of naming food after women and body parts. Within the piece, she opens a community-oriented discussion on food and language.
North of Essen, there is St. Marien, which, in contrast to Gethsemane-Kirche, has fallen into a state of disrepair and is no longer an active church. The space is a towering brick building almost hiding behind a park. Pieces of the roof are missing, and parts of the stained-glass windows have broken off. Within, works by Alicja Kwade, SUPERFLEX, Jason Dodge, and others fill the unused space. One piece in particular is William Engelen’s Variation on Godspeed in 4/4 (2026), which consists of tubes hanging down into the space, recalling the church organ. Another interpretation of this instrument can also be found in Abbas Zahedi’s work, Ouranophobia 47051 (2026), located in Duisburg’s Kulturkirche Liebrauen.
Making your way to each church requires a grand tour through the Ruhr region. Traveling by bike reveals the dense foliage that seems to touch every corner. Going by public transport exposes the shifting face of western Germany. With every site, a new view of the region comes into view—one that has long been on the precipice of change, yet holds onto relics of the past. By bringing these religious spaces into view, Manifesta 16 reveals the history of this European region through art, participation, and community.
creative mediators: Anda Rottenberg, Krzysztof Kosciuczuk, Josep Bohigas, Gürsoy Doğtaş, René Block, Henry Meyric Hughes, Leonie Herweg, and Michael Kurtz
This article is part of designboom’s MODES OF HABITATION chapter, exploring how the spaces we inhabit can reshape the ways we live together. Discover more stories rethinking domesticity, shared living, and the many forms a home can take here.
from zucchini ballet flats to shoes covered in flowers and dandelion seed heads, the artist turns fleeting plant materials into playful studies of footwear.

Unknown Publisher

30 August 2026•Update: 30 August 2026
Approximately 85 American citizens remain missing in Nepal and China's Tibet region following a massive glacial collapse that triggered catastrophic flash floods on Aug. 26, the US State Department said on Sunday.
"This morning, I can say we now have 85 Americans, approximately, that are unaccounted for," Spokesman Tommy Pigott told ABC News.
He noted that while nine Americans have been successfully evacuated, Washington is "currently unaware of any US citizen deaths at this time."
Pigott said the US embassies in Kathmandu and Beijing are working "24/7" to coordinate with local officials and obtain reliable information.
Washington announced more than $3.6 million in humanitarian assistance for the affected region on Saturday, including emergency food aid for up to 10,000 households.
The disaster occurred when a sudden glacial collapse, the rapid breaking or melting of a glacier, sent powerful surges of water and debris through Himalayan valleys, destroying villages and major infrastructure.
The overall death toll from the floods has climbed to more than 800, while nearly 3,300 people remain missing across the border region.

US forces strike Iranian launchers on Larak island in Strait of Hormuz
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
20:27:09 UTC
05:27:09 KST

US forces strike Iranian launchers on Larak island in Strait of Hormuz
US forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz in the first military action in a month, a US official said Sunday. Iran's Revolutionary Guards said the US attack on Larak island killed and wounded several Iranian fighters and civilians, and vowed to punish those responsible.
US forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz in the first military action in a month on Sunday, according to a US official, breaking a lull in fighting during an intermittent war that has lasted more than six months.
Forces with the Revolutionary Guard Corps were observed preparing to launch rockets with sea mines into the strait, according to the official, who spoke on condition of anonymity to detail sensitive military movements.
The US military last week completed clearing sea mines from the strait’s international shipping routes.
Semiofficial news outlets in Iran reported sounds of explosions near Larak island on the strait. The Guard in a statement carried by Iran's state broadcaster noted “the martyrdom and injury of several of our fighters and compatriots.”
The statement said the attack will “result in punishment of the aggressor.”
The fighting comes just days after the Trump administration said it would turn its focus to increasing economic pressure — rather than military action — to try to end its war with Iran. The shifting strategy centers on threats to punish any country or entity that continues to conduct business with Tehran.
The turn to using sanctions as the cudgel of choice comes as the administration weighs diminished munitions stockpiles after months of war, sparking concerns that the prolonged conflict could undermine US military readiness in other parts of the globe.
Read moreTrump says Strait of Hormuz demined, warns of ‘zero tolerance’ for new mines
As the conflict grinds on, Trump’s talk of finding a quick end to the war also appears to be fading. He stressed last week that he’s “not in a hurry” to get Iran back to the negotiating table, and he continues making the case that the Islamic Republic’s leadership is on the ropes.
Appointments to Iran’s senior security leadership in the past month, however, have signaled Tehran’s defiance after weathering decades of sanctions as well as a lack of tolerance for dissent at home.
Trump has consistently emphasised that the US and Israel campaign has been devastating for Iran’s navy and air force. Iranian officials have said the country has suffered $270 billion in direct and indirect damage. Israeli military strikes in the first weeks of the war wiped out much of the theocratic government’s leadership structure.
But Iran has found leverage through its own strikes in the critical Strait of Hormuz where relatively few vessels carrying oil and liquefied natural gas are risking passage. Iran still has enough drones and missiles to fire at vessels transiting the vital energy waterway, through which 20% of the world's oil normally flows, effectively controlling much of the traffic in the strait.
Tehran continues to assert that even after it works out a management plan for the strait with Oman, its neighbor on the other side of the waterway, the US can't use it until it fulfills its obligations under the memorandum of understanding the countries signed in mid-June.
Trump has repeatedly declared that the “Strait of Hormuz is open,” saying 24 vessels passed through last week. But that’s a fraction of the roughly 130 vessels that transited daily before the war began.
Earlier on Sunday, a multinational coalition overseen by the US Navy said commercial traffic through the strait remained at “reduced levels.”
And a monitoring agency run by the British military said an unknown projectile struck a tanker ship on Saturday north of Khasab, Oman, in the strait. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Organisation said no casualties or environmental impact had been reported, and cited unspecified military authorities. There was no immediate claim of responsibility.
The US military said that as of Sunday, it had redirected 83 commercial vessels and disabled three under its blockade of Iranian ports.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

Taylah Preston advances in US Open as Storm Hunter, Talia Gibson and Adam Walton crash out
In short:
Taylah Preston has advanced to the second round of the women's singles at the US Open for the first time.
Qualifier Storm Hunter was defeated by 11th seed Marta Kostyuk, while breakout Aussie Talia Gibson went down in three sets to Donna Vekic.
Adam Walton also bowed out early in the men's draw, missing two set points in the third set of a tight loss to China's Yibing Wu.
Taylah Preston is the first Australian into the second round of the US Open, claiming a straight-sets win over American Alycia Parks.
The 20-year-old from Western Australia, whose only previous second-round appearance in a grand slam was this year's Australian Open, produced a terrific performance to secure a 6-3, 6-3 victory.
The Australian faced three break points in the fourth game of the opening set, but was able to rally and level at 2-2. Preston then applied pressure to Parks's serve in the very next game, getting a 15-40 lead before winning the game on her second break point.
Preston broke Parks's serve in the ninth game to win the opening set.
Parks responded immediately by breaking Preston in the opening game of the second set.
Down 0-2 and facing, Preston roared back to win five games on the bounce, on her way to another 6-3 set win to close out the match.
Preston, world number 100, will either face Polish 20th seed Maja Chwalinska or American Taylor Townsend in the second round at Flushing Meadows.
Gibson, Hunter and Walton out in first round
A dejected Talia Gibson is doing her best to extract the positives after Donna Vekic crashed the rising star's US Open party in a rough start for the Australian contingent.
Storm Hunter and Adam Walton also made early exits on day one at Flushing Meadows as Gibson was unable to disguise her anguish at an opportunity lost.
The 22-year-old rallied from a set and a service break down to look poised to claim her maiden grand slam victory outside Australia before Vekic steadied to post a 6-2, 4-6, 6-3 in two hours and 33 minutes.
The veteran Croat and 2024 Wimbledon semifinalist seemed to be unravelling after blowing a set and 4-1 lead, cursing herself and berating her box as Gibson roared back into the contest.
But Gibson was unable to wrestle back control after failing to convert any of four break-point chances in the second game of the deciding set.
She had Vekic down 0-40 serving at 4-2, only to miss five straight returns to ruefully let the Paris Olympics silver medallist off the hook.
"It's a hard one to swallow," Gibson said.
"Most of the time it's who makes the most unforced errors on the court who comes away with the loss and today that was me, so it's just something to learn from."
But after starting the year well outside the world's top 100, Gibson has slashed her ranking in half after racking up some 30 match wins, including over former No.1 and dual Australian and US Open champion Naomi Osaka.
"Days like these are really tough. It's hard not to be disappointed. When it comes to the slams, every player wants to do well," said the world No.63.
"But if I'm looking at my entire year so far, I've been able to achieve some things that probably at the start of the year I probably wouldn't have thought I'd be able to do.
"So to still be in the position ranking that I currently have and moving forward to these next tournaments, I don't really have any points to defend, so it's kind of just no pressure and more opportunities."
Aussie qualifier Storm Hunter was defeated by 11th seed Marta Kostyuk in straight sets.
After stumbling at this year's Australian Open, Kostyuk has been in sublime form at the grand slams, making the semifinals of the French Open and Wimbledon to arrive at Flushing Meadows as a genuine contender in the women's draw.
The 11th seed got down to business quickly once the match began and powered to a 4-1 lead before overcoming a wobble to close out the first set when Hunter produced a double fault on set point.
Kostyuk tightened her grip on the clash in the second set, breaking early and never allowing Hunter a route back into the match as she wrapped up a 6-4, 6-1 victory in 67 minutes.
"I'm very happy to be back to this amazing place," Kostyuk said on court.
"It's not easy to play a qualifier, they've played a whole tournament [already]. I'm very happy with my performance today. I try to keep myself grounded. There's still a long way to go, I'm enjoying my tennis."
Adam Walton also bowed out early, missing two set points in the third set of a tight 7-6 (7-2), 6-2, 7-5 loss to China's Yibing Wu.
Aleksandar Vukic, up against Japan's Rei Sakamoto, is the only other Australian in men's action, while Kim Birrell faces Petra Marcinko.
World number seven and three-time US Open quarterfinalist Alex de Minaur opens his title quest on Tuesday against Italian qualifier Andrea Guerrieri.
