Russia has burned millions of Ukrainian books, striking at the infrastructure of Ukrainian culture
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:28:23 UTC
01:28:23 KST

Another Russian strike has destroyed tens of thousands of Ukrainian books around Kyiv, adding to a summer of attacks that has wiped out millions of copies and damaged the warehouses, printing plants and markets that keep Ukraine’s publishing industry running.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022, Ukrainian publishers, printers, bookstores, warehouses and other parts of the literature industry have repeatedly been hit by Russian attacks.
The destruction has drawn comparisons to earlier Russian and Soviet efforts to suppress the Ukrainian language, culture and national identity, with publishers and cultural figures warning that the current attacks are damaging not only businesses and infrastructure but the means through which Ukrainian culture is produced and preserved.
The latest loss came on 28 August, when a Russian drone struck a Nova Post fulfillment and sorting center in Sviatopetrivske, Kyiv Oblast. More than 60,000 books stored there were destroyed, including books belonging to Ukrainian publishers and retailers such as Vivat, A-BA-BA-HA-LA-MA-HA, Osnovy, Readeat and Book.ua.
The destruction is taking a growing toll on Ukrainian culture
Nova Post director Yevhen Tafiichuk said the strike destroyed the company's most modern robotic fulfillment center, along with books from several publishers and stores. He said the company is working with affected partners to compensate their losses and is moving toward a decentralized fulfillment system to reduce the risk of losing large inventories in a single strike.
“For centuries, the enemy has tried to destroy the Ukrainian language, culture and memory. Once, it burned libraries and banned printing; today, it launches missiles at printing plants and warehouses filled with books,” Tafiichuk said.
The latest destruction comes after the Ukrainian publishing industry estimated that Russian attacks had already destroyed about 13 million books in July and August – nearly a third of the number of books Ukrainian publishers printed during all of 2025.
Russia has burned 13 million Ukrainian books in three months, nearly third of everything country printed in 2025
Another warehouse full of books goes up in flames
The Sviatopetrivske strike hit a logistics facility rather than a publishing house itself, but the consequences spread across much of the book market.
Readeat founder Dmytro Feliksov said more than 60,000 physical books were destroyed and estimated his company's losses at more than UAH 23 million. The warehouse held stock for several publishers and booksellers.
Vivat CEO Yuliia Orlova said the publisher also lost books stored at the Kyiv warehouse in the attack. The company had already begun moving some print runs to other parts of Ukraine, including Lviv, after earlier Russian strikes destroyed publishing infrastructure. But many new releases and books by Ukrainian authors remained in Kyiv.
The same attack destroyed a warehouse used by A-BA-BA-HA-LA-MA-HA to fulfill direct orders. The losses came as publishers were already trying to spread their inventories across multiple locations to reduce the risk posed by Russian strikes.
Millions of books destroyed across Ukraine, publishers hit again and again
On 1 August, a Russian strike on the warehouses of RNK-Ranok destroyed nearly 8 million books, including hundreds of thousands of school textbooks. The Ukrainian Book Institute said the loss from that strike alone was equivalent to about 30% of the country's annual book production.
A separate Russian strike on 19 July destroyed the Konvi printing facility and about 250,000 books belonging to Knyholav, along with print runs and materials belonging to numerous other publishers.
BookChef has suffered some of the largest losses around Kyiv. A Russian strike in July destroyed about 800,000 books at its main warehouse. A second strike in August hit a backup warehouse opened after the first loss, destroying more than 100,000 additional books, Interfax-Ukraine reported.
The attacks have also damaged publishing offices and warehouses. On 16 August, Russian strikes near Kyiv’s Pochaina metro station damaged the offices and warehouses of BookChef and RM, including areas where books were stored.
Kyiv’s Pochaina market also burned
The damage is not limited to modern distribution centers.
On 16 August, a Russian strike set fire to Kyiv’s Pochaina book market, one of the capital’s best-known places to buy new, used and second-hand books. Much of the market burned, with the fire covering more than 2,000 square meters of commercial space.
The market, formerly known as Petrivka, had operated for about 30 years and was a major hub for second-hand books and other goods. Dozens of thousands of books were destroyed, according to local reporting.
The destruction was extensive enough that 60–70% of the market's commercial space was lost. The surviving Bukinist section began reopening later in August, with booksellers returning to trade where their stock had survived, RBC reported.
The market's destruction also meant the loss of a part of Kyiv's book culture that cannot simply be replaced by reprinting new editions. Second-hand books, older editions and used collections had been traded there for generations.
The losses are hitting an already fragile industry
The Ukrainian publishing sector had been growing before Russia's latest attacks, helped in part by rising demand for Ukrainian-language books during the full-scale invasion.
But publishers now face the repeated cost of replacing destroyed print runs, warehouses and equipment while also trying to keep books moving to stores and readers.
Olesia Ostrovska-Liuta, director general of Mystetskyi Arsenal, said the Ukrainian book industry had only recently begun to grow, making the latest losses especially painful.
“Losses are accumulating, while the tools to minimize them are being built extremely slowly,” she said. “Culture will not disappear, but it will once again be drained of its strength.”
Publishers seek help to rebuild and protect a supply chain under attack
The Ukrainian Publishing Association has called for additional support, including war-risk insurance for book stocks, affordable financing to rebuild printing capacity and the restoration of state purchases of books for libraries.
The Ukrainian Book Institute has also appealed for international support for the publishing sector, saying Russia has systematically targeted publishing houses, bookstores, printing facilities and warehouses since the start of the full-scale invasion.
For publishers, the latest strikes show that moving books from a printer to a reader has itself become a wartime vulnerability. A single warehouse can contain the output of dozens of publishers, and losing it can erase months of work and leave books unavailable even when the companies themselves survive.
Nova Post says it is responding by distributing inventory across more locations rather than relying on large centralized facilities. The strategy may help reduce future losses, but it also reflects how deeply Russia’s ongoing attacks have altered the basic infrastructure through which Ukrainians produce, store and buy books.

James Cleverly has pledged to run a “classically Conservative” campaign to become the mayor of London, insisting that his victory in the capital would be a stepping stone for Kemi Badenoch to become prime minister.

However, in a series of interviews on Sunday he avoided speaking about culture war issues, which have been a focus for the Conservative leader.
“I am going to put forward a classic Conservative case to be the mayor of London, and it’s about enterprise, it’s about opportunity,” Cleverly told Times Radio.
“That is a classically Conservative vision, and it will run in parallel to and supportive of Kemi’s plans for the country as a whole.”
If he wins his party’s nomination, Cleverly is expected to run a more moderate campaign than the last Tory candidate, Susan Hall. She drew criticism for claiming there was a “problem with crime” in the black community and was forced to apologise for liking a tweet in 2020 that had a picture of Enoch Powell captioned: “It’s never too late to get London back.” Hall lost to Labour’s Sadiq Khan in 2024, who won with 43.8% of the vote.
Cleverly, who lost the Conservative leadership race to Badenoch, is considered a more moderate voice in a party that has moved to the right as support for Nigel Farage’s rightwing Reform UK has grown.
Giles Dilnot, the editor of Conservative Home, who has worked closely with Cleverly in the past, denied a rift and said he thought it unlikely the MP for Braintree was using his attempt to become mayor as a route to become the next Conservative leader. “There is not a hidden side order of ‘what’s next’ here,” he said.

“Mayoral campaigns are often focused on the person – the personality is that extra 10% rather than just the rosette,” Dilnot said. “James is gloriously normal and I wouldn’t be surprised if he’s selling what he is: a normal Londoner who wants the city to succeed.”
Prof Tony Travers, of the London School of Economics, said the restoration of the supplementary vote system in the 2028 London mayoral election – where voters have a preferred first and second choice, with the second choice counted if no one wins more than 50% of the vote – meant Cleverly had to win over voters whose first choice was the Liberal Democrats.
“The last thing Cleverly would want to do is put off Liberal Democrats, whose party has been the main beneficiaries of the Conservatives’ shift to the right in the south of England,” Travers said. “I think we are likely to see him adopt a pre-Brexit traditional, centrist Conservative position.”
The entrance of a Conservative big-hitter into the May 2028 contest will raise further questions about whether Khan, who was first elected in 2016, will run for a fourth term, a question he has thus far avoided.
A YouGov survey this month found that 56% of Londoners thought he should step down and allow a different Labour candidate to stand.
A recent poll for the Mile End Institute, Queen Mary University of London, found that Khan would win a fourth term if he stood despite a surge in support for the Greens. The Savanta survey put Labour on 33%, Reform on 20%, the Conservatives on 18%, the Greens on 14% and the Liberal Democrats on 10%.
If Khan steps out of the running, Dawn Butler, Labour MP for Brent East, is expected to stand, while other potential candidates in the Labour ranks include Rosena Allin-Khan and David Lammy, the former justice secretary.
Cleverly told LBC he thought Khan had “really lost passion for the job”, adding that as a Londoner he wanted to stand against “very anti-London” Andy Burnham.
“Andy Burnham just doesn’t get it,” he said. “He’s got a war with London, and London needs someone to fight its corner.”

Vance, Rubio, or Hegseth? Trump's inner circle quietly prepares for fierce US 2028 race - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:23:11 UTC
01:23:11 KST

Who in US President Donald Trump’s inner circle will succeed him as president in 2028?
That appears to be the question on much of his cabinet’s mind, as Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Vice President JD Vance, and now Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth each weigh presidential runs.
However, voters this November may cut one, or all, of the three men’s political ambitions short.
Trump is placing a significant amount of pressure on Republicans to win the upcoming November midterms to maintain the party’s congressional majority.
Notably, the president is currently polling at a 33% approval rating, an August Reuters/Ipsos poll found.
Trump pressures Republicans to win midterms to maintain congressional majority
Trump has repeatedly said that Republicans have “got to win the midterms,” and has implied that losing them would lead to “very bad things” for US voters.
"I'm here because I love Iowa, but I'm here because we're starting the campaign to win the midterms. Got to win the midterms," Trump said in a January speech in Iowa.
"If we lose the midterms, you'll lose so many of the things that we're talking about, so many of the assets that we're talking about, so many of the tax cuts that we're talking about – and it would lead to very bad things.”
In a separate interview in January with Reuters, Trump expressed frustration that the GOP could lose control of the House of Representatives or the Senate, and cited historical trends that have seen the party in power lose seats in the second year of a presidency.
“It's some deep psychological thing, but when you win the presidency, you don't win the midterms,” Trump said. He boasted that he had accomplished so much that “when you think of it, we shouldn't even have an election.”
But even Trump, though he has tried before, cannot stop an election.
So the question remains: who will his successor be?
Trump has not directly endorsed anyone yet, though he has said he will when the time is right and has privately shared his preferences.
Trump has publicly egged on a contest for his endorsement between Vance and Rubio, and has said that the two running on the same ticket would be his “dream team.”
“By the way, I do believe that’s a dream team. But these are minor details. That does not mean you have my endorsement under any circumstance. But you know … I think it sounds like presidential candidate and vice presidential candidate,” he said in May.
Vance: MAGA heir apparent or Trump's whipping boy?
Trump has praised and disparaged Vance in front of audiences, at times making him seem more like a whipping boy than an heir apparent. In one instance, he notably said he would blame Vance if a deal with Iran fails.
But Vance is still largely seen as the frontrunner to inherit the GOP, and Trump has reportedly said as much in private conversations.
Notably, The Washington Post reported in August that Trump privately told investors in the Oval Office that “at the end of the day, we need to elect JD.”
Some White House sources told the Washington Post that Trump will not endorse any candidate until much later, and that his mind is constantly changing on who to endorse.
Trump later denied the report, saying: “I think he’s great, but we’re way too early to even be thinking about that.”
A March Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 79% of Republicans held a favorable view of Vance, while 19% held a negative view. Some 71% viewed Rubio positively, while 15% viewed him unfavorably.
Vance is associated with MAGA’s younger wing, which helped get Trump into office in 2024 but is reportedly eroding over issues like rising inflation. He courted several Silicon Valley businesspeople for their support in the 2024 election and has continued to court business moguls to help fundraise for the Republican Party.
Additionally, he could attract more working-class voters, given his roots in Ohio and his familial ties to rural Appalachia.
Although his deal with Iran fell through, Vance told his advisers that he believed his role in the talks put him at a political advantage because he helped create a popular agreement to end an unpopular war, according to the Washington Post.
However, some voters have said that Vance is unlikeable and too much of a yes-man for his current role as vice president.
He notoriously called Trump “America’s Hitler” during the president’s 2016 run, before he became his political ally.
Rubio: Tenured international policy hawk who polls better than Vance
Marco Rubio, as previously mentioned, is besting Vance in some hypothetical matchups against Democrats. A May Emerson College survey put Vance with 36% of conservative voter support, with Rubio at 35%.
If Rubio decides to run, he could point to the myriad of global crises that he managed as proof of his leadership skills. In the first half of the term alone, Rubio has managed diplomatic relations regarding Iran and the US’s allies, assisted in rebuilding Venezuela after devastating earthquakes and the ousting of former authoritarian president Nicholas Maduro, and explicitly redefined the US’s foreign aid strategy.
According to the May Emerson College survey, he tends to receive support from older, more educated Republicans and Hispanic voters.
In terms of polls, conservative voters appear to prefer Rubio to Vance in hypothetical head-to-head races against Democrats. In a survey done by Emerson College, Rubio beat Vance in all but one hypothetical race.
Rubio defeated both former vice president Kamala Harris and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez in hypothetical races by the same margin, 48% to 43%. Vance, by comparison, narrowly defeats Ocasio-Cortez, 46% to 44%, but loses to Harris by four percentage points.
However, Rubio legally cannot run for president while serving as secretary of state or as a national security adviser.
He has indicated that he intends to finish out the rest of his term in the role; sources close to him told the Washington Post that he has no political campaign waiting in the wings.
Sources close to the secretary of state told the Washington Post that he had reduced his speaking availability to avoid talking about the 2028 election.
Wild card or Liability? Hegseth weighs presidential run
And then, there’s the administration’s current wild card: former Fox News anchor and current Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.
NBC reported on Friday that Hegseth has floated the idea to his close associates within the past few months. He reportedly believes that he has attributes that made Trump popular with his core voter base, like his tough-guy attitude and conservative stance on social issues.
“Pete Hegseth should consider running for president,” Chairman of the American Conservative Union Matt Schlapp told NBC. “He’s an impressive guy and has a tremendous amount of energy.”
However, his handling of the conflict with Iran, Signalgate, and conditions aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln could potentially affect his polling with voters. Hegseth hasn't been mentioned in any recent polls about the 2028 elections, since the NBC report came out on Friday.
“MAGA really loves Hegseth because they love the cut of his jib. But you’ve got to deliver the goods. If you want to be secretary of war, you’ve got to win wars,” one pro-Trump operative close to the White House told NBC.
Hegseth, along with Pentagon and White House officials, has discredited the rumors that he is weighing a presidential bid.
The secretary said on Friday that any reports of him weighing a presidential bid were "100% false," adding that his "only job" was making the Department of Defense great.
Be that as it may, he is currently mobilized on the campaign trail during the middle of the US’s conflict with Iran, something that former defense secretaries have abstained from.
Three former defense secretaries, Leon Panetta, Chuck Hagel, and William Cohen, told NBC that Hegseth’s partisan political appearances are something that they deliberately abstained from in the past.
“My God, we’re at war. We’ve got a huge problem,” Hagel, Obama’s defense secretary and former Nebraska senator, told NBC.
“We’ve got a global issue here that we’ve gotten ourselves into with this mess, and what are you doing going to Iowa and campaigning when you should be paying attention to your job?”
It is also worth noting that no defense secretary has ever been president, while several vice presidents and secretaries of state have later made the jump to be commander in chief.
Additionally, Hegseth had several scandals before he was confirmed as secretary of defense, including his drinking habits.
What comes next?
For now, all three men appear to be shrugging off any questions about their candidacy. Rubio has repeatedly downplayed his presidential ambitions despite his previous run against Trump, and has said that he will not run in 2028 if Vance does.
Vance has said he would wait until after the midterm results, and that he doesn’t make decisions “until I absolutely must.”
Hegseth said that reports of him weighing a presidential run were “100% false,” but then campaigned for Republicans in Iowa and Kentucky during an active conflict.
Trump’s popularity has also taken hits for incidents that the three men were directly involved in. Most specifically, the White House’s handling of the war with Iran.
The war has rapidly reshaped the midterms and has affected thousands of Americans’ bank accounts because of the rising cost of gas.
One Reuters/Ipsos poll found that only 31% of US voters approve of the Pentagon’s handling of the war, which has not technically ended.
Another Reuters/Ipsos poll found that 69% of Americans believe Trump had not clearly explained the goals of US military involvement in Iran.
Whoever inherits the mantle will not only have to answer for their role in the conflict, but also accept responsibility for others’ perceived mistakes in the administration. While Vance, Rubio, and Hegseth all successfully tied themselves closely to Trump in 2024, it might hurt their chances of running as individual candidates.
The midterms will help clarify which of these three men can effectively communicate to voters what the GOP looks like post-Trump, and who can distance themselves from the administration’s shortcomings or spin their mistakes in a marketable way.
The race to be the 2028 GOP nominee doesn’t technically start until after the midterms, but in effect, it already has.
Trump’s endorsement will have an enormous impact on the race, but it won’t come anytime soon. In the meantime, the president who remade the GOP in his image may discover that choosing who inherits it is more difficult than choosing who serves beneath him.
Idan Kweller and Reuters contributed to this report.

The Durban Conference 25 years later: A blueprint for anti-Israel demonization - interview
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:22:26 UTC
01:22:26 KST

“Durban was the restarting of the Zionism is Racism campaign. It was the blueprint for accusing Israel of genocide and starvation and war crimes,” Gerald Steinberg, founder and president of NGO Monitor, told The Jerusalem Post on Sunday.
Monday marks 25 years since the “Durban” Conference, officially the UN World Conference Against Racism, Racial Discrimination, Xenophobia and Related Intolerance, held in South Africa from August 31 to September 8, 2001.
Over 12,000 representatives came together to forge a common strategy against discrimination.
However, ironically, the conference has become synonymous with discrimination of the anti-Zionist kind, and is considered by many the birthplace of modern anti-Israel rhetoric.
Preceding the conference was the NGO Forum, which had over 7,000 participants gather to create a pre-planned and coordinated anti-Israel strategy. It was here that the intentional use of words such as “genocide,” “war crimes,” and “apartheid” entered the scene.
UN Resolution 3379 equated Zionism with racism
Six months before Durban, a preparatory conference had taken place in Tehran, although the Islamic Republic of Iran had refused to grant permission to Israeli and Jewish organizations.
In their absence, the delegates drafted a summary document accusing Israel of “ethnic cleansing,” of implementing “a new kind of apartheid” and “a crime against humanity,” and saying Zionism was “based on race superiority” – a document that formed the basis for the NGO declaration at the main conference in Durban.
Ahead of Durban, Secretary of State Colin Powell warned the UN officials that the US would not participate if the agenda was used to restart the Zionism is racism campaign.
The UN high commissioner at the time, Mary Robinson, promised them that this would not happen, but when they arrived, they found no change. The US and Israel ultimately walked out of the conference.
The final NGO declaration called for the restoration of UN Resolution 3379 equating Zionism with racism and demanded the application of all measures used against apartheid South Africa to Israel.
Steinberg told the Post that Durban was the restarting of the Zionism is Racism campaign that had been run 26 years earlier in 1975 by the Soviet Union and the Arab League.
The language itself can actually be traced back to 1948, and the use of the term Nakba and “Israel is doing to the Palestinians what Germans did to the Jews.” However, this did not gain so much traction outside of Palestinian spheres.
The difference at Durban, Steinberg continued, was that it became legitimate, mostly due to the commandeering of non-governmental organizations under the label of human rights.
“And that has been the engine that has driven the demonization of Israel and language like genocide, starvation, deliberate killing of children, war crimes,” Steinberg told the Post.
Steinberg said the specific strategies developed during Durban have been refined and expanded over the last 25 years, and that NGOs keep coming back to the same language and the same processes that were first used at Durban.
“At the Durban NGO forum there was no debate – they adopted a plan of action naming Israel specifically and repeatedly as a genocidal state, committing war crimes, ethnic cleansing, apartheid, and then they established mechanisms for the complete isolation of Israel. Nothing there was incidental or accidental.”
Durban is also where the BDS movement began, and where the International Criminal Court was chosen as the appropriate body to label Israel as the “world’s biggest violator of international law,” Steinberg continued.
Implementation of strategy
Steinberg said the first time NGOs rolled out the new strategy was six months after the Durban conference with the Jenin Massacre myth.
In April 2002, multiple international media outlets and NGOs spread unverified claims that the Israeli military deliberately killed hundreds of civilians during the Battle of Jenin. Rumors claimed 500 people had been massacred and buried in mass graves.
Amnesty International and Christian Aid were instrumental in spreading the rumor.
However, subsequent investigations by human rights organizations (including Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International) found no evidence of a massacre.
“It was obviously a lie, but it got a lot of traction. Journalists picked it up. NGOs spoke of Israeli war crimes, and they repeated that all the way through the last 25 years,” said Steinberg.
“Durban was a blueprint which went beyond calling Zionism racism, but added genocide, starvation, war crimes, and all those other elements.”
The same thing has happened time and time again, he continued.
“Every single time there was a military clash or a terrorist clash, and Israel responded – the 2006 Lebanon war, the 2008-2009 first Gaza war, Operation Cast Lead, the Goldstone Report, Operation Protective Edge – all those mechanisms were trotted out.
“The condemnation of Israel, the fact-finding commissions, the NGO reports, social media.
“Then, when October 7 started, they had already practiced all of the elements of the Durban strategy. It just exploded in a much greater magnitude, but it was all there in all of the years before.”
Launching NGO Monitor
In response to what he was seeing and the bastardization of the role of NGOs, Steinberg launched NGO Monitor.
“Having watched this process take place and expressing my concerns and seeing the amount of power and influence of NGOs, and how the UN went along with it, I thought I could do a project and document the political role of NGOs, and particularly the manipulation of the language of human rights and the mechanisms of human rights,” he told the Post.
“I thought, ‘I can do that for a few years as an academic, write a couple of articles, maybe a book, and have some graduate students.’
“It was supposed to be a three-year project at a university, and it turned into NGO Monitor, because the deeper that I dug in understanding the NGO industry, and I began to see it as an industry, the more I realized how much power and influence they have, and how little attention was being paid.
“There are huge amounts of money going into these organizations which have no accountability, no democratic frameworks; all of their decisions are made in secret, behind closed doors.”
Antisemitism at Durban
Another key part of the Durban conference, aside from the targeting of Israel, was the shocking and overt displays of antisemitism.
At the forum, NGOs sold copies of The Protocols of the Elders of Zion.
Pamphlets were also distributed showing Hitler’s photograph with text reading: “What if I had won? The good thing is there would have been no Israel and no Palestinian’s [sic] bloodshed.”
There were multiple reported examples of Holocaust revisionism and Jewish members being told: “Blood was on their hands.”
Holocaust survivor and US Congressman Tom Lantos called the Durban Conference “the most sickening display of hate for Jews I have seen since the Nazi period.”
Former minister of justice and attorney-general of Canada Irwin Cotler said, “If 9/11 was the Kristallnacht of terror, then Durban was the Mein Kampf.”
There was one notable outcome of this Jew-hatred: the gradual writing of what’s now called the Working Definition of Antisemitism of the International Holocaust Remembrance Alliance (IHRA).
In the immediate aftermath of Durban, Steinberg said many Jewish leaders came together and discussed the urgency of developing a modern definition of antisemitism to reflect what they saw at the forum.
The definition was first published in 2005 by the European Monitoring Center on Racism and Xenophobia. It was then officially adopted by the IHRA in 2016.

AI’s worst disasters will arrive unannounced | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:17:40 UTC
01:17:40 KST

Timothy Garton Ash is right that serious artificial intelligence risks demand international action, but “AI Hiroshima” may be the wrong picture (Would even an AI disaster on the scale of Hiroshima be enough to make humankind protect itself? I fear not, 22 August). Hiroshima was not technology going rogue. Human beings designed the bomb, authorised its use and dropped it. The technology worked much as intended.
AI may one day behave in ways we cannot control, but many of the gravest harms could happen without any dramatic moment when “the AI takes over”. AI might help design a pathogen, find a vulnerability in critical infrastructure or improve a weapons system while people still decide what happens next. Other harms may build almost invisibly through thousands of ordinary decisions – more autonomy here, one safeguard removed there, another consequential task handed over because the system has worked well so far. By the time the danger is obvious, the important decisions may already have been made.
That is also where international agreement could begin. We do not need countries to agree about superintelligence or the probability of human extinction before agreeing that there are some doors AI should never be allowed to open by itself. Weapons systems, critical infrastructure and biological synthesis are obvious places to start. Governments could agree minimum safeguards, require clear human authority for the most consequential actions, keep records of who authorised what and share serious failures and near-misses internationally.
The greatest AI dangers may not arrive with a mushroom cloud. They may arrive quietly, one apparently reasonable step at a time. If we want effective AI governance, we need to fight the right battle, not the most cinematic one.
Dr Simon Nieder
Chesterfield, Derbyshire
Prof Jonathan Michie (Letters, 26 August) reminds us that the Serbelloni group, led by the author’s father, Donald Michie (when he was at Edinburgh University), was weighing the social dangers of artificial intelligence as long ago as 1972. Nor is AI technology itself new, since its roots run back through to Frank Rosenblatt’s perceptron of 1957, to the Dartmouth workshop of 1956, and to Alan Turing before that. What is new is that we now have the hardware and software infrastructures to drive it forward at what can sometimes seem to be a terrifying speed.
The Lighthill report of 1973 duly delivered an AI winter in the UK, and the field’s centre of gravity crossed the Atlantic, with the consequences that we all now live with. Donald Michie had worked alongside Turing at Bletchley Park and argued forcefully against the cuts, in the televised Lighthill debate that followed the report, to no avail. The quip attributed to him, perhaps apocryphally, “Let there be Lighthill. And there was darkness”, still resonates strongly in our country today.
As a double-hatted academic (computer scientist and humanities scholar), I would argue for the return of a “Serbelloni debate” that, as Jonathan Michie observes and as his father recognised, requires the involvement of both the sciences and the humanities.
Dr Anthony Harris
Emmanuel College, Cambridge
In his article about regulating AI (I worked at OpenAI. Here are the guardrails we need now, 21 August), Miles Brundage failed to mention an international effort seeking broad political support for a global AI treaty. This effort is carrying forward a compelling address at the inaugural UN Global Dialogue on AI Governance in Geneva last month, where the secretary general called for human control of AI as its applications spread in weaponry and subversive, prejudicial public surveillance
A fragmented approach, as described by Mr Brundage, is likely to greatly increase the difficulty of implementing AI controls that are timely, internationally negotiated, and therefore effective.
AI, corporate agendas, diverse national defence and economic goals, and the proliferation of energy-intensive datacentres are entangled in interlocking systemic interrelationships that cannot be resolved through disjointed incrementalism. This is especially true as the pace of innovation accelerates, exacerbating worst-case scenarios of advanced AI technology, posing increasingly dire risks.
No matter how well intended, fragmented efforts will be diversionary and cause crucial delays, impeding the diligent pursuit of a systemic global strategy to pre-empt destructive outcomes. Such outcomes could result from malicious use of AI by humans and/or subversive and deceptive activities of renegade algorithms – examples of which are already alarming.
Another troubling aspect of this systemic dilemma must be addressed. Mounting bipartisan opposition to datacentres – well-justified and well-substantiated – is diverting the political attention needed to control AI and implement appropriate restraints (bans or moratoriums) until reliable AI safeguards can be established. This is analogous to focusing on treating a serious symptom in lieu of urgently seeking a remedy for the critical disease that’s causing it. Surely it’s possible to employ a multifaceted strategy, recognising that the sooner rigorous AI guardrails are established, the fewer datacentre harms will be suffered.
Like climate change, the threats of advanced AI are inherently global, making an international approach essential.
David Kyler
Saint Simons Island, Georgia, US

Making the British countryside more accessible and inviting to all | Letters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:17:23 UTC
01:17:23 KST

What a joy to read John Harris’s piece on the cultural changes taking place in rural areas (Walking the Peak District, I discovered a wonderful rejection of the right’s monotone vision of England, 23 August. My husband and I have walked many miles in the Peak District and we would comment on the monocultural nature of other walkers. Nina Young

Why solar bonds are a bright idea | Letter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:16:57 UTC
01:16:57 KST

The UK proposal to use “solar bonds” to make rooftop solar more affordable is a smart solution to a fundamental problem: the rising cost of capital (Cut cost of loans for solar panels on UK homes, ministers urged, 21 August).
A household that can pay for solar upfront saves money from day one. For everyone else, high-interest financing can consume much of those savings and ultimately deter people from installing the technology. A solar bond structure changes that equation: investors receive a modest, guaranteed return, and homeowners get access to cheaper capital. Because the loan is attached to the property rather than the individual, there’s no issue if the person moves.
The model is worth considering in the US too. Leases and power purchase agreements already let homeowners install solar with no money down, and green banks in states like Connecticut and New York offer below-market loans. But leases mean homeowners never own the system, forfeiting long-term savings, and even the best green bank loans are attached to the borrower, not the home. A solar bond wouldn’t replace these tools; it would fill the gap they leave.
The bond mechanism itself isn’t a stretch – it’s similar to the state and municipal bonds already financing infrastructure, just retail-facing and earmarked for solar. The bigger challenge is repayment. The UK can tie the standing charge on a national energy bill, while the US has thousands of utilities with different rate structures. That makes a federal programme harder, but a state-by-state approach is realistic.
The need is growing. The 30% residential solar tax credit expired at the end of 2025, as did the federal Solar for All programme. States that build this now won’t just be filling a financing gap; they’ll be shaping what energy independence looks like over the next decade.
Alexis Abramson
Dean, Columbia Climate School, US

India and Uzbekistan deepen ties, eye $5bn trade and long-term uranium supplies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:16:38 UTC
01:16:38 KST

The two governments also broadened cooperation on critical minerals, defence, digital payments and transport. A new foreign minister-level mechanism will oversee implementation, alongside expanded education and regional links.
India and Uzbekistan have upgraded relations to a Comprehensive Strategic Partnership and set a $5bn (€4.29bn) trade target for 2030 during Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s state visit to Tashkent. New Delhi also says the two sides are close to signing a new long-term uranium supply agreement.
The talks produced agreements and commitments across trade, energy and security, expanding cooperation in critical minerals, defence and digital infrastructure.
India’s Ministry of External Affairs said there had been “positive discussions” and that an agreement could be signed “very shortly”. The ministry also said a memorandum on mining and geological resources signed during the visit would support cooperation on critical minerals, including uranium.
India already imports uranium from Uzbekistan under a 2019 contract covering 1,100 metric tonnes of natural uranium concentrate for delivery through 2026. A parliamentary answer published in March 2025 said India had received 600 metric tonnes under the agreement by then.
India uses imported uranium in civilian nuclear power reactors placed under International Atomic Energy Agency safeguards. New Delhi plans to expand nuclear generating capacity to 100 GW by 2047.
Trade and digital payments
President Mirziyoyev said bilateral trade rose by 33% last year to $1.3bn (€1.12bn). The two leaders now want that figure to reach $5bn (€4.29bn) by 2030.
The joint statement calls for steps to remove non-tariff barriers, improve market access and strengthen manufacturing and supply-chain links. The two governments will establish a working group to address trade and investment barriers and examine the next steps after completing a feasibility study on a possible Uzbekistan-India Preferential Trade Agreement.
Digital payments also emerged as a specific outcome. A commercial agreement between India’s NPCI International Payments Limited and Uzbekistan’s National Interbank Processing Centre would allow Indian travellers to use UPI-enabled payment apps in Uzbekistan once implemented. Indian officials expect the rollout within about a year.
The two sides also backed greater use of multimodal transport routes aimed at lowering freight costs between India and landlocked Uzbekistan.
Other agreements covered education, environmental cooperation and closer links between Indian and Uzbek regions.
Defence and regional cooperation
A new foreign minister-level mechanism will oversee the expanded partnership, while the existing Intergovernmental Commission will be upgraded to ministerial level.
The two countries also agreed to expand defence and security cooperation. The joint statement identifies new opportunities for cooperation between their defence industries, while India and Uzbekistan already hold the Dustlik joint military exercise.
Both sides reaffirmed a zero-tolerance approach to terrorism and called for greater cooperation in intelligence-sharing, law enforcement and counter-terrorism.
On multilateral affairs, Uzbekistan reaffirmed its support for India’s bid for permanent membership of a reformed UN Security Council.
The two leaders also pledged closer coordination within the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation and on Global South issues.
Education, culture and people-to-people ties
Tourism is also set to expand. The Uzbek presidency highlighted a 30-day visa-free regime and 14 weekly flights between the two countries, while the governments adopted a tourism cooperation programme for 2026–2028.
Four Indian universities operate in Uzbekistan and around 16,000 Indian students, many studying medicine, are enrolled in the country. India also announced 100 scholarships for Uzbek students studying Hindi.
Modi also attended a session organised by the Yoga Federation of Uzbekistan.
Modi was also awarded the Oliy Darajali Do‘stlik Order, which the Indian government describes as Uzbekistan’s highest honour for foreign leaders. It was his fourth visit to Uzbekistan, as the two countries marked 15 years of strategic partnership.
“A stronger India-Uzbekistan partnership will be a powerful force for peace, progress and prosperity in Central Asia,” Modi said after the talks.

Google Maps Now Shows ‘Lake America’ Instead of Lake Ontario
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:16:24 UTC
01:16:24 KST

Lake Ontario is no more on Google Maps in the US. Google changed the name of easternmost of the Great Lakes to “Lake America” late Saturday, days after President Donald Trump ordered its rebranding in official government databases.
Trump issued the executive order on Thursday as part of an ongoing feud over tariffs with Canada, whose capital province is called Ontario. It followed a similar order he issued in January 2025 to rename the Gulf of Mexico as the Gulf of America as part of a fight with the US trading partner to the south.
Google, Apple, Microsoft, and other maps providers adopted the Gulf of America naming as soon as the US Department of the Interior updated its records, which came a couple of weeks after Trump’s order. So it was no surprise that when those records—which are used to determine names on roadway signs and in government literature—reflected Lake America, digital maps from Google also quickly took on the new name.
Apple Maps and Bing Maps have not yet reflected the change but are expected to. In fact, the map for the federal government’s Geographic Names Information System database, which informs these changes, still showed Lake Ontario as of Sunday morning, with a note that the maps are “in the process of being updated to reflect this name change.”
While Google and other private organizations that provide maps are not bound by law to use official names, they generally follow government databases like GNIS. The location names a user sees depends on their own geography.
“People using Maps in the US will see ‘Lake America,’ those in Canada will continue to see ‘Lake Ontario,’ and those outside of the US and Canada will see both names,” Google said in an unsigned statement. “These updates follow our long-standing policy for bodies of water with names that vary from country to country, and are starting to roll out now.”
Trump’s efforts to rewrite maps have generated considerable public debate in open-source mapping communities such as OpenStreetMap, whose technology is used by companies such as Uber and Lyft. Ultimately, OpenStreetMap recognizes both the US and foreign names and gives organizations using its maps the choice over which to show.
One map provider that has so far declined to make the change is MapQuest, which said in a social media post in response to Trump’s order that “we’re not changing it.”

British woman killed in stabbing at German railway station

A British woman has died after being stabbed at a railway station in southern Germany in the early hours of Sunday morning, police have said.

Officers arrested a 27-year-old German man at the scene immediately after the incident. The background and motive for the attack is under investigation, the statement added.
Police have asked anyone who may have witnessed "an argument or physical altercation" at the station late on Saturday or early on Sunday to contact them.

The Rosenheimer Herbstfest - an event similar to the Oktoberfest beer festival - is currently taking place in the area.

"The criminal investigation department is working closely with the public prosecutor's office to investigate the circumstances and motive behind the crime as a matter of urgency," he wrote in a statement.

What’s behind Netanyahu’s condemnation of this weekend’s settler pogroms?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:06:15 UTC
01:06:15 KST

What’s behind Netanyahu’s condemnation of this weekend’s settler pogroms?
The Israeli prime minister blames a ‘handful of rioters’ for the West Bank pogroms, but analysts say his statements mask a state-sponsored campaign of massive settlement expansion.
A wave of coordinated Israeli settler attacks swept across the occupied West Bank over the weekend, leaving dozens of Palestinians injured and properties torched.
The pogroms have seen little or no response from Israeli police and soldiers.
Dozens of settlers attacked a Palestinian home in the village of Qusra, south of Nablus, with tear gas and stones, injuring seven people. A Palestinian Red Crescent Society ambulance that attempted to reach the besieged families was also attacked.
Simultaneously, Israeli forces fired tear gas during incursions into the Far’a refugee camp, el-Bireh, and al-Mughayyir. Soldiers also attacked journalists in Hebron’s Old City.
A Palestinian family and an American NBC news crew were assaulted in the village of Jalud. In Arrabeh, two Palestinians were also beaten near the Mevo Dotan settlement, in a weekend of violence against locals by Israeli settlers.
The Palestinian Ministry of Foreign Affairs strongly condemned the escalation, particularly the 20-day siege on al-Mughayyir, describing it as a systematic policy of forced displacement and colonial expansion.
Surgical isolation
Israeli politicians have launched a coordinated campaign to minimise the public relations damage after the pogroms.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu issued a statement strongly condemning the “criminal acts of violence” in Qusra and Jalud, blaming it on a “handful of rioters” who violated the law, interfered with the military, and harmed Israel’s standing in the world.
He publicly stated that he expected law enforcement authorities to “arrest the rioters and bring them to justice”.
However, this public outrage contrasted sharply with the reality on the ground.
Documented footage captured masked settlers storming the villages of Qusra and Jalud in open pickup trucks, according to Israeli media reports. Despite this visual evidence and Netanyahu’s stated demands, the Israeli police’s West Bank district, under the command of Moshe Pinchi, made zero arrests.
President Isaac Herzog echoed the sentiment, calling the events a “red line”.
Former US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee praised Herzog’s statement and claimed that the half-million Israelis living in the West Bank are “most disgusted by a small group of thugs”.
The Israeli Ministry of Foreign Affairs declared that the violence carried out by “extremists” stands in complete contradiction to the values of Israel.
Opposition leader Yair Lapid described another weekend of violent rampages as a “moral stain” and said the government’s failure to tackle Israeli violence in the West Bank is a “national disgrace”.
Experts told Al Jazeera that this chorus of condemnation from the Israeli establishment represents a calculated political manoeuvre by the government, which is actively engineering the annexation of the West Bank.
Ehab Jabareen, a writer, analyst, and Palestinian citizen of Israel, said that Netanyahu is pursuing a “political surgical isolation process” to shield the broader settlement project from international scrutiny.
“He puts forward a political equation stating that there are 500,000 legitimate settlers, alongside a few dozen deviants or anomalies,” Jabareen said.
“He wants to punish, or give the illusion of punishing, the most blatant link in order to protect the wider system.”
By defining the latest pogroms as a criminal anomaly, Netanyahu aims to isolate this from the wider settler enterprise, Jabareen added.
Security fears
Few see the prime minister’s statement as anything more than a practical response to fears among the military that unchecked settler pogroms could ignite a massive Palestinian uprising in the occupied West Bank.
Recent closed-door security assessments by Major General Avi Bluth, head of the Israeli military’s Central Command, warned that “nationalistic crime”, such as the pogroms, could spark a massive response from Palestinians.
“The army speaks to Netanyahu in the language of cost-benefit analysis,” Jabareen noted.
“Dozens of settlers create an open front that requires the mobilisation of thousands of soldiers. Netanyahu did not say this is unacceptable because it targets Palestinians, but rather said it obstructs the army.”
Mamoun Abu Amer, an analyst on Israeli politics, dismissed the idea that the state has lost control over the settlers.
He emphasised that the military consistently protects the settlers during these attacks while heavily punishing Palestinians who attempt to defend themselves.
“The settlers are too cowardly to carry out any attack without the sponsorship and cover of the government,” Abu Amer said, pointing to instances where the military demolished Palestinian homes simply because the residents resisted settler assaults.
Engineered expansion
While top Israeli officials publicly distance themselves from individual attacks, the government is still systematically funding, legalising, and expanding the settlers’ presence.
A report by the Israeli organisation Peace Now detailed how successive governments, heavily influenced by Netanyahu, have thrived on expanding settlements since the 1993 Oslo Accords.
Thirty years ago, there were approximately 110,000 settlers in the West Bank and 140,000 in East Jerusalem.
Today, those numbers have skyrocketed to 465,000 in the West Bank and 230,000 in East Jerusalem.
The current far-right Israeli government has accelerated this process to unprecedented levels.
According to a 2025 European Union report, the Israeli government officially approved the establishment of 54 new settlements in the West Bank in a single year, a more than tenfold increase from the five approved in 2024.
In parallel, 86 new outposts were erected, and a record-breaking 63,311 units were also approved across the occupied territories.
Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who holds sweeping administrative powers over the territory, recently declared a “revolution in settlement” expansion, openly linking the construction to the prevention of Palestinian statehood.
The government recently passed a record $271bn national budget that bypassed legal frameworks to allocate 400 million shekels ($134m) to the Ministry of Settlement and National Missions, which officially authorises illegal outposts.
This massive infrastructure investment includes advancing the strategic E1 settlement project, which could sever the West Bank in two and effectively kill any hope for the establishment of a Palestinian state.
The government recently issued tenders for 1,234 homes as part of a larger plan to build 3,401 units connecting the Ma’ale Adumim settlement to occupied East Jerusalem, as part of this plan.
International complicity
The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) reported that settler violence is on the rise, recording over 1,540 attacks that caused Palestinian casualties or property damage this year alone.
OCHA noted that the monthly average of these attacks is now higher than in any other year on record.
Despite this historic surge in state-sponsored pogroms and land theft, Western responses have largely remained confined to rhetorical outrage.
While European nations and the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) strongly condemned the recent settlement approvals, including the E1 project, analysts note a glaring double standard.
Abu Amer highlighted that Western countries have failed to impose meaningful economic sanctions on the Israeli state, opting instead to issue travel bans against a few individual settlers.
“There are political positions issued recently by Western countries condemning the Israeli behaviour in reviving the E1 project, but these positions have not translated into practical measures,” Abu Amer said.
He contrasted this hesitation with the immediate actions taken by 28 Western nations to defund the UN agency for Palestinian refugees based on unproven Israeli allegations.
By decoupling the violent acts of individual settlers from the state machinery that arms, funds, and protects them, Israel continues to advance its broader strategic goal: the permanent, irreversible annexation of Palestinian land.

At least 9,796 people have become victims of enforced disappearances as a result of Russia’s war against Ukraine since 2014, according to human rights defenders

An enforced disappearance occurs when a state representative or persons acting with its authorization, support, or tacit consent deprive a person of their liberty and then refuse to acknowledge the fact of their detention or provide information about what happened to them and where they are.
In this way, a person is placed outside the protection of the law, while their loved ones may remain in the dark for months or years.
On the International Day of the Victims of Enforced Disappearances, we remind everyone of the people who have suffered from this crime. People are not numbers. Every case must be investigated. Educated? Skilled? Ambitious? Traffickers are looking for you
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:03:27 UTC
01:03:27 KST

Educated? Skilled? Ambitious? Traffickers are looking for you
Young jobseekers are being recruited into scam compounds. Urgent action is needed to disrupt these trafficking schemes.
Good salary. Visa sponsored. Flight included. Applicants must be educated, fluent in English and confident online.
It sounds like a great opportunity for a young graduate, but it is the bait in a trafficking operation.
The advertised job does not exist. On arrival, the person’s passport is taken. They are moved to a compound they cannot leave and are forced to run online scams: impersonating strangers, building false relationships and persuading people thousands of kilometres away to send money.
Those who miss their targets may be beaten, starved or placed in solitary confinement. Their families may sell land or take on debt to raise money to pay for their release.
I heard versions of this story firsthand during a recent visit to Rwanda, where I met two survivors who had been trafficked through fraudulent job offers. They were fluent in English and comfortable with technology. They had been looking for the same thing as millions of other young people: a good job and the chance to build a better future.
Those qualities made them valuable to the traffickers. They were given scripts and forced to impersonate women online, build romantic relationships with people in Europe and persuade them to send money.
Today, after returning home with support from the International Organization for Migration (IOM), they are working alongside us to warn communities and other young people. They are using some of the same platforms on which traffickers search for recruits to help others recognise the danger.
Their experience exposes a crime that creates victims on both sides of the screen. One person is held under threat and forced to deceive. Another has their trust exploited and may lose their savings. The criminal network profits from both.
At least 300,000 people are estimated to have been trafficked or coerced into scam compounds across Southeast Asia. People from at least 80 countries and territories have been identified among them.
Across the Asia Pacific, scams cost people an estimated $88bn to $114bn in 2025. Those losses cover a wider range of scams, but they show the scale of the criminal economy in which these compounds operate.
The threat is also reaching further into Africa. IOM and its government partners are identifying a growing number of victims from countries like Ethiopia, Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania. During recent visits to Tanzania and Rwanda, leaders told me of fraudulent job offers reaching young graduates and other jobseekers through social media.
These networks are global by design. Recruitment may happen in one country, travel through another and exploitation in a third. The scams can target people anywhere. When an operation is disrupted, it moves and starts again elsewhere.
Government responses are often divided. Labour authorities see an unlicensed recruiter. Border officials see suspicious travel. Police see online fraud. Consular teams see citizens stranded abroad. Traffickers exploit the gaps between them.
These gaps need to be closed. Governments should provide trusted ways to verify overseas employers, recruiters, contracts and visas. Labour, border, police and consular authorities need to share alerts quickly and investigate the networks together.
Technology companies have an equally important role. Fraudulent recruitment happens openly on social media, messaging services and job platforms. Companies should detect and remove deceptive advertisements, make them easy to report and preserve evidence that can help identify those responsible. Awareness campaigns designed with survivors must reach young people in those same spaces.
Above all, people forced to run scams must be treated as victims of trafficking. Some escape the compounds only to be detained or prosecuted for immigration offences or crimes committed under threat. No one should be punished for acts they were compelled to carry out because they were trafficked.
From 2022 to 2025, IOM assisted more than 3,500 victims from 39 countries who were trafficked for forced criminality in Southeast Asia. Survivors need protection, medical and psychological care, a safe way home and support to rebuild their lives.
Jobseekers can take precautions. A legitimate employer should have a verifiable address. The contract should describe the work, and the visa should match the job. A recruiter should not pressure someone to travel immediately, keep the offer secret or surrender their passport.
But polished deceptions are designed to appear credible. The burden of defeating sophisticated international criminal networks cannot rest on jobseekers alone.
Before someone boards a flight, there must be a reliable way to verify the offer. When trafficking is suspected, authorities must act together. When a victim escapes, they must be met with protection rather than punishment.
For many people, trafficking now begins with an ordinary message on an ordinary phone. Our response must reach them there.
Every jobseeker should be able to ask: Is this really a job, or is someone trying to lure me into a trap?
None should be left to answer that question alone.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

Pioneering Care After Crisis: It All Starts with the People
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:00:23 UTC
01:00:23 KST

Pioneering Care After Crisis: It All Starts with the People
How CityUHK’s innovative Community Chilling Hub is reimagining human care in Hong Kong
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
When the devastating fire broke out at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po on 26 November, the response from City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK) did not begin with a strategy memo. “In fact, since the very beginning, it was not a strategy,” says Professor Cherry TAM, Associate Professor from the Department of Social and Behavioural Science (SS). “We viewed it as our expertise, our responsibility … our aim is to care for people and society.”
Within five days—by 1 December—the university had organised a public lecture on resilience, mobilised psychosocial support for affected primary school pupils and begun planning trauma-informed workshops for frontline professionals. What started as an instinctive response soon evolved into something more ambitious: the CityUHK Community Chilling Hub, an innovative model demonstrating the synergies among private and public sectors, academia, public health and social care in Hong Kong. At its heart, the new model demonstrated how crisis exposes the urgency of human care and how universities can help innovate the possibilities.
 
From Academic Department to First Responders
Tam resists the language of “strategy”. The response, she insists, was embedded in CityUHK’s DNA. “At CityUHK, we have the very important mission to engage with the community ... we generate knowledge and we need to contribute to society,” she says.
In this instance, that ethos translated into speed. The resilience lecture was held just days after the fire. Senior management, academic staff and technical support units worked across time constraints and boundaries. “This kind of interdisciplinary, cross-departmental collaboration … happened in a minute,” Tam recalls.
In governance terms, that agility matters. Complex crises rarely fit neatly into existing silos. CityUHK’s response showed how mission-driven institutions can act responsibly across established structures. 
Trauma Support Rooted in Humanity
Beyond public messaging, the department provided direct psychosocial support, particularly for affected primary school pupils. “When we provide professional services for this kind of traumatic experience, the very important first step is to understand, to listen,” Tam explains.
Her team, partnering with an NGO and the University’s senior management, invited students onto campus, offering distance from the disaster site and emotional breathing room. Using adapted cartoon storytelling, facilitators helped children externalise their fears. “Let them know that their reaction is common, it’s normal,” Tam says. Artistic drawing allowed quieter students to express what words could not: “Silence is a very, very important signal.”
This layered approach—listening, normalising, identifying and referring—demonstrates sustainable recovery at the human scale. Rather than imposing solutions, the team built support around lived emotional realities.
Hope, Tam emphasises, is central to recovery. “Hope is very important. Without hope, maybe they would keep declining.” Bringing children to campus was therefore symbolic as well as being therapeutic. 
“Even though university feels like it’s a long way off,” she says, “bringing them onto campus gives them hope for the future.” Exposure reframed identity not around trauma, but possibility.
It is understandable that the fire’s psychological impact extended beyond residents. “Even many helping professionals felt it was totally out of their capacity to handle such a big trauma,” explains Tam. By early January, the department launched a full-day trauma-informed workshop using a “train the trainer” model. The aim was not just immediate intervention, but strengthening the professional ecosystem.
“This kind of training is very sustainable,” Tam explains. “With more professionals equipped, when we have other issues they can take action more immediately.” Rather than relying solely on centralised emergency responses, the university invested in distributed capacity—networks of practitioners ready to respond to future crises.
From Fragmentation to Integration
The early initiatives made clear post-traumatic recovery after such an unprecedented fire was not short-term but challenging. Long-term and continuous support to guide affected people to overcome and develop post-traumatic growth is indispensable. With this mission—and made possible through the generous and timely contribution of China Hongqiao Group Limited—CityUHK established the Community Chilling Hub, drawing on interdisciplinary expertise in social work, counselling, psychology, criminology and sociology, as well as technologies in health screening, to offer longer-term and sustainable support for the affected communities in a welcoming, stigma-free space.
“The services nowadays in Hong Kong to handle mental wellness-related issues are quite fragmented,” Tam says. Many are limited by age or socioeconomic criteria. The hub aims to be different: “Without age limit, without economic limit. Anyone can come here. It is a very inclusive service.”
The hub’s model integrates physical health screening, mental health support, social services and spiritual well-being. “It’s a one-stop shop—physical, social, mental and spiritual wellness support,” Tam says. This integrated design aligns with sustainable development goals: breaking down silos, reducing inequalities in access and addressing well-being holistically.
Beyond the Medical Model
Central to the hub is social prescribing, first developed in the United Kingdom. Traditionally, mental health systems have been “very diagnostic oriented, very medical oriented”, Tam says, but after acute intervention, people need community and social support. Social prescribing connects residents not only to therapy, but to social resources through trained community link workers—volunteers drawn from university students and residents.
“We provide basic volunteer training,” Tam explains, linking them with families to co-design tailored “social prescriptions”. The volunteers also build social capital, becoming “the pool of resources in the community to serve in Hong Kong”.
If evidence demonstrates effectiveness, the university hopes to present the model to the government as a scalable alternative. “We can prove the model … and let the government have more alternatives to improve the existing services,” she says.
Enhancing Human Care Through Community
Innovating for better human care is often framed around digital platforms or policy reform. CityUHK’s Community Chilling Hub suggests another path: human care with community capacity, interdisciplinary collaboration and human dignity. “It’s in our DNA … to work with the community, to break through existing silos. Unfortunately, people fall through these cracks,” Tam reflects.
The hub is an attempt to close the cracks. If it succeeds, it may offer Hong Kong—and beyond—a blueprint for human care that is responsive, more inclusive and more sustainable because it begins where all sustainable development must: with people.

Social Transformation in the Sands

Social Transformation in the Sands
The afforestation project around Inner Mongolia's Malan Lake has grown into a fine example of how ecological engineering, economic incentives and institutional cooperation can reinforce one another
[The content of this article has been produced by our advertising partner.]
On the southeastern rim of the Tengger Desert, where dunes can rise 30 metres high and advance significant metres a year, a private afforestation effort is attempting something larger than tree planting. At Malan Lake in Alxa, Inner Mongolia, founder Mr YUEN Shu Wah is testing whether desert restoration can succeed by redesigning not only landscapes, but also livelihoods and governance.
Battling Moving Sand
“Countries, cities and villages have been annihilated by the desertification,” Yuen says, describing the stakes in stark historical terms and adding the spread of desert conditions affects communities “very, very much” and must be stopped.
Malan Lake lies along an ecological corridor where unchecked expansion can intensify sandstorms and push degradation outward. Greening this frontier, Yuen argues, helps “hold the desert expansion” at a critical point. His aim is afforestation, which is the process of planting trees where there have not been any for a long period of time, as opposed to reforestation where new trees are planted to replace old or missing ones in existing forests.
Yuen began exploring desert restoration in the late 2000s and formally established Alxa League Springfield Forest Limited in 2011 to scale the Malan Lake initiative. When he first surveyed the site around 2010, he encountered moving dunes up to 30 metres high, advancing roughly 12 metres a year.
Early planting efforts revealed how technically complex the terrain was: seedlings on the windward side could be uprooted, while those on the leeward side risked burial. After more than two years of experimentation and hesitation, Yuen committed significant capital in and around 2013–2014, shifting from small-scale trials to systematic afforestation.
The project has since expanded dramatically. At its most intensive recently, it reported planting up to 150,000 mu—approximately 100 square kilometres—of desert in a single year. Planting density is intentionally low, at about 50 plants per mu (roughly 750 per hectare), reflecting dryland forestry practices designed to maximise survival under limited rainfall.
Yet Yuen is quick to temper any sense of triumph. Against the vastness of the Tengger Desert, he says, even these gains remain “a drop in the bucket”. Nevertheless, what began as a cautious pilot has evolved into a structured operation involving partnership between full-time staff, seasonal workers, university, research organisations and government, demonstrating both scale and organisational maturity.
What distinguishes the Malan Lake model is not only its scale but its structure. It is largely privately funded, operating with the discipline of a business while pursuing public ecological objectives.
“The unique point is, firstly, it comes from a private source of funding,” Yuen explains. In addition, the emphasis is very much on keeping costs down and maintenance needs low. The team focuses on planting indigenous, drought-resistant species capable of surviving harsh conditions with little or no irrigation. “The plant needs to survive on its own,” Yuen says, adding that the aim is to tackle “the most harsh conditions” at minimal cost.
This technical discipline is matched by a social one. For Yuen, desertification cannot be separated from human behaviour. Overgrazing has long contributed to land degradation, but simply restricting herds without offering alternatives risks undermining livelihoods. “We try to green the desert and keep the people happy,” he says. “We need people to look after the land.”
That philosophy has led to the development of what he calls a “sand industry” - economic activities adapted to arid conditions. Cultivating Tremella mushrooms, using local shrubs as a growing medium, has become one example of an alternative income stream. The initiative also promotes indigenous plant propagation and cultivating medicinal species suited to desert environments. These ventures are designed to reduce dependence on expanding herds while giving residents a stake in ecological recovery.
“In order to let people stay there without relying only on overgrazing, we developed a sand industry,” Yuen says. “Since we're able to develop the Tremella industry, this is an innovative sort of livelihood for the local people.”
He acknowledges that policy efforts to curb overgrazing face limits if livelihoods are not addressed, pointing out that without viable alternatives, behavioural change is difficult to sustain. Yuen has called on enterprises and educational institutions to help develop more desert-based industries that align economic incentives with conservation.
“The government also knows that they need to change the herdsmen’s habit of overgrazing. But if they cannot find a good livelihood for the herdsmen… their achievement is limited,” he says.
Participation extends beyond local communities. Universities have reserved plots of land where students can take part in greening efforts over several years. Corporate partners contribute not only funding but also procurement support, for example by purchasing desert-grown products as gifts. In this way, ecological restoration is woven into supply chains and ESG strategies.
Technology is increasingly central to the project’s governance model. In its early years, operations relied heavily on field experience and practical experimentation. Now, in collaboration with City University of Hong Kong (CityUHK), the team is introducing environmental sensors and exploring satellite assessment to monitor larger areas. The goal, Yuen says, is to improve predictive capability, to understand better what can and cannot be done under volatile desert conditions, and to make the project more productive.
“We always wish to make better predictions of what we can do, what we cannot do. I think it helps to make the project more productive,” he explains.
He situates the work within a broader ESG and SDG framework. Environmental gains include biodiversity restoration and carbon sequestration; social benefits include employment and education about sustainable land use; governance innovation lies in cross-sector collaboration between private funders, public institutions and research partners.
“To find out ways and means to do this is by itself an achievement,” he reflects.
A Model for All
The project has made considerable progress, but Yuen acknowledges its limitations and emphasises that the ambition is not to conquer the desert single-handedly, but to demonstrate that restoration is possible—and replicable.
“We want more companies, enterprises, foundations, individuals to realise it is possible to forest the desert land,” he says, “and hopefully they can chip in and do the same.”
After more than a decade of work, Yuen believes the team has gradually found its way. Malan Lake now stands as more than a green patch against a shifting horizon: it is a test case for how ecological engineering, economic incentives and institutional cooperation can reinforce one another.
In a landscape defined by wind and sand, the project suggests that the more durable force may be governance—the careful alignment of people, capital and purpose towards a common environmental goal.

Data to Direction: How Vietnam is Reinventing the Strategic State
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
