Ukraine Hits Russia’s Refineries So Bad Moscow Is Now Importing Fuel for Its Warplanes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:24:49 UTC
00:24:49 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hits Russia’s Refineries So Bad Moscow Is Now Importing Fuel for Its Warplanes
Systematic Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries have sharply reduced the country’s aviation fuel production, forcing Moscow to import Jet A-1 from South Korea and Egypt to support both military and civilian aviation, Ukraine’s Defense Intelligence said on August 29.
According to HUR, Russia has also temporarily banned exports of its own aviation fuel as it attempts to preserve domestic supplies.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“To meet the needs of combat and civilian aviation, Russia, which for decades positioned itself as an energy superpower, has officially introduced a temporary ban on exports of its own aviation fuel and is forced to seek ways to import foreign Jet A-1 aviation fuel,” Ukrainian intelligence said.
Jet A-1 is broadly comparable to the Soviet- and Russian-standard TS-1 and RT kerosene fuels used in gas-turbine aircraft engines, allowing it to be used by a wide range of aircraft operated by the Russian military.
HUR said the imported fuel is suitable for aircraft including the MiG-29, Su-34, Su-35S, Su-30SM, Su-57 and Su-24M, as well as Tu-95MS strategic bombers.
The fuel could also be used by Russia’s newer jet-powered Geran-4 and Geran-5 attack drones, which employ Telefly TJ2000A turbojet engines or Russian-made equivalents designated TRD-2000.
Ukrainian intelligence said three tankers linked to Russia’s shadow fleet have already delivered approximately 70,000 metric tons of Jet A-1 from South Korea and Egypt to Russian ports in St. Petersburg and Vladivostok.
The shipments were reportedly arranged for Russia’s Independent Oil and Gas Company, which supplies large quantities of fuel to TZK-AERO.
TZK-AERO, in turn, provides fuel under government contracts to the Russian military, the Federal Security Service and other Russian security formations, according to HUR.
Ukrainian intelligence said the supply chain for South Korean aviation fuel involved UAE-based Caliph Energy Trading FZE.
The Egyptian supply route reportedly involved the Middle East Oil Refinery, known as MIDOR, the Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation and UAE-based trading company Vernal Overseas FZE.
Earlier, reports emerged that Russia was considering easing aviation fuel standards in an effort to increase production following Ukrainian strikes on the country’s oil refineries.
Russia’s Transport Ministry has proposed allowing aviation fuel with a freezing point of up to minus 50 degrees Celsius, compared with the current requirement of minus 60 degrees Celsius.

Ukraine Hammers Two Russian Airfields in One Night, Triggering Fires and Ammunition Blasts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Ukraine Hammers Two Russian Airfields in One Night, Triggering Fires and Ammunition Blasts
Ukrainian forces struck two Russian military aviation sites overnight on August 30, hitting the Yeysk airfield in Krasnodar Krai and a facility used to store, prepare and launch attack drones in Millerovo in the Rostov region, Ukraine’s General Staff confirmed on August 30.
Fires were recorded at both locations following the strikes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
At Yeysk, footage published by the OSINT community Exilenova+ showed a large fire inside the military airfield as secondary explosions consistent with detonating ammunition could be heard.
NASA’s FIRMS satellite fire-monitoring system also detected a blaze at the facility at around 4:02 am local time. Satellite data indicated that the affected area extended from the aircraft parking section toward the runway.
A drone warning had been issued across the region at approximately 2:58 am, including for the city of Yeysk. The alert remained active until 5:33 am, lasting roughly three hours.
Ukraine’s General Staff subsequently confirmed that the Yeysk military airfield had been hit and that a fire broke out on the site.
The Russian military uses Yeysk to support aviation operations, including aircraft capable of launching missiles and guided aerial bombs against Ukraine.
The base also hosts Russia’s 859th Center for Combat Application and Retraining of Naval Aviation Flight Personnel, making it an important training and support facility for Russian naval aviation.
Another distinctive feature of Yeysk is its NITKA ground-based aviation training complex, which replicates an aircraft carrier’s flight deck and landing systems. Russian naval aviators use the facility to practice carrier takeoffs and landings without operating at sea.
Repeated Ukrainian attacks have made Yeysk increasingly vulnerable, and Russian forces do not appear to station combat aircraft there permanently. However, aircraft can still be temporarily redeployed to the base ahead of operations.
Ukraine simultaneously struck a Russian drone operations facility in Millerovo, roughly 170 kilometers, or 105 miles, from the front line.
The General Staff said the target was used for the storage, preparation, and launch of Russian attack UAVs. A fire was recorded following the strike.
NASA FIRMS detected a fire in the Millerovo area at approximately 3:33 am local time after drone warnings were issued shortly after midnight.
The Millerovo military airfield is associated with Russia’s 31st Fighter Aviation Regiment, which operates Su-30SM multirole fighters.
The site has repeatedly come under Ukrainian attack because of its proximity to Ukraine and its role in supporting Russian military aviation and drone operations.
Russian forces also use infrastructure in the area to store ammunition, house personnel and maintain fuel and lubricant supplies.
Rostov regional governor Yuri Slyusar acknowledged a drone attack on Millerovo but did not publicly mention the military facility or the fire there.
Previously, Ukrainian drones struck a Russian Nebo-U radar station at the Millerovo military airfield in Russia’s Rostov region, a facility used to launch Shahed drones and other UAVs against Ukraine.

'A close partner': EU offers muted reaction after Iceland rebuffs accession talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:21:49 UTC
00:21:49 KST

The EU institutions say they fully respect the choice of the Icelandic people after voters said "no" to reopening accession negotiations. The result threatens to dampen the momentum on enlargement policy.
The European Commission has issued a muted reaction after Iceland rejected the reopening of accession negotiations with the bloc in a hotly contested referendum, a decision that risks dampening the momentum on enlargement.
The vote came down to the wire: 52.8% chose "no" and 47.2% chose "yes".
"The European Commission takes note of the outcome of Iceland's referendum," a Commission spokesperson said in a brief statement.
"The Commission respects the choice of the Icelandic people. Iceland remains a close partner of the European Union."
Meanwhile, European Council President António Costa exchanged messages with Iceland's Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir during which "both leaders expressed their desire to continue to strengthen the relationship between the EU and Iceland", according to Costa's spokesperson.
"President Costa stressed that the EU fully respects the democratic choice of the Icelandic people in today's referendum. Iceland remains one of the EU's closest and most trusted partners," the spokesperson said.
Frostadóttir had previously said she would abandon the matter of EU membership entirely for the remainder of her term if voters rejected the proposal.
"47% of the population was interested in it," Frostadóttir said on Sunday. "I think it is important that we go into the coming months and weeks and respect that point of view."
Officials and diplomats in Brussels had seen in Iceland a five-star candidate that could have proven enlargement sceptics wrong. The Nordic country was all but guaranteed to become a frontrunner, given its extensive degree of integration with the bloc.
In the lead-up to the vote, the Commission, which oversees accession, had kept a low profile but signalled its intention to find "creative" solutions with Iceland to address what would have been the two most contentious issues: fisheries and agriculture.
Though Iceland enjoys broad access to the single market, the arrangement excludes the Common Fisheries Policy (CFP) and the Common Agricultural Policy (CAP).
Those two chapters were left untouched the last time that Reykjavík and Brussels engaged in accession talks, a process put on hold in 2013.
It remains to be seen how large an impact the Icelandic referendum will have on the bloc's enlargement drive, which, after years of stagnation, jumped to the top of the political agenda in the aftermath of Russia's invasion of Ukraine.
Montenegro is the current frontrunner, having provisionally closed 18 of the 33 accession chapters. The country aspires to become the 28th member state in 2028, an ambition that has inspired the "28 by 28" slogan.
Even if Brussels refuses to commit to artificial deadlines, it recognises the importance of delivering on the promise of enlargement before candidates run out of patience. Coupling Montenegro with Iceland was considered a potential avenue.
The Commission is preparing reforms to bring tangible benefits to candidates, such as access to certain EU programmes, before they become full-time members.

Libya’s political representatives have welcomed the signing by the country’s 4+4 Small Dialogue Committee of a final agreement to restructure the High National Elections Commission and review election laws.

In a statement on Sunday, Abdulhamid Dbeibah, prime minister of the Tripoli-based, UN-recognised Government of National Unity (GNU), hailed the move as “an important step that reinforces the path we have called for from the outset, based on ending transitional phases and moving towards elections”.
“Our vision is clear: the decision should rest with the Libyan people through elections that end the state of division and give all institutions their true legitimacy,” he added.

Saddam Haftar, deputy commander-in-chief of the LNA in the country’s east, also welcomed the agreement in a separate statement.

4+4 committee
Earlier, the 4+4 committee announced the signing of a draft agreement that provides for restructuring the board of the High National Elections Commission and appointing Dhaou Ibrahim Attia as chairman of the commission’s board and Sana al-Lishani as deputy chairwoman.
The latest agreement is part of UN-led efforts to create the conditions for holding elections and ending Libya’s political division between two administrations.

It has been holding UN-sponsored talks since April 2026 aimed at breaking the country’s political deadlock and advancing the implementation of a UN roadmap for holding elections and unifying executive authority.

It also permits military personnel to participate in presidential elections as candidates and voters and requires presidential candidates to secure 20,000 endorsements from registered voters across Libya.

It also stipulates that sessions of the elected House of Representatives and the executive authority be held periodically, according to a fixed rotation, in Tripoli, Benghazi in the east and Sabha in the south.

Niger junta, aided by Russian paramilitary forces, regains control after mutiny

Niger junta puts down mutiny with help from Russia's Africa Corps
Life returned to normal in Niger's capital on Sunday, a day after mutineers stormed the presidential palace and a military base at Niamey's main airport, resisting forces loyal to the ruling junta until Russia’s Africa Corps intervened. State TV reported that dozens of soldiers were killed or arrested, with some paraded in front of cameras live on television.
Niger’s capital of Niamey on Sunday appeared calm with normalcy restored after a day of unrest as young soldiers staged a mutiny that threatened the ruling military junta before being repelled by loyalist forces aided by Russian troops.
In what was seen as a major threat to the junta in power since a 2023 coup, the soldiers engaged loyalist forces in sustained gunfire overnight from Friday till late Saturday. Most of the clashes took place at Niamey’s main airport that houses the military air base and in a district where the presidential palace is located.
The unrest culminated in the arrest or killing of dozens of soldiers who were paraded in front of the cameras live on state television. The fate of the mutineers was not immediately clear and authorities did not disclose any charges against them.
Watch moreNiger's junta says 'regaining control' after clashes in capital
On Sunday, military trucks and check points were seen across the city, particularly along major roads between the airport and the presidential district. Junta leader Abdourahamane Tchiani was yet to make any public comments or appearance.
Here’s what we know about the mutiny, according to witnesses, analysts and diplomats:
Nigeriens were awoken around midnight on Friday into Saturday by bursts of gunfire and explosions that started at the Diori Hamani International Airport. The airport is a strategic hub that hosts a key military air base, known as Base 101, as well as the headquarters of Russia’s Africa Corps in the country. It was the third time this year the airport has experienced unrest.
Gunshots were also heard near the presidential palace in the Plateau district of Niamey as a group of soldiers confronted forces loyal to the junta.
Niger’s defence ministry said its forces were gradually regaining control of the situation after a group of soldiers took their “comrades” hostage at the air base and fired at “sensitive” sites, without specifying cause of the unrest.
The chaos persisted for hours late into Saturday as the presidential guard and other loyalist forces secured the air base and the presidency, analysts and diplomats said.
Some of the mutineers came from hot spots in the south and west, among the areas worst-hit by jihadi violence, and were rallying support from others stationed outside the city, according to one European diplomat, who spoke on condition of anonymity because they were not allowed to speak publicly about the matter.
The unrest appeared to have been triggered by grievances over rising insecurity, including rampant jihadi attacks that have led to the mass killing of soldiers in the last year.
Deadly attacks are “becoming commonplace (in the country) and will continue to fuel unrest and aggravate tensions within the army ranks”, said Héni Nsaibia, senior West Africa analyst at Armed Conflict Location and Event Data, a conflict monitor.
Jihadi violence has worsened in the wider Sahel region, including in neighbouring Burkina Faso and Mali, where the military also seized power from civilian governments. The junta in Niger promised to stabilize the country but instead security has deteriorated. Attacks on military positions have increased, including one about a week ago when at least 18 soldiers were reportedly killed in the southern Dosso region.
Far below the expectations that followed their forceful takeover of power from their barracks, the junta led Niger into a “critical security situation” fueling discontent and the mutiny was led by soldiers mostly deployed on the ground against the jihadis, said FRANCE 24's terrorism expert Wassim Nasr.
Watch moreSituation in Niger 'not stabilised yet' as security forces deploy around airport
“Deteriorating insecurity drove the coups that swept across the central Sahel, and the latest events show how these same pressures are now fueling unrest within the militaries that seized power,” said Nsaibia.
The mutineers remained camped at the military base within the airport complex for several hours, resisting efforts from loyalist forces, until Russia’s Africa Corps intervened with ground and aerial support, several analysts said.
The Africa Corps is believed to have between 200 to 300 personnel in Niger where it is primarily protecting the junta and its interests, and also supporting the fight against jihadis.
In interviews broadcast on Russian media, Moscow’s ambassador to Niger, Viktor Voropayev, said Niger had requested support from the Russian force and the mutineers were “neutralized particularly thanks to the intervention” of Africa Corps.
The mutineers outnumbered the elite presidential guard that was deployed to retake the air base and it was unclear who was in control until the Russians intervened, according to Nasr.
“At the end of the day, it is easier to go full-blown on repression when it’s a foreign force,” Nasr said.
The regional Alliance of Sahel States (AES) that includes Burkina Faso and Mali issued a statement late Saturday expressing its “full support” to Niger and condemning the “betrayal” from the soldiers.
“Thanks to the bravery and professionalism of the loyalist republican forces, this latest attempt was contained and thwarted,” it said
Algeria, the first country on Saturday to express support for Niger, its southeastern neighbour, assured it of its “full solidarity and firm support”.
Turkey, another key ally of Niger, expressed solidarity with the country and its people, called for “restraint” for the preservation of the country’s security and stability.
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:17:06 UTC
00:17:06 KST

1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
A 1.4-million-year-old footprint trail reveals a surprisingly large group of ancient human relatives traveling together along a Kenyan lakeshore.
- Date:
- August 30, 2026
- Source:
- Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology
- Summary:
- Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.
- Share:
A remarkable set of fossil footprints from northern Kenya is offering scientists a rare glimpse of how an extinct human relative may have moved and interacted about 1.4 million years ago.
The tracks, preserved near an ancient lakeshore, appear to record eight Paranthropus boisei individuals occupying the same place at roughly the same time. Researchers describe the discovery as a snapshot of "fossil behavior" because, unlike bones that can accumulate over long periods, footprints can capture a brief moment in the lives of individuals.
The international team, made up of researchers from the US and Kenya, concluded that all eight trackmakers were likely adults. Several also appear to have been considerably larger than earlier estimates of Paranthropus boisei body size based on the limited skeletal remains available.
Ancient Footprints Reveal Unexpected Body Size
The researchers used analytical techniques first developed by their team in 2024 to identify the footprints as belonging to Paranthropus boisei. The classification was based on clues in foot anatomy as well as the way the individuals appear to have moved.
The size of the tracks came as a surprise.
"The sizes of the footprints indicate human-like body sizes - up to 1.8 meters tall and around 75 kilograms," says lead author Kevin Hatala, of Chatham University and an associated researcher of the Department of Human Origins at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Leipzig.
For decades, most known fossils of Paranthropus boisei consisted of skulls, including specimens with exceptionally large jaws and teeth. Much less has been known about what the species looked like below the neck because fossils from the rest of the skeleton are far rarer.
The new tracks now challenge earlier research suggesting that Paranthropus boisei was substantially smaller than Homo erectus, another hominin that lived during the same general period and is considered a possible direct ancestor of modern humans.
A Rare Glimpse of Ancient Social Behavior
Footprints can reveal more than anatomy. Because a walking surface may be formed and preserved over a very short span of time, fossil tracks can provide direct evidence about movement, group size, and possible social interactions.
In this case, the eight individuals appear to have been traveling together. Most were likely adult males, with no obvious evidence of females or children among them.
"The fact that eight, mostly adult male, Paranthropus boisei individuals seemingly traveled together as a group, without females or children, hints at a complex social structure in this species," says co-author Neil Roach of Harvard University. "They may have lived in large groups, where males competed for mates, but also tolerated each other at times for safety in a dangerous environment."
That possibility adds a new dimension to what scientists know about Paranthropus boisei. The species shared its world with early members of the genus Homo but followed a very different evolutionary path.
Why Ancient Hominins Returned to the Lakeshore
The new discovery is part of a much larger collection of hominin footprints found in ancient lakeshore environments around Lake Turkana.
That pattern suggests these areas were important habitats that offered resources valuable enough to draw extinct human relatives back repeatedly.
"To me, it is amazing that we have the same kind of lake margin deposits in two areas of East Turkana that are 40 kilometers apart, at about the same age," says co-author Kay Behrensmeyer of the Smithsonian Institution.
Researchers have now documented hundreds of hominin footprints at more than a half-dozen sites across the region. Understanding why those tracks survived could also help explain why ancient hominins continued visiting the lakeshore over such a long span of time.
Behrensmeyer predicts that, "if we can understand what geological conditions allowed these tracks to be preserved, we should know more about why hominins continued to return to the lake shore environment over more than 100,000 years."
Building a Record of Life 1.4 Million Years Ago
The research team plans to return to Kenya this year to continue investigating the fossil footprint sites.
Each newly documented surface can preserve a different moment from the distant past, giving researchers evidence about anatomy, walking behavior, social interactions, and environmental conditions that traditional fossils cannot always provide.
"Each site represents a snapshot of our past, and we are quickly building a photo album with several different windows to hominin anatomy, locomotion, behavior, and environments during the Early Pleistocene," says Hatala.
The discoveries are also reinforcing the importance of the Lake Turkana region as one of the world's richest areas for studying human evolution.
Co-author Purity Kiura of the National Museums of Kenya adds, "The discovery of these fossil footprints along the margins of Lake Turkana reinforces the region's global importance in understanding human evolution, preserving remarkable evidence of how our ancient relatives lived 1.4 million years ago. It further strengthens Kenya's position as one of the world's leading paleoanthropological landscapes and highlights our responsibility to protect this irreplaceable heritage."
By combining new analytical methods with unusually well-preserved footprint sites, researchers are gaining access to details that bones alone often cannot provide. These ancient tracks can reveal how extinct human relatives were built, how they moved, where they spent their time, and even how they may have interacted with one another.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Kevin G. Hatala, Neil T. Roach, John W. K. Harris, Purity Kiura, Emmanuel K. Ndiema, Ben Sila, David Kipkebut, Joyce Waweru, Philiphine Kisale, Apolo Alkoro Longaye, Hilary Sale, Anna K. Behrensmeyer. Insights into hominin body size, locomotion, and behavior from Early Pleistocene trackways in northern Kenya. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 2026; 123 (31) DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2530996123

EU wants drones to spray pesticides — but it could backfire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:11:00 UTC
00:11:00 KST

EU wants drones to spray pesticides — but it could backfire
August 30, 2026
In theory, the idea doesn't sound bad: Instead of using tractors to spray large quantities of pesticides over fields, drones could precisely spray herbicides, fungicides and insecticides only where they are actually needed.
The plan would be to scan a field, identify affected areas and treat them selectively — significantly reducing pesticide use, according to the European Union's Omnibus X legislative package, which aims to simplify EU food and feed safety rules. After all, the bloc aims to halve the use of chemicals for plant protection by 2030.
Until now, however, the EU had a decades-old ban on spraying pesticides from the air over agricultural land. Exceptions applied only to difficult-to-work terrain, such as steep vineyard slopes. Omnibus X is now set to change that. In May, the European Council gave the legislative package the green light.
Drone use doesn't automatically mean less pesticides
"I think it makes sense in principle to distinguish spray drones from conventional aerial application from a regulatory perspective," said Thomas Daum, an agricultural economist and human ecologist at the School of Global Studies at the University of Gothenburg. Daum studies new technologies and their impact on agriculture. Compared with an airplane or helicopter, he said drones can generally spray more precisely.
However, Daum also cautioned that "the drone itself does not save any pesticide." He sees potential for using drones to respond more selectively to pest infestations — and thus reduce overall pesticide use. Another advantage for farmers could be the ability to respond quickly to an infestation "even when soils are wet or in difficult-to-access terrain."
"At the same time, this flexibility lowers the barriers to treatment and could therefore also lead to spraying being carried out more frequently overall," Daum said. This could result in a technological lock-in — meaning that more efficient application could reinforce dependence on chemical crop protection.
Omnibus X aims to save administrative costs, cash
Chemical pesticides have been cause for concern for many researchers. Omnibus X is intended not only to make it easier to use spray drones, but also to change the way pesticides are approved.
When the European Council approved Omnibus X in May, a group of researchers from 27 European research institutions voiced strong criticism. Among them was Carsten Brühl, a biologist at the Institute for Environmental Sciences at the Rheinland-Pfalz Technical University of Kaiserslautern-Landau. Brühl, who studies the effects of pesticides on the environment, called Omnibus X a "deregulation package" and is deeply alarmed by it.
To date, pesticide active substances have generally been approved at the EU level for a period of 10 years. Once that period expires, manufacturers can apply for renewed approval and must once again submit data on the safety of the active substance. Since this review process was introduced in 2011, it has resulted in 59 active substances not being reapproved, as they were deemed harmful to human health and the environment.
The main aim of the Omnibus X package is to cut administrative costs, reduce bureaucracy and "ensure fair treatment for companies while safeguarding fair competition within the internal market [...]," according to an EU press release.
Researchers warn Omnibus X could harm people, environment
European scientists have been critical of the EU proposal to cut red tape and deregulate the industry, because it could lead to many active substances being approved indefinitely, eliminating regular reassessments. They also say the transition periods after an approval expires would be extended from 18 months to three years.
Brühl called the idea "reckless." It would mean that even active substances suspected of being harmful to human health could remain on the market — like weedkiller glyphosate, for example, which has been linked to cancer in humans.
But the precautionary principle should apply, Brühl argued. This political principle holds that potential harm to people and nature should be prevented proactively, even when there is not yet conclusive scientific evidence.
The scientific evidence on pesticides is already incomplete. The risks posed by an active substance are inferred from the results of laboratory studies, Brühl said. But how that substance actually behaves over the long term under different environmental conditions and in combination with other pesticides is unclear at the time of approval. That is why regular reassessments are so important.
Brühl now fears Omnibus X could undermine scientific interest in studying these active substances. It would be unappealing for researchers "to engage with a system that can no longer be influenced anyway," he said.
Agriculture can work without pesticides
Brühl is certain the new EU legislation will not lead to lower pesticide use — not even with the help of drones and more targeted spraying. This approach, for example, does not work at all with fungicides, he pointed out. Fungicides combat fungal infections and have to be applied preventively because once a plant has become infected, it can no longer be saved.
But Brühl stressed there is another way: doing without pesticides entirely, through what is known as "integrated pest management." And this isn't some hippie eco-fantasy, but rather a concept for the sustainable management of harmful organisms enshrined in German law in 2012.
Shortly after the European Council gave the green light to Omnibus X and its new rules on drones and pesticides in May, the Scientific Advisory Board of Germany's National Action Plan for the Sustainable Use of Plant Protection Products reminded the German government of its own law in a statement. Brühl was the lead author.
Researchers wrote that integrated pest management calls for the use of synthetic chemical pesticides only as a last resort. The goal is to secure yields and quality while also minimizing negative consequences for people and nature and preventing resistance to plant protection products. This can work if certain crop rotations are taken into account and mixed cropping is favored. Pests can be controlled by attracting natural predators through flower strips or hedges, while weeds can be removed mechanically.
The problem: Spraying pesticides is often the less time-consuming and therefore cheaper option. There is also a persistent narrative that pesticides are necessary to ensure food security.
What this narrative leaves out is that monocultures and ecosystems disrupted by pesticides make agriculture more vulnerable to changing environmental conditions. That threatens food security, said Brühl, "because you have a system in place that can't cope with climate change."
This article was originally written in German.

Venezuela’s interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, has defended her government’s highly controversial energy deal with Donald Trump, insisting the South American country will maintain ownership and sovereignty over its massive oil reserves.
Rodríguez, who assumed power in January after Trump ordered the abduction of the president, Nicolás Maduro, took to the airwaves on Saturday to push back against criticism of what the US president has called “the biggest oil deal in world history”.
“The benefits are endless,” claimed Rodríguez, a former vice-president whom Trump backed after ordering Maduro’s capture during a special forces raid on the capital, Caracas.
During a six-minute television broadcast, Venezuela’s acting leader claimed the deal would help her resource-rich country develop its economy, earn revenues of more than $209bn (£154bn), and become “an energy powerhouse”.
Rodríguez said: “As everyone knows, our country has the biggest oil reserves in the world. But having resources underground isn’t enough. We need investment, technology, infrastructure [and] production capacity to convert this wealth into wellbeing for our people.”
She added: “It’s no use having our oil reserves underground, only to appear in statistics or bookkeeping … and for us not to be able to convert and translate them into development for Venezuela.”
Trump announced the “groundbreaking” deal on Friday, calling it a “historic transaction [that] more than doubles American oil reserves … while helping to continue to set Venezuela on a course toward Tremendous Success and Great Prosperity”.
On Sunday, Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform: “One of the things I am going to do with the Venezuelan Oil is fill up the Strategic National Reserves which, because of Sleepy Joe Biden, has been virtually emptied.”
Trump added: “The ‘topping out’ process will begin very shortly, and is a Gift from Venezuela to the People of the United States.”
Hours after seizing Maduro on 3 January, Trump warned Rodríguez she would face an even worse fate if she failed to toe the US line. “If she doesn’t do what’s right, she is going to pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro,” Trump said.
Details of the agreement – struck during months of secret talks – remain sparse but it will reportedly see Washington take control of 65bn barrels of Venezuelan oil reserves.
The South American country has the world’s largest proven crude oil reserves, with an estimated 303bn barrels, compared with Saudi Arabia’s 268bn and Iran’s 208bn. Rodríguez said the deal involved 17 “strategic oilfields” where it was hoped more than 1.5m barrels could be produced each day.
But the deal has provoked outrage, both among members of Venezuela’s opposition and within the Chavismo political movement of which Rodríguez is part.
Speaking on Friday, one prominent opposition figure, who asked not to be named, called the agreement “a massive land grab” by a “rapacious, mafioso United States”.
Writing on X, Rafael Ramírez, the former head of Venezuela’s state-owned oil company PDVSA, accused Rodríguez’s administration of “driving a dagger straight into the heart of the homeland” with the “neocolonial” transaction. “They are handing over 65bn barrels of our reserves to the United States. That has never happened in Venezuela, and I think nowhere else in the world,” Ramírez added in an interview with the newspaper El Nacional.
On Saturday, dozens of leftwing protesters marched through Caracas with banners reading: “We are neither a colony, nor a back yard” and “Yankees go home!”
Critics of the agreement shared an ironic meme on social media suggesting the state oil company’s name should be changed from PDVSA to “PDUSA”.
In her broadcast, Rodríguez, the daughter of a Marxist guerrilla who spent years denouncing “imperialist” attempts to snatch her country’s oil reserves, countered claims she was surrendering Venezuela’s natural resources to a foreign power. She thanked Trump and the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, for striking the deal but added: “There is something that must be made absolutely clear: Venezuela retains the ownership and sovereignty over its resources.”
“We are thinking of Venezuela’s future,” claimed the politician, whose country was plunged into authoritarian rule and one of the world’s worst peacetime economic crises during Maduro’s 13-year rule.
The deal represents an astonishing U-turn from Rodríguez and the socialist, anti-imperialist political movement she and Maduro inherited from Hugo Chávez after his death in 2013.
In one 2024 speech, footage of which circulated on social media after Friday’s announcement, Rodríguez lambasted the Venezuelan opposition, accusing it of seeking to surrender the country’s oil, natural gas and gold reserves to its “masters” in Washington.
Last September, as the US tightened the screws on Maduro, Rodríguez told the New York Times: “The Pentagon always had a strategic objective of obtaining Venezuelan reserves.”
The deal will reportedly involve the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital, which channels funds into projects seen as important for national security. It will also involve a private company owned by Alejandro Betancourt, a controversial UK-based tycoon who has emerged as a key intermediary between the Trump administration and Rodríguez.
Opposition politicians fear the deal will scupper attempts to recover Venezuela’s democracy and hold fresh presidential elections. Maduro is widely believed to have stolen the last vote, in 2024, and Rodríguez has deflected questions about a future election, saying vaguely that it will happen “some day”. Trump has also said Venezuela is “not really ready” for elections.
Writing on X, the opposition leader Juan Pablo Guanipa, said: “The only way to truly reactivate the Venezuelan economy in the long term and make this agreement benefit both parties is through a free election that leads to a representative government, clear rules of the game, rule of law, and institutions that allow our resources to be managed transparently and for the benefit of the nation.”
Without that, the energy deal was like “a skyscraper [built] on pillars of clay”, Guanipa added.

NASA launches powerful new Roman Space Telescope from Florida
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:08:00 UTC
00:08:00 KST

NASA launches powerful new Roman Space Telescope from Florida
- NASA launched the US$4 billion Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope to study dark energy, dark matter, and exoplanets from its orbit beyond the moon.
- Roman will survey the sky much faster than Hubble, capturing wide-angle views and mapping over two billion galaxies in 3D.
- The mission aims to solve cosmic mysteries, discover thousands of exoplanets, and begins science operations after a 90-day commissioning phase.
AI generated
CAPE CANAVERAL, Florida – NASA’s new flagship astronomical observatory was launched into space from Florida on Aug 30 on a mission to probe some of the biggest mysteries in astrophysics and cosmology.
The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope, a roughly US$4 billion (S$5 billion) project, was carried aloft from NASA’s Kennedy Space Center aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket through blue skies just after sunrise, embarking on a potentially decade-long observation mission.
The telescope, which will park itself beyond the moon, is designed to investigate cosmic enigmas such as dark energy and dark matter, while also testing gravity at vast scales and searching for exoplanets, as planets beyond our solar system are called.
The launch marked “an endpoint for the engineers, but it’s a starting point for the scientists”, Julie McEnery, Roman telescope senior project scientist, told reporters at a post-launch news conference. “It feels like I’m on the edge of a precipice, and we’re just about to set a foot off into the unknown.”
Roman will travel through space towards an orbital location called Lagrange Point 2, situated about 1.6 million km from Earth. Its mission is planned for five years, though the US space agency said the telescope may have enough fuel for five additional years.
Mission scientists will spend the next 90 days commissioning the spacecraft and preparing the observatory for its science operations. It is expected to beam back its first high-resolution images “before the winter holidays”, Roman telescope project manager Jackie Townsend told reporters.
Roman will build on the capabilities of other orbiting observatories such as the James Webb Space Telescope, launched in 2021, and the Hubble Space Telescope, launched in 1990.
“It will be as if Hubble and James Webb kind of peered through a keyhole at the universe, while Nancy Grace Roman will kick the door down,” Nicola Fox, chief of NASA’s Science Mission Directorate, told reporters on Aug 29.
“Roman has broadly the same sensitivity and sharpness of vision as Hubble, but we survey the sky much faster,” McEnery told reporters at a briefing in July.
She said one month of Roman observations can survey the entire home galaxy.
“One month of observations to survey our Milky Way galaxy would take about a century with Hubble,” McEnery said.
Wide angle and zoom lenses
Webb has provided a new understanding of the early history of the universe, finding among other things that primordial galaxies formed sooner and were bigger than previously known. Webb is capable of looking across vast distances and back into deep time, because of the time it takes light to travel.
Roman instead is able to take panoramic views. NASA likens Roman to a camera’s wide-angle lens and Webb to a zoom lens.
“Webb is designed to be able to probe very deeply and with exquisite sensitivity into the universe, so we can find rare things in the early universe,” McEnery said, while Roman offers “the large vision that complements the deep views that Webb provides”.
Roman will help in the understanding of two mysterious cosmic components – dark energy and dark matter – by creating the most comprehensive 3D map of the universe to date. Its main survey, to take more than a year to complete, will cover more than two billion galaxies.
The Big Bang event roughly 13.8 billion years ago initiated the universe, and it has been expanding ever since. Scientists in 1998 disclosed that this expansion was actually accelerating, with an invisible force called dark energy as the hypothesised reason.
The universe’s contents include ordinary matter – stars, planets, gas, dust and all the familiar stuff on Earth – as well as dark matter and dark energy. Ordinary matter represents perhaps 5 per cent of the contents. Dark matter, known through its gravitational influences on galaxies and stars, may represent about 27 per cent. Dark energy may represent about 68 per cent.
Using Roman to gauge dark matter’s pull and dark energy’s push across the universe will bring scientists closer than ever before to solving both mysteries, according to NASA.
Roman also will conduct one of the most comprehensive searches ever for exoplanets. It is expected to discover thousands of new ones and provide the first statistical census of planetary systems similar to our own.
“One of the most exciting aspects of Roman is its discovery potential. Historically, major astronomical observatories have often made their most important breakthroughs in areas that scientists did not anticipate before launch,” cosmologist Mustapha Ishak of the University of Texas at Dallas, a member of Roman’s scientific collaboration, told Reuters.
President Donald Trump’s administration tried during both his first and second terms to reduce or eliminate funding for Roman, but Congress preserved it. Roman’s launch comes nine months ahead of schedule, according to NASA. REUTERS

Personality trait of openness linked to lower antisemitic attitude, more Jewish contact study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:06:43 UTC
00:06:43 KST

A new study claims that individuals possessing higher levels of the personality trait openness are less prone to antisemitic attitudes, and that this relationship is partially mediated by interpersonal contact with Jewish individuals. This is based on research published in the August issue of Personality and Individual Differences.
Talia Morstead and Anita DeLongis from the Department of Psychology at the University of British Columbia conducted the study. The researchers set out to explore the psychosocial mechanisms underlying antisemitic attitudes, noting that “antisemitism is an enduring phenomenon with parallels to other forms of prejudice yet demonstrates a distinctive capacity to adapt in rhetorical form to the prevailing sociocultural context."
According to the authors, while previous literature has established a clear link between personality traits and prejudice, “compared to work examining effects of intergroup contact, the role that individual differences play in the propensity to seek out contact is under-examined.”
The study was prompted by the need to identify “potential intervention targets that are contextually enduring and less tied to the prevailing socio-cultural climate,” particularly in the context where “recent years have witnessed surges in antisemitic incidents across Western democracies.”
To test their hypotheses, the researchers utilized data from non-Jewish individuals collected as part of the Understanding America Study, which is an internet-based probability panel study administered by the Center for Economic and Social Research at the University of Southern California.
Interpersonal contact accounts for 25% of effect between openness, antisemitism
The analyzed dataset included 1,442 non-Jewish participants from a nationally representative sample of Americans.
Openness was assessed using 10 items from the Big Five Inventory, while antisemitic attitudes were measured using an 11-item scale developed by the Anti-Defamation League (ADL) to “quantify global acceptance of antisemitism.”
Interpersonal contact with Jewish individuals was measured by asking participants how often they interact with Jewish people, with responses coded on a scale from one to six.
The researchers performed causal mediation analyses while controlling for demographic covariates including age, gender, political orientation, education, and household income.
According to the results, openness positively predicted Jewish contact and negatively predicted antisemitic attitudes.
The mediation analysis indicated that interpersonal contact with Jewish individuals partially mediated the relationship between openness and antisemitic attitudes, accounting for “approximately 25% of the total effect.”
Additional pathways for antisemitism exist independent of contact with Jews
The authors noted that a significant direct effect of openness on antisemitic attitudes remained even when controlling for Jewish contact, pointing to “additional pathways beyond interpersonal contact through which openness might contribute to reduced antisemitic attitudes.”
In their discussion specifically addressing the challenge of fighting antisemitism, the authors note that because antisemitism features a “uniquely conspiratorial nature” that makes it “often resistant to change through educational interventions or appeals to reason,” behavioral approaches are vital.
They highlight that “interpersonal contact predicted reduced antisemitic attitudes,” which “highlights the potential value of behavioral intervention approaches” as alternatives or complements to traditional education.
Furthermore, the researchers point out that contact interventions have “proven effective in reducing endorsement of antisemitic conspiracies.”
However, the authors also acknowledge methodological limitations, including the cross-sectional nature of the data, which “precludes examination of causality, including whether the assumptions of temporal ordering hold.”

Google Maps has changed the name of "Lake Ontario" to "Lake America" for US users to reflect US President Donald Trump's executive order renaming the lake, according to a Google statement.
Trump announced on Thursday that he was changing the name of the smallest of the five Great Lakes, part of an escalating trade feud with Canada that has prompted the two countries to impose reciprocal tariffs on billions of dollars in goods.
The president's order affects the US Geographic Names Information System (GNIS), which sets the standards for official US maps. It does not have any impact on Canadian naming conventions or how the rest of the world refers to the lake.
Canadian users will continue to see lake labeled as 'Lake Ontario'
"Since we update Google Maps to reflect name changes in official government sources, which is GNIS for the US, people using Maps in the US will see 'Lake America,' those in Canada will continue to see 'Lake Ontario,' and those outside of the US and Canada will see both names," Google said in a blog post issued on Saturday.
The White House, Carney's office and Ford's office did not immediately comment on Sunday on Google's decision.
Google Maps made a similar change to the Gulf of Mexico last year, labeling it the "Gulf of America" following Trump's executive order on his first day in office renaming the body of water.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney immediately rejected the lake's name change on Thursday. Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul of New York, which shares a long border with Canada, declared that "New York won't be calling it that," while Phil Scott, the Republican governor of neighboring Vermont, called Trump's decision "petty and disappointing" on social media.
The premier of Ontario, Doug Ford, on Saturday unveiled a large lakeside sign that reads, "Lake Ontario: Now and Always," in both English and French.
"President Trump can call it whatever he wants, but I can tell you, the rest of the world will always call it Lake Ontario," Ford said.

This strange “spacetime crystal” can suddenly become a black hole
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:05:09 UTC
00:05:09 KST

This strange “spacetime crystal” can suddenly become a black hole
A strange crystal like state of spacetime could transform into a microscopic black hole, and physicists have finally found a way to describe the process mathematically.
- Date:
- August 30, 2026
- Source:
- Vienna University of Technology
- Summary:
- Physicists have mathematically captured a bizarre “spacetime crystal” that can either dissolve or collapse into a microscopic black hole after only a tiny change in energy. Their breakthrough came from an unusual trick involving infinitely many dimensions, potentially giving researchers a new tool for studying primordial and microscopic black holes.
- Share:
Physics allows for black holes far smaller than the enormous objects typically found at the centers of galaxies or created when massive stars collapse. Under the right conditions, microscopic black holes could also form when spacetime enters an unusual critical state and organizes into a repeating, crystal-like pattern.
Researchers from Goethe University Frankfurt and TU Wien have now found a way to describe this process mathematically. For the first time, they derived an exact formula for the phenomenon by using an unconventional mathematical approach.
Microscopic Black Holes and Critical Collapse
Most familiar black holes are associated with violent cosmic events, including the deaths of massive stars. In theory, however, there is no strict lower size limit. Extremely small black holes could arise from special critical states in which even a tiny addition of energy can determine whether the system disperses or collapses.
Conditions like these may have existed in the early universe, shortly after the Big Bang, when matter and energy were packed into an intensely chaotic environment. Such circumstances could potentially have produced primordial black holes.
Computer simulations had already shown that these unusual critical structures should be possible. The challenge was finding a mathematical description that could reproduce what the simulations revealed. Researchers at Goethe University Frankfurt and TU Wien have now done that with a formula that can be worked out analytically, using what the scientists describe as essentially paper and pencil.
How a Tiny Change Can Trigger Collapse
"Sometimes a tiny, seemingly insignificant cause is enough to trigger a huge and dramatic change," says Prof. Daniel Grumiller from TU Wien. "Take liquid water at zero degrees Celsius, for example. A very small change is enough to make the water freeze. The water molecules then spontaneously arrange themselves into a regular pattern and form an ice crystal."
Einstein's theory of relativity suggests that spacetime can undergo something conceptually similar. Matter influences the geometry of spacetime, and changes in the distribution of particles can therefore alter its curvature.
"We say that spacetime is curved by mass," explains Christian Ecker from the Institute for Theoretical Physics at Goethe University Frankfurt. "Large objects such as stars curve spacetime strongly -- for example, we can observe this when light rays are deflected by massive stars. But smaller masses also produce spacetime curvature, just to a lesser extent."
Under critical conditions, that curvature can arrange itself into a repeating pattern across space and time. The researchers describe the resulting structure as a kind of "spacetime crystal." The process that produces this finely balanced state is known as critical collapse.
"This spacetime crystal is a very peculiar and fascinating object," says Grumiller. "It is a kind of intermediate state, an unstable point that can evolve in two different directions. It may simply dissolve again, leaving behind ordinary spacetime filled with freely moving particles. But if a tiny amount of energy is added, the evolution takes a completely different path: the inconspicuous spacetime crystal turns into a black hole."
A Black Hole Prediction Dating Back to 1993
Computer simulations first indicated in 1993 that black holes could form spontaneously through this kind of critical behavior. Physicists have spent decades trying to reproduce the process with mathematical equations, but deriving the necessary formulas proved exceptionally difficult.
The Vienna and Frankfurt researchers found a way around the problem by changing the number of dimensions in which they performed the calculations.
"Our universe has four dimensions -- three dimensions of space and one dimension of time," explains Christian Ecker. "But in principle, nothing prevents us from writing down physical equations for a larger number of dimensions -- five dimensions, forty-two dimensions, or even infinitely many."
It might seem that adding dimensions would make an already difficult problem even more complicated. Surprisingly, the opposite can happen. The researchers found that certain complex calculations become much easier when the number of dimensions approaches infinity.
Solving Four-Dimensional Physics With Infinite Dimensions
The team first analyzes the problem in this hypothetical setting with infinitely many dimensions. Researchers can then investigate whether the resulting solution can be translated back toward a universe with fewer dimensions, including the four-dimensional spacetime in which we live.
This mathematical detour allowed the scientists to extract information about critical collapse that had previously been extremely difficult to obtain analytically.
"Our technique turns out to be remarkably stable. Depending on the desired precision, we can systematically improve our formulas using additional approximation methods," says Florian Ecker from TU Wien. "This gives us a new method for studying black-hole-related phenomena that could previously not be analyzed analytically."
The approach could give physicists a new way to study black hole formation and other extreme behaviors of spacetime without relying entirely on numerical computer simulations.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Vienna University of Technology. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Christian Ecker, Florian Ecker, Daniel Grumiller. Analytic Discrete Self-Similar Solutions of Einstein-Klein-Gordon at Large D. Physical Review Letters, 2026; 136 (19) DOI: 10.1103/qgl5-5l3t

Kyiv • UNN

Details

“My beautiful, kind, intelligent, trusting daughter had the misfortune of stumbling across a link in a Discord server that led her to your evil and cruel group.
“The grooming of her started immediately, and what followed was unimaginably harrowing and traumatic. You were just one of the group members who abused her, who made her do things that no young person should ever be made to do.”
These are the words that came to an Australian mother, Olivia*, as Kyle Spitze was sentenced to 77 years in prison this month in Tennessee – the longest federal sentence yet imposed on what the US government has called a “nihilistic violent extremist”.
Spitze, 27, pleaded guilty to abetting the distribution of animal crushing videos and child sexual exploitation material (CSAM) offences, with victims around the world – some who have still not been identified. His lawyer said he plans to appeal the sentence.
The US Department of Justice said Spitze’s crimes occurred as part of his association with an online network known as “764”, known for its sadistic extortion of young and vulnerable people around the world.
Olivia told the Guardian the early days after she discovered her child’s abuse by these networks were terrifying.
“I had no idea what was happening or what to do, so I just focused on trying to keep my child as physically safe as possible while I tried to figure out what to do next,” she said
The platforms where her daughter had interacted with this network were not the “dark web”. They were apps like Discord, Telegram, Instagram and Snapchat. At the time, local police did not seem able to assist because the offenders were overseas.
Years later, she could not believe it when she heard Spitze had received such a long sentence.
“Pretty soon the tears started as I was flooded with relief, but also as I reflected on how long and hard we’d fought to get to this point,” she said.
Normalising explicit material
In December 2023, the chat platform Discord sent the FBI a 29-page report with a list of accounts it said were involved in “high harm activities”.
The users were, in Discord’s words, engaged in “sextortion, solicitation of minors to perform online sexual acts, self-harm coercion, swatting and conspiring to commit real world acts of violence”. Swatting is when someone calls in a fake threat to provoke an armed police response.
One username was “CRIMINALOLI”, prosecutors said. This was Spitze, then in his early 20s. Earlier that year, others had also sent tips to police alleging he was “grooming minors”.
Police found a video on a Telegram channel he ran that showed minor girls exposing their breasts and bodies, with his moniker sometimes “written in blood or carved on their bodies”.
He demanded one girl kill animals on video. If she hesitated, according to the prosecution, he threatened to dox and swat her and her parents. She was 12 when they met online, and thought she was his girlfriend.
In May, his father was sentenced to nearly six years’ imprisonment for attempted tampering with a victim, including asking her to destroy any evidence. Michael Spitze called the victim, 15, and told her to set up an account to speak to his son in prison, which she did out of fear. Kyle Spitze then called her 51 times.
In court documents, the prosecutor said 764 and similar groups “work in concert” to normalise explicit material to minors and “groom them towards future violence”, creating video records of victims: “Ultimately, these videos are placed on the network servers to gain notoriety and spread fear.”
According to Discord, the company has shared insights about these “harm groups” to law enforcement since it became aware of their activity in 2021.
“Discord is continuing to invest in new ways of detecting these groups, including if they attempt to return to Discord after being removed,” the company said.
Grooming manuals
About one year before authorities received tips about Spitze, in June 2022, a teenager in Australia sent an email to police in Inglewood, California.
The thread was disturbing. She alleged that a man called Dong Hwan Kim had sent her explicit messages, according to the criminal complaint, urging her to show him her body on camera. She said he threatened to send photos and videos of her to her father and even to her work if she did not show him naked imagery again.
The tip-off was one of several that led to a police investigation, and in April, Kim, who was 27 when he was arrested, pleaded guilty to two counts of producing child sexual exploitation material. He is yet to be sentenced. His lawyer did not respond to a request for comment.
The government says in court records that Kim’s crimes also occurred as part of his association with 764, and that he and his associates ran multiple online forums in which they “enticed, persuaded, and coerced minors” into creating CSAM.
Both US cases, and others currently before the courts, demonstrate the complex global nature of these crimes, with victims and perpetrators spread across borders. There have been a spate of global arrests but these groups and their propaganda continue to spread and change.
Groups such as 764 are understood to be part of the Com – the term for a broad online network that engages in cybercrime, extortion and violence.
This network does not have a traditional organised crime structure; it is decentralised and very fluid. “The other primary difference is that predominantly it involves young people, both as perpetrators and victims,” said AFP cybercrime commander Graeme Marshall.
Sadistic online exploitation as part of these groups can be driven by “gamification”, as well as a means to build status and notoriety. It is this type of Com activity that the AFP observes most often in Australia, although the scale is unclear.
The typical perpetrator, according to the AFP, is a young white male aged between 11 and their early 20s. The victim will often be a young woman in a similar age bracket.
The Guardian has seen Telegram channels that claim to be new iterations of 764, as well as manuals that provide guidance about how to groom and extort young people and where to store files. Court records suggest “content” is often traded, and allegedly used as means of entry to certain closed online spaces.
Marshall said the AFP has worked to increase awareness of the Com from local police, who need to know what questions to ask – and from parents and caregivers, who need to be aware of the warning signs.
“I still find it hard to believe that kids as young as 13 are even involved in these criminal groups, let alone perpetrating crimes,” Marshall said. “So, it’s completely understandable that parents, educators and health professionals would have that type of reaction as well. It is a broader education and awareness piece that is needed.”
Warning signs
The conviction of Spitze and others in 764 and other extortion networks often came off the back of tips from victims, families and their friends, court records show.
Before Spitze was arrested, a video spread online of him being shot in the ear during an altercation with his mother’s partner. He even gave interviews about the incident on YouTube.
This was when Olivia was able to “put a face to the name”.
“I couldn’t believe that he’d exposed himself so publicly, and after that more and more people started speaking out on [social media] about who he really was and what he’d been doing to young girls,” she said.
Olivia believes there is increasing awareness about how serious these groups are “and how easily kids can accidentally end up in contact with a predator”.
Some of the potential warning signs she wants parents to look out for include: increased time on devices, as well as distress and anger if separated from those devices; a child becoming extra secretive or distrusting of those closest to them; self-harm; and, random gifts or deliveries.
Olivia said that in her experience, the most significant thing a parent can do to help a child in this situation is to not blame them and to help them feel safe. “It sounds simple, but unfortunately it’s something that a lot of parents struggle with,” she said.
Today she would tell Spitze that although he was just one of the group members who abused her daughter, this doesn’t absolve him of responsibility for the “wilful destruction of lives that [he] gleefully participated in”.
“We’re doing a lot better, but our lives are forever changed,” she said. “Life is still incredibly difficult most days.”

As a therapist, here’s why I sometimes advise couples to end their marriage | Nicholas Purcell
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:00:02 UTC
00:00:02 KST

I’ve killed every garden I’ve neglected, which is all of them: bring me a struggling houseplant and watch it die. But bring me a struggling marriage and I will sometimes encourage it back to life. Other times, when the conditions are right, by which I mean when something is wrong, I will kill it. Intentionally. Or, in more professional language, I will advise it to end. Not every plant gets to flower. Not every marriage should be saved.
I have come to realise that care and attention, the fundamentals that keep both plants and relationships alive, are absent from many marriages that survive anyway. I call them cactus marriages: alive, but I couldn’t tell you how.
Jess* and Pete* came to see me: they had raised their kids and always turned up for their jobs – at least with work someone writes down what is required of you. Neglect, it turns out, takes longer to kill a marriage than it does a garden. When couples remember how to be loving, the cactus thrives, and sometimes it even flowers, which surprises everyone, including me.
But not every struggling marriage I see is a neglected cactus. Sometimes the soil has gone sour. And sometimes the roots have been severed, intentionally, and no water reaches a severed root. From across the room, neglect and its harder cousins, soured and severed, look the same: quiet and unhappy. Up close, the difference is everything.
Sour soil looks like Diane* and Thomas*, married more than 30 years, whose fighting had become a script neither could stop performing. She raised her voice. He corrected her grammar. She brought up his breath. A trade economy where no one wins. There was no innocent party in that room.
Underneath, this is mechanical failure. Contempt has become the default; the repair cycle – the small, ordinary apologies healthy couples make without noticing – has broken down and nothing is ever absorbed. But sour soil can be sweetened. Good gardeners do it all the time.
This is the marriage I fight for because it so nearly wasn’t necessary; if only they had come in sooner, before the habit hardened into the marriage’s personality. Despite bitterness and distance, these marriages often contain two people who would each say they would be lost, not relieved, if the other walked out. And the honest news is that they are probably repairable if both are committed, and the equally honest news is that the window does not stay open for ever.
The severed root marriage is different. This marriage houses a person clinicians have names for: narcissist, abuser, controller, none of which quite closes over the thing itself: a way of being that depends on the other not fully having a self, let alone flourishing. These are the marriages you won’t see on TV shows like Couples Therapy: the erosion of a life that’s hard to capture on film. The soured marriage saddens me; this one disturbs me.
The marriage with two people behaving badly worries me less than the marriage with one person doing real harm. Here the question is not how to love better. It is when to leave.
An ordinary-looking couple came to me, Michael* and Liz*. It had begun small enough to mistake for love: his need to know where she was. He counted the seconds it took her to answer his texts. The tracking devices came next. Before long he was throwing her against walls, and worse. I challenged Michael privately: is your behaviour making your marriage more or less likely to last? His head turned to me, his breathing slowed and his eyes went black, the light stopped coming back out of them. I hesitate to use the word evil, but I’ve sat with it, there isn’t a better one. It is the look of someone who does not care whether you are alive, or whether they are the reason you stop being.
This is not a relationship with a problem, the relationship is the problem. This marriage’s continuation requires one person’s diminishment, one person’s harm. To stay is a form of self-erasure. For anyone inside one, couples therapy is the wrong tool entirely. When only one person is being hurt, calling it “our relationship issues” launders the harm, and can keep a person in danger for years while they wait to become a better communicator.
Almost everyone inside a marriage like this does the arithmetic and gets it wrong, not because they are foolish, but because the sums are rigged. The cost of leaving is concrete: money, housing, the children and even shame. The cost of staying is paid invisibly, in instalments of health and the self that keeps getting smaller. And the children, so often the reason given for staying, are there, absorbing what a husband is and what a wife is, and how one is allowed to treat the other.
So let me say it plainly, because this kind of marriage depends on it never being said plainly: some relationships must be left.
But leaving is not the same as safe. The part people rush past, because it’s frightening to hear: the time around leaving is often when this kind of partner is most dangerous. Which is exactly when you need a safety plan, a domestic violence service, a friend or counsellor who knows the whole truth, not the version that’s easiest to say out loud.
Liz left Michael. She survived. He repartnered.
Sometimes I advise couples to end their marriage.
*All clients are fictional amalgams
In Australia, support is available at Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, Lifeline on 13 11 14, and at MensLine on 1300 789 978. The Domestic Violence hotline is 1800 RESPECT. In the UK, the charity Mind is available on 0300 123 3393 and Childline on 0800 1111. In the US, call or text Mental Health America at 988 or chat 988lifeline.org

Israelis still believe in unity - now they need to elect leaders who do, too - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

At first glance, the latest Israeli Society Barometer offers an encouraging picture. Nearly three-quarters of Israelis (73%) believe that Israel can be a cohesive society despite the divisions within it. This is the highest figure recorded since the Center for Jewish Impact began conducting the barometer in 2024, and a notable increase from 67% in February.
After years of political turmoil, the trauma of following the October 7 massacre and a prolonged multi-front war, Israelis have not given up on the possibility of a shared future.
However, beneath this optimism lies a warning that must not be ignored. Israelis may believe in cohesion as a national ideal, yet they are far less confident that the country’s different communities can actually live together.
Only 64% believe that secular and haredi (ultra-Orthodox) Jews can coexist in Israel. More troublingly, just 42% currently believe in Jewish-Arab coexistence. The differences between communities are stark. While 74% of Arab respondents and 48% of secular Jews believe Jewish-Arab coexistence is possible, only 7% of religious and haredi respondents share that view.
These figures do not mean that Israel is destined to fragment. On the contrary, the broad belief in the possibility of national cohesion provides a foundation on which to build.
Nonetheless, they demonstrate the distance between supporting unity in principle and trusting one another in practice.
Ahead of Israel’s fateful elections in October, it is clear that national cohesion cannot remain a slogan reserved for campaigns or moments of emergency. It must be translated into sustained engagement between communities that too often encounter one another through political arguments, social media or stereotypes.
Israel needs spaces in which Jewish and Arab citizens – across all religious backgrounds – can meet around shared responsibilities and common interests. Education, national or civic service, employment, local government and civil society can all become arenas for cooperation rather than competition. This does not require communities to abandon their identities or disagreements.
A cohesive society is not one in which everyone thinks alike. It is one in which differences do not prevent people from recognizing a common destiny.
The barometer also reveals that Israel’s internal crisis of confidence is being compounded by a serious failure abroad.
Although 64% of Israelis consider the strategic relationship with the US to be strong, only 23% believe Israel effectively communicates its policies and positions internationally fully, and 70% regard Israeli public diplomacy as ineffective.
This is not merely a matter of Israel receiving unfavorable media coverage. It is now affecting the daily lives and personal decisions of Israelis. More than half, 52%, report some level of concern about identifying as Israeli while traveling abroad. Since October 7, 2023, 41% have changed their behavior overseas, including altering destinations, canceling trips, or avoiding certain activities.
When Israelis feel compelled to hide their nationality, the problem is no longer abstract. It represents a profound deterioration in the environment surrounding Israel and the Jewish people.
The response cannot consist solely of better slogans, faster reactions, or additional social media content.
Israel needs a strategy for international communication
Israel needs what the public itself is demanding: a long-term national strategy for international communication. One-third of respondents identified such a strategy as the most important measure needed to improve Israel’s global standing, while another 25% pointed to changes in government policy and decision-making.
We need to strengthen our ties with our allies who know us, even if they do not necessarily voice strong opinions or wield significant influence. Just as there were volunteers in the 1960s and 1970s whose positive impact is evident today, we now have individuals, whether foreign workers, Christian volunteers, or people in the hi-tech industry working with Israelis, who will return to their home countries and serve as our ambassadors.
Nevertheless, public diplomacy cannot compensate for poor policy, but even necessary and defensible policies will lose international support if they are not explained within a coherent strategic framework.
Israel must invest in research, professional communication, credible international partnerships and engagement with audiences beyond its existing supporters. It must explain not only what it does, but who Israelis are, what Israel stands for and why its security and future matter to the democratic world.
This effort must be closely connected to Israel’s relationship with global Jewry. Seventy percent of Israelis believe the state should invest resources in Diaspora Jewish communities. Their priorities include encouraging aliyah, protecting Jewish communities and supporting civil society organizations.
That finding reflects an important truth. Israel and the Diaspora are not separate constituencies connected only by sentiment. They are part of a single, interdependent people. Antisemitism abroad affects Israel, just as Israel’s policies and international standing affect Jewish communities worldwide.
Strengthening Jewish security, identity and resilience must therefore be treated as a strategic national interest, including smaller communities, particularly those in countries with modern Islamic societies.
None of this can be separated from the economic and security concerns facing Israeli families. The public’s leading priority for the next government is reducing the cost of living and strengthening the economy, selected by 38% of respondents. National security follows at 25%, while 13% prioritize unity and bridging social divisions and 11% the IDF enlistment crisis.
These issues are interconnected. Economic hardship deepens social resentment. Unequal obligations weaken solidarity. Internal division damages national resilience, while diplomatic isolation threatens both security and prosperity.
The barometer does not describe a society that has lost hope. It describes a society that still believes in itself but is increasingly impatient for leadership equal to its challenges.
Israelis have demonstrated extraordinary courage and mutual responsibility during the most difficult period in recent memory. The task now is to transform the solidarity shown in moments of crisis into a permanent national strategy.
This must be front and center for any incoming government after the elections.
The choice is not between unity and disagreement, nor between Israel’s domestic resilience and its global standing; we must strengthen both.
Israel must build trust among its citizens, renew its partnership with world Jewry and explain its purpose to the world with confidence, professionalism and moral clarity.
The Israeli public still believes that a cohesive society is possible. That belief is a precious national asset, but it is not guaranteed to endure.
We must act before optimism becomes exhaustion and distance becomes division. Israel’s future will be secured not simply by defeating its enemies, but by ensuring that its citizens, its global Jewish family and its friends around the world understand what holds us together and why that bond is worth defending.
The writer is the chairman of the Center for Jewish Impact and a former CEO of the World Jewish Congress and World ORT.
