‘Pakistan's port capacity, an advantage for Iran's trade with East Asia’
TEHRAN- The Head of Iran's Trade Promotion Organization (TPO) described the visit of a Pakistani delegation to Iran—aimed at holding a bilateral meeting and following up on the approvals of the 10th Joint Trade Committee—as the beginning of a brilliant era in the development of economic and trade cooperation between the two countries, and emphasized the need for a long-term perspective on Tehran-Islamabad relations.
According to the TPO Public Relations Department, a bilateral meeting to follow up on the approvals of the 10th Joint Trade Committee was held with the delegation from Pakistan's Ministry of Maritime Affairs at the Isfahan Hall of the Tehran Permanent International Fairgrounds. The meeting was attended by Mohammad-Ali Dehghan Dehnavi, Head of the Trade Promotion Organization, along with TPO deputies and managers, as well as Shahid Ahmed, Chairman of the Karachi Port Trust, and a number of high-ranking representatives from Pakistan's Ministry of Maritime Affairs.
At the start of the meeting, Dehghan Dehnavi emphasized the need to chart a long-term vision for Iran-Pakistan trade, stating: "This meeting should go beyond technical and short-term issues and pursue all matters with a long-term horizon, keeping in view the 10-billion-dollar trade target agreed upon by the leaders of the two countries."
The Head of TPO stressed the necessity of developing shipping lines and land transport between the two countries and said: "In the past, Pakistani goods were transported to Iran through third countries. In line with the long-term vision, direct routes between the two countries should be established and strengthened."
Dehghan Dehnavi spoke of Iran's willingness to diversify its foreign trade routes and make greater use of Pakistan's capacity, and clarified: "Achieving this goal requires the development of cooperation in transport infrastructure and ports."
He also referred to Iran's considerable volume of trade with East Asia, particularly China, and said: "Pakistan's port capacity and transport routes can be utilized to transfer a portion of these goods to Iran via sea and land routes."

The Head of TPO concluded by recalling that the approvals of the 10th Joint Trade Committee—held in Islamabad with the presence of the Minister of Industry, Mining and Trade—can pave the way for the development of trade cooperation between the two countries.

Germany news: Politicians call for ban on radical AfD state branches

Germany: Merz warns of 'problems' in Saxony-Anhalt under AfD
Published August 29, 2026last updated August 30, 2026
What you need to know
- Merz predicts 'significant problems' for Saxony-Anhalt under AfD
- Merkel calls on Germans to 'fight for this democracy'
- German politicians call for ban on radical AfD state branches
Here is a roundup of top stories from and about Germany on Saturday, August 29, and Sunday, August 30.
Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add DW as a Preferred Source on Google.
Gamescom attendance comes close to record high
The international video games trade fair Gamescom came to a close in the western German city of Cologne on Sunday after being attended by an almost record number of visitors.
Around 368,000 gamers attended the event, 11,000 more than in 2025 and 33,000 more than in 2024. The record attendance of 373,000 set in 2019 wasn't quite reached — but Gamescom is getting closer.
Digital reach was once again substantial, with various online formats recording 624 million views worldwide — roughly the same number as before. On the ground in the sprawling halls of Cologne's trade fair, there were 1,743 physical exhibitions — a significant increase on last year (1,568).
"Gamescom has solidified its position as the biggest event in the gaming world," said Felix Falk, Managing Director of the industry association Game.
"At the same time, the unique atmosphere and enthusiasm on site demonstrated how games forge a strong, creative, and diverse community out of people from all walks of life," he added.
Merz: Germany to respond to hybrid threats 'in coming days'
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has said that Germany will respond to Russian hybrid threats in the coming week — in coordination with international allies.
"We're largely in agreement within the government as to how to react and we will make this known in the coming days," he told public broadcaster ARD as part of Sunday's summer interview.
The Chancellor's remarks come following the recent drone attack on Leipzig/Halle Airport. While an explosive-laden drone failed to detonate on August 5, the incident has put Germany's security and defense infrastructure in the spotlight.
Asked whether Germany was in any position to respond to such threats in an appropriate manner, Merz responded: "Let's wait and see what we mean by an appropriate response."
Either way, he continued, any German response will be coordinated with allies. "Our European Union and NATO partners will not be surprised," he said.
Merz predicts 'significant problems' for Saxony-Anhalt under AfD
Election victory for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in Saxony-Anhalt next week would do serious damage to the eastern German state, according to Chancellor Friedrich Merz.
"Should it come to that, this state would face significant problems," Merz told public broadcaster ARD in his annual summer interview.
"I cannot imagine that international investors would want to be seen attending the first spades in the ground for new factories or businesses in Saxony-Anhalt alongside an AfD state premier," he said.
According to the latest polls ahead of next Sunday's vote, the AfD maintains a commanding lead with 40% — far ahead of Merz's conservative Christian Democratic Union (CDU) with 23%, the Left Party (13%), the Social Democrats (SPD) (9%) and the Greens (6%).
Merz said he would be appearing twice himself in Saxony-Anhalt over the coming week in order to convince undecided voters (which still make up a good 20% of the electorate, according to polls) not to vote for the far-right.
"We will do everything we can to prevent Saxony-Anhalt falling to extremists," he said, adding: "And that applies to the Left Party, too."
Asked how the CDU intended to form a coalition government in Saxony-Anhalt with such low ratings and while refusing to work with either the AfD or the Left Party, Merz said: "We will look at that once we have the results."
The current state premier, Sven Schulze (CDU), however, has expressed a willingness to form a coalition with the SPD, Greens and the Left Party.
Hockey: Germany's men retain World Cup title
Germany retained their men's field hockey World Cup title with a hard-fought 1-0 victory over Spain in Sunday's final in Wavre, Belgium. The triumph secured Germany's fourth World Cup crown, moving them level with Pakistan as the tournament's joint-record winners.
Michel Struthoff scored the decisive goal in the 44th minute, beating the Spanish goalkeeper to turn the ball into the net and give Germany the lead. Spain pushed for an equalizer, but Germany's disciplined defense held firm through the closing stages.
Goalkeeper Jean-Paul Danneberg was instrumental in preserving the advantage, making several crucial saves and keeping out all four of Spain's penalty corners. Germany, who are also the reigning European champions, absorbed increasing pressure late in the match to see out the victory.
The title adds to Germany's previous World Cup successes in 2002, 2006 and 2023. Argentina secured third place earlier on Sunday with a 2-1 win over co-hosts the Netherlands in the bronze-medal match.
Cologne-Mallorca Eurowings flight forced to land in Paris
A Eurowings plane was forced to make a landing in Paris on Saturday evening after steam was detected in the aircraft's galley, the airline said.
The Boeing 737 with 131 passengers on board was flying from the western German city of Cologne to the Spanish island of Mallorca.
The unscheduled landing at Charles de Gaulle Airport was made as a precaution and under "normal" flight priority status, according to Eurowings.
"The safety of the passengers and crew was at no time at risk," a Eurowings spokesman said on Sunday.
German politicians call for ban on radical AfD state branches
High-ranking German politicians have advocated for proceedings to ban the most radical regional branches of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party.
Defense Minister Boris Pistorius and Baden-Württemberg's state premier, Cem Özdemir, called for bans to be initiated swiftly in a joint guest op-ed in the newspaper Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung.
"We once again strongly urge that proceedings to ban the party be initiated as soon as possible, with a particular focus on the AfD's clearly ethno-nationalist state branches in Thuringia, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, and Brandenburg," Pistorius and Özdemir said.
Their comments come just days before the September 6 election in Saxony-Anhalt, where an AfD victory could result in a far-right party leading a German state government for the first time since the end of Nazi rule in 1945.
Pistorius and Özdemir argue that it is important to distinguish between different factions within the AfD.
The two politicians say that the party's more radical, ethnically based wing rejects the constitutional principle. In their view, this wing should be subject to legal scrutiny.
They refer to this faction of the AfD as "völkisch" — a German adjective derived from das Volk, meaning "the people." The völkisch movement was an ethno-nationalist movement and precursor to Nazism. Today, the AfD is often accused of holding völkisch views because its officials repeatedly distinguish between Germans with and without a history of migration.
However, Green Party lawmaker Irene Mihalic warned against a selective ban.
"I see a risk that the idea might eventually take hold that there is an unconstitutional part of the AfD and a constitutional one," she told the Handelsblatt newspaper. "In my view, it is now clear that the entire AfD is at odds with our democratic constitution."
British woman stabbed to death at railway station in Bavaria
A British woman was stabbed to death overnight at a railway station in the southern German state of Bavaria, police said on Sunday.
The 31-year-old was taken to hospital but later died from her injuries.
Police reported that a 27-year-old German man was detained at the scene in Rosenheim — the third-largest city in Upper Bavaria after Munich and Ingolstadt.
Authorities are investigating the circumstances and motive behind the attack and have appealed for witnesses to come forward.
WATCH: AfD and the battle for young voters
For the first time since the end of World War II, a far-right politician could become a state premier in Germany.
In Saxony-Anhalt, the Alternative for Germany (AfD) party is well ahead of the other parties, with its lead candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, especially popular among young voters.
Siegmund presents himself as a fresh and positive figure who wants to "get Germany back on its feet."
We speak to young people in Saxony-Anhalt to find out what they like about Siegmund and the AfD.
To what extent are young people being politicized by the right? Or are they simply disillusioned with the established parties?
Three Germans among those missing in Nepal-Tibet flood, China says
Three Germans are among those missing following Wednesday's flash flood in the Himalayan border region between Nepal and China, Chinese authorities said on Sunday.
A total of 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were unaccounted for.
Those missing include:
- 
	104 people from Nepal
- 
	49 from India
- 
	33 from Latvia
- 
	18 from the United States
- 
	15 from Britain and several dozen from other countries
"Chinese authorities have notified the respective embassies and consulates of these countries in China," state media CCTV said, citing officials.
The Nepal Tourism Board, however, said eight Germans are missing. It is unclear if the three German nationals reported as unaccounted for by Chinese authorities are included in the number reported by Nepal.
The Foreign Office in Berlin has said "a high single-digit number of German nationals" are missing in the devastating flood.
On Sunday, the combined death toll rose to 750, with more than 3,000 people still missing, local authorities said.
Several scientists believe a glacier collapse high in the Himalayas on Wednesday may have triggered a tsunami-like wall of water which swept away entire villages in the Himalayan region.
Merkel calls on Germans to 'fight for this democracy'
Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel has called on her compatriots to "stand up" for democracy ahead of next weekend's state election in Saxony-Anhalt.
The far-right Alternative for Germany party (AfD) is leading polls raising questions about what kind of government will be formed.
Despite this, the majority of Germans are not AfD voters, Merkel said at a political event in Berlin on Saturday night.
"I believe that now, once again — something we haven't had to do for many decades — we must really fight for this democracy, simply stand up for it, be a little brave, stand by our word and say that this is a wonderful way to live," she said.
Merkel said the AfD had, to some extent, managed to "dominate all our discussions from morning to night" about politics in Saxony-Anhalt. This meant that many voters no longer knew the policies of the other parties, she said.
But while the AfD has long polled strongest in the eastern states, Merkel — who herself hails from the former East Germany — said the rise of the AfD was not limited to those areas.
"It has become a pan-German phenomenon," she said.
German government expected to hold Moscow responsible for Leipzig drone incident, reports say
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government plans to officially hold Moscow responsible for the Leipzig drone incident in early August, several German news outlets owned by media company Axel Springer SE reported on Saturday.
Berlin is expected to announce the planned move in the coming days, including "extensive" sanctions, three officials familiar with the matter told German newspaper Welt am Sonntag and the media outlet Politico.
However, the three sources did not elaborate on what the specific measures could be. It is also unclear to what extent Berlin plans to hold Russia responsible for the Leipzig incident.
On August 4, a drone loaded with explosives was discovered near Ukrainian cargo planes at Leipzig/Halle Airport, which serves as a hub for military aid shipments to Ukraine for its war against Russia.
Merz told RTL in an interview on Thursday that the federal government would soon identify those responsible for the incident.
Sick leave now costs Germany twice as much as in 2010
The total amount of wages German firms paid in sick and maternity leave has more than doubled over the past 15 years, a study from the Cologne-based German Economic Institute (IW) shows.
IW estimated that German companies paid a record-high €85.6 billion ($111 billion) in wages to employees who were out sick last year. This compares to €36.9 billion in 2010.
Of the larger figure, €72.5 billion represented gross wages, while €13.1 billion was earmarked for social security contributions.
IW said several factors have contributed to the rise, including wage hikes and inflation in other employee costs.
The institute said the total number of employed people has also grown since 2010, meaning more workers are eligible for sick leave.
IW, however, said it had noted a "significant" rise in recorded sick leave since Germany moved to electronic medical certificates in 2022.
Separate research by the Berlin-based IGES Institute in January showed that German workers now take an average of 19.5 working days as sick leave per year, a noticeable increase from about 13 days in 2018.
In an effort to stem the rise, Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government will from January ban patients from receiving sick notes from doctors by phone.
In Germany, employers are generally required to pay workers' salaries for up to six weeks before the statutory health insurance fund takes over by paying sickness benefits.
Lower Saxony premier seeks deal on VW restructuring
Volkswagen's second-biggest shareholder has called on all sides to agree on a restructuring plan for the German auto giant in the next few days.
Olaf Lies, state premier of Lower Saxony — which holds 18% of VW's shareholder voting rights — said he was convinced "a viable solution" can be found.
"I strongly urge that we use the time remaining until the next meeting to bring the different positions together," Lies told journalists on Friday.
The state leader noted that VW must face its numerous business challenges head-on, namely costly tariffs, falling demand and intense competition from China.
But he said the group's position in Germany's industrial landscape also had to be considered.
"With its sites in Lower Saxony and across Germany, its tens of thousands of employees and their families, and its suppliers and service providers, Volkswagen also bears an enormous responsibility for the wider economy and society," Lies said.
VW's management now thinks they may need to cut up to 100,000 jobs and that several German factories may face closure.
The supervisory board of Europe's largest automaker is due to meet on September 4 to discuss a turnaround plan.
Survey: Trump's return increased US influence over Germany
Two-thirds of residents think the United States has more influence on Germany since US President Donald Trump returned to the White House.
A poll by the Forsa research institute found that 67% of respondents agreed, while just 11% thought there was less US influence. Around 18% thought it was the same.
The survey for the German-language Internationale Politik (International Politics) magazine found only 2% of 18 to 29-year-olds and 6% of 30 to 44-year-olds think US influence in Germany is lower than before Trump's second term. That's versus 18% of respondents aged 60 and over.
Germany-US ties have soured since Trump's reelection, due to surprise tariffs, talk of seizing Greenland and open sniping over Russia's war in Ukraine and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz during the Iran war.
Report: Taliban team in Berlin to aid Afghan deportations
The Taliban has sent a team of three people to Germany to help facilitate the deportation of Afghan nationals, public broadcaster NDR reported.
NDR said the delegation arrived in Germany on Wednesday and is staying at the Afghan embassy in Berlin.
The broadcaster said their mission is to provide documents recognized by the Taliban in Kabul to Afghan nationals being deported from Germany.
The delegation is also due to spend time in Bonn and Munich, where Afghanistan has consulates general.
The arrival of the delegation is contentious as Germany — along with most of the rest of the world — does not recognize the Taliban government.
Chancellor Friedrich Merz calls the contacts a purely technical necessity to return people with no right to stay.
Critics, however, say his government is legitimizing the Taliban to help raise deportation numbers.
Germany suspended deportations to Afghanistan when the Taliban returned to power in 2021.
They resumed three years later, initially for convicted criminals.
According to German government data, 15,343 Afghan nationals in Germany are required to leave the country, as of the end of June, including more than 1,500 children.

Hundreds of hidden earthquakes found at Antarctica’s Doomsday Glacier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
13:07:17 UTC
22:07:17 KST

Hundreds of hidden earthquakes found at Antarctica’s Doomsday Glacier
- Date:
- August 30, 2026
- Source:
- The Conversation
- Summary:
- Hundreds of previously overlooked seismic events have been detected beneath Antarctica, including 245 near the marine edge of the Thwaites Glacier. Many appear to be glacial earthquakes caused when huge icebergs break off, capsize, and collide with the glacier. The surge in activity coincided with a period when Thwaites was flowing faster toward the ocean, hinting that changing ocean conditions may be destabilizing the ice.
- Share:
Glacial earthquakes are a special type of earthquake generated in cold, icy regions. First discovered in the northern hemisphere more than 20 years ago, these quakes occur when huge chunks of ice fall from glaciers into the sea.
Until now, only a very few have been found in the Antarctic. In a study published in Geophysical Research Letters, I present evidence for hundreds of these quakes in Antarctica between 2010 and 2023, mostly at the ocean end of the Thwaites Glacier – the so-called Doomsday Glacier that could send sea levels rising rapidly if it were to collapse.
A recent discovery
A glacial earthquake is created when tall, thin icebergs fall off the end of a glacier into the ocean.
When these icebergs capsize, they clash violently with the “mother” glacier. The clash generates strong mechanical ground vibrations, or seismic waves, that propagate thousands of kilometres from the origin.
What makes glacial earthquakes unique is that they do not generate any high-frequency seismic waves. These waves play a vital role in the detection and location of typical seismic sources, such as earthquakes, volcanoes and nuclear explosions.
Due to this difference, glacial earthquakes were only discovered relatively recently, despite other seismic sources having been documented routinely for several decades.
Varying with the seasons
Most glacial earthquakes detected so far have been located near the ends of glaciers in Greenland, the largest ice cap in the northern hemisphere.
The Greenland glacial earthquakes are relatively large in magnitude. The largest ones are similar in size to those caused by nuclear tests conducted by North Korea in the past two decades. As such, they have been detected by a high-quality, continuously operating seismic monitoring network worldwide.
The Greenland events vary with the seasons, occurring more often in late summer. They have also become more common in recent decades. The signs may be associated with a faster rate of global warming in the polar regions.
Elusive evidence
Although Antarctica is the largest ice sheet on Earth, direct evidence of glacial earthquakes caused by capsizing icebergs there has been elusive. Most previous attempts to detect Antarctic glacial earthquakes used the worldwide network of seismic detectors.
However, if Antarctic glacial earthquakes are of much lower magnitude than those in Greenland, the global network may not detect them.
In my new study, I used seismic stations in Antarctica itself to look for signs of these quakes. My search turned up more than 360 glacier seismic events, most of which are not yet included in any earthquake catalogue.
The events I detected were in two clusters, near Thwaites and Pine Island glaciers. These glaciers have been the largest sources of sea-level rise from Antarctica.
Earthquakes at the Doomsday Glacier
Thwaites Glacier is sometimes known as the Doomsday Glacier. If it were to collapse completely it would raise global sea levels by 3 metres, and it also has the potential to fall apart rapidly.
About two-thirds of the events I detected – 245 out of 362 – were located near the marine end of Thwaites. Most of these events are likely glacial earthquakes due to capsizing icebergs.
The strongest driver of such events does not appear to be the annual oscillation of warm air temperatures that drives the seasonal behaviour of Greenland glacier earthquakes.
Instead, the most prolific period of glacial earthquakes at Thwaites, between 2018 and 2020, coincides with a period of accelerated flow of the glacier’s ice tongue towards the sea. The ice-tongue speed-up period was independently confirmed by satellite observations.
This speed-up could have been caused by ocean conditions, the effect of which is not yet well understood.
The findings suggest the short-term scale impact of ocean states on the stability of marine-terminating glaciers. This is worth further exploration to assess the potential contribution of the glacier to future sea-level rise.
The second largest cluster of detections occurred near the Pine Island Glacier. However, these were consistently located 60–80 kilometres from the waterfront, so they are not likely to have been caused by capsizing icebergs.
These events remain puzzling and require follow-up research.
What’s next for Antarctic glacial earthquake research
The detection of glacial earthquakes associated with iceberg calving at Thwaites Glacier could help answer several important research questions. These include a fundamental question about the potential instability of the Thwaites Glacier due to the interaction of the ocean, ice and solid ground near where it meets the sea.
Better understanding may hold the key to resolving the current large uncertainty in the projected sea-level rise over the next couple of centuries.
Story Source:
Materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Thanh-Son Pham, ARC DECRA Fellow in Geophysics, Australian National University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Cite This Page:

Icelanders Reject Resuming EU Accession Talks - RUV
Kyiv • UNN
52.8% of Icelanders voted against resuming negotiations on joining the EU, while 47.2% supported the initiative. Reykjavík was the only region to vote "yes".
Iceland rejected the resumption of membership negotiations with the European Union in the referendum. This was reported by the public broadcaster RUV, according to UNN.
Details
The question on the ballot was: "Should Iceland resume negotiations on joining the European Union?" Some 47.2% voted in favor of resuming the negotiations, while 52.8% of Icelanders voted against. The difference was approximately 12,700 votes
According to RUV, the voting results are already known in all constituencies. The only region where a majority of voters supported the referendum was the country's capital, Reykjavík, reports Associated Press.
Context
On Saturday, August 29, Iceland's residents began voting on whether to resume membership negotiations with the European Union in a referendum testing the bloc's geopolitical appeal.
As of the morning of August 30, 50.4% had voted in favor of the referendum, while 49.6% voted against.
Earlier, 51.3% of Icelanders supported resuming negotiations on joining the EU.

Inside Kourou: how Europe's satellite is prepared to watch skies and prevent natural disasters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
13:05:17 UTC
22:05:17 KST

Engineers from ArianeGroup, Arianespace, CNES, Eumetsat, ESA and Thales Alenia Space describe, step by step, how an Ariane 6 rocket and a 3.8-tonne weather satellite were brought together to the launch pad at Europe's Spaceport.
After two flights and more than 7,000 kilometres from Paris, we have witnessed first-hand a launch that has put Europe at the forefront of global space technology: the placing in orbit of a state-of-the-art satellite that speeds up mapping of the Earth’s surface to monitor disasters and help prevent floods and fires from continuing to devastate countries across the Old Continent.
The heart of the Ariane 6 launch system is not on the pad, but in a windowless control room several kilometres away. That is where we are received by the deputy launch director, Frédéric, whose surname we are withholding to protect him from cyberattacks, and several engineers who walk us through the details of the milestone. The rocket that is about to place the new European weather satellite in orbit was built on a very specific premise: to be cheaper and more versatile than its predecessor, Ariane 5, in a far more competitive international environment than a decade ago.
The launcher: a rocket designed not to waste time in Kourou
The key, the engineers explain, lies in where each task is carried out. The Ariane 6 core stage is manufactured and fully tested in France; the upper stage in Germany. Both arrive in Guiana already "ready to fly", with no need for any further functional tests once they are unloaded from the Canopée. Transport is handled by the dedicated cargo ship Canopée, the same one with the large sails that made the shipping line famous, which also picks up parts in Bordeaux and Rotterdam before completing the route to South America.
The solid-fuel boosters that assist at lift-off, by contrast, are manufactured in French Guiana itself, at the Regulus and Europropulsion plants. "It is much more practical and convenient to manufacture the boosters here than to ship that type of propellant from Europe," the engineers sum up. Once all the pieces are on the ground, the ArianeGroup team needs only between seven and nine days to assemble the launcher’s central core and have it ready to fly.
"It is not like pulling up at a petrol station, filling the tank and driving off. Filling the launcher takes two hours, and then another hour and a half of thermal stabilisation, because the liquid oxygen is at about -150°C and the liquid hydrogen at -250°C," Frédéric tells us.
The MTG-I2 flight also featured two rare technical characteristics. It was the first time an Ariane 6 had flown to a geostationary transfer orbit (GTO), the most distant orbit reached by the rocket so far, in its A62 configuration with two side boosters. And, for the first time since the maiden flight, the mission had a launch window of two hours and 30 minutes instead of a fixed lift-off instant, giving the team some leeway to deal with unexpected issues.
The rocket’s upper stage, powered by the Vinci engine, can also be re-ignited in mid-flight thanks to a helium pressurisation system, which settles the propellant at the bottom of the tank before each re-ignition: a capability Ariane 5 did not have and which Ariane 6 is debuting on this type of mission.
The build: robots assembling a rocket horizontally
The rocket is assembled horizontally, not vertically. Guided vehicles move the lower and upper stages into a common position, where the two pieces are joined with a tolerance of barely a millimetre. "It is not a fully automatic process, it is assisted: there are many steps that the staff have to check and validate before triggering the next automatic sequence," the experts stress.
From the moment the two stages arrive in the facility, it takes around ten days until the central core is ready to be moved to the pad. The facility has two parallel assembly lines, which makes it possible to start putting together the next rocket as soon as the previous one heads out to the launch platform. The goal of the programme is to reach a cadence of nine to ten launches a year from 2027.
The satellite: the most sensitive passenger ever to fly on an Ariane 6
A few metres away, in the encapsulation building, the air is filtered, temperature-controlled and its humidity finely regulated. It is the last room where technicians have direct physical access to the satellite before it is sealed inside the rocket’s fairing. For MTG-I2, an optical meteorological observation instrument that is extremely sensitive to contamination, that cleanliness is not a minor detail: any particle can degrade the quality of its future images.
The process even includes a system of light traps for insects and birds: when the container with the satellite arrives at night and the gigantic doors of the building open to let it in, any animal that slips inside could jeopardise the cleanliness of the payload. "We cannot just open the container and let it out with a bird inside, obviously," explains one of the managers of the facility, who has spent almost a year coordinating this final stretch of the campaign with the spacecraft team.
The Júpiter control room: the chain of command for the countdown
Eleven hours before lift-off, the final timeline begins and the centre of gravity shifts to the Júpiter control room at CNES, the French National Centre for Space Studies. A large operational screen shows the status of all systems in green, the planned trajectory and the countdown clocks.
In the centre sits Maxime André, the launch operations director, responsible for coordinating safety across the entire launch range (people, assets, environment) and, together with the quality team and the measurements officer who monitors telemetry, radar and tracking, providing the final voice and eyes that give the go-ahead.
Right up to the last minute, the mission team remains in contact with the satellite’s own control centre, located some four kilometres from the Júpiter room, to confirm that everything remains nominal and pass that confirmation up, step by step, to the operations director.
Lightning veto: the weather that can stop a launch
A few metres from the launch complex, a small team is watching the sky as closely as the engineers watch the rocket. François Laforge, meteorological analyst at the spaceport’s station, keeps his eye on two parameters above all others: lightning and wind. "Rain or temperature are not so important; what really matters are thunderstorms and wind, both at the surface and at altitude."
The criteria are strict: no storm within a ten-kilometre radius around the base, either during preparations or during lift-off itself; and no cloud above 6,500 metres in that same radius, because as the rocket passes through such a high cloud it can generate static electricity capable of triggering lightning. To monitor this, the team combines radars that measure cloud height with a triangulation system of three antennas that pinpoint every electrical discharge in real time.
Weather balloons with radiosondes, launched several times during the countdown, measure the wind profile at altitude, data that Leonard Bouchaillot, flight safety engineer, uses together with the rest of the team to ensure safe conditions so that the pre-calculated "launch corridor" – the zone where, for safety, a possible flight termination of the rocket is simulated – remains valid.
This, he explains, is a requirement set out in French space law to guarantee public safety. The final weather check comes barely ten minutes before lift-off. Once in the air, the risk changes in nature: the rocket passes the speed of sound in under 50 seconds and 50 kilometres in altitude in under two minutes, so wind very quickly ceases to be a real threat. The real risk, they insist, lies on the ground.
A 6-billion-euro programme with benefits topping 61 billion
James Champion, head of the MTG project at the European Space Agency (ESA), set out the 16 years of work on the Meteosat satellite programme. It has meant almost two decades anticipating technology that did not yet exist but had to be factored in when placing MTG-I2 in orbit.
The cost of the programme in today’s economic conditions has been around 6 billion euros, while its benefits exceed 61 billion, once infrastructure is taken into account, not to mention the number of lives that will be saved thanks to satellite data helping, for example, to trigger evacuation plans. This family of satellites will be key to forecasting and preventing adverse weather events.
The science: a watchful hawk’s eye over Europe every 2.5 minutes
With the satellite just hours away from being placed in orbit, Cristian Bank, director of programme preparation and development at Eumetsat, sets the launch in its real context: that of a continent increasingly hit by extreme weather events. "In the past five years we have seen losses of 10 billion a year in damage in Europe and thousands of deaths. Fortunately, the number of fatalities is falling as our forecasts and warnings improve, but the damage to infrastructure remains. We need to be more resilient," he warns.
MTG-I2 is the third part of a complementary trio: the first satellite, launched in 2022, offers a hemispheric view – Europe, Africa, the Atlantic as far as the Indian Ocean – feeding global weather models; the second, launched in 2025 and almost operational, measures the atmosphere in depth (humidity, temperature, wind, pressure); and the third, whose launch we have just witnessed, will focus on Europe and in particular the Mediterranean basin, which is heavily affected by adverse weather events, updating its data every two and a half minutes.
"That frequency is crucial for local weather forecasting in Europe and the Mediterranean, but also for civil protection: firefighters detecting forest fires, droughts, or Mediterranean tornadoes, which are becoming more frequent and more violent.
Bank estimates that the new satellite will need around half a year of commissioning before it can be integrated and calibrated with its two siblings. From then on, probably around April 2027, the three will operate as a single system.
The technical specifications: 500 million pixels every ten minutes
Graeme Mason, head of meteorological programmes at ESA, laid out the figures that make MTG-I2 one of the most advanced observation instruments ever placed in orbit. While the first satellite in the family scans the entire visible Earth disc every ten minutes at a resolution of 500 metres – around 500 million pixels per full sweep, distributed across 16 channels – MTG-I2 will focus solely on the upper quadrant centred on Europe, repeating the scan every 150 seconds.
Its second instrument, the lightning detector, operates in a very narrow band of the spectrum, the oxygen emission line at 777 nanometres, taking 1,000 samples per second. To resolve features 500 metres across from an orbit 36,000 kilometres above the Earth, the satellite needs extreme stability across its three axes.
This programme is an example of the strength of the European aerospace industry: with more than 17 European countries and 70 companies involved; over 200 subcontracts; and more than 2,200 people working on the project.
"This image generator is the best geostationary 'imager' in the world. The lightning detector is the best 'lightning imager' in the world, a technology that is ahead even of that of the United States. In ten years, ESA expects to send the next family of satellites to continue leading the way in monitoring and analysing the climate and its impacts.
Between the Ariane 6 control room, the satellite encapsulation facility and the weather station that tracks every cloud over Kourou, the launch of MTG-I2 has in fact been the sum of dozens of technical decisions taken by teams that rarely share the spotlight with the lift-off itself.
With this satellite in orbit, Europe completes the first operational trio of its third-generation meteorological constellation, a system that is set to support climate monitoring of the continent at least until well into the 2040s.

Barrier lake above mudslide-hit Xizang port basically drained: ministry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:03:50 CST
22:03:50 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- The barrier lake above mudslide-hit Gyirong Port in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region has basically drained, forming a flowing state of the river channel, China's Ministry of Water Resources said Sunday, citing drone footage and panoramic images captured in the morning and reports from emergency response teams.
The barrier lake was formed by a fast-moving chain mudslide that struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border. The mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse on the Nepali side, has caused heavy casualties and left many missing.
The ministry said an impact crater upstream of the barrier lake still warrants attention. Located about 5.6 km upstream at an altitude of around 3,700 meters, the crater is roughly 800 meters higher than the barrier lake.
At 11:23 a.m. Sunday, the crater had a water surface area of about 108,000 square meters, down 19,000 square meters from 7 a.m., with a storage volume of about 1.4 million cubic meters.
Water was flowing out continuously about 180 meters downstream of the crater's dam, and three water accumulation areas within 2.5 km downstream had a combined surface area of less than 70,000 square meters.
The crater and the three downstream water accumulation areas still pose risk hazards and require continued monitoring, the ministry said.
A new barrier lake formed on Saturday about 2.8 km downstream of the previous one after a landslide on the Nepali side. The barrier dam has been breached by upstream water flow, forming a flowing state of the river channel, according to drone footage and panoramic images. ■

Czechia's Lukes claims men's gold at 2026 Modern Pentathlon World Championships
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
21:03:47 CST

GUIYANG, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- Czechia's Matej Lukes won the men's title at the 2026 Modern Pentathlon World Championships on Sunday, finishing with 1,586 points in the final in Guiyang, southwest China's Guizhou Province.
Lukes, 24, entered the final as the world No. 1 and improved on his bronze medal at last year's World Championships. He was followed by Russia's Egor Gromadskii with 1,581 points and South Korea's Seo Chang-wan with 1,576.
Speaking after the competition, Lukes said: "It's crazy feelings to win this gold. I am so happy, and we did maximum to be this place. We trained a lot and this is the end, so I'm so happy and proud of my team and myself too."
"It's super challenging for athletes, of course. But challenge is what we came for and what the fans want to see. My strategy is to be like the best in every discipline, like how can I manage it and to push maximum," he added.
Asked about the key to his strong performance and decisive comeback in the laser run, Lukes said: "It's like a one piece painted on. It's not like I'm even running fast as I can, I will swim fast as I can. It's like you must swim a little bit slower to run fast. So, this is the strategy. It is just like focus on the run in your tunnel, and don't look around or care about others. Just be focus on yourself."
Looking ahead, Lukes said qualifying for the Olympic Games was his main goal.
"The most important goal and the biggest goal for every pentathlete, it's Olympic Games especially. Next year, I will start to Olympic qualifications. So, I will do a lot of training for collecting the points to the Olympics in LA." Lukes said.
The 2026 World Championships were held in Guiyang from Aug. 24 to 30. ■

Iceland applied for EU membership in 2009. Accession talks were suspended in 2013 after a Eurosceptic government took office. However, according to Icelandic parliamentary documents, the European Commission has maintained that the application was never formally withdrawn.
After the rejection of the accession talks, Iceland's relationship with the EU would continue largely through the European Economic Area and Schengen frameworks. ■

Niger’s military-led government says it contained mutiny: What next?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
13:01:20 UTC
22:01:20 KST

Niger’s military-led government says it contained mutiny: What next?
The mutiny began at a military base in Niamey and spread near the presidential palace and state broadcaster.
In the latest turmoil to hit Niger in West Africa, the military-led government says it has contained a mutiny in the capital, Niamey, after hours of gunfire and explosions near key military and government sites.
A military base at Diori Hamani International Airport was first targeted on Saturday by renegade soldiers, followed by attacks on the state broadcaster and presidential palace.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Niger military says it is regaining control after attempted mutiny
- list 2 of 3Gunfire, blasts in Niamey as soldiers mutiny in Niger’s capital
- list 3 of 3Tuareg rebels free more Malian soldiers in prisoner swap, sources say
State TV said security forces gradually regained control, while dozens of rebel soldiers were reportedly killed or arrested.
The mutiny is another blow to Niger’s military leadership, which has failed to bring stability to the country since it took over in a coup three years ago. Since then, the military ruler and president, General Abdourahamane Tchiani, has pivoted the country away from the West, including its former colonial ruler, France.
He has forged close security ties with Russia in efforts to tackle the growing threat from armed groups, but that has not deterred fighters linked to al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS) from mounting attacks.
So what happened, who was behind the mutiny, and what does it mean for Niger’s military government?
What happened?
The attacks started shortly after midnight on Saturday at Base 101, a major military facility inside Niamey’s international airport complex previously used by United States forces.
General Salifou Mody, Niger’s defence minister, said a group of soldiers detained some of their comrades and opened fire at “certain sensitive sites” in the capital.
The fighting lasted for several hours, during which the state broadcaster was temporarily taken off air, while gunfire and explosions were reported around the airport and presidential palace.
Authorities said security forces responded quickly and helped regain control. The ruling military council, known as the National Council for the Safeguard of the Homeland, urged people to remain calm.
“Our Defence and Security Forces are mobilised for the Defence of the Fatherland. Let us remain united, vigilant and supportive,” it said.
By late Saturday, military authorities and state TV said the mutiny had been contained. Dozens of soldiers had been killed or arrested. Africa Corps, the Kremlin-backed force, received a request for assistance in neutralising the mutineers in the capital, said Viktor Voropaev, the Russian ambassador to Niger, in an interview with TASS news agency on Saturday.
Africa Corps is a Russian state-controlled paramilitary organisation established by the Russian Ministry of Defence, replacing and absorbing the African operations of the privately run Russian militia, the Wagner Group.
The whereabouts of military leader Tchiani have not been confirmed.
Base 101 houses the general staff of the unified force of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), which includes Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso. The AES was established in 2023 to combat armed rebellion in the Sahel region.
It also houses the headquarters of the Africa Corps, which supports Sahel states in combating armed groups.
Who were the renegade soldiers behind the mutiny?
The mutineers appear to have included young soldiers from areas outside Niamey, particularly the southwest of Niger.
Reuters news agency reported that the operation involved soldiers from Ouallam, Tera and Dosso, citing analysts and security officials. Troops from those areas have suffered heavy losses fighting armed groups, particularly the regional ISIL affiliate.
The exact size of the mutinous force, and who led the mutiny, was not immediately clear. But analysts said the involvement of front-line troops points to growing frustration within the military.
“These mass-casualty overrun attacks on the Nigerien military are becoming commonplace and will continue to fuel unrest and aggravate tensions within the army ranks,” said Heni Nsaibia, senior West Africa analyst at Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (ACLED).
Timeline of unrest in Niger
July 2023 – Niger’s military government seizes power in a coup, saying the elected government had failed to contain armed groups.
August 2023: Regional bloc the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) imposes sanctions and threatens military intervention; Tchiani proposes a three-year transition.
September 2023: Niger, Mali, and Burkina Faso establish the Alliance of Sahel States (AES). France agrees to withdraw its ambassador and 1,500 troops.
January 2024: Niger, Mali, and Burkina Faso announce their withdrawal from ECOWAS.
June 2024: An attack in western Niger kills 20 soldiers and a civilian, one of the deadliest assaults on the military since the coup.
September 2024: Niger suspends its military pact with the US. Washington subsequently withdraws its troops and closes its two bases – Air Base 101 in Niamey and Air Base 201 near the northern city of Agadez. Built at a cost of more than $100m, Air Base 201 was used for manned and drone surveillance flights and other operations in efforts to target ISIL fighters and Jama’at Nusrat al-Islam wal-Muslimin (JNIM), a regional affiliate of al-Qaeda.
October 2025: Kevin Rideout, a pilot with the evangelical missionary agency SIM International, is abducted in Niamey.
January 2026: ISIL claims responsibility for an attack on an air force base at Niger’s Diori Hamani International Airport and the adjoining military base in Niamey.
June 2026: An armed attack on Niamey airport kills 11 soldiers and two civilians.
August 29, 2026: Soldiers mutiny at Niamey’s Base 101, with gunfire around the airport, presidential palace and other sensitive sites.
Why is there unrest in Niger?
Niger’s military invoked increasing armed violence to seize power in the 2023 coup. It accused the elected government of failing to quash armed rebellion.
However, three years later, armed groups remain a major threat – fighters affiliated with al-Qaeda and ISIL have continued to carry out attacks.
The military-led government boosted its ties with Russia as Niger told France and the US to withdraw their forces. Niger has also joined Burkina Faso and Mali in the AES in order to put up a united fight against armed groups.
Nevertheless, the shift has not stopped unrest. The repeated attacks and heavy military casualties have fuelled frustration among front-line troops.
ACLED’s Nsaibia described the mutiny as a sign of a wider problem.
“Deteriorating insecurity drove the coups that swept across the central Sahel, and the latest events show how these same pressures are now fuelling unrest within the militaries that seized power,” he said.
What has been the response of the international community?
The AES expressed support for Niger’s military leadership, saying in a statement that the mutineers had been “contained and thwarted”, calling the mutiny a “betrayal by a group of soldiers involved in a destabilisation plot”.
It was unclear whether Mali or Burkina Faso provided direct military assistance to their ally.
Algeria condemned the events and expressed its “full solidarity and firm support” for Niger.
Turkiye’s Foreign Ministry called for restraint and posted on X that it hoped “calm would be restored as soon as possible” while pledging to continue supporting Niger.
Why did the attack happen, and what comes next?
The mutiny “speaks of deeper institutional and structural challenges within the military”, Kabir Adamu, an Abuja-based security expert, told Al Jazeera.
There is an argument that “persons who have received significant training, both within and outside [the military], are now occupying political positions and are not on the front line where they are needed to address the complex security challenges facing the country”, he said.
There are also the issues of equipping and rotating military forces.
“The grievances grew to a point where this mutiny sort of occurred,” said Adamu, the managing director at Beacon Security Innovations, adding: “As part of that mutiny, based on the places they targeted, it was clearly an attempt to overthrow the government.”
“If [Tchiani] does not address the deep-rooted socioeconomic, cultural, environmental and security challenges that he promised when he took over power in July 2023, then those issues will continue to rear their head,” Adamu said.
Rida Lyammouri, a senior fellow and Sahel expert at the Policy Center for the New South, based in the Moroccan capital Rabat, says Niger’s military leadership has devoted resources to protecting its grip on power rather than addressing the country’s security and other challenges.
The Africa Corps, Lyammouri pointed out, has been paid to fight groups affiliated with al-Qaeda and ISIL (ISIS), but instead, the Russian group has been used to protect the military during the “recent coup” attempt.
Lyammouri warned against growing threats from armed groups, with some of them also expanding into new areas along Niger’s borders with Benin and northeast Nigeria.
“There are no clear signs of the military bringing stability and security to the country, as they promised following the coup they carried out in 2023,” he told Al Jazeera.

Ratko Mladić, the ‘Butcher of Bosnia’, could not escape death. But his fascist ideas and ideology live on | Ed Vulliamy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
13:00:58 UTC
22:00:58 KST

Men age and die, but in the Balkans, time stands still and is stuck. General Ratko Mladić, who died in prison in The Hague on Thursday aged 84, remains a hero in the Republika Srpska statelet – the Serbian half of dismembered Bosnia that he carved out with a hurricane of violence between 1992 and 1995 – and in Serbia itself.
Too many Serbs in whose name Mladić carried out his mass murder of other ethnicities – mainly Muslim Bošniak and Roman Catholic Croats – adore him and mourn his passing.
Since Bosnia’s war ended, Mladić’s portrait has adorned posters, gable ends, mantelpieces and football fans’ flags. Supporters of Red Star Belgrade marked his death at a match against Viktoria Plzeň on Thursday night with banners reading: “General: Eternal glory. Thank you.”
Republika Srpska’s former president Milorad Dodik extended his condolences to the Mladić family and paid tribute: “Republika Srpska will not forget his role, just as it has not forgotten it to this day. A man has died who was the commander in the struggle for the freedom of the Serbian people here, a commander who led the honourable army of Republika Srpska from the first day of its establishment. A man who demonstrated his human and military character.”
Conversely, in the 30 years since the war ended, there has been scant apology from Serbian quarters to those people, most of them Muslims, who survived Mladić’s massacres, and no reckoning. Au contraire: across Republika Srpska, hatred of what remains of “the other” and for federal authority in the capital of Sarajevo is palpable and quotidian. A friend writes to me from Bosnia: “We’re still living with the legacy every day. Listening to Republika Srpska, to Dodik, to [Serbia’s president] Vučić, the same old lies, the same old denial.” There is mass collective amnesia, denial of or – nonsensically – justification for what was done.
Mourners who gather annually at the mass cemetery of victims of the Srebrenica massacre of some 8,000 men and boys in July 1995, and for commemorations at concentration camps, are routinely harassed by police and onlookers. It is made clear to Muslims and Croats who have dared to return to Republika Srpska in the north-west and east of the bitterly divided country that, if they could, the Serbs would do it all again.
Mladić had a singular, and singularly nasty, squint. You can see it in the footage of him as he prepared the Srebrenica massacre, and in photo portraits that abound this weekend. For very many, it was a death sentence; for me, it was a stab across a courtroom at the international war crimes tribunal in The Hague as I took the witness stand in 2012 to testify against him. Having delivered that terrifying gaze, Mladić never met my eyes again during a half day of evidence from the ground of atrocities committed by those under his command. He sent a shiver of fear down the spine of anyone near him, and he knew it.
Mladić was the military wing of an unholy trinity: at its apex, Serbia’s then president, Slobodan Milošević, resurrected the insane idea of a “Greater Serbia”, a form of nationalist fascism whereby wherever the Serbs lived, only Serbs would live – everyone else would leave or die, and every vestige of their culture and religion (Muslim or Catholic) would be erased. His political co-commander in Bosnia was Radovan Karadžić, president of the self-declared Bosnian Serb republic. Milošević died while on trial at The Hague; like Mladić, Karadžić was convicted of genocide and other war crimes and remains jailed – surreally, on the Isle of Wight.
If Milošević and Karadžić were dangerously deranged, Mladič was bloodthirstily effective. He was the killer, the “Butcher of Bosnia”. To invoke and invert Hannah Arendt, if the others were the evil of banality, Mladić was the real thing: the banality of evil.
Mladić was a military more than an ideological man, a career officer in the Yugoslav army. He knew what he was doing. Transcripts of the Bosnian Serb assembly submitted to The Hague by an historian at the University of Michigan, Robert Donia, show Mladić expressing concern in 1992 that the political leadership was setting goals that would be hard to achieve. “We cannot cleanse, or sift with a sieve, so that only Serbs would stay, or that the Serbs would fall through and the rest leave. I do not know how … Mr Karadžić would explain this to the world. People, that would be genocide.” And so it was – at Srebrenica at least, according to The Hague tribunal – and as a good military commander, Mladić obeyed his political masters and enforced his own orders.
Mladić was convicted at The Hague in 2017. The media talked about “closure” for his victims. Wishful nonsense: there is no “closure”, nor can there be as long as the Serbs celebrate this creature.
Most discussion of Mladić since his passing has inevitably invoked Srebrenica, the infamous massacre. There is the TV footage of him smirking, knowing what was to come. But it was not only Srebrenica. Srebrenica was the most egregious war crime, but it was a denouement: more than 55,000 Muslims and 7,000 Croats had already been killed in other places over those three years, and two million had fled their homes. Foca and Višegrad (sites of rape camps for the indulgence of Mladić’s soldiers); Rogatica, Vlasenica and Sokolac; Bjeljina and Brcko, Kozarac, Sanski Most, Ključ … the list goes on. The siege of Sarajevo counted 11,541 deaths, including 1,600 children.
Mladić achieved most of what he set out to do. The “international community” granted the Bosnian Serbs a large part of what they killed, raped, tortured and burned for with the Dayton peace agreement, signed in 1995. There was baffling agreement from the Muslim-led government, apparently more anxious to establish its own sectarian fiefdom than unite the republic in a war that the Bosnian army was – actually, finally – winning by that summer (in a counteroffensive that put Mladiċ’s soldiers to flight, liberating territory then returned at Dayton to Republika Srpska).
Mladić succeeded in persecuting a very Bosnian, casually convivial interpretation of Islam into something more identitarian and polemical. In the absurd waltz of aspirant accession to the EU, Serbia leads the Balkan queue, ahead of truncated Bosnia, despite Belgrade’s open allegiance and subservience to Russia.
Above all, Mladić has succeeded in death, as he did in life, because of the adoration he still commands. His mission to establish an ethnically “pure”, fascistic Greater Serbia remains a dream, and a plan. Through public celebrations, he continues to terrorise the lives of those mostly Muslims and a few Croats brave enough to return to live under the insignia of those who mass murdered their families.
Mladić’s funeral will probably tell us more than his death. Several Serbian government officials and ministers urge a “state and military funeral, and day of mourning”. The president, Aleksandar Vučić, says he will leave arrangements to the general’s son, Darko, who is of the faith. If Darko decides on full national honours, that is what will happen. Mladić is dead, but lives on.
- 
  Ed Vulliamy is an author who reported on the Balkan war for the Guardian and Observer

Why is 'vegan' suddenly being used as a slur? | Emma Beddington
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
13:00:57 UTC
22:00:57 KST

Cool news, fellow soy boys and girls – we’ve been promoted from feeble, tofu-eating wokerati to dangerous radicals unfit for public office. Politico reports that US Republicans have started throwing “vegan” around as a tactic to tarnish their political opponents. “He’s a vegan,” Trump warned of Democratic Texas senatorial candidate James Talarico in May, while Talarico’s opponent, state attorney-general Ken Paxton, is trying to get the nickname “Tofu Talarico” to stick. Paxton also called him “a vegan who thinks God is non-binary”, which I find hilarious as a political put-down – give the man a Netflix special. (Sidenote: I investigated, and according to the Catholic catechism, God is “neither man nor woman”.)
Republicans have also been digging up past pro-plant-based statements from Colorado congressional candidate Manny Rutinel: a campaign committee press secretary described him on X as “a far-left vegan activist who wants to end animal agriculture”, posting an old pic of Rutinel bare-chested and wearing a Peta anti-meat banner. Other Dems have also been accused of, erm, liking animals and eating plants: Arizona congressional candidate Amish Shah has been attacked for his “wacky liberal agenda pushing vegan policies” and Lindsay James in Iowa drew heat for merely supporting the idea of “meatless May”.
It’s ridiculous but also depressing. Because hang on: does America actually think veganism disqualifies a person for political responsibilities? Apparently, when you look at how these candidates reacted. A Talarico spokesperson issued an official response to “vegan accusations” (“accusations” – the word you’d use for say, corruption or sexual assault): a picture of him wrapping his face around a giant hunk of meat. The candidate himself joked, spicily, “I’ve been eating barbecue since before Ken Paxton’s first indictment” (despite many years of legal issues, Paxton has never been found guilty of any crime).
Rutinel, meanwhile, clarified he’s not vegan now, saying he needs to “enjoy the delicious products that Colorado ranchers make”. His Reddit posts supporting animal rights, he said, were “the views of a 22-year-old kid,” giving the impression his veganism was youthful folly, like taking a puff of a joint in college – he tried a tempeh wrap, but he didn’t finish it! A spokesperson for James said she has “always sided with Iowa farmers”.
Obviously harbouring vegan sympathies plays badly in agricultural communities (claiming your opponent is a seitan worshipper is a canny strategy when you’re appealing to ranchers), so I understand the emphatic denials. But rather than playing into this notion that vegans are extreme-left fantasists who can’t be trusted, I wish someone would defend the idea that they’re actually perfectly well qualified for political office.
Why wouldn’t they be? Sure, people think we’re pleased with ourselves and boring (guilty), but that never excluded other politicians from power. We’re not so weakly undernourished that we couldn’t survive the rigours of the job, either – these days, plant proteins are thrust at us from every angle.
And actually, there are plenty of reasons why vegans can make great public servants. For a start, anyone who has gone vegan for planetary or animal welfare reasons is OK with a spot of self-denial for the greater good. You think we’ve forgotten how delicious butter is? Believe me, I remember. I’m not suggesting vegans live heroic lives of self-sacrifice (there are vegan pistachio croissants now!), or that not eating animals makes us better people. But any politician with a sense that there are things more important than their own gratification is welcome.
Vegans are used to ridicule, and being the target of people’s strongly voiced opinions – that’s always handy in politics. We’re also – and apologies for veering into classic vegan self-righteousness – basically right, no? Talarico’s 2022 comment, that reducing meat consumption to fight climate change is an “existential” matter, has been weaponised against him, but meat production alone accounts for nearly 60% of agriculture’s greenhouse gas emissions. Thomas Poore, lead author of the landmark 2018 study on the environmental impact of agriculture from which that statistic comes, concluded that excluding meat and dairy from your diet is “the single biggest way to reduce your impact on planet Earth”.
Politicians who think individuals can make a difference, and that collectively we can mitigate the worst impacts of climate breakdown and stop things getting even worse, are exactly who I want to see in power. Because they give us something even better than a plant milk that doesn’t curdle in hot tea: hope.
Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnist

Why some young people stick with social causes while others fade away
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
13:00:07 UTC
22:00:07 KST

Young adults in the United States who support social causes due to internal moral convictions are more likely to anticipate staying engaged over time than those driven by a desire for social approval. Research published in Social Psychology Quarterly indicates that political ideology shapes these motivations, with liberals often acting from empathy and conservatives frequently relying on community approval. The researchers found that external motivations can still foster lasting commitment when tied to enduring social networks like religious groups.
When people participate in social, political, or religious causes, their reasons for getting involved typically fall into two categories. Internal motivation involves a deep personal commitment or moral dedication to an issue. External motivation involves acting to gain social approval or avoid punishment.
External motivation is often debated under the term performative activism on social media. Observers often view performative activism as actions that have minimal actual impact while maximizing public visibility for the person performing them.
Psychologists classify these motivational differences using self-determination theory. This framework suggests that while both internal and external motivations can prompt short-term action, internally motivated behaviors are generally more persistent.
Researchers E. Ashby Plant and Kyle Rose of Florida State University led a team to explore how these motivational sources affect participation among young adults. The researchers wanted to understand whether specific emotional responses to social causes encourage people to act for internal or external reasons. They also sought to determine how a person’s political ideology might influence their emotional and motivational approaches to social engagement.
The research team began by conducting a survey of 934 young adults between the ages of 18 and 29. The participants answered questions about their online and offline involvement in political, religious, and civic activities over the past year. They also rated their intended engagement in these areas over the next twelve months.
Each person identified a primary cause that mattered most to them. They then rated statements assessing their internal and external motivations to act. For example, they indicated whether they promoted the cause because it was personally important or because they wanted to gain approval from others.
The participants also provided their political orientation and rated how strongly they felt certain emotions when thinking about their primary cause. The researchers categorized these emotions as either self-focused, such as pride and guilt, or other-focused, such as empathy and anger directed at wrongdoers.
The survey results showed that both internal and external motivations were associated with participants taking action in the past. When predicting future behavior, however, only internal motivation was linked to intended ongoing engagement.
Emotions played a distinct role in these motivational pathways. Participants with high internal motivation tended to experience other-focused emotions, alongside feeling positive about themselves and reporting lower levels of guilt. Those with high external motivation were more likely to report self-focused emotions, including both pride and guilt.
Political ideology strongly influenced these patterns. Liberal participants reported higher levels of empathy, negative emotions directed at others, and internal motivation. The data indicated that their tendency to experience empathy and anger statistically accounted for their higher internal motivation.
Conservative participants reported higher levels of pride and external motivation. The researchers found that feelings of pride statistically explained their tendency to rely on external motivation for their activism.
To gain deeper insight into these survey patterns, the researchers conducted follow-up interviews with 30 of the participants. They selected ten liberals, ten moderates, and ten conservatives to answer open-ended questions about their motivations and feelings regarding social engagement. Two independent researchers coded the interview transcripts to identify expressions of motivation and emotion.
During the interviews, liberal participants frequently emphasized their internal motivations and explicitly rejected the idea of acting for social reputation. They framed their participation as a moral responsibility and expressed anger about injustice, along with frustration toward people who remained apathetic.
Liberal interviewees also highlighted the emotional toll of their activism. As one liberal participant explained about managing anger, “There’s two types of anger. There’s anger that fuels you, and there’s anger that burns you.”
Conservative participants often described their engagement in terms of social interaction and community building. Many of these respondents tied their activism to their religious faith, which provided a supportive network that encouraged their involvement.
These individuals often expressed pride and satisfaction in seeing the tangible results of their group’s efforts, such as distributing donations to people in need. Another participant described the tangible satisfaction of directly helping people, such as bringing coats to those in need, saying, “It feels like, okay, this is actually making a difference.”
The interview responses suggested that the traditional divide between internal and external motivation might be less rigid for individuals motivated by faith. For many conservative participants, a desire for approval from their religious community or God functioned as a highly stable form of external motivation.
The study relied on survey data collected at a single point in time, which restricts the researchers from establishing a cause-and-effect relationship between emotion, motivation, and engagement. People’s feelings and motivations might evolve as they spend more time participating in a cause.
Participants reported their own past and future behaviors, which can sometimes differ from objective reality. Tracking actual activities, such as measuring the time spent on specific digital platforms or logging attendance at community events, could provide a more accurate picture of engagement.
Finally, the external motivation driven by a religious community might operate differently than external motivation aimed at impressing peers or the general public. A religious community or a belief in an ever-present deity might offer a permanent audience, making that specific type of external motivation unusually stable over time.
The study, “Social Engagement for Oneself and Others: The Roles of Motivation, Emotion, and Political Ideology,” was authored by E. Ashby Plant, Kyle Rose, Yuki Maynor, Levi Mitzen, Bayla K. Thompson, Deana A. Rohlinger, and Grant W. Bailey.

13-year-old among 321 arrested as Hong Kong police seize drugs worth HK$130m
19 boys and nine girls under the age of 18 among those taken into custody during seven-week citywide crackdown
Hong Kong police have arrested 321 people, including a 13-year-old, and seized HK$130 million (US$16.5 million) worth of suspected illegal drugs during a seven-week citywide crackdown.
Code-named “Tailbacker”, the operation ran from July 12 to August 29, and uncovered 234 drug-related cases, police said on Sunday.
The 321 suspects, aged between 13 and 72, comprised 228 men, 65 women and 28 minors. They were arrested for suspected offences that included the manufacturing, possession, and trafficking of dangerous drugs, as well as operating a drug den and possessing Part 1 poisons. Some have already been formally charged.
The underage suspects comprised 19 boys and nine girls, all under the age of 18.
Over the course of the operation, officers seized 231kg (509 lbs) of suspected illegal drugs with a market value of HK$130 million, including 76kg of cocaine, 65kg of ketamine, 3.7 litres of liquid etomidate, and 6,400 etomidate vape pods, as well as some heroin, cannabis and methamphetamine.
Police noted a significant increase in etomidate seizures compared with similar operations last year.

Libya rivals agree roadmap for elections within 24 months at UN-led talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30

Libya rivals agree roadmap for elections within 24 months at UN-led talks
TRIPOLI, Aug 30 - Representatives of Libya's rival political parties on Sunday signed an agreement on holding long-delayed national elections within two years to resolve contentious issues over electoral laws and reform the national elections body.
• The political process to resolve more than a decade of conflict in Libya has been stalled since an election scheduled for December 2021 collapsed following disputes over the eligibility of the main candidates.
• Sunday's signing ceremony was held at the United Nations Support Mission in Libya, UNSMIL, in the Libyan capital Tripoli.
• It followed talks in a smaller format, known as the 4+4, that involved two representatives of each of Libya's four main institutions: the Government of National Unity, the High Council of State, the House of Representatives and the Libyan National Army.
• Walid Ellafi, state minister of political affairs and communications in the Government of National Unity, said legislative and presidential elections should be held "within a period not exceeding 24 months" under a single executive authority and unified national institutions.
• Shibani AbuHamoud, head of the army's general command delegation, said the 4+4 would work with UNSMIL "to develop a framework within one month of the signing of the agreement to follow up on all matters related to its implementation".
• The agreement says that if Libya's House of Representatives and High Council of State fail to approve the deal within a month, the parties will seek to adopt it nationally as a constitutional document through broad national mechanisms and secure international backing through the U.N. Security Council.
• Libya has had little stability or security since a 2011 NATO-backed uprising.
• It split in 2014 between warring eastern and western factions but there has been little major warfare since a 2020 ceasefire.
• All Libya's major political players have repeatedly called for elections, but many Libyan people have voiced doubts that they would want a vote that could push most of them from positions of authority. REUTERS

South Africa urges ICJ to act on Israel's ongoing Gaza violence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
12:47:52 UTC
21:47:52 KST

Breadcrumb
South Africa urges ICJ action over Israel's non-compliance with Gaza orders
South Africa has submitted a dossier to the International Court of Justice (ICJ), accusing Israel of continuing to disregard court orders intended to protect Palestinians amid the Gaza conflict, which is set to enter its third year.
The South African Foreign Ministry said on Friday that the dossier was submitted on 25 August to assist a committee of judges responsible for monitoring the implementation of provisional measures and recommending possible action to the court.
Pretoria said it presented the evidence after concluding that Israel had failed to comply with three legally binding provisional measures issued by the ICJ to protect the rights of Palestinians under the Genocide Convention.
South Africa launched legal proceedings against Israel at the ICJ on 29 December 2023, alleging violations of the 1948 Genocide Convention.
The court subsequently issued three separate provisional measures orders on 26 January, 28 March and 24 May 2024, after South Africa requested urgent intervention over the humanitarian situation in Gaza.
The rulings required Israel to take all necessary measures to prevent acts prohibited under the convention.
The court also ordered Israel to implement safeguards against potential genocidal acts, halt military operations in the southern Gaza city of Rafah where such operations could cause physical destruction to the Palestinian population, and provide regular reports on its compliance with the measures.
In its latest statement, South Africa said it would continue pursuing “all avenues available” to seek Israel’s full and immediate compliance with the court’s orders.
“Regrettably, Israel has not complied with the Orders,” Pretoria stated in the filing.
South Africa warned that the rights of Palestinians in the Gaza Strip could be “destroyed before [the ICJ] renders its final decision”, a situation it said threatened the "legitimacy of the ICJ itself".
The dossier stated that, as of August, at least 73,407 Palestinians had been killed and 174,335 injured, together representing "over 10% of the Palestinian population" of the Gaza Strip.
It also said that, since the announcement of a "so-called ‘ceasefire" in October 2025 the Israeli military had killed an average of one Palestinian child per day.
The submission further stated that miscarriage rates among Palestinian women had "increased more than three-fold" in 2026.
South Africa also said that Israel had “arbitrarily detained and deported Palestinians” who were subsequently “tortured, subjected to sexual and gender-based violence, and to cruel, inhuman and degrading treatment”.
The department additionally accused Israel of killing local journalists and preventing foreign journalists and UN-mandated investigative bodies from entering Gaza.
Israel has repeatedly rejected allegations that it is committing genocide in Gaza, despite rights groups warning that the scale and nature of its violence, including killings, restrictions on humanitarian aid, mass displacement and the destruction of medical services, could amount to genocidal acts.
Rights groups have also pointed to statements by Israeli officials that they say indicate genocidal intent.
Despite a ceasefire in Gaza that has been in place since October 2025, Israeli attacks have continued across the devastated Palestinian enclave. Israel's military has killed at least 1,313 Palestinians since then, according to Gaza's health ministry.
