Train drivers have secured a significant pay rise after the threat of strike action was floated on busy routes across the UK, including on the busy London-Manchester line.
The deal, which was agreed on Saturday between Avanti West Coast and the Associated Society of Locomotive Engineers and Firemen (Aslef) union, is the first to be approved by Andy Burnham in his premiership.
As well as the London-Manchester line – likely to see increased ministerial traffic after the establishment of the No 10 North office – the company also operates services to other big British cities such as Birmingham, Glasgow and Liverpool.
Coming after Aslef announced plans in June to ballot members about possible strike action over pay, the deal – first reported by the Sunday Times – will be seen as a victory for the union. It includes a 3.6% pay rise for drivers, 0.7 percentage points higher than the latest inflation rate, as well as time and a half pay for working Sundays, and £720 if drivers work a fifth day in the week.
Avanti is to be renationalised under the Labour government by spring 2027, with all rail companies due to be under government control by the end of that year. The operator, which is seen as having the worst punctuality rating for any major rail company in the UK, based on figures from the Office of Rail and Road, has cut multiple services in the past year, including the 7am train between Manchester and London, which it cut and brought back in the space of a few days after public scrutiny.
The government said it had “prioritised resolving the rail union disputes, improving services for passengers and saving hundreds of millions in lost revenue to ease the burden on taxpayers”.
But the shadow transport secretary, Richard Holden, said the government was “totally capitulating to their union paymasters” and that “taxpayers are being asked to stump up millions simply to save Burnham’s blushes”.
An Aslef spokesperson said on Saturday: “Our job is to enhance our members’ terms and conditions and this deal, struck with Avanti West Coast and approved by the DFTO (Department for Transport Operator), has been accepted.”
A Department for Transport spokesperson said: “We are pleased to see Avanti West Coast work with Aslef to enable a fair and affordable settlement to keep Britain’s railways moving and prevent disruption for passengers.”

Ratcliffe made an unannounced trip to Moscow on August 25. The following day, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov confirmed that contact between the two countries’ intelligence services had taken place, but said Putin had not met with the CIA chief. “Of course, President Putin is immediately briefed on everything,” Peskov said, calling the meeting “a positive phenomenon” while declining to give further details.

Earlier last week, Trump described the visit as “semi-routine.” When asked by talk show host Glenn Beck whether Putin planned on “testing NATO resolve,” or whether Ratcliffe discussed US sanctions on Iran, Trump replied “none of the above.”
Ratcliffe’s visit was the first known trip to Moscow by a CIA director since William Burns traveled there in November 2021. The last known face-to-face meeting between the CIA and SVR chiefs was in Ankara in November 2022, when Burns met Naryshkin to discuss nuclear escalation risks and detained US citizens.
The last publicly disclosed contact between Ratcliffe and a senior Russian official was a March 2025 phone call with SVR chief Sergey Naryshkin. ====================================================================================================

Why the Hottest New Wearables Want to Be Ignored
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
10:30:00 UTC
19:30:00 KST

There’s a new kind of gadget on shelves, designed for you to ignore it 99 percent of the time—it only needs attention when its battery is low. I'm talking about the screen-free wearable. You rarely look at it or touch it, yet it collects health stats day and night so you can view them later on in an app, when you get the time—if you can find the time. No pressure.
They have been exploding of late and are only set to grab more attention in the coming months, with the promise of demanding less of your attention once you actually buy one. Today there’s the Garmin Cirqa, Google Fitbit Air, Polar Loop, the Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Whoop series, the original pioneer of this category. Apple is considering its own version of the concept, according to Bloomberg. One answer to that big question of why? Many of us are sick of attention-hoarding tech and social media, not least realizing it is probably doing us no good.
I have reviewed wearables since they went mainstream the first time around with the early waves of Fitbits from 2009 and onward. In some ways this new generation of trackers feels like a callback to those days. Back when I used the Fitbit Ultra, a 2011 tracker that clipped to your jeans, I paid so little attention to it that two days passed before I realized I’d lost it somewhere on the streets of Zagreb, Croatia. While, like many, I fell for the sub-Tamagotchi little cartoon faces of the 2012 Fitbit Zip’s screen, it—like a Fitbit Air—wasn't something you were meant to pay attention to more than a couple times a day, max.
Over the last few years, though, I’ve spent most days referring to a Garmin, Samsung, Fitbit, Coros—the list goes on—dozens or hundreds of times a day. WhatsApp messages and emails buzz on their little screens and my wrist reflexively raises to see what’s up. When I wear a Garmin watch, I’m also lulled into the rhythm of checking evening and morning “reports,” and pathologically looking at my sleep score as soon as I wake up. And let’s not even get into the move alerts, an eye-rolling nag wearables have had for years now.
What Wearables Have Become
Part of the sell-in of new-breed wearables is that they're, in some ways, the antithesis of what other watches have grown into. Fitness watches are more smartwatch-like than ever. OLED screens are near-ubiquitous even in health trackers; hardcore running wearables let you communicate with AI assistants. And this is all even though smartwatches have never really fulfilled the original promise of a life-changing app or feature beyond what people used the first Apple Watch for back in 2015: not much.
Sure, Apple Watches may have saved a life or two, but that’s not necessarily what you’re buying them for. I waited years to report on smartwatch apps that would change things and instead saw entire wearable app ecosystems wither like neglected houseplants. Screen-free wearables want to hit “reset” on the entire category.
The most interesting factor isn't that bands like the Fitbit Air exist now, but why this is all happening now, in 2026. These wearables are largely a case of design subtraction. They are much like a normal fitness tracker—heart rate sensor, battery, accelerometer, Bluetooth transmitter, and whatever other sensors are packed in on a per-case basis—with the display excised.
Whoop has made screen-free wearables since its first proper release in 2015, but the shift in what Whoop considers itself to be about mirrors the change we see in the wider market. Today a Whoop band is made for just about anyone with the spare cash to pay for its $199 annual subscription. It’s a system to “help you improve how you sleep, train, and feel—starting day one,” to use Whoop’s own words. This couldn’t be further removed from the self-serious way Whoop described itself in 2015, as a “performance optimization system exclusively designed for elite athletes and teams.” What a change a decade makes.
Even if Whoop has always been grounded in the now-common concept of “training readiness,” things have altered drastically. So while it’s tempting to say Google's Fitbit and company are playing catch-up with Whoop, that’s not quite it. It has homed in on the “low-distraction” lifestyle selling point just as the other bigger tech companies have.
On at least three fronts this can be attributed—or blamed—on AI, to some extent.
AI as the Good and Bad Guy
AI is a way for these wearable companies to upsell and make money, and on the other side, a major contributor to why a lot of us feel like we need low-distraction tech these days in the first place. While virtually every Whoop rival says it can be used without a subscription, some of these companies lean heavily on AI as an upsell.
Take Google and the Fitbit Air. Without a subscription, the app looks cute enough but is fairly spare. You get stats and charts, but if you want chatty explainers of what any of it means, you need Google Health Premium at $10 a month. Numbers and graph lines become paragraphs that reference specific quirks or events of the day because, to steal a line from humorist and podcaster John Hodgman, specificity is the soul of narrative.
And this is just the beginning. “The use of AI in monitoring and guiding health and wellness is still at the early stage of development but will likely become significantly more advanced as AI matures,” says Peter Richardson, vice president and cofounder of Counterpoint Research.
I find Google Fitbit’s chatbot ramblings quite annoying, with not-that-rare dips into the condescending, and I may even prefer the subscription-free experience. But my job has pushed me through the unenviable task of learning what VO2 Max actually means, what heart-rate variability trends indicate, and so on: not the norm.
AI could solve that long-standing issue with wearables—people glazing over data as soon as they see anything more than their daily step count. This AI use will be better represented on the phone than the watch screen, too, making the lack of screen a strength. It lets the AI shine.
Technostress
The most important influence of AI here is on the other side of the equation, though, as just the latest stage in the tech-ification of our daily lives. I’ve heard from multiple friends about how their recent work appraisals focused on higher-ups demanding greater AI use within their “personal workflow.” Perhaps you’ve had a similar experience.
Elizabeth Marsh, a doctoral researcher at the University of Nottingham who studies the dark side of the digital workplace, finds that digital tools consistently trigger a familiar cluster of harms: technostress, information overload, constant interruption, and blurred work–home boundaries.
“These appear to have become the predictable by-product of environments where the volume and pace of digital demand has risen faster than people's capacity to absorb it,” Marsh tells WIRED, noting that information overload and FOMO correlate strongly with lower well-being and higher strain.
It’s a good argument for not having notifications and alerts pop up on your wrist, phone, and work PC—and wherever else your to-do list of responsibilities takes on a digital form.
“Participants described them in visceral terms—one said the notifications “make me feel sometimes on edge and it does make me feel anxious and it affects my mental health;” another described feeling angry at the sender for taking their time, while simultaneously feeling bad for not replying immediately,” Marsh says about her study on “digital workplace technology intensity.”
But she found simply cutting off notifications wasn’t necessarily a solution either, as people worried they would miss something. Screen-free wearables are a parallel development to this kind of tech cold turkey of banishing wearables from your wrist entirely. You can still get your sleep scores and step count, but without it being advertised consciously through the day. With a Garmin Cirqa, you can even see maps of runs and walks without ever having tapped a “start workout” button. Nothing needs to buzz away or, at a simpler level, require the daily charge coddling of an Apple Watch.
This is perhaps the key. So many tech companies are making these low-distraction wearables because so many of us are close to wanting to opt out altogether, at least in the areas of tech in which we can.
Digital Mindfulness
Marsh’s suggested strategy for dealing with tech strain is what she calls “digital mindfulness,” which is all about having an “awareness of how you engage with technology, rather than operating on autopilot.” That mindless social media feed scrolling? In most cases, you won't convince anyone that’s a digitally mindful practice. Marsh says it involves three things.
“Intention—having a clear purpose for picking up the device in the first place, rather than reaching for it reflexively and then wondering where twenty minutes went,” she says. “Attention—staying with what you've chosen to do and resisting the pull of whatever else is competing for your attention. And attitude—responding to yourself with a bit of kindness and patience when it goes wrong, as self-criticism about our own tech habits tends to make the relationship worse rather than better.”
Buying a screen-free tracker like a Fitbit Air isn’t digital mindfulness in itself. But it’s more intuitively compatible with adopting that mindset than a notification-spewing, buzzing smartwatch.

Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
10:28:59 UTC
19:28:59 KST

Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
- Date:
- August 30, 2026
- Source:
- University of Copenhagen
- Summary:
- Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.
- Share:
An international research team has identified seven previously undescribed species of Madagascar's elusive diamond frogs (Rhombophryne), adding new evidence that this unusual amphibian group is far more diverse than scientists once realized.
Accurately identifying species and understanding where they live are essential for measuring biodiversity and protecting it. To sort out the identities of these frogs, researchers combined field observations, museum specimens, and advanced DNA analysis. The work revealed previously hidden species diversity and helped resolve a taxonomic problem that had remained unsettled for years.
By determining which frogs belong to which species and mapping where they occur, the researchers have also created a stronger scientific basis for conservation in Madagascar, where many forests are rapidly disappearing.
"Diamond frogs have been hiding their diversity beneath our feet," said Dr. Mark D. Scherz, Curator of Herpetology at the Natural History Museum Denmark and lead author of the study.
"Many species spend most of their lives beneath the leaf litter, and even when they emerge they can look deceptively similar," he added.
Madagascar's Secretive Diamond Frogs
Diamond frogs are some of Madagascar's most distinctive amphibians. Certain species are extremely round and resemble the rain frogs found in mainland Africa, spending much of their time concealed beneath the forest floor. Other species have long legs and live among moss, while some are sturdier frogs adapted to life on the ground.
Most diamond frogs look brown at first, but several species have vivid markings that remain hidden until the frogs move. These can include bright orange flashes or bold white and black patterns on the thighs and lower back. Researchers think these markings may help startle predators.
Because these frogs are so difficult to find and observe, diamond frogs remain among the least studied vertebrates in Madagascar.
A 12 Year Scientific Puzzle
The research effort began more than twelve years ago, when scientists repeatedly encountered frogs that clearly appeared to represent species that had never been formally described. Identifying them was not simple, however, because researchers had trouble matching older species names with the genetic lineages found in modern specimens.
"When I started this project twelve years ago, we already knew there were several species waiting to be described, and almost every expedition to Madagascar revealed another one. Some were relatively straightforward to describe, but others were complicated by uncertainty surrounding older species names. Untangling that puzzle took years," Scherz said.
A major breakthrough came from museomics, the use of DNA sequencing on historical museum specimens. Researchers compared genetic information from old collections with DNA from newly collected frogs. They also examined external features, skeletal anatomy, and frog calls.
Together, those lines of evidence allowed the team to connect historical species names with the correct evolutionary lineages and clear up taxonomic confusion that had persisted for decades.
Museum collections played a central role in establishing the identities of several of the species.
"Museum collections are far more than archives of the past - they are essential scientific resources for understanding biodiversity today," said Dr. Alice Petzold of the University of Potsdam, who led the museomics work.
"By sequencing historical specimens, including the original type specimens, we were able to answer questions that have persisted for generations," she added.
New Species Could Shape Conservation
The study was carried out through close cooperation among scientists and institutions in Madagascar and Europe. It also highlights the direct connection between biodiversity research and conservation.
Many diamond frogs live in forests that are becoming increasingly fragmented by deforestation. At the same time, scientists still know very little about the basic biology of many of these species.
"For many species, we still know almost nothing about their breeding biology, population sizes or ecological requirements. Without that knowledge, it becomes much more difficult to assess their conservation status and protect them effectively," said co-author Dr. Andolalao Rakotoarison of the Institut d'Enseignement Supérieur de Soavinandriana Itasy, Madagascar.
The new findings are already contributing to conservation planning in Madagascar. At a protected area planning workshop held in March 2026 as part of the country's Biodiversity 30x30Program, several of the newly described frogs, including Rhombophryne quentini, directly informed proposals aimed at strengthening and expanding protected areas.
More Frogs May Still Be Waiting
With the addition of seven new species, the number of known Rhombophryne species has risen to 27. Even so, the researchers believe more unnamed species are almost certain to remain undiscovered and undescribed.
The new study resolves many long-standing questions, but Scherz views it as the start of a much larger effort.
"Every newly described species represents millions of years of unique evolutionary history. The more we learn about Madagascar's remarkable amphibians, the clearer it becomes that there is still an enormous amount left to discover," he said.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Copenhagen. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Mark D. Scherz, Frank Glaw, Alice Petzold, Franco Andreone, Jörn Köhler, Achille P. Raselimanana, Carl Hutter, Francesco Belluardo, Andolalao Rakotoarison, Michael Hofreiter, Miguel Vences, Angelica Crottini. A wealth of riches: A comprehensive revision of diamond frogs, genus Rhombophryne Boettger, 1880 (Microhylidae: Cophylinae), with the description of seven new species. Vertebrate Zoology, 2026; 76: 485 DOI: 10.3897/vz.76.e172567

Why obsessing over self-improvement could be sabotaging your brain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
10:27:48 UTC
19:27:48 KST

If you want to improve yourself, your health or your lifestyle, you need to do it to the “maxx”—according to social media, at least.
If you want to better your appearance, you need to try “looksmaxxing”. If you want to fix your diet and look after your gut, you should be “fibermaxxing”. And if you want to improve your social skills and be more charming, you really ought to be “personality-maxxing”.
But all of this maxxing might not actually be a good way to motivate yourself into healthier habits. In fact, it may have the opposite effect—and may even cause stress.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The language of “maxxing”has roots in the gaming concept of “min-maxing”, in which players strategically maximize desirable attributes while minimizing less useful ones to create the most effective in-game character. The concept then made it’s way to the mainstream, most notably through “looksmaxxing”: making focused, and sometimes extreme, efforts to maximize physical attractiveness.
The suffix has since been adapted in multiple health and wellbeing spaces. If there is an aspect of life that could be improved, it can probably be maxxed.
The “maxxing” trend encapsulates our increasingly intense optimization culture, in which we systematically seek to improve different aspects of our thinking, feeling and functioning. This pursuit is often aided by commercial products and services that promise to produce the “best version” of ourselves.
But there’s an interesting conundrum that arises from the terminology itself. Maxxing implies there is a maximum – a point at which you have reached the peak, or perhaps even “won.”
But health, wellbeing, social relationships and lifestyle habits aren’t really something we complete. They’re continuing and fluctuating processes. Things happen outside our control, our lives and circumstances change – and we change with them.
This makes maxxing something of a double-edged sword. It can make healthy behavior engaging, provide a sense of identity and encourage people to connect with others pursuing similar goals.
But if self-improvement turns into constant self-surveillance, self-criticism and the pursuit of an idealized “optimal” self, it may come with psychological costs.
When social media constantly reminds us there’s another metric to optimize, healthy self-improvement risks fueling self-criticism and anxiety around our bodies, health and self-image. Examples of this have already been seen in “looksmaxing spaces”—online communities in which people can connect and exchange advice on improving appearance.
Social media use, particularly engaging with content or communities which glorify fit and idealized bodies, has also been associated with greater risk of experiencing muscle dysmorphia (a preoccupation with muscle and physique) and orthorexia (an obsessive preoccupation with healthy eating). Constantly focusing on how to maximise ourselves may inadvertently cause us to become more focused on what is wrong with us.
Moderation-maxxing
So perhaps we need to start moderation-maxxing instead?
This doesn’t mean you should stop caring about health or abandon your goals. Rather, it’s about recognizing the mindset motivating your aim for improvement.
If a maxxing trend encourages awareness of healthy behavior, that can be genuinely useful. But if pursuing one optimal health behavior begins to compromise your psychological wellbeing or social connections, it’s worth checking in with yourself and exploring the motivations behind your efforts.
For example, positive motivations for trying to improve your personal appearance could be a desire to boost your self-esteem or feel more open to connecting with those around you. But if the reason you’re being drawn to improve your appearance comes from a place of in inadequacy and constant comparison to others, then this motivation may leave you at risk of developing restrictive or harmful behaviors.
This is where ideas such as self-compassion and mindful awareness become particularly important. Self-compassion involves having kindness of yourself, recognizing common humanity, reducing self-judgement and practicing mindfulness (a focus on living in the present moment).
Rather than ignoring our difficulties or giving up on improvement, self-compassion allows us to recognize imperfection and change as part of being human. It also means speaking to ourselves without excessive judgement and trying not to over-identify with the idealized version of health we see on social media.
And, importantly, accepting ourselves doesn’t mean that we have to stop growing. We can want to improve while still appreciating who we are now – and not constantly feel stressed to maximize every component of our lives.
“Maxxing” is just a new and catchy repackaging of a much older impulse towards health and self-improvement. While it can be a fun trend to engage with, just remember that optimization is never supposed to become the purpose of life. After all, there’s little point in building a character with all the highest stats if you stop enjoying the game.
This article was first published by The Conversation. Read the original article here.

'We never thought they were Muslims': Mohan Bhagwat recalls 1996 Charkhi Dadri mid-air collision
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

10:25:50 UTC
19:25:50 KST

'We never thought they were Muslims': Mohan Bhagwat recalls 1996 Charkhi Dadri mid-air collision
Edited by: Vijaya Srivastava / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 30, 2026, 15:55 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
RSS Chief Mohan Bhagwat addresses at 'One World One Humanity' event, in New York on Saturday. (One World One Humanity/ ANI Video Grab)
NEW DELHI: Nearly three decades after one of the world’s deadliest aviation disasters, RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat returned to the memory of the Charkhi Dadri mid-air collision in Haryana.He recalled the chaos that followed the crash. He spoke of injured passengers, bodies that had to be recovered and families arriving from far away, searching for their loved ones and trying to identify those they had lost. And he remembered the RSS volunteers who, according to him, reached the site and began helping.
They treated the injured. They helped recover the dead. They assisted relatives who arrived later. They also helped arrange funeral rites.Many of the victims were Muslims. But Bhagwat said that was never a consideration for the volunteers who were serving them.Speaking at the "One World One Humanity" event in New York on Saturday, Bhagwat recalled the tragedy as an example of what he described as the RSS's philosophy of unconditional humanitarian service."Two planes collided over Haryana, which is part of Bharat, over the place named Dadri. Both were from Arab countries. Most of the passengers were Muslims. After that collision, our Swayamsevaks reached there first, and they served. Served in treating the injured... Recovering their bodies, arranging for the funeral rites when their relatives come, helping them in identifying. We never thought at that time that these were Muslims," said the RSS Chief.
The disaster took place on November 12, 1996. A Saudi Arabian Airlines Boeing 747 and a Kazakhstan Airlines Ilyushin Il-76 collided in the skies over Charkhi Dadri, Haryana.There were no survivors.All 349 people aboard the two aircraft were killed. The crash became the deadliest mid-air collision in aviation history.For Bhagwat, the tragedy was not only about the terrible loss of life. It was also about what happened after the aircraft came down.He recalled a moment when grief and devastation had stripped away every distinction between people. Those at the crash site needed help. Families needed answers. The dead needed dignity.Bhagwat said the volunteers did not ask who the victims were before helping them.He also said the RSS did not publicise such work because it did not expect anything in return."The prominent working organisation was RSS. We could do this because we are not in politics. And we don't go on making these things famous because we don't want anything from this. No return... In Sangha, we only give. We don't want anything. That is why in publicity matters, we are way behind."The RSS chief was speaking in New York as he began a three-nation global outreach tour covering the United States, Canada and the United Kingdom. The visit has been organised as part of the organisation's centenary year celebrations, following invitations from overseas local organisations.Bhagwat also used the occasion to speak about perceptions of the RSS. He said the organisation was often viewed through narratives that, in his view, did not reflect its work on the ground."There are many perceptions created by wrong narratives. But when you come and see us from inside, all those will be disbelieved in the day."He then broadened his argument beyond the RSS and its work during disasters. He spoke about the kind of social change he believes is necessary to create greater unity.Bhagwat said political systems alone could not bring about such change. In a democracy, he argued, political leaders ultimately respond to public opinion. The first step, therefore, had to be taken within society itself."Politics today, especially in a democracy, depends on the public view. If there is public opinion, then no politician will dare to go against it. Therefore, I think after taking a common resolve today, we have to act in these societies, and we have to act first locally."He argued that social harmony could not be built simply by gaining political power. It had to grow from everyday interactions and acts of service.For Bhagwat, the idea was rooted in what he described as the traditional thought of Bharat, where the unity of humanity is placed above individual interests."This is the traditional thought of Bharat--unity of humanity. All our leaders, at any point in time, have emphasised that too. After independence, we got the constitution, which emphasises this, but that is not happening. Because these things do not happen through politics. I'm sorry to say, but the fact is, politics has now become a game of self-interest. And where there is me and I, there is no solution. We and ours are the solution. So our experience in Bharat is that we have to start with society."He called for such efforts to begin locally. Small pockets of people working together, he said, could eventually become larger networks of service and unity."Whatever we decide to do today, we should start in our own country and create pockets of such selfless service, such an atmosphere of unity, and then this dialogue should continue. Through this dialogue, we should connect them, and then we should grow."
Nearly 30 years after the Charkhi Dadri crash, the scale of the disaster remains difficult to comprehend. Hundreds of lives were lost in a matter of moments.But Bhagwat chose to remember what happened in the aftermath.Amid the wreckage, he said, volunteers came forward to help people they did not know. They treated the injured. They recovered bodies. They helped families search for answers.And, in his telling of that day, they did so without first asking whether the person in front of them was Hindu or Muslim.That memory formed the emotional centre of Bhagwat's message in New York: that in moments of profound human suffering, service can begin before identity does.

Her stories explore how policy, technology, economic shifts and social change influence people's everyday lives. Her work also focuses on bringing depth, context and a human perspective to complex issues.
Her reports primarily cover society, healthcare, safety, public policy and emerging trends, alongside other political developments.

Salary deductions for Odisha government employees defaulting on alimony
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
10:11:27 UTC
19:11:27 KST

BHUBANESWAR: The Odisha government on Sunday issued an order mandating automatic deduction of alimony payments from the salaries of its employees who default on maintenance obligations to their estranged wives and children despite clear court directives. Officials said the order, applicable to only govt employees, is aimed at ensuring timely financial support and dignity for distressed beneficiaries.“Chief minister Mohan Charan Majhi has ordered strict enforcement of court‑mandated alimony and maintenance payments by government employees. Defaulted amounts will now be deducted directly from monthly salaries and transferred to the bank accounts of the estranged wives or children concerned,” Majhi’s office said in a statement.The order followed repeated complaints from women in distress reaching the chief minister’s office. “Several male employees failed to provide maintenance grants or alimony even after divorce, ignoring explicit court instructions. On average, two to three such complaints are received during the CM’s grievance hearings,” the statement noted.The CMO added: “Despite repeated judicial directives, many women and children were left without financial support.
The chief minister has taken a stern stance against government employees who defy court orders and neglect their families.”Majhi himself underscored the moral dimension of the directive. “It is unacceptable for government employees to act unjustly towards their spouses and children while drawing salaries from the state exchequer,” he said.Following the order, the government issued detailed guidelines. Once a court order is received, the departmental drawing and disbursement officer (DDO) will deduct the specified amount from the employee’s salary bill and transfer it electronically to the beneficiaries. The CM has further directed that such cases be integrated into the state’s centralized human resource management system (HRMS) to ensure automated compliance and eliminate delays.Officials said they will track such errant husbands from complaints received by victims.
Legal experts welcomed the initiative. “Salary deductions will ensure that court orders are not reduced to mere paperwork,” said senior advocate Pramod Mishra.Women’s rights activists also hailed the decision. “For years, women have struggled to enforce maintenance orders. This mechanism will bring relief and dignity to many households,” said activist Sunita Patnaik. She added: “By linking alimony enforcement to the HRMS system, the government hopes to prevent harassment of affected women and children.The move will not only uphold judicial authority but also ease the distress of families who often face prolonged battles for rightful support.”

Judge rules against Trump bid to deport pro-Palestine students

Judge rules against Trump bid to deport pro-Palestine students
A federal judge in California said Saturday that the US government is unconstitutionally silencing critics of Israel's genocide in Gaza and others as part of the Trump administration 's quest to deport international students who it says disrupted college campuses while expressing their views.
Judge Noël Wise, in a ruling Friday, delivered a victory for the student newspaper at Stanford University, which has said some international students were afraid to speak out because of the deportation threat.
The decision largely piggybacks on findings from nearly a year ago by a US district judge in Boston, who ruled that the Trump administration violated the Constitution when it targeted people who are not citizens for deportation solely for supporting Palestinians and criticising Israel.
Wise wrote that the freedoms of speech and the press are "foundational to America’s enduring democracy". The judge cited free-speech and vagueness flaws that violate the First Amendment and Fifth Amendment as she struck down portions of the provisions that the federal government follows regarding deportations.
Wise cited retaliation in March 2025 by US immigration authorities against people who engaged in speech supporting the Palestinians and against Israel's actions - which a growing number of experts, including those commissioned by a UN body, have said amount to genocide. The judge also cited retaliation against people who were critical of Charlie Kirk after the Turning Point USA co-founder was assassinated last September.
"Tomorrow, or perhaps even today, targets may include anyone in the United States who exercises their freedom of speech to simply express opinions the government does not like," the judge in San Jose said.
"This downward spiral is antithetical to our Constitution that recognises our right to speak freely," she added. "Here you can simultaneously hate the content of a person’s speech and love the country that cherishes the freedom to allow it. Zealous protection of our Constitutional right to free speech is a provocative demonstration of our country’s powerful lack of fear."
The Justice Department did not respond Saturday to a message seeking comment on the decision.
Conor Fitzpatrick, an attorney with the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, which brought the lawsuit, praised the ruling.
"In America, free speech doesn’t just belong to the people who say things the government agrees with," Fitzpatrick said in a release.
(Associated Press and TNA staff)

Israel's Ben-Gvir boasts of worse prison conditions
Israel's far-right national security minister on Sunday boasted of worsening conditions for Palestinian prisoners as he visited female inmates.
Two months before elections, Itamar Ben-Gvir posted a video in which a veiled woman, her face blurred out, said that prisoners had "extremely bad" conditions and "don't get any rights, and we have particular needs as women".
"We haven't bathed for three days and we haven't changed our underwear," she said, warning of the risk of disease.
Ben-Gvir responds approvingly as he compares the treatment to that of captives held for up to two years by Hamas and other fighters in Gaza following the 7 October 2023 attack.
"Our hostages had no shampoo and had no such conditions. I am proud that we have succeeded in reducing the terrorists' prison conditions to the bare minimum. The summer camps in the prisons are over," Ben-Gvir said.

The activists reported physical abuse, with an Australian saying Israeli authorities sexually assaulted her. Israel denied the allegations.
Ben-Gvir again drew international condemnation recently when he said Israel should kill 30 to 40 Palestinians each night in Gaza.
According to her husband, the prisoner speaking in the video is Yasmine Shaaban, who was re-arrested by Israeli forces in May 2025 during a raid on her home near Jenin, months after being released as part of a Gaza ceasefire agreement.
The Palestinian Authority's Commission on Detainees Affairs accused Ben-Gvir of "brutality, hatred and racism".
The Gaza prisoners ministry under Hamas said Ben-Gvir's video "reflects the depths of depravity to which the occupation regime has sunk".
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's coalition is struggling in some polls ahead of 27 October elections, and Ben-Gvir has refused his pleas to boost the right-wing's chances by running jointly with a fellow ultranationalist.

Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Pakistan to hold first defence pact meeting, source says
- Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Pakistan will hold their first defence committee meeting on Aug 31 in Istanbul under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed in August.
- The pact aims to strengthen collective defence, treating an attack on one as an attack on all, similar to NATO's Article 5 clause.
- Discussions will focus on enhancing defence capabilities, interoperability, and joint defence industry projects amid regional security concerns involving Iran and Israel.
AI generated
ISTANBUL - Top officials from Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan will gather in Istanbul on Aug 31 for a first committee meeting under the joint defence accord that they signed in August, a Turkish foreign ministry source said.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed on Aug 7, brought together Sunni Muslim US allies concerned by the Iran war and regional conflict that has led to Iranian missile fire on Gulf oil exporters.
It is intended to strengthen collective deterrence against any act of aggression and stipulates that an armed attack against any of the three would be regarded as an attack on all, similar to NATO’s Article 5 collective defence clause.
Foreign and defence ministers, as well as the chiefs of staff, of the three countries will attend the meeting in Istanbul, the ministry source said.
“International security issues will be on the agenda,” the source said, with discussions expected to cover enhancing defence capabilities, greater interoperability among their armed forces and deepening cooperation in the defence industry, including joint production and development.
The three nations share concerns about the military stances of Israel and revolutionary Shi’ite Iran, as long-time ally the US struggles to contain regional upheaval that has caused a global energy crisis.
Six months after the US and Israel launched the war against Iran, negotiations are at an impasse and President Donald Trump’s administration has stepped up efforts to punish Iran financially with what it has billed as an “economic D-Day”.
Turkey, which has NATO’s second-largest military, has said the pact with nuclear-armed Pakistan and top oil exporter Saudi Arabia was open to expansion — with Egypt as a potential candidate — and did not seek to replace existing alliances. REUTERS

US Treasury's Bessent faces G20 diplomacy test amid tariffs, Iran war, bond turmoil
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
10:05:37 UTC
19:05:37 KST

US Treasury's Bessent faces G20 diplomacy test amid tariffs, Iran war, bond turmoil
ASHEVILLE, North Carolina, Aug 30 - U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent faces a major test of his economic diplomacy skills this week as he presses finance leaders from the G20 major economies to shrink global trade imbalances, boost growth and sever business ties to Iran, while trying to calm worries about rising U.S. debt and bond yields.
After shunning the Group of 20 process last year in South Africa, Bessent is seeking to revamp it under U.S. leadership to push the Trump administration's worldview in the Blue Ridge Mountains city of Asheville, North Carolina.
The meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors on Monday and Tuesday comes at a time of massive uncertainty over the Trump administration's next tariff moves, its festering trade war with close ally Canada, and high energy and commodity prices due to the Iran war.
The unresolved conflict has kept the Strait of Hormuz closed, sapping growth from nearly all G20 economies. And Bessent has warned that countries face secondary U.S. sanctions if they continue to buy Iranian oil or facilitate other transactions with Tehran. On Friday he imposed curbs on a bank based in G20 member Egypt over links to Iran through its branches in the United Arab Emirates.
The combination of pressures adds up to potentially more discord in the widely diverse forum that includes China and Russia and has a hard time agreeing on any collective action while largely ignoring geopolitical tensions such as the war in Ukraine.
"Secretary Bessent will want to put Iran front and center and talk about tightening sanctions on Iran, and many countries around the G20 table will want to talk about anything else," said Josh Lipsky, international economics chair at the Atlantic Council. "They'll want to talk about tariffs."
After the Supreme Court struck down President Donald Trump's broad global tariffs in February under a national emergencies law, his administration has been rebuilding the levies under different legal authorities.
All of the G20 countries and the European Union were among 60 economies hit in July with 10% or 12.5% U.S. tariffs for allegedly lax enforcement of forced labor bans. Sixteen top U.S. trading partners -- more than half of them G20 members -- are in line for more tariffs to counteract alleged excess industrial capacity under a separate trade probe.
CUTTING IMBALANCES
The tariffs are central to the Trump administration's effort to reduce global trade imbalances, which a senior Treasury official said were the result of distortive government economic policies "that prevent fair competition" and that would be a major discussion topic at the Asheville meetings.
European officials are keen to discuss the growing flood of Chinese exports that is threatening their industries, including autos, a European official due to attend the meetings said.
With chronically weak domestic demand, China has doubled down on exports of electric vehicles, semiconductors and other goods, and its total exports rose 23.9% in July year-on-year. With high U.S. tariffs and an outright ban on Chinese vehicles, China's exports have flooded into Europe, prompting growing calls in the EU for tougher curbs on Chinese imports.
But G20 member China has shown little interest in longstanding calls for it to reduce industrial subsidies and rebalance its economy away from exports to internal consumer demand, while the International Monetary Fund estimates that China's yuan is undervalued by 21%.
But economists say that the U.S. has shown little interest in the other side of the equation: a major reduction in fiscal deficits that would help quell demand for imports. Total U.S. public debt crossed the $40 trillion mark on August 19 after doubling since 2017 during Trump's two terms and the intervening presidency of Joe Biden, and markets are growing edgy about the future U.S. debt trajectory.
Yields on 30-year debt reached their highest levels in 19 years this month, but Bessent surprised markets by announcing a doubling of scheduled buybacks of longer-dated Treasuries to $4 billion per operation, which cooled yields briefly.
The move drew criticism from Bessent's former Wall Street mentor, Stanley Druckenmiller, and has raised concerns among central bankers the Treasury may make more interventionist moves in a massive market known for its "regular and predictable" debt issuance.
Asked how Bessent would discuss the debt market concerns with G20 counterparts, a senior U.S. Treasury official said that the long-bond yields had "risen above what we consider fair value," and the Treasury was committed to bringing yields lower.
Bessent's corrective market tactics also have extended to G20 currencies, with an August 1 joint U.S. intervention with Japan to support the yen and October 2025 purchases of Argentine pesos.
G20 ministers attending the meeting "won’t buy into soothing words," said Mark Sobel, a former U.S. Treasury official who negotiated G20 communiques during both Republican and Democratic administrations.
"Further, their economies are being adversely hit by Trump’s war on Iran, which their countries don't support," said Sobel, now U.S. chair of the OMFIF monetary policy think tank. "No amount of US diplomacy can change those realities."
The U.S. push for more global growth, which the Treasury official said was anchored by reduced regulation, more energy production and private sector innovation, is part of an effort to return the G20 to its roots after focusing on issues promoted by host countries in recent years.
South Africa pressed G20 countries to address the climate crisis last year, while Brazil in 2024 pushed proposals to raise taxes on the wealthy.
The G20 got its start as a leaders-level forum during the 2008 global financial crisis to unleash measures to end the deepest recession since the 1930s. Its last major collective action came during the COVID-19 crisis in 2020, when member countries agreed to inject another $5 trillion into the global economy to combat job and income losses. REUTERS

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s Tzu Chi Foundation is providing emergency medical assistance and disaster relief in Nepal following catastrophic flash floods triggered by a glacier collapse.

A Tzu Chi medical team made up of local medical personnel and volunteers traveled to Dhading District, about 87 kilometers west of Kathmandu, to provide assistance and assess medical needs. The foundation has also mobilized local volunteers to purchase rice, beans, cooking utensils, and other necessities in Kathmandu for delivery to affected communities, per CNA.
Tzu Chi teams are also assisting hospitals in Chitwan District, where large numbers of bodies have been recovered following the disaster. The foundation said local volunteers reported shortages of cold-storage facilities and protective equipment needed for handling remains.
Tzu Chi said its headquarters in Taiwan has prepared additional relief supplies and is ready to dispatch aid as transportation conditions allow. Its Nepal teams are continuing to assess needs in affected communities and hospitals.

Norway’s churches hold memorial services to pay tribute to late King Harald

- King Harald was praised for his modern, modest monarchy despite family scandals, and a national mourning period has been declared.
- King Haakon will take an oath on Sept 1; no coronation is planned, but a consecration ceremony at Trondheim Cathedral is possible.
AI generated
ASKER, Norway – Norway’s new King Haakon VIII attended a memorial service on Aug 30, as churches across the Scandinavian kingdom paid tribute to his father, King Harald, who passed away two days before.
Members of the public lined up to catch a glimpse of the new king, 53, as he arrived with the royal family for a service in the church of Asker, just south of the capital.
The late king enjoyed massive support despite the slew of scandals that dogged his family in the final stretch of his 35-year reign.
Memorial services were planned in churches across the country, and outside Oslo Cathedral – where the government attended the service – hundreds started lining up in the morning to try and get a seat.
Standing in line, Aud Ragnhild Skar, a lecturer at University of Oslo, told AFP that it felt “natural” to take part in the service.
“I’ve been deeply affected by the fact that King Harald has died. I felt a desire to be part of the community and to share the grief over his passing,” Skar said.
‘Beloved’
Also waiting in line was nurse Sissel Engedal, who said Harald had been “a very significant and important and beloved king”.
A national period of mourning has been declared. No date has been set for the funeral.
On Sept 1, King Haakon will swear an oath of allegiance in Parliament.
King Haakon and his wife, Queen Mette-Marit, are not expected to be crowned in a ceremony – Norway abolished coronations in 1908.
But, like his father and grandfather before him, Haakon could opt for a consecration ceremony at Trondheim Cathedral, where Norwegian monarchs were crowned between 1814 and 1906.
Harald was widely seen as the embodiment of an open and tolerant Norway, and praised for leading a monarchy that was modern and modest.
“Above all, you were a person who remained committed to your values and dedicated to your duties,” Haakon said of his father in his first public speech which was broadcast on Aug 29.
The new monarch also said it had been “deeply moving to see all the people, candles, messages and flowers filling up the Palace Square”.
“We greatly mourn his loss. At the same time, it gives us consolation and strength to know that there are so many who are grieving with us,” the king said.
Harald had been in hospital in Oslo since Aug 17, suffering from haemolytic anaemia, a condition caused by an abnormally rapid destruction of red blood cells that leads to fatigue and shortness of breath.
He faced mounting health problems in his final years, forcing him to scale back his official schedule.
The past year has been a turbulent one for the Norwegian royal family. Queen Sonja, also 89, was herself briefly admitted to hospital in May due to heart problems.
Haakon’s wife, Mette-Marit, is under scrutiny for her ties to the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
And in June, Mette-Marit’s son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Hoiby, was sentenced to four years in prison for two rapes, a sentence he is appealing against.
Mette-Marit, 53, who suffers from a serious lung disease, underwent a lung transplant in July. AFP

19:05:00 KST

The death toll from a Russian strike on an ammunition depot in Ukraine's Kyiv region has risen to 38, with four people still missing, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Sunday.
The deadliest Russian strike in the Kyiv area this year took place late Friday as Moscow launched an intense campaign of attacks on the Ukrainian capital, which has continued over the weekend.
Friday's blast hit a military facility that held artillery shells, mines, drones and other ammunition.
Zelenskyy said on Telegram that first responders had managed to extinguish most of the fires. However, the scale of contamination in the area was significant and this work would continue for as long as necessary.
The president released video footage showing firefighting teams battling blazes and removing debris from destroyed buildings.
In its intensified attacks on the country, Russia over the last week launched nearly 2,000 strike drones, more than 1,600 aerial bombs, and 31 missiles, including North Korean ballistic missiles, Zelenskyy said.
"We are seeking just responses to every Russian strike and crime. They will certainly come," he said.
Overnight Saturday, plumes of black smoke poured over the capital's western suburbs, while videos published by Ukraine's rescue services showed homes near the blast epicenter in flames, reported Agence France-Presse (AFP).
The attack was the second to hit a munitions depot near Kyiv in less than two months, with officials expressing anger that arms were still being stored so close to residential areas.
Both Russia and Ukraine have intensified long-range strikes on each other in recent months, pushing civilian casualties to their highest level since Moscow invaded in 2022.
"Those who allowed this to happen must be held accountable for their decisions ... ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas," President Zelenskyy said in a post on X.
The blast forced hundreds to evacuate and damaged multiple homes, including a care facility for elderly and disabled people, he added.
The mayor of the nearby town of Dmytrivka were also among the dead, Kyiv region Gov. Tymur Tkachenko said on Telegram.
Residents in the area told AFP the explosion was "terrifying."
"We thought we were being bombed. No one knew it was a detonation," said Yana Doneli, resident of a nearby town.
Zelenskyy blamed the incident on "horrific negligence," saying ammunition should not have been stored there.
Ukrainian prosecutors said they had opened an investigation into criminal negligence.
"On Aug. 28 at around 8:10 p.m. (1710 GMT), an unmanned aerial vehicle ... fell on or struck the grounds of an enterprise in the town of Myla," the office of Ukraine's prosecutor general said.
Myla is a small town on the outskirts of western Kyiv.
"A large-scale fire broke out on the enterprise's grounds and detonation began," prosecutors added.
The prosecutor's office said that its investigation would focus on "the legality of the ... storage of explosive objects and materials on the enterprise's grounds," as well as whether the owner, whom it did not name, had the "necessary permits and approvals."
Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergiy Koretsky expressed regret that a "lesson" had not been learned following a previous deadly strike on a munitions depot near Kyiv in July.
That investigation revealed serious failings on the part of a state-owned company, which did not comply with regulations regarding the proximity of residential buildings.
"In the fifth year of the full-scale invasion, making the same mistakes over and over is criminal negligence," he said on Telegram.
"Everyone responsible, without exception, must face severe punishment so that such situations never happen again," said Koretsky.

The Best Label Makers for an Organized Home
Featured in this article
There’s something oddly satisfying about a perfectly labeled spice rack or a pantry with bins that specify exactly what they contain—even if it’s plain as day that the “pasta” bin contains boxes of dried penne. Taking a label maker to the most clutter-laden corners of my home helps me feel organized. And frankly, feeling organized externally often helps me feel organized internally, too.
With that in mind, I researched, selected, and tested some of the top home label makers to see how intuitive different devices were to use and how well their labels stuck to my kids’ dresser drawers, toy bins, water bottles, and lunchboxes. Read on for my thoughts about the best machines for various needs. Just beware that household organizing with a label printer can get addicting and lead to joy-inducing clean spaces.

Also Tested
Nelko P21 for $22: This adorably pocket-sized, affordable, direct thermal label maker is easy to keep at the ready (or even in a tote bag for on-demand label-making emergencies), but actually using it is kind of a lot of work. Its companion app offers plenty of fun templates, but a lot of them are behind a paywall. I only discovered this when I printed a “Pasta” label for a pantry bin, and it came out with a watermark-like overlay. Once I made my own simple label, I struggled to calibrate the label tape to get the pre-cut stickers appropriately centered for my design. Even after I did figure it out, I realized I had to recalibrate the tape for each subsequent print. That’s because there’s no perforation or internal cutting mechanism, so you have to pull out the label tape a bit after it’s printed, which then moves the rest of the pre-cut roll of labels off-center. If you don’t remember to recalibrate, your next label will print off-center as well. I’m sure with enough trial and error, this process would become second nature, but the learning curve for the Nelko was nonetheless the steepest of all the label makers I tried.
FAQs
What Are the Different Kinds of Label Makers?
The top label makers I’ve included in the list use either thermal transfer printing or direct thermal printing. Direct thermal printing works by heating special paper, which is a process that yields labels that are less durable under various conditions and also more likely to fade over time. Thermal transfer printing works by melting ink from a ribbon cartridge onto a label. These labels tend to be more durable and longer-lasting. Thermal-transfer label makers also typically require slightly larger, more expensive machines.
Are Bluetooth or Traditional Label Makers Better?
Neither is inherently better, but each offers its own benefits. Traditional label makers have on-device keyboards where you type your label and customize font sizes, styles, symbols, and borders. Bluetooth-enabled label makers work by pairing the device with a mobile app on which you design your label, and then print it remotely. Often, these apps feature a wider variety of templates and font options than traditional label makers. Apps also typically show a more accurate preview than LCD screens on label makers themselves. Some label makers, like the best overall Brother PT-n25bt, offer both on-device and app-enabled designing.
Can You Use Label Maker Labels on Clothing?
It’s not recommended unless the label tape in question specifically mentions being able to work with fabric, like the TZe fabric label tape for the P-touch Cube Plus. Some label tape does claim to be heat-resistant and water-resistant, but even in this case, the label’s adhesive quality is likely to degrade after a bunch of cycles in the washer and dryer.
How I Tested These Label Makers
I considered popular options, and I received some testing units as samples from the company and bought others. I tested the functionality of each device by creating labels with an on-device keyboard, designing labels in a companion app and printing via Bluetooth compatibility, or both, depending on the label maker in question’s capabilities. I tested the durability of the top machines’ labels by sticking them on various surfaces, seeing if they could get wet and handle heat without fading or losing their adhesive strength over the course of at least one week, often longer.

Documents leaked by Trump official to bolster a conspiracy show ‘absolutely nothing’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
10:00:53 UTC
19:00:53 KST

A botched leak of purportedly explosive government files to a prominent conservative online personality was supposed to offer proof of what the Trump administration and its allies have long alleged: that a little-known office inside the US state department, created to fight foreign propaganda, had secretly become a tool for domestic censorship.
Two former high-ranking officials at the Global Engagement Center (GEC), a target of Republican ire that lost its funding in 2024 and was disbanded after Donald Trump’s return to office in 2025, say the documents show nothing of the kind.
Instead, they argue, the files are a symptom of a protracted and bitter political fight over an office that spent nearly a decade tracking and countering foreign influence operations, particularly from Russia, China and Iran.
And the state department is now resuming some of this work in other parts of its operation, including plans – laid out in a proposal reviewed by the Guardian – to pay social media influencers across south-east Asia as part of an $11m campaign to counter Chinese propaganda.
Sarah Rogers, the state department’s undersecretary for public diplomacy, provided the so-called “GEC files” to Jennica Pounds, a rightwing online data analyst known as DataRepublican – only for Pounds to claim earlier this month she was leaked the documents as part of a bid to “entrap” her.
Rogers, who denied this claim, then published the files herself, claiming officials inside the center “betrayed their stated mission”. The files included a 2022 GEC report on “gendered disinformation”, a flashpoint in the culture wars.
“These guys have consistently misrepresented what the GEC did, and this was a great example of that,” said Daniel Kimmage, who served as the center’s principal deputy coordinator and acting coordinator from its founding in 2017 until its complete dissolution in 2025. His own congressional testimony was included in the leaked files.
Kimmage and Carrie Goux, a Joe Biden appointee and the center’s former acting deputy coordinator, say nothing in the material shows the GEC, whose mandate was explicitly foreign-facing, ever turned its tools on Americans.
“If the smoking gun was a gendered disinformation report, that feels like they came up short,” Goux said. “There seems to be absolutely nothing here.”
Weaponization
The dispute is the latest chapter in a years-long campaign by conservatives to portray the GEC as part of a broader effort by the US government and technology companies to suppress rightwing speech.
Republican congressmen including Michael McCaul, former chair of the House foreign affairs committee, argued in a July 2024 letter that the GEC was “at best indifferent to, and at worst complicit in” stretching the definition of disinformation to “censor” conservative speech in the US.
Trump’s return to the presidency drew this view into the heart of the federal government. The center was abolished in 2025, and what remained of its work scattered across the state department.
Much of that Republican-led campaign centered on how the GEC had funded the Global Disinformation Index (GDI), a UK-based non-profit that rates media outlets by how likely they are to spread disinformation, to help monitor propaganda in Asia. But in 2022 the GDI separately published its own study of the US media market that rated several conservative outlets, including Newsmax, One America News and the New York Post, as high-risk – a finding its critics have cited ever since as evidence that a foreign-facing office had funded a group meddling in domestic politics.
The question raised by the files leaked this month is narrower, however: whether they show the GEC itself ran a domestic censorship operation. Kimmage and Goux insist they do not.
Kimmage said his own congressional testimony, which Rogers included in the leak, had been selectively read. “If you look at the transcript, [the question was], ‘Does GEC take positions on US outlets?’ And I said, ‘No, it didn’t,’” he said.
Rogers “tried to twist that into something that it wasn’t”, according to Kimmage. “For people who talk a lot about weaponization of government, this seems a lot closer to the weaponization of government and psy-opping of the American people than anything that the emails from the Global Engagement Center show.”
‘False’ allegations
Pounds, the rightwing analyst, is not a neutral bystander. Days after the documents were released, she disclosed that she had been quietly working since July as a special government employee for the defense department.
On Friday, Pounds released a database to track US citizens in the Democratic Socialists of America. The Pentagon did not respond when asked whether the database is included in her scope of government work.
Both former senior officials, Kimmage and Goux, draw a sharp line between the accusations made by critics of the GEC and what the center actually did. “We were not ever looking at Americans,” Goux said. “We were looking at the foreign actors and what their [tactics, techniques and procedures] … are doing overseas.”
The GEC “did what its congressional mandate charged it to do, which is to fight foreign [misinformation and] disinformation”, added Kimmage. “This allegation that it’s censoring Americans is false.”
During its almost decade-long existence, the center published eight detailed public reports on Russian and Chinese information operations and ran four major exposures of Russian disinformation campaigns – in Latin America, Africa and Moldova, and on the Kremlin-linked network RT.
Its largest such operation traced a Kremlin-backed effort called the “African Initiative”, which the center said had recruited local journalists, bloggers and public figures to spread conspiracy theories about US-funded health programs across the continent.
In January 2024, the GEC helped broker an international pact on countering foreign state disinformation that eventually drew more than two dozen government signatories, among them Moldova, Spain, Estonia, Poland and Finland – a framework its backers hoped other countries would use to build their own version of the office.
A 2022 inspector general review found the GEC “generally effective” at supporting counter-disinformation programs overall, while flagging weaknesses in its internal controls, contractor oversight and strategic planning. That record was enough to sustain bipartisan support: senators Rob Portman, a Republican, and Chris Murphy, a Democrat, repeatedly pushed to fund and strengthen the center, and its authorization survived multiple renewal fights before House Republicans, increasingly focused on the domestic-speech question, declined to extend it again in 2024.
That mandate cost roughly $61m per year. The GEC employed about 120 people before Congress declined to reauthorize it, letting the office lapse at the end of 2024. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, later folded what remained of its work into a new counter foreign information manipulation and interference office, framing the closure as an end to wasteful, censorious government overreach.
Trust exercise
Now, less than a year after the GEC shut down, a proposal reviewed by the Guardian shows the state department preparing to pay up to 30 online influencers across 11 countries in south-east Asia $2,500 apiece as part of an $11m, multi-year campaign to counter Chinese propaganda.
The project, which would be operated by the US Mission to USEAN, has three parts: a $5m messaging campaign, a $3m program training influencers and journalists to counter Chinese propaganda, and a $3m trip bringing about 180 participants to studios in Washington and Houston “for intensive collaboration, studio production and first-hand engagement with US institutions and creators”.
The proposal’s planning materials describe the ideal recruit as starting from a “welcoming” position of what one document calls the “rejecting-affirming continuum”: someone not yet sold on the US, but not hostile either. As participants move through the accelerator, the materials say, exposure to evidence of US commitment in the region and training in spotting propaganda from China (which has reportedly invested billions of dollars in disinformation efforts globally) is meant to carry them toward the “affirming” end of that scale, publicly backing closer ties with Washington on trade, tech standards and the South China Sea.
The document cited the rightwing analyst and new Pentagon special government employee, Jennica Pounds, the DataRepublican, as an ideal model to seek out in other recruits abroad.
Contacted for comment, the state department declined to directly address questions about the documents released by Rogers, the influencer proposal, the department’s current foreign influence programs and whether other regions are being targeted as well.
A state department official said: “Undersecretary Rogers has been clear that the department will continue to confront censorship, anti-American propaganda and coercive influence directly while demonstrating the enduring advantages of freedom, accountability and open communication.”
Meanwhile, the office of policy, planning and resources for public diplomacy (R/PPR) was separately shopping for commercial help with a similar mission this spring. A government filing from May 2026 shows the R/PPR requesting information from vendors on software that can mine open-source data, map “adversarial propaganda influence networks” and detect deepfakes.
That apparent contradiction is not lost on the GEC’s former staff.
“Are they trying to re-create it? Probably,” Goux said. “But now they’re spending a lot more tax dollars doing that, trying to get contractors to do some of the stuff that we were doing.”
Goux put the broader cost in plainer terms still. “The US has lost their seat at the table to do that, and that’s unfortunate,” she said. “I hope we can gain it back, but we’re losing trust too, and that’s significant.”

Emotional infidelity is linked to a surprising mix of dark and light personality traits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
10:00:49 UTC
19:00:49 KST

A recent study indicates that the tendency to become emotionally and mentally preoccupied with someone outside of a romantic relationship is driven by a complex mix of personality traits and relationship dynamics. The research suggests that this type of infidelity is not just tied to dark or impulsive personality traits, but also to generally positive characteristics like emotional sensitivity. The findings were published in Psychological Reports.
Infidelity is a common issue in romantic relationships, often leading to emotional distress and couples therapy. Historically, people have defined infidelity through physical acts, but modern perspectives recognize that subtle psychological behaviors also play a major role in relationship disengagement. One such phenomenon is extradyadic infatuation. This term describes a state where a person maintains their primary relationship but becomes cognitively, emotionally, and motivationally preoccupied with someone else.
To better grasp why some people develop these alternative attractions, scientists look at individual personality differences and relationship quality. For instance, a 2019 systematic review found that a combination of personal background and relationship dynamics strongly influences whether someone engages in infidelity.
Personality traits are often categorized into broad frameworks to understand interpersonal behavior. The Dark Triad consists of Machiavellianism (a tendency toward manipulation and emotional detachment), narcissism (an inflated sense of importance), and psychopathy (impulsivity and a lack of empathy). On the other hand, the Light Triad focuses on prosocial human characteristics. Introduced in a 2019 study, the Light Triad framework includes Kantianism (treating people as ends rather than means), humanism (valuing the dignity of individuals), and faith in humanity (believing in human goodness).
Another relevant trait is sociosexuality, which describes a person’s willingness to engage in casual sex without emotional commitment. Research, such as a 2021 study of young adults, indicates that dark personality traits and an openness to casual sex frequently interact to influence how people pursue short-term romantic encounters. The authors of the new study aimed to see how this blend of dark traits, light traits, sociosexuality, and relationship satisfaction predicts the specific experience of extradyadic infatuation.
“What initially caught our attention was the idea that infidelity is not always as straightforward as we tend to think,” said study author Teodora-Elena Huțanu, a PhD student at the Faculty of Psychology and Education Sciences at Alexandru Ioan Cuza University of Iași in Romania. “Rather than viewing infidelity simply as a matter of ‘good’ versus ‘bad’ people, we wanted to explore a more nuanced picture that considers Dark and Light Triad personality traits, sociosexuality, and relationship quality.”
The research involved a sample of 303 Romanian adults. Participants were between 19 and 64 years old and were currently in a committed romantic relationship. A key requirement for participation was that respondents had to report liking or feeling attracted to someone they knew personally, other than their current partner. Most of the participants were women, and the majority were married or in long-term relationships.
The respondents completed several questionnaires. They answered items assessing their Dark Triad and Light Triad traits. They also completed measures of their sociosexuality, rating their attitudes, behaviors, and desires regarding uncommitted sex. Finally, participants rated their current relationship satisfaction and the intensity of their extradyadic infatuation, which included their thoughts, emotions, and desires regarding their outside attraction.
In their initial analysis, the scientists found that people scoring higher on any of the Light Triad traits tended to report less extradyadic infatuation. Those scoring higher on Dark Triad traits, sociosexuality, or who had lower relationship satisfaction tended to report higher levels of infatuation.
When the researchers analyzed all these factors together to see which ones independently predicted extradyadic infatuation, a more complicated picture emerged. High psychopathy, high sociosexuality, and low relationship satisfaction reliably predicted greater preoccupation with an outside person. A lack of faith in humanity also predicted higher infatuation, suggesting that people with cynical views about others might invest less in their primary relationship and look elsewhere.
Interestingly, two traits behaved differently than expected once other variables were accounted for. Humanism, which initially seemed protective, became a positive predictor of infatuation. The researchers suggest that the emotional sensitivity and openness characteristic of humanism might make people more receptive to forming deep, emotionally meaningful connections with alternative partners.
In contrast, Machiavellianism became a negative predictor in the final analysis. Because extradyadic infatuation requires sustained emotional and cognitive energy, people high in Machiavellianism might avoid such intense attachments due to their preference for strategic, detached interactions. Narcissism and Kantianism did not emerge as statistically significant predictors in the final model.
“What surprised us most was that, even when looking at extradyadic infatuation as a more cognitive, emotional, and motivational form of infidelity, rather than simply as a behavioral transgression, some less adaptive psychological characteristics still remained relevant,” Huțanu explained. “At the same time, the unexpected changes in direction for Machiavellianism and Humanism were also particularly informative.”
“Our findings showed that both Dark and Light Triad traits contributed to its prediction, but in different directions,” Huțanu noted. “This is particularly interesting because it suggests that extradyadic infatuation cannot simply be understood as the result of being manipulative, impulsive, or otherwise ‘dark’.”
“Some of the characteristics involved may also reflect greater emotional receptivity and openness to meaningful interpersonal connections,” she added. “So, rather than asking whether someone who experiences extradyadic infatuation is simply a ‘good’ or ‘bad’ person, we may need to look at what kind of psychological and relational processes are making another person emotionally salient in the first place.”
The study has a few limitations to consider. The sample consisted mostly of women, which might restrict how well the results apply to men. Additionally, the researchers did not account for different relationship agreements, such as whether participants were in strictly monogamous partnerships or consensually non-monogamous arrangements. Open relationship structures might alter how traits like sociosexuality interact with relationship satisfaction.
“An important caveat is that we assessed extradyadic infatuation rather than actual infidelity behavior; therefore, we cannot determine whether participants acted sexually or otherwise on their attraction to an extradyadic person,” Huțanu said. “In addition, extradyadic infatuation may partly reflect an idealized or imagined representation of the other person, particularly when the actual interpersonal bond is limited.”
Because the data was collected at a single point in time, the findings cannot determine whether these personality traits cause infatuation, or if they simply tend to co-occur. “In my future research I would like to clarify how these cognitions and emotions unfold over time and whether extradyadic infatuation ultimately translates into behavioral infidelity or sustained extradyadic relationships,” Huțanu explained. “I am quite confident that this research is only the beginning of a broader effort to highlight more nuanced and comprehensive perspectives on infidelity, which may be psychologically more complex than its behavioral expression suggests.”
The study, “Personality, Relationship Quality, and Infidelity: Extradyadic Infatuation as Predicted by Dark and Light Triad Traits, Sociosexuality and Relationship Satisfaction,” was authored by Teodora-Elena Huțanu and Andrei Corneliu Holman.
