The home front: How Israel, Iran, and US leaders have been hit by the war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
09:32:26 UTC
18:32:26 KST

The home front: How Israel, Iran, and US leaders have been hit by the war
Six months into the US-Israel war on Iran, the governments in the three countries are all fighting political wars at home.
Six months ago, the United States and Israel struck targets across Tehran, killing Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other Iranian leaders.
It fulfilled a long-held ambition of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for a joint attack with the US on Iran, with Washington now locked in a war from which it is unable to extricate itself.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4US-Israel war on Iran, six months down the line: In numbers
- list 2 of 4After six months of war, what have US, Iran gained and lost?
- list 3 of 4Six months into the Iran war, a new Gulf security architecture is emerging
- list 4 of 4Iran’s leaders acknowledge economic toll of war, pledge diplomacy, defence
The US’s stated war aims also appear not to have been achieved, with President Donald Trump’s initial claim that Iran’s nuclear capacity had been destroyed now appearing false.
Netanyahu might have hoped that the fall of the government in Tehran would be part of his election campaign. And in Iran, the consequences of six months of war have done little to reverse the struggling economy, which appears to be the government’s Achilles heel.
United States
The cost-of-living crisis was the mainstay of Trump’s criticisms of the previous administration of Joe Biden during the 2024 US election, but petrol prices alone have risen by 50 percent since the war on Iran began on February 28.
Trump’s repeated empty claims that a deal with Iran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz is imminent appear to be doing little to help his struggling Republican Party ahead of midterm elections due to take place in November.
Numerous surveys show Trump’s approval rating is at a record low, with criticism of his foreign policy competing with disapproval of his domestic record.
“The economic cost of the war is becoming a key issue for many,” Shibley Telhami, government and politics professor at the University of Maryland, told Al Jazeera.
Adding to the pressure on Trump are reports that he entered the unpopular war on Iran at the behest of Netanyahu, with fewer than one in three Americans supportive of the conflict, according to a recent Ipsos poll.
“There was a perception, certainly among Democrats but initially young Republicans, that this was a war that Israel had dragged the US into,” Telhami said. “The issue of Israel has risen in public priorities, as it is now not just a foreign policy issue but also a pocketbook and core values issue.”
In a bid to pile pressure on the Iranian government to agree to a deal that is more favourable to the US, Trump imposed new sanctions on Tehran last week, which he dubbed “Economic D-Day”.
Still, despite the costly effects of the war and sanctions on the Iranian economy and the destruction to its military, American author and diplomat Aaron David Miller pointed out that the government in Tehran has survived.
“The highly enriched uranium is still in the country and could still be enriched. Iran has also weaponised geography, in that it’s essentially closed off the Strait,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Likewise, their proxies in Hamas and Hezbollah, while much reduced, are still in place and still have capacity. The public unrest or internal dissent the US had hoped for hasn’t arisen. In terms of Iranian deterrence, it’s been a huge success for Tehran.”
The failure of Trump and Netanyahu’s military endeavour in Iran could have long-term effects on US foreign policy.
“No future administration is likely going to consider such a military campaign again,” said Miller.
Israel
Ahron Bregman, an Israeli security analyst and senior teaching fellow at King’s College London, said Netanyahu is viewed as having failed in Gaza, Lebanon and now in Iran. For Netanyahu, the war in Iran is perceived by many Israelis as a major security error.
“Netanyahu is trailing in the polls and for good reason,” Bregman said. “Instead of concentrating on stopping Iran from getting the bomb, he focused on – and convinced Trump to join him – regime change. It all failed, and Iran is now closer than ever to having the bomb.”
The US decision to sign a memorandum of understanding with Iran, without Israel’s involvement in June, provided Netanyahu’s political opponents with multiple reasons to attack the prime minister.
“I think Netanyahu was hoping this would be the electoral game-changer,” former Israeli government adviser Daniel Levy told Al Jazeera. “The war hasn’t gone as planned, so it hasn’t given him that momentum. If anything, it joins the list of things where he’s overpromised and underdelivered, given how much was expected of it as a decisive moment.”
The view that Iran still poses a fundamental threat to Israel, and the war has done nothing to minimise this, is a widely held belief among Israelis.
“I think [Netanyahu is] in favour of the economic ‘D-Day’ measures, not because he believes they’ll be decisive or that Iran will capitulate in talks, but because he’s hoping they’ll drive Trump’s frustration and put re-escalation back on the agenda, and that this time, things will look different,” Levy added.
Iran
Despite the Iranian government remaining in place, the sanctions and the US siege on Iranian ports do appear to be affecting the Iranian economy.
By Iran’s own reckoning, the war had already cost the economy upwards of $145bn by April, with annual inflation hitting 66 percent just last month. Taken in isolation, the US blockade could be inflicting $435m a day on the country. But the economy is still proving resilient to these challenges.
“I don’t want to downplay the effects of a crippled economy and of inflation, but my sense is that these pains remain manageable,” Shervin Malekzade, an academic and author on Iran, told Al Jazeera.
Iran’s entire political and military system was rooted in “the timeless task of preserving Iranian sovereignty and dignity against the world”, he added, helping it manage any economic challenges.
But there are still differences on economic issues within the Iranian government and a public rift between hardliners and moderates on the future of talks with the US.
Irrespective of the domestic political challenges thrown up by the war, none of the belligerents can concede defeat.
For Iran, the standoff with the US and Israel has gone beyond establishing deterrence and is a matter of survival.
Trump’s failure to deliver a short and decisive victory against Iran, and the economic and political costs of the war, will likely affect Republicans’ performance in the upcoming midterms.
For Israel, Iran remains no less of a perceived profound and existential threat than it did on February 27.

🔴 Iceland rejects restarting EU accession talks in referendum
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
09:31:40 UTC
18:31:40 KST

Iceland rejects restarting EU accession talks in referendum
Icelanders voted to reject reopening EU membership talks, official results showed Sunday, dealing a blow to the government's push to join the bloc and handing a win to those who argued the country's prized fishing waters were too important to risk. The results will disappoint Brussels, which had hoped to welcome the Nordic country as a new member.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Iceland's voters rejected restarting negotiations to join the European Union in a referendum that pitted concerns about geopolitical stability against keeping national control of Iceland’s prized fisheries, officials said Sunday.
Opponents defeated the measure by a margin of 52.8% to 47.2%, the National Electoral Commission said. The result puts the divisive issue to rest for now — more than a decade after a euroskeptic government ended EU talks that had begun after the 2008 financial crisis.
The vote Saturday was held in the shadow of repeated threats by US President Donald Trump to take control of nearby Greenland. Although Iceland is a NATO member, supporters said European solidarity would provide greater protection if Trump ever made similar threats toward the volcanic island.
Iceland’s left-leaning coalition government, elected in 2024, moved up the EU referendum it had planned for next year after Trump mistakenly named Iceland four times while speaking about his designs on Greenland.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadóttir said she did not see the loss as a setback for her coalition government but as a win for democracy as more than 82% of the eligible 270,000 voters cast ballots. She said she would respect the result but would not rule out a future attempt to reopen the issue.
“Things happened in the past couple of years, though, that I could not have predicted,” she said. “But this government will not go forward with it. And something big has to change in the next 24 months for this to be at the top of the agenda.”
Guðrún Hafsteinsdóttir, leader of the opposition Independence Party who opposed the measure, said the result is a blow to the government but not European relations.
“The best way to heal the wounds is for the government to listen to the conclusion and put this path aside,” she told RUV, the national broadcaster. “Because we want to remain in close contact with the European Union, Europe and as many other countries as possible, the nation is sending a clear message that we intend to steer that course ourselves.”
Voters faced a simple yes-or-no question: Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?
The capital of Reykjavik was the only area in the island nation of 400,000 people where a majority supported the referendum.
The influential fishing industry led opposition to the referendum over fears the bloc’s common fisheries policy would open its waters to Spanish, Dutch and other trawlers.
Descendants of Vikings, Icelanders, who won their independence from Denmark in 1944, have lived off the sea for centuries, and fishing is central to their national identity. Iceland has a proud history of refusing to be pushed around by bigger and richer European nations, winning the so-called Cod Wars with Britain in the 1970s over the right to control its waters.
Opponents also rallied around the fact that Iceland already reaps benefits from being in the EU’s frictionless single market and the Schengen free-travel zone without the sovereignty compromises that come with full membership. They argued that Iceland’s voice would be muted in the large European Parliament and that it would be better off cutting its own trade deals, such as one with China.
Backers said EU membership would lower inflation and interest rates, and the euro would bring more stability than Iceland’s volatile króna currency. They said it was also in the nation’s interest to get closer to its European neighbors to tackle issues that don’t respect borders, such as climate change.
If the proposal had been approved, it would have been a preliminary step to revive the lengthy negotiating process with the EU’s executive branch, the European Commission, to discuss areas from the economy to human rights. Voters would have needed to approve any negotiated deal.
The result is sure to disappoint many in the European Union. As a wealthy, stable and democratic country with vast fishing grounds, Iceland could have joined the bloc relatively quickly. Croatia was the last country to join, in 2013.
Most of the other candidates waiting — including several countries in the Balkans, plus Moldova and conflict-torn Ukraine — must still undertake time-consuming reforms to bring their laws and standards into line with those of the EU.
Getting Iceland into Europe’s rich club, perhaps along with Montenegro and possibly Moldova, over the next two years could have helped to lay to rest the damage to the EU caused by the departure of Britain in 2020, even though London now appears willing to mend ties.
Voter Daniel Bjarkason, who opposed the measure, said Iceland should wait a decade or two before trying again to join the EU.
“For now we’re too divided and that’s not a good look,” he said. “It should be 70-30 Yes if we’re going to do it.”
(FRANCE 24 with AP)

Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
09:30:18 UTC
18:30:18 KST

Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
Ancient Egyptian princesses may have been skilled archers and weapon users, not simply royals buried with symbolic arms.
- Date:
- August 30, 2026
- Source:
- Frontiers
- Summary:
- Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.
- Share:
For years, archaeologists have debated why some ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. The bows, arrows, daggers, and maces found in their tombs were often interpreted as ceremonial objects rather than equipment the women had actually used. A new examination of royal mummies from Egypt's Middle Kingdom now suggests that at least some of these women were physically trained to handle such weapons.
"Members of the royal family, especially the women, were active participants in skilled, physically demanding activities such as archery and hunting," said Dr. Zeinab Hashesh, lead author of the article in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. "This conclusion is supported by the way their bones developed to sustain heavy muscle use, which corresponds directly to the weapons discovered in their tombs."
Royal Mummies Rediscovered at Dahshur
The research focused on six royal mummies originally uncovered during the 1890s at Dahshur, an Egyptian burial complex containing pyramids and shaft tombs. The remains later disappeared from scholarly attention for many years before being identified again in the Egyptian Museum during a curation project in 2020.
Four of the six individuals were sisters and daughters of the pharaoh Amenemhat II. They had been placed in matching underground burial chambers. Princess Ita was buried beside Princess Khenmet, while Princess Itaweret was interred alongside an unidentified woman who has tentatively been identified as Princess Sathathormeryt.
Their tombs contained objects more commonly associated with male burials, including bows and arrows. Princess Ita's coffin also held an especially ornate dagger. Similar royal objects were found with the two other individuals included in the investigation, Princess Noub-Hotep and King Hor.
All six bodies had been carefully mummified, but preservation was incomplete. Their soft tissues had deteriorated into powder, while portions of the skeletons were also missing. The princesses' skulls, for example, were lost during the early 1900s.
Even so, enough skeletal material survived in good condition for researchers to estimate age at death, height, and sex. The bones also provided evidence of past injuries, illnesses, and other aspects of the individuals' health.
Bones Reveal Archery and Weapon Use
"Princess Ita was a young woman aged between 28 and 34 with strong upper-body muscle attachments, suggesting she habitually used weapons like maces or daggers," said Hashesh. "Princess Khenmet was a woman in her late 30s or 40s who showed signs of thinning bones, but had very robust ligament attachments. Princess Itaweret was a young woman aged between 20 and 34 who survived broken ribs and foot fractures; her skeleton shows she was a skilled archer."
The sisters' skeletons contained unusually robust muscle attachments, indicating that they regularly performed strenuous physical activities. Those patterns closely match the movements required to use the weapons placed in their graves. Comparable skeletal evidence also suggests that Princess Noub-Hotep and King Hor practiced archery.
"We found pronounced development in the upper limbs of these individuals, which correlates to repetitive, high-intensity actions like pulling a bowstring or stabilizing a weapon, proving these activities were habitual throughout their lives," explained Hashesh. "This directly explains the presence of bows, arrows, and maces in the women's tombs; these were not just symbolic gifts but tools they actively used."
The findings suggest that repeated weapon use was part of these royals' lives rather than an occasional activity. Their physical development points to long-term practice involving demanding movements such as drawing a bowstring or controlling a weapon.
Injuries Point to Physically Demanding Lives
Several of the individuals also showed evidence of trauma, infections, and nutritional deficiencies. Princess Itaweret had suffered broken ribs, probably caused by a blow or a fall from a height, as well as fractures in her feet.
The sisters shared rare abnormalities in their spines as well. Researchers say this pattern indicates that their parents and the broader royal family were closely related.
"These injuries were most likely caused by accidents, falls, hard blows, or other impacts linked to an active lifestyle, whether through hunting, military training, or other demanding activities," said Hashesh. "What is remarkable is that the injuries healed well, which suggests they had access to advanced medical care for their time."
The fact that these injuries healed successfully provides another clue about royal life. Despite experiencing significant physical trauma, the princesses appear to have received medical treatment that allowed them to recover.
Reconstructing the Lives of Egypt's Royal Women
There are still important limits to what researchers can learn from the remains. The loss of the princesses' skulls restricts the kinds of analyses that can be performed, and the team has not yet completed every type of investigation it hopes to conduct.
One planned approach is stable isotope analysis, which could provide additional information about diet and help researchers better understand evidence of nutritional deficiencies.
"Our dream would be to go far beyond simply identifying the Dahshur royals," said Hashesh. "We would try to tell their full life stories, their families, health, and even their political roles, with as much detail as possible. Beyond the science, we would preserve the remains, create 3D prints for teaching and virtual exhibitions, and display them alongside their jewelry, weapons, and funerary objects. All of this would be done with respect, ensuring the remains are presented ethically, just as they were originally buried.
"Their objects and jewelry are truly fascinating, breathtaking in their craftsmanship. Yet, while archaeologists have long focused on preserving these treasures, the people themselves were often forgotten. Our study seeks to change that."
Story Source:
Materials provided by Frontiers. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Zeinab Hashesh, Ahmed Gabr, Roxie Walker. Bioarchaeological reassessment of Dahshur royal skeletal remains from the Late Middle Kingdom (c. 1850–1700 BCE). Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology, 2026; 5 DOI: 10.3389/fearc.2026.1844402

Ukrainian drone maker lands $10.4 million funding round
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
09:30:08 UTC
18:30:08 KST

- Buntar Aerospace raised $10.4 million from Axon Enterprise and Munkene AS, ranking among Ukraine's six largest disclosed funding rounds this year.
- Ukrainian defense tech funding rose 119 percent to more than $129 million in 2025, with foreign investors providing 49 percent of it.
Ukrainian drone maker Buntar Aerospace raised $10.4 million in funding from Axon Enterprise and Munkene AS, placing the round among the six largest disclosed funding rounds in Ukraine this year, according to venture capital firm Defence Builder, citing data from Vestbee.
The full list, in order of size: language-learning platform Preply at $150 million, UFORCE at $50 million, streaming platform HolyWater Tech at $22 million, quantum computing startup Haiqu at $11 million, Buntar Aerospace at $10.4 million, and Farsight Vision at $7.9 million. Four of the six companies on the list work in defense technology.
Buntar Aerospace said the funding will go toward scaling its reconnaissance drones and mission software. The round was led by Axon Enterprise, the U.S. company best known for making Tasers and police body cameras, along with Munkene AS, a Norwegian investment vehicle whose sole disclosed investment to date is Buntar. Munkene has also been involved in setting up Gardar, a separate $92 million Norwegian fund launched this year specifically to back Ukrainian defense startups.
Defence Builder, an early-stage venture fund, said it invested in Buntar before rounds of this size were available to Ukrainian defense companies.
“That is the part of the work we care about: the capital that arrives when the technology is validated but the market has not yet priced it,” Defence Builder wrote. “Strategic investors like Axon come in after that question is answered, and the gap between those two moments is exactly where an early fund is either useful or it is not.”
Defence Builder said the rounds raised by Buntar, UFORCE and Farsight Vision show that Ukrainian defense financing is shifting from small individual checks toward institutional venture capital and strategic corporate investment, describing the shift as a change in the type of capital entering the sector rather than simply the total amount.
Ukrainian defense technology companies attracted more than $129 million in grants and equity funding in 2025, an increase of 119 percent from $59 million the year before, according to figures cited by Defence Builder. Foreign investors accounted for 49 percent of that funding. Separately, professional services firm KPMG recorded four Ukrainian defense tech transactions above $5 million in the first half of 2026, compared with one such transaction in the first half of 2025.
Defence Builder credited Buntar Aerospace co-founders Ivan Kaunov and Bohdan Sas in its announcement. The firm did not disclose Buntar’s valuation following the round or specific production or delivery targets tied to the new funding.

China Focus: Ice-rock avalanche in Nepal triggers deadly mudslide in China's Xizang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
17:29:04 CST
18:29:04 KST

GYIRONG, Xizang, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- An ice-rock avalanche originating from a high-mountain glacier in Nepal has been identified as the cause of a devastating mudslide that struck Gyirong Port in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Aug. 26, local authorities said Sunday.
A glacier on the north slope of Mount Langtang Lirung in Nepal fractured at an altitude of about 5,200 meters, triggering an ice-rock avalanche, according to a press conference held by the information office of the regional government.
The avalanche plunged rapidly to an altitude of around 4,000 meters, scouring the mountainside and developing into a massive debris flow, which surged about 22 kilometers before reaching Gyirong Port at an altitude of around 1,800 meters.
The disaster flattened an area of about 0.7 square kilometers, destroying 27 buildings and related facilities in the area.
The findings were made by a cryosphere emergency disaster response team from the Institute of Mountain Hazards and Environment under the Chinese Academy of Sciences, based on the analysis of remote-sensing monitoring data and field-transmitted data, as well as on-site surveys and investigations.
The deadly mudslide had claimed 16 lives and left 546 others missing at Gyirong Port as of 6 p.m. Saturday, the regional government said on Sunday morning.
Su Pengcheng, a researcher with the institute, said the disaster is the result of glacier instability under the long-term effects of climate warming.
A post-disaster investigation found that the narrow valley and steep vertical drop in the area where the ice-rock avalanche occurred gave the collapsing mass enormous potential energy. As it descended rapidly, friction and impacts generated large amounts of heat and meltwater.
The resulting mixture swept up moraine and other loose material along the valley and rapidly developed into a debris flow. It reached Gyirong Port at around 10:59 a.m. on Aug. 26, only six to seven minutes after the initial collapse, Su said.
The debris flow caused blockage and backwater near the port before continuing downstream into Nepal.
Su said the disaster was marked by its sudden onset, large peak flow, high speed, strong destructive force and wide impact area, characteristics that he described as a notable new feature of cryospheric disasters on and around the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau.
Meanwhile, a barrier dam above the core area of Gyirong Port is currently stable and unlikely to suffer a sudden complete breach, according to the press conference.
Radar monitoring showed that the dam has an average height of 60 meters and a length of about 1,100 meters. The lake behind it covers about 0.1 square kilometers and has a storage capacity of around 2.2 million cubic meters.
Authorities said that the dam has begun discharging water through overflow and is generally stable.
Rescue operations remain difficult because of the high-altitude terrain, steep valleys and volatile weather, while the surrounding area still faces potential risks from glaciers, glacial lakes and geological hazards, Su said.
So far, a total of 2,141 personnel have joined search and rescue operations, including personnel from the People's Liberation Army, the People's Armed Police Force, the China Search and Rescue Team, China Anneng, border defense units and police, according to the press conference.
A total of 269 rescue vehicles and 3,922 sets of rescue equipment have also been dispatched to the front line, where rescue teams have searched an area of 90,000 square meters. ■

Asia-Pacific Community: A Myanmar vocal coach orchestrates harmonies beyond borders
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
17:28:22 CST
18:28:22 KST

Local students attend a Chinese singing class at the China Cultural Center in Yangon, Aug. 28, 2026. (Xinhua/Myo Kyaw Soe)
YANGON, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- In a modest classroom in Yangon, voices rise not just in songs but in quiet connection -- weaving together two cultures through the simple, universal language of music.
Phyo Nyein Zaw has become a familiar figure at the China Cultural Center in Yangon, teaching singing lessons to nearly 40 students from different backgrounds over the past two years.
"Music is a universal language," he said in an interview. "Even if you don't understand the lyrics, you can feel the energy and emotion. It brings people together."
Born and raised in Yangon, Phyo Nyein Zaw developed a love for singing at an early age, inspired by his father, who has been singing for more than 40 years.
He studied Myanmar literature at university and began performing at temples in 2012. In 2018, he was selected through a singing competition held at the center to perform at a television station in Nanning in China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region.
That experience in China, he recalled, was a turning point. "It opened my eyes to how music can carry culture across borders," he said.
Now back in Myanmar, he teaches a growing number of students at the China Cultural Center. The singing course runs for over two months, with classes covering everything from breathing exercises and vocal registers -- including chest voice, head voice and mixed voice -- to music theory.
To keep students engaged, he weaves popular songs from social media platforms such as TikTok into his lessons.
"These songs often blend traditional Chinese elements with modern styles," he explained. "They help my students understand not only the music but also the culture behind it."
Among the 13 students in his current class is 16-year-old Aung Min Zaw, a local teenager who speaks Chinese but had never received formal vocal training before joining the class.
"I can speak Chinese, but I can't sing, so I joined the singing class," Aung Min Zaw said, adding that the techniques he has learned have transformed the way he performs.
For Aung Min Zaw, the class is more than just music. "We have a lot of fun during the training because we meet people from different backgrounds. We cheer for each other while learning," he said.
The events and classes held at the center offer a glimpse into cultural exchange between Myanmar and China. Visitors include Myanmar locals as well as members of the Chinese community. Teachers and students from the National University of Arts and Culture also frequently visit the center. Together, they share stories, compare musical traditions and discuss ideas for future cultural collaborations.
"Sometimes we talk about how we can work together to create something new between artists from the two countries," the teacher said with a smile.
Looking ahead, he hopes to train students who will not only sing well themselves but also go on to teach others. "I want to share what I've learned and help more people become vocal coaches," he said. "That way, the bridge between our two countries will only grow stronger.
For now, in his classroom in Yangon, the sound of voices rising in harmony is a reminder that music knows no borders, and that one teacher's passion can echo far beyond the walls of a single room. ■
Local students attend a Chinese singing class at the China Cultural Center in Yangon, Aug. 28, 2026. (Xinhua/Myo Kyaw Soe)

Nepal seeks to advance electricity import arrangement due to floods

An electrical equipment at a power plant is partially buried in slush brought in by the Trishuli river in flash floods, in Dhading District, Nepal, Sunday, Aug. 30, 2026. (AP Photo)
NEW DELHI: Nepal has sought advance approvals to import electricity from India, effective Sept 2026, in view of generation deficits caused by flash floods, govt said.Power ministry officials said India will provide any additional electricity that Nepal may need and relevant authorities are processing these requests.
India imports hydropower from Nepal during summer and exports electricity in the dry winter, when rivers freeze and generation is impacted. Both countries currently have a 1,000 MW electricity import-export capacity through the Dhalkebar-Muzaffarpur 400 kV cross-border transmission line and have recently agreed to increase it to over 1,400 MW.Following flash floods in the Trishuli/Lhende Khola river basin on Aug 26 that caused severe local infrastructure damage and disrupted specific generating stations, officials said Kathmandu has requested India to advance the export mechanism, which otherwise begins during peak winter.The impact of the damage on India’s national power grid, however, is minimal and fully manageable, an official said.“Major cross-border transmission corridors, such as the high-capacity 400 kV Dhalkebar-Muzaffarpur link (with a transfer capacity of 1,000 MW), remain operational,” said a power ministry official. According to assessments, domestic generation capacity in Nepal has seen a reduction of approximately 550 MW due to damaged facilities.
Cross-border power flow to India is currently reduced by approximately 400 MW, from previous peak export levels of around 950-1,000 MW.“We do not foresee any requirement for exceptional emergency procurement or alternative arrangements to balance domestic demand. India’s vast national grid capacity and robust generation reserve margins are capable of absorbing a temporary shortfall of 400 MW seamlessly without disrupting grid stability or retail supply,” the official said.
Some of the key under-construction projects, including the 900 MW Arun-3 and 669 MW Lower Arun projects in the Arun River basin, which are being executed by central public sector companies, are located in an unaffected catchment and continue on schedule without disruption, said an official.

Russia is preparing strikes beyond Ukraine’s borders; British companies are at risk — Daily Mail

Unknown Publisher

Russia is preparing strikes beyond Ukraine’s borders; British companies are at risk — Daily Mail
Kyiv • UNN
Companies supplying weapons and drones to Ukraine have been informed about the risks of espionage, cyberattacks, and sabotage. Some have already tightened security.
British defense companies supplying Ukraine with weapons and drones have warned of possible operations by Russian special services against their executives, employees, and production facilities. These could include espionage, cyberattacks, sabotage, and potential assassination attempts. This is reported by the Daily Mail, according to UNN.
Details
According to the publication, the warning was issued during a closed roundtable that the United Kingdom’s Foreign Office held with defense company executives earlier this summer.
The meeting’s participants were allegedly warned of the risk of surveillance of employees, attempts to obtain classified information, cyberattacks, sabotage at facilities, as well as possible physical attacks on company executives.
Afterward, some companies tightened personnel screening, access controls at production sites, and security measures during overseas trips by senior executives.
The British government has not officially commented on the holding of such a closed briefing.
Among the enterprises that may be of particular interest to Russia are manufacturers of drones and long-range weapons supplied to Ukraine.
In particular, the Ukrainian company Ukrspecsystems opened production facilities in Suffolk, Britain, in 2026. The facility is intended to manufacture unmanned systems, including for Ukraine’s needs.
Another British company, Callen-Lenz, which is owned by BAE Systems, is working on unmanned platforms, some of which are procured by the British Ministry of Defense.
MBDA, the manufacturer of Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missiles, is also attracting particular attention. At the end of August, the United Kingdom allowed the company to provide Ukraine with classified data on the British components of these missiles in order to deepen cooperation with Kyiv and Paris.
Context
The warning came amid a sharp escalation in Moscow’s rhetoric toward the United Kingdom.
In August, the Russian side repeatedly threatened London with "consequences" over the supply of drones and long-range weapons to Ukraine. Officials in Russia also stated that strikes on British military facilities could be possible in response to Ukraine’s use of British weapons.
London’s concerns are also grounded in previous incidents in Europe.
In 2024, U.S. intelligence uncovered a Russian plan to assassinate Armin Papperger, the CEO of the German defense contractor Rheinmetall. A NATO representative later confirmed that the plan was part of a broader Russian campaign that included sabotage, arson, and possible assassination attempts against representatives of the defense industry.
Germany is also investigating the possible preparation of an assassination attempt against Stefan Thomann, the head of Donaustahl, a company that manufactures drones for Ukraine.
Britain’s counterintelligence service MI5 previously warned that Russia is increasingly using intermediaries recruited online for sabotage and espionage. This includes surveillance, arson, infrastructure damage, and other operations against facilities and people linked to support for Ukraine.
In 2024, a warehouse containing humanitarian aid and Starlink equipment intended for Ukraine was also set on fire in London. British prosecutors said that the organizers were acting in the interests of the Russia-linked private military company "Wagner."
Reminder
Several days earlier, Stefan Thomann, the founder of the German defense startup Donaustahl, said that he feared an assassination attempt by Russian special services.

Nepal-China flood disaster: What’s the latest toll, how many are missing?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
09:24:46 UTC
18:24:46 KST

Nepal-China flood disaster: What’s the latest toll, how many are missing?
More than 3,000 people remain missing days after the devastating floods triggered a collapsed glacier near China-Nepal border.
The death toll from devastating floods near the border between Nepal and China has risen to nearly 800, with thousands missing following Wednesday’s disaster.
Rescue efforts are under way to locate more than 900 missing workers at hydropower projects in central Nepal.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 38-year-old Nepal flood survivor reunited with mother after rescue
- list 2 of 3Before and after images show catastrophic impact of Nepal flash floods
- list 3 of 3Nepal and China resume flood rescue as death toll surpasses 600
Authorities from Nepal and the Tibet region of China have put the total number of missing at just over 3,000, with some bodies washing up in neighbouring India.
A glacier collapse high in the Himalaya mountains in Nepal near the border with Tibet triggered Wednesday’s catastrophic flooding and landslides, which buried villages and towns along the Trishuli and Bhotekoshi river systems.
On Friday, rising water levels in a new lake formed by the build-up of debris prompted a temporary halt to search efforts amid fears of a second flood. Rescue operations resumed after the lake threat was deemed manageable.
Al Jazeera’s Katrina Yu, reporting from Beijing, said that Chinese authorities say the risk seems to have been reduced, but it has not disappeared.
“They are closely monitoring the barrier lake, located one km upstream at the port of Gyirong and the border area. They are closely monitoring using satellites, radars, and drones,” she said, adding that “authorities are confident that if the situation around the barrier lake should deteriorate, they will be able to give notice of about 30 minutes to rescuers below”.
Here’s what we know about the latest rescue efforts and the victims:
Where are the 900 workers missing?
As of Sunday morning, around 933 people are missing or unaccounted for, according to the country’s Independent Power Producers’ Association. They were working at 11 hydropower project sites and tunnels in Nepal’s Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts, which are among the worst-hit areas.
The workers include citizens of Nepal, India, South Korea and China. How many are trapped or missing at each individual hydropower site remains unclear.
“After complaints emerged that people were trapped inside the tunnel, the government prioritised the deployment of a rescue team and has been advancing the work to clear the entrance by removing debris and rubble,” Nepal’s prime minister’s office said late on Saturday.
“To expedite the digging of the tunnel entrance and the search operations, a joint team of 82 personnel – including 62 from the Nepali Army and 20 from the Armed Police Force Nepal and Nepal Police – has been continuously deployed since last night. However, with adverse weather conditions persisting in the area, the rescue efforts have become quite challenging,” the statement added.
Nepal’s Foreign Secretary Amrit Bahadur Rai said that 19,000 security personnel and 16 helicopters have been mobilised in the search and rescue operations.
Videos on social media show Nepali soldiers wading through mud trying to rescue workers trapped at the 216-megawatt Upper Trishuli-1 hydropower project. The army has rescued 254 workers there.
But rescue efforts have also proved challenging at other hydropower sites, such as the 22MW Chilime Hydropower project in Rasuwa district, 133 km (82 miles) north of the capital, Kathmandu.
“We have not been able to carry out a rescue. The tunnel is filled with mud and it is impossible to enter,” Baburaj Maharjan, executive director of Chilime Hydropower Company, told the Kathmandu Post. “We are working to mobilise a rock-climbing rescue team,” he added.
India has sent teams to help rescue trapped workers.
According to Indian media reports, an 11-member team of medical personnel and tunnel-rescue specialists reached Nepal on Saturday to begin aerial assessments in the Chilime and Langtang regions.
What else do we know about the victims and the missing?
According to Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, the death toll from the floods has risen to 781.
The Kathmandu Post reported that bodies are turning up far downstream and local morgues are running out of space to store others until they are identified.
Rojita Adhikari, a freelance journalist and filmmaker from Nepal, told Al Jazeera that authorities are facing a challenge.
“Yesterday [Saturday] I was at a press conference with Nepal’s foreign minister and he said the country is struggling to store and identify dead bodies – whose numbers are mounting. He said Nepal does not have enough refrigerators to store the dead bodies and identify and test their DNA,” she said.
Unidentified bodies have been sent to 21 hospitals in different districts for preservation and identification, says the Kathmandu Post.
Chinese authorities in Tibet told reporters that 16 people had died in Gyirong County, as of Saturday evening.
As of Sunday morning, 2,498 people remain missing in Nepal. They include 589 foreigners and 127 Nepali citizens travelling with them, 45 personnel from Nepal’s army, 27 from Nepal’s police and 13 from the armed police force.
Reporting from Nepal, Al Jazeera’s Samer Allawi said Nepal’s disaster management authorities have evacuated thousands of people, including foreign nationals, with the help of the army and police.
In China’s Tibet region, authorities said on Sunday that 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries are missing. They include 104 from Nepal, 49 from neighbouring India, as well as 33 Latvians, 18 Americans, 15 Britons, six from Canada, six from Australia, three each from Russia, Malaysia and Germany, 10 from the Netherlands, New Zealand, Estonia, France and Ireland and one each from Finland, Lithuania, Portugal, Ukraine, Spain, Hungary and Kazakhstan.
Al Jazeera’s Yu said that getting a picture of the full scale of the devastation on the Chinese side of the border is difficult because foreign journalists are not allowed to enter the area. “We are completely reliant on the government and state media,” she said.
“The government says teams have desperately been searching the worst-hit area of the port of Gyirong since teams arrived there late on Friday after days of trekking through the mountains,” she said, adding that they have “searched at least 90,000 square metres using life monitoring equipment, search dogs and drones”.
Chinese authorities say that a team of hundreds of technical operators are using heavy machinery to slowly repair roads as access to the port of Gyirong is blocked following the flooding and landslides.
What do we know about rescue efforts?
Nepal and China are working together to identify missing citizens and foreign nationals.
But the efforts have proven to be challenging, with roads and bridges destroyed.
On Sunday morning, water levels in the Trishuli River rose after more rain, prompting residents and rescue workers to seek higher ground, a Nepalese police official said.
Al Jazeera’s Allawi said authorities “have not yet moved to the second phase of relief operations, which includes humanitarian assistance and reopening roads”, because of “the rugged terrain and the lack of sufficient resources”.
He added that Nepal’s finance minister [Swarnim Wagle] estimated losses from the disaster at “more than $4bn”, while warnings remain in force for potential flooding along rivers in northern Nepal.
“Local relief efforts are also very limited because of the difficulty of reaching the affected areas,” he said, adding that “dozens of kilometres of roads have been destroyed, as well as bridges over rivers”.
Al Jazeera’s Minelle Fernandez, reporting from the Nepalese capital, said the government has requested specialist help from India and China to “fill gaps” in its rescue operations.
“The reason the [Nepalese] foreign ministry spokesman said that this decision has been taken is because lives are at stake and that it is very, very urgent,” she said.
“The reason that initially Nepal had said they didn’t want assistance is they didn’t want the chaos which comes with huge teams being fanned out in different areas.”
Nepali journalist Adhikari accused world leaders of not prioritising the threats posed by the climate crisis. “This catastrophe is not Nepal’s fault. The country is paying the price for how world leaders have been dealing with climate change.”
“Nepal has had floods and disasters like earthquakes before, but I have never seen anything like what happened on Wednesday. Entire families have been swept away. People are devastated and have lost everything – their property, their security, their lifelines. They have no homes to return to in the flood-affected areas.”
China has mobilised 2,100 rescue workers and allocated at least 220 million yuan ($32.7m) to support relief efforts, according to CCTV news. Beijing is also using heavy-lift drones and helicopters to airdrop equipment and supplies to frontline rescuers near the border crossing.
International aid has arrived from the United Nations, the Red Cross Federation, Australia, India, South Korea and the United States.
The US and Canada said they would provide $3.6m each in humanitarian aid. The United Kingdom has offered $6.8m in aid, while the UN released $2.5m in emergency funding.
On Friday, the European Union pledged $2.3m and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said it had allocated more than $1m and launched an emergency appeal for $31m.

Sweden to Deploy Gripen Fighter Jets and Naval Ships to Guard Finnish Border With Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

18:24:16 KST

- Category
- World
Sweden to Deploy Gripen Fighter Jets and Naval Ships to Guard Finnish Border With Russia
The Swedish government has decided to send military units to Finland to strengthen patrolling operations along the border with Russia.
According to Swedish public broadcaster SVT on August 28, the action comes after a direct request from Finnish authorities for military assistance to respond to ongoing air space threats tied to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Over the past year, Finland has recorded several instances of Ukrainian drones straying into its territory due to electronic warfare, alongside repeated air space violations by Russian military aircraft.
To handle these security concerns, the Swedish Armed Forces will soon deploy JAS 39 Gripen fighter jets and naval vessels to patrol regions along the Finnish-Russian border.
Additional ground support may also follow later in the year. Swedish air defense and counter-drone units could be sent to Finland during the autumn if the operational situation requires further force integration.
The entire deployment is organized alongside NATO and relies on bilateral agreements between the two nations. These legal frameworks give the Swedish government the mandate to deploy armed forces directly for the defense of Finnish territorial integrity.
This operation sits within a larger expansion of regional security ties in Northern Europe. Sweden is set to assume command of NATO forward land forces in Finland, where international troops will form a core element of the alliance's enhanced defense presence.
This framework includes a primary battalion task group stationed in Finland alongside a permanent multinational headquarters.
Previously, Sweden's parliamentary defense commission warned in a report covered by Bloomberg on June 12 that Russia could seek to test NATO's cohesion and commitment to mutual defense through a military attack in the "relatively near term."
The commission stated that such action could come if the Kremlin assessed that "political conditions are favorable," even when the balance of forces fell short of the traditional threshold for an attack, Bloomberg reported.

‘Stuck’: Canada ends Hong Kong migration pathway, some turn to US and UK
‘Moving to the US is geographically convenient, but it is expensive,’ agent says, recommending UK BN(O) visa as Ottawa closes 2021 pathway
The closure of Canada’s “lifeboat” migration scheme for Hongkongers has left some applicants who are struggling to meet permanent residency requirements in limbo, prompting others to consider alternative destinations such as the US and Britain.
Hong Kong-based immigration agents made this observation after Ottawa announced on Friday that its dedicated pathways for Hongkongers would stop accepting new applications on Monday. Applications submitted before the deadline will continue to be processed.
Launched in 2021 in response to Beijing’s imposition of the national security law in Hong Kong, the pathway allowed applicants to qualify for permanent residency either by completing a diploma or bachelor’s degree at designated Canadian institutions, or obtaining an open work permit and working full-time in the country for at least one year, or accumulating 1,560 work hours.
Benny Cheung Ka-hei, director of immigration consulting firm Goldmax, said on Sunday that the scheme’s closure was widely expected amid Canada’s tightening immigration policy.
He noted that some Hongkongers who moved to the country failed to meet the requirements, particularly struggling with the English proficiency test, and that the closure could shut down their route to permanent residence.
“Some of our clients moved to Canada but are busy or need to take care of children and remain unable to pass the English test despite multiple attempts,” Cheung said. “Some of them are stuck at this stage.”
He said some Hongkongers unable to qualify for permanent residency had begun seeking alternatives, prioritising the United Kingdom and the United States.

MOSCOW, August 30. /TASS/. The Russian Armed Forces have begun preparing massive strikes against Ukraine’s energy facilities in response to the Kiev regime’s attacks on civilian infrastructure and the energy sector, the Defense Ministry reported.
"In accordance with the received instructions, the Russian Armed Forces have begun preparing to launch massive strikes against Ukraine’s energy facilities in response to the Kiev regime’s ongoing attacks on civilian infrastructure and Russia’s fuel and energy complex," the statement said.
At the same time, Russian servicemen continued to launch coordinated strikes against Ukrainian military-industrial facilities that support the Ukrainian military overnight, the ministry emphasized. In particular, over the past night, the Russian miltiary struck an asbestos-cement products plant in Kiev, whose warehouses were being used to store explosives. "An industrial facility, an asbestos-cement products plant in Kiev, whose facilities were used to store explosives on behalf of the Smart Ammunition LLC scientific, technical, and engineering company, which manufactures drones and ammunition for them, was attacked with strike drones," the statement noted.
In the meantime, the Russian Armed Forces struck the Flamingo missile launch site, fuel and energy infrastructure facilities, and logistics centers used by the Ukrainian military over the past 24 hours, the ministry pointed out.
"The Russian Armed Forces struck the preparation and launch site for the Flamingo long-range cruise missiles, Ukrainian fuel and energy infrastructure facilities, ammunition production facilities, logistics centers used by the Ukrainian military, assembly and storage sites for drones and their components, as well as temporary deployment sites for Ukrainian servicemen and foreign mercenaries in 143 areas," the statement said.
In addition, Russian servicemen established control over the settlements of Velikiy Prikol and Sadki in the Sumy Region over the past 24 hours, the Defense Ministry reported.
Meanwhile, Ukraine has lost approximately 1,425 troops in the special military operation zone over the past 24 hours, the ministry stressed. According to its statement, Russia’s battlegroup North wiped out more than 230 Ukrainian servicemen, the battlegroup West eliminated up to 210 enemy troops, the battlegroup South wiped out up to 240 military, the battlegroup Center eliminated up to 375, the battlegroup East destroyed up to 340 troops, and the battlegroup Dnepr wiped out up to 30.
Moreover, Russian air defenses shot down five HIMARS rockets and 804 Ukrainian fixed-wing drones over the past 24 hours, the Defense Ministry said. For the first time ever, Russia’s battlegroup West destroyed Ukraine’s Canadian-made Titan-S armored vehicle in the special military operation zone, the statement concluded.

Voltaic Marine equips its robotic ship with weapon turret
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
09:20:41 UTC
18:20:41 KST

- Voltaic Marine completed live trials integrating a Moog RIwP remote weapon turret onto its AEU39 uncrewed surface vessel.
- The turret drew power from the vessel's 300 kilowatt-hour battery bank through the AEU39's open payload architecture.
Voltaic Marine has completed live trials pairing its AEU39 uncrewed surface vessel with a Moog Space and Defense RIwP remote weapon turret, the company said this week.
During the trials, the turret drew power directly from the AEU39’s 300 kilowatt-hour battery bank through standard interfaces, while the vessel held position on the water. The RIwP, or Reconfigurable Integrated-weapons Platform, is an existing remote weapon station already fielded on other platforms.
Footage released alongside the announcement shows the weapon turret housed inside the AEU39’s bow, concealed beneath a hinged armored hatch that opens upward when the system needs to engage. With the hatch closed, the turret sits flush within the hull, giving the vessel a low profile until the weapon station is called into use.
The integration ran through the AEU39’s open payload architecture, which Voltaic Marine describes as built around two modular bays with a combined 4,000-pound (1,814-kilogram) capacity. The bow bay, where the RIwP was mounted for these trials, is designed to accept modular turret systems for maximum reconfigurability. A separate enclosed midship bay is built to launch and recover uncrewed aircraft from a stabilized deck, with its own set of reconfigurable payload options.
The vessel runs on electric propulsion, which Voltaic Marine says gives it a low acoustic and thermal signature, allowing the AEU39 to hold position without generating the noise or heat associated with a conventional engine. Power for the payload bays runs through an 800-volt to 12-volt conversion system, paired with open data and communications standards intended to let different payloads plug into the same architecture.
For autonomy and command and control, the company describes the AEU39 as agnostic to both, supporting waypoint transit, area patrol, loitering on station and repositioning on command through open interfaces meant to work with whatever autonomy or C2 systems a customer already operates.
Voltaic Marine said the platform is designed to deploy using standard commercial logistics rather than specialized transport. The company said the AEU39 can move by road trailer, launch from a boat ramp, or ship inside a 45-foot high-cube container, and is sized to fit aboard a C-17 or C-130 aircraft.
Voltaic Marine said the combination of the AEU39 and the RIwP turret is intended to let a fielded weapon system remain on station for extended periods, describing the vessel as capable of keeping the turret “on watch for weeks at a time.”
The company did not disclose the specific date or location of the trials, the customer or program involved, whether the RIwP was armed with live weapons during testing, or what performance data the trial produced.

Israelis can flee Israel, but they cannot escape their Jewish destiny - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
09:19:05 UTC
18:19:05 KST

The recent, mysterious disappearance of mother and daughter Mali and Liel Yahalomi held the nation of Israel spellbound for more than a week. Everyone wanted to know: Where have they gone? Have they been kidnapped? Are they lying dead in some remote field, the victims of yet another antisemitic crime?
Israelis love suspense stories – the more sordid, the better – perhaps because it gives us temporary pause and takes us away, for a few exciting hours, from the more serious, harrowing headlines that we encounter every day.
One of the many conspiracy theories held that Mali had absconded with huge sums of money drawn from the Bank of Jerusalem, where Mali worked.
So pervasive were these rumors that shares of the bank actually dropped, as investors feared there might be a run on the bank.
They undoubtedly recalled the 2002 scandal when Eti Alon, the deputy head of investments at the Tel Aviv-based Trade Bank, embezzled more than $65 million (over NIS 250 million) over a five-year period, to cover the massive illegal gambling debts of her brother, Ofer Maximov.
Speculations found to be false
None of these wild speculations turned out to be accurate. The two were found – by an Israeli police officer “on loan” to Argentina – on a bus in Buenos Aires. They were unharmed and, according to the bank, no money was missing.
They had ditched their cellphones to avoid being traced or contacted by their family, and were headed from Prague to Vienna to Argentina to an unspecified country to “start life over again.” They had seemingly deserted their loved ones and planned to take on new identities with new passports in a new country.
Many of the questions still remain unanswered, but perhaps the key question – “Why?” – has a simple response: They wanted to escape the life they knew; they wanted out.
There’s nothing all that earthshaking about this. Let’s be truthful: how many of us have, at one time or another, fantasized about going off the grid and fleeing to some remote corner of the planet? To a place that is serene, free of war or terrorism, a place where no one asks – or cares – what God we worship or what flag we fly. Just a place where passersby casually smile at us and go about their business as if we don’t exist.
We have prominent role models to draw from.
Jonah – we’ll soon recount his tale – hopped on a boat and descended to its lowest deck to escape his responsibility as a prophet and avoid his mission of saving the Assyrian capital of Nineveh.
Prophet Elijah ran to the desert, not only to evade evil Queen Jezebel, but to reconnect with God after a life of frustration.
I might even conjecture that Moses took a full 40 days on Mount Sinai – rather than a brief weekend – because he needed a real break from being our leader – we can be a difficult people, you know!
Sadly, no small number of Israelis have indeed fled the Holy Land since we became a state. The Institute for Jewish Policy Research estimates that roughly 630,000 Israeli citizens – our population when the state was founded! – live outside of Israel (about 6% of the country’s population). When you include their foreign-born children, that number nears one million.
Many of them maintain they are “just visiting,” and almost all claim they will come back at some point. Many indeed do, especially if it’s to join a war in progress, or to vote. But many others are quite comfortable blending into their new habitats.
In Koh Samui, Thailand, which we recently visited (thank God, we came back), there are no less than 17 kosher restaurants, and the lingua franca is Hebrew. And Israeli-Americans are the backbones of many Jewish communities in the US, often keeping the Jewish day schools there viable.
In fact, has anyone reading this article actually been in a place where there are no Israelis at all? (North Korea, maybe, unless you count the Mossad agents.)
Yet I maintain that, ultimately, the expat Jews will someday return. This will happen for two reasons – one negative, one positive.
On the negative side, the odious effort to isolate, demonize, and make life miserable for the Jews is increasing exponentially.
It is led and funded by radical Islam, but is also avidly supported by any number of non-Muslim Jew-haters, as well as general crazies who just love to hate Jews. This even includes no small number of delusional Jews themselves; as Hawkeye of MASH fame once said, “If we had more people like you, we’d have less people like you!”
Historically, Jews – sooner or later – become primary targets throughout the Diaspora, and that will not change. Pressed to either engage in self-immolation – condemning their own people and culture – or pick up and leave, significant numbers of Jews will choose the latter. It’s really not fun being in a place where you are not wanted.
Even in docile Koh Samui last week, an Israeli family was denied entry and ordered to leave an animal park, after the owners learned of their nationality when they heard Hebrew being spoken.
But on the positive side, Israelis (and Jews) abroad will come to see Israel as the long-awaited fulfillment of ancient prophecy, and the natural habitat we have always longed for. They will sense that history is reaching out to them, and they will want to be part of the miracle that Israel embodies every day, in every way.
This movement will be led by the young, who are always in the forefront of risk-taking, pioneering, and the ability to discern and desire the future.
These two approaches are indicated in the famous verse from Isaiah 60:8, “Who are these that fly along like clouds, like doves to their coves?” Some of our brothers and sisters will return here, pushed and driven by gloomy clouds and ill winds; others will flock here, pulled like birds who swiftly fly to their welcoming nests.
The Talmud in tractate Sukkah tells the story of two of King Solomon’s scribes who were “wanted” by the Angel of Death. They decided to escape to the city of Luz, a place where the angel had no power to enter. But as they approached the gates of Luz, it was precisely there that the Angel of Death was waiting for them.
The Talmud concludes, “Where a person is meant to be, there his feet will take him.”
A very different kind of angel awaits us here, in the holiest of all lands, and it is here that we shall find our destiny. The inevitability of God – and Israel – cannot and will not be denied.
The writer is director of the Jewish Outreach Center of Ra’anana. rabbistewart@gmail.com

Eisenkot, Bennett continue race toward 61 seats, but could a team-up with Netanyahu be necessary?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
09:18:26 UTC
18:18:26 KST

B’Yachad leader Naftali Bennett and Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot are no longer waiting for candidate lists to be finalized and have begun competing directly as both seek to define their political camps and coalition paths ahead of the coming election.
Speaking at an event in Rishon Lezion, Bennett drew a clear right-wing line against Eisenkot, saying he supports E1 construction between Jerusalem and Ma’aleh Adumim and that “anyone who opposes a Palestinian state should support settlement in E1.”
He also made clear that he opposes a Palestinian state “under any constellation.”
Regarding haredi (ultra-Orthodox) conscription, Bennett positioned himself against both Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Eisenkot.
“Bibi is talking about a 50% exemption, Gadi is talking about a 30% exemption, I am talking about 0 exemption,” he said, stressing that any framework that leaves 30% outside the draft would ultimately collapse into a much broader exemption.
Bennett also hardened his security stance, stating, “Anyone who launches terror balloons into Israel deserves death,” while noting that, as prime minister, he ordered the purchase of munitions intended to help Israel contend with Iran’s air defense system as part of preparations for a strike.
He also proposed targeting the Iranian regime with a sustained military, economic, diplomatic, and cyber campaign.
Eisenkot aims to lead governing coalition
Eisenkot, for his part, has sought to present himself as a candidate who can translate his polling advantage into a governing coalition.
In Maariv’s weekend poll, his Yashar party received 25 seats, compared with 15 for Bennett’s B’Yachad and 20 for Likud. Eisenkot also led Netanyahu in the question of suitability for prime minister, 48% to 37%, while Bennett led Netanyahu 45% to 40%.
Eisenkot has spoken of a target of 63-65 seats for his camp and attacked Netanyahu’s approach, which he described as “victory through not losing.”
He has also hardened his position on conscription, setting a goal of at least 10,000 haredi recruits in each cycle, most of them to the IDF and some to national service, alongside personal sanctions against those who do not serve.
Eisenkot pledged that if his camp failed to reach a 61-seat majority, he would work to expand his coalition rather than default to another election.
In doing so, he is leaving himself the option of trying to assemble a majority even after the election if the results do not give his camp 61 seats.
Eisenkot also claimed that when he was IDF chief of staff, Netanyahu asked him to appoint Ofer Winter as military secretary. The request was made in part because of the importance of having someone who wore a kippah at his side.
Eisenkot said he refused because he was unwilling to make a military appointment based on political or sectoral considerations.
THE DIFFERENCES between Bennett and Eisenkot have become sharper as the two continue to campaign for overlapping groups of voters.
Bennett is offering soft-right voters an alternative to Netanyahu without moving closer to the Left. Eisenkot is seeking to hold the political Center while persuading right-wing voters that he is not dependent on Yair Golan.
E1, the conscription law, and the approach to the Palestinians have highlighted the clear dividing lines between Bennett and Eisenkot, with the conscription issue emerging as one of the primary tests facing the next government.
Shas has already raised the stakes, as MK Yoav Ben-Tzur said the party would demand that a conscription law be passed before the next government is formed.
“If we have to enter a coalition, a conscription law will pass before the government is formed. Unequivocally,” he said.
Netanyahu, therefore, faces conflicting demands even before coalition negotiations have begun.
Bennett and Eisenkot are competing over who can present the stricter conscription framework; Shas is demanding that the issue be settled as a condition for joining the government; and Likud is already signaling that it is prepared to discuss that demand even before the government is sworn in.
Liberman keeps his distance
Yisrael Beytenu leader Avigdor Liberman has once again maintained his independence and has not declared support for any prime minister candidate.
In Maariv’s weekend poll, Yisrael Beytenu received nine seats. Regarding the question of suitability for prime minister, Netanyahu led Liberman 40% to 37%.
Separately, Yair Golan is operating from the other end of the political spectrum.
The Democrats have invested in a campaign aimed at young voters and in consolidating an independent left-wing camp, while Golan, for now, is also maintaining his political independence ahead of what comes next.
The Zionist opposition’s advantage still does not automatically produce a majority for an alternative government.
The Arab parties received a combined 13 seats, eight for the Joint List of Hadash, Ta’al, and Balad, and five for Ra’am.
The Zionist opposition’s advantage still does not automatically produce a majority for an alternative government.
Eisenkot could emerge as the leader of the largest party and still discover that the numbers do not add up to a coalition.
Bennett wants to remain an independent alternative. Liberman does not want to become an appendage to another candidate. Golan wants to preserve his party’s independence.
Benny Gantz and Gilad Erdan, meanwhile, are preoccupied, first and foremost, with their own political survival.
The battle for the premiership has already begun, even though the composition of a potential alternative government to Netanyahu remains far from settled.
This is how the political system looks on the eve of the new week: on the Right, parties are trying to prevent votes from being lost; in the Center, parties are trying to assemble lists that will be able to clear the electoral threshold; and among the larger parties, the battle over leadership of the respective camps is already underway.
The approaching deadline for submitting candidate lists will force the parties to finalize their alliances, but the question of coalition formation will remain open even afterward.
Even before Election Day, several questions that will directly affect the result will be decided: which lists will clear the electoral threshold, how many votes will be lost below it, and which party leaders will reach the ballot box with a plausible path to a 61-seat majority.

Israel must bring Diaspora Jews home before assimilation takes them - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
09:18:11 UTC
18:18:11 KST

Lamenting the crisis under which world Jewry finds itself, The Jerusalem Post’s editor-in-chief Zvika Klein’s recent Friday column was devoted to the subject of why Israeli politicians just don’t get it.
Quoting different leaders, what stood out the most was the staggering 70% of intermarriage that is happening in the US. If that trend continues, within a reasonably short period of time, the Jewish community will simply disappear. Who wouldn’t be concerned by such troubling news?
But there is hope, and it’s what no one feels comfortable talking about. While agencies such as Nefesh B’Nefesh are wholly devoted to the cause of aliyah, at the same time, they do their best to weed out Jews they deem less qualified to live in the Jewish homeland. That includes those who are intermarried, do not identify with Orthodox Judaism, and have possibly shifted over to another set of religious beliefs. It also includes those who are not fully Jewish.
The problem with that weeding process is that, short of bringing them to Israel so that they can become reacquainted with the holidays, customs and traditions – not to mention giving their kids a much better chance of marrying a Jew – that massive sector will assuredly be lost as future Jews.
Conversely, bringing such families to Israel will almost guarantee a completely different outcome! Once here, they will be confronted with the traditional Friday night Shabbat dinner, where families gather together, light candles, and connect in a meaningful way.
Rebuilding Jewish identity
They will learn to relax on Saturdays, because few things are open. It won’t be their usual day to wash the car, run to the mall or catch up on jobs they’ve been putting off.
With so many biblical, cultural, and national holidays and observances, they will begin to solidify and take on a new identity – one which is more aligned and unified with their people.
Of course, as their children attend school, they will learn Hebrew, often speaking with no detectable accent, unlike those who arrived at a later age. Their friends will be other Jews, and their orientation will be geared towards teaching them their history as they slowly become part of the country’s future.
Those kids will serve in the military, study in our universities, and choose their marriage partner from the vast pool of Jewish candidates who live here. This is the right recipe for saving Diaspora Jewry, for those who are truly interested in doing so.
For those who are, instead, fixated on the purity and percentage of Jewish blood running through the veins of individuals, and for those who are closed off to anyone other than the religiously observant, saving world Jewry might already be a cause which has been written off.
That is because they no longer consider Diaspora Jews as Jews worth saving. Years ago, I had this very conversation with one such person who I thought shared my own passion for bringing every Jew home, regardless of what they believe. Their only criteria had to be what is written in the 1950 Secular Law of Return – being the child or grandchild of a Jew.
Sadly, once the conversation turned toward the unaffiliated and intermarried, the response was that they should remain in the Diaspora as they were, in his mind, not eligible to come. From his point of view, they had made their choice to abandon Judaism and were not worth saving, even if another Holocaust were to happen.
He was, in effect, closing the door to hundreds of thousands of his own people who, irrespective of their religious affiliation or marital status, remain ethnically Jewish – a distinction which no one can erase or deny.
For anyone who has been paying attention, the accounts of antisemitic attacks, denigrating verbal sentiment, or attempts to disenfranchise Jews from many segments of society are only widening, with no signs of letting up.
Sure, you may not attend a synagogue and may even be married to a gentile, but what happens if your last name is Rosenberg or Levine? Will you get any special dispensation just because you have assimilated and no longer closely identify with the traditions of your people? Probably not!
The truth of the matter is that assimilated Jews will still be looked upon as strangers, different from all others. Born with that Jewish gene, they will never be able to scrub it out of them, and that is why their lives will still be in peril despite the choices they have made.
Anyone who thinks they are not worth rescuing either has no heart or conscience and has a misplaced perspective as it relates to what Judaism teaches us about loving our neighbor as ourselves.
World Jewry is truly at a crossroads on so many levels. There is danger when it comes to their safety, their continuity, appreciation for their identity and, most especially, the survival of their homeland.
While some may see them as an extra burden, their presence here can make such a great difference. As they are strengthened in a new way of life, we, too, will receive that benefit by the sheer numbers, replacing others who have left.
Yes, they will need lots of help learning the language, the customs, and the uniqueness of our society, but once they do, they will become an asset in so many ways that it will be a mystery why no one considered this sooner.
Regrettably, Klein is right. Many Israeli politicians are unable and unwilling to confront this issue, almost accepting the loss of Diaspora Jews as a foregone conclusion. It’s sad to say, but those who feel that way are simply lacking the vision that is needed to see the great potential that could bless this nation by embracing the “lost” of their people.
Each one of us who has made our own aliyah journey should reflect on just how fortunate we have been to be gathered to our people and be part of the Zionist dream, becoming the envy of nations, as we pooled our collective resources to build an enviable society.
There is no reason this cannot and should not happen. It already exists in our Law of Return. The real tragedy for world Jewry is that it’s just not being done. We can change that, and we must!

Russia says preparing ‘massive strikes’ on Ukraine’s energy sector
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
09:13:39 UTC
18:13:39 KST

Police officers inspect the area, after a Russian attack struck a warehouse, followed by an explosion, in the village of Myla, Kiev region, Ukraine, Saturday, Aug. 29, 2026. (AP Photo)
Russia’s Defense Ministry said on Aug. 30 that it was gearing up for large-scale attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure in a tit-for-tat response to strikes by Kiev.
“Russian forces have begun preparations for massive strikes against facilities in Ukraine’s energy sector in response to the ongoing attacks by the Kiev regime on civilian infrastructure and on Russia’s oil and energy complex,” it said on Telegram.
Last winter, Moscow repeatedly hit Ukrainian power plants, devastating the country’s energy sector and plunging millions of people into cold and darkness in sub-zero temperatures.
Both sides have for several months escalated long-range strikes, targeting infrastructure such as warehouses, businesses, oil and port facilities, as well as ships, increasing civilian casualties.
On Aug. 30, the Russian army claimed to have struck a plant in Kiev producing asbestos and cement whose warehouses, it said, were used to store explosives, as well as a manufacturer of drones and munitions.
On Aug. 29, a Russian strike on an ammunition depot in the suburbs of the Ukrainian capital triggered a huge explosion and killed at least 37 people.
The attack was the second to hit a munitions depot near Kiev in less than two months, with officials expressing anger that arms were still being stored so close to residential areas.
“Those who allowed this to happen must be held accountable for their decisions. Ammunition cannot be stored near homes or other residential areas,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on X.
Ukraine for its part attacked an oil refinery with drones in northwestern Russia, causing a fire, according to the local authorities.
