TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Hwa Mei Food purchased nearly 2 hectares of industrial land in Tainan’s Qigu Science and Technology Industrial Park and plans to invest NT$600 million (US$18.9 million) in a new frozen food factory.
The Tainan Economic Development Bureau said Sunday that the company plans to build an automated factory using smart manufacturing and high-standard cold-chain technology, with two main production lines for frozen pastries and rice-based products, per CNA.
The project is part of its parent group’s efforts to develop next-generation frozen foods and upgrade traditional food manufacturing through automation and intelligent production. Tainan Mayor Huang Wei-che (黃偉哲) said the industrial park is an important engine for industrial development along Tainan’s coast. Its transportation links and access to local agricultural and fishery resources were among the factors attracting companies, per a press release.
Huang said that since the investment promotion campaign began in 2024, the Qigu Science and Technology Industrial Park has completed five rounds of land auctions, attracting 38 companies. The investments are expected to create more than 6,000 jobs.
As of May 2026, seven companies were under construction in the industrial park, 24 had submitted landscape review applications, and three were expected to be completed by the end of the year. The park has already begun to form industrial clusters in automotive parts, metal products, and plastic products, showcasing its attractiveness as a high-value-added, low-pollution industrial hub.
The Tainan Economic Development Bureau said changing consumer habits have increased demand for convenient, ready-to-eat frozen foods. This has encouraged traditional food manufacturers to adopt smart manufacturing and improve production efficiency.
The city said it will provide companies with assistance through a single investment window, including coordination of water, electricity, gas, and other industrial infrastructure. The park also features a service center integrated with a Taiwan Power Co. substation to provide stable electricity for manufacturers.
The Qigu Science and Technology Industrial Park covers 141 hectares and is located near Provincial Highway 17 and National Freeway 8. It is positioned as a supporting industrial area for the Southern Taiwan Science Park and is expected to attract about NT$29 billion in investment.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s 205th Arsenal has established automated production lines for six key components of the military’s T112 combat rifle as it increases output of the new weapon.
The arsenal expects to supply tens of thousands of rifles over the next five years, with robotic arms and automated machinery now handling portions of the machining process, per CNA.
Private manufacturers supply accessories such as slings and stocks, while the arsenal keeps production of six critical T112 components in-house. These include the firing pin, upper and lower receivers, barrel, bolt mechanism, and bolt.
Most machinery on the new lines comes from Taiwan suppliers, although the arsenal imported its forging equipment. The six-component automation project was finished in 2025 with technical assistance from the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology, per Radio Taiwan International.
A T112 bolt component is machined on five types of equipment before undergoing heat and surface treatment, while barrel production spans 11 stages. Robotic arms move workpieces between parts of the production line, and optical systems are used to check machining quality.
Military units receive the rifles only after they clear final testing. Officials said automation has increased production capacity while reducing manpower requirements.
The arsenal also plans to seek overseas orders when domestic demand leaves capacity available.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — National Security Council Secretary-General Joseph Wu (吳釗燮) warned that China’s new entry and exit rules would strengthen its transnational repression efforts.
Wu said in a post on X that mandatory access to personal digital data, combined with other ambiguous provisions and recent legislation, would provide China with “new legal tools” to enforce transnational repression. “Those who plan to visit China should think twice,” he said.
An accompanying infographic provided more details about the rules:
- Expanded identity and data collection allows authorities to require documents and access to devices and account information.
- Technology and export control considerations can be used as grounds to restrict travel, including cases involving alleged violations of what the Chinese government defines as “industrial or technological security.”
- The “one China” principle has been weaponized, allowing authorities to restrict individuals’ ability to leave the country during investigations into cases deemed to involve national security or major public interests.
- Individuals accused by Chinese authorities of illegal activities overseas could be barred from leaving China for six months to three years after entering the country.
- Authorities are not required to disclose reasons for denying entry or exit in cases deemed sensitive.
- The rules encourage cross-agency information sharing regarding immigration, public security, and other areas.
- Individuals placed on sanctions or surveillance lists may also be denied entry.
Mainland Affairs Council Minister Chiu Chui-cheng (邱垂正) said earlier this month that the rules lack clear legal standards and are worded vaguely, allowing them to be enforced unfairly. Chiu said this uncertainty may affect people’s basic right to travel in and out of the country and raise risks for Taiwanese travelers. He urged them to carefully assess those risks before visiting China.

First serial HÜRJET jet completes maiden flight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
09:08:59 UTC
18:08:59 KST

- Turs first production HÜRJET jet trainer completed its maiden flight on Victory Day, August 30, moving the program from prototype to production.
- Spain has agreed to buy 30 HÜRJET aircraft, Türkiye's first jet trainer export to a NATO country, with deliveries targeted for 2028.
The first production-standard HÜRJET jet trainer, distinct from the program’s two earlier flight-test prototypes, completed its maiden flight on Victory Day, August 30, marking the transition from prototype testing to a working production line for the Turkish Air Force, according to a social media announcement.
The HÜRJET is a single-engine, tandem-seat supersonic jet trainer built by Turkish Aerospace Industries, designed to replace the Turkish Air Force’s aging T-38 and F-5 aircraft. The jet is capable of Mach 1.4 with a service ceiling of 45,000 feet (13,716 meters), and is powered by a single General Electric F404 engine, the same engine family used on the F/A-18 Hornet.
The program has been in development since 2017. The first prototype made its maiden flight on April 25, 2023, followed by a second prototype in November 2024. Between them, the two prototypes have logged around 340 test flights and nearly 260 flight hours, according to Turkish state media reports cited by Daily Sabah. During testing, the aircraft has flown demonstration flights with the Turkish Stars aerobatic team and in formation with the Anka-3 stealth drone prototype, and it has also completed transonic and supersonic test flights.
Turkish Aerospace has said it plans to ramp up its production line to two aircraft per month once serial manufacturing is fully underway. First deliveries to the Turkish Air Force are targeted for the end of 2026, with initial jets going to the Turkish Stars aerobatic display team before wider fleet deliveries follow.
Spain has agreed to purchase 30 HÜRJET aircraft, marking Turkey’s first jet trainer export sale to a fellow NATO member. Turkish Aerospace CEO Mehmet Demiroglu told Spanish outlet El Español that a final supply contract covering roughly 45 aircraft, intended to replace Spain’s own aging F-5 fleet, is expected soon, with an estimated value of $3.6 billion. Spanish deliveries are targeted for 2028, a year after the Turkish Air Force is expected to begin receiving its own production aircraft. The memorandum of understanding covering the Spanish deal was signed in 2025 between Turkish Aerospace, Spain’s Ministry of Defense and Airbus, on the sidelines of Spain’s FEINDEF defense exhibition.
Turkish Aerospace is also developing light attack and naval variants of the HÜRJET. The aircraft has previously been discussed as a possible candidate for operations from the Turkish Navy’s TCG Anadolu, a hybrid assault ship and drone carrier, though further specifications and timelines for the naval or light attack configurations have not been disclosed.

Greece, Turkey clash over protected Aegean marine areas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
09:07:00 UTC
18:07:00 KST

Greece, Turkey clash over protected Aegean marine areas
August 30, 2026
A stint of unfamiliar calm between Greece and Turkey lasted less than three years.
After a devastating earthquake struck Turkey in February 2023 and Greece provided substantial aid, the two countries came closer together. They then signed the Athens Declaration on Friendly Relations and Good-Neighbourliness in December 2023, a further step to improved relations.
During this unusual time of calm, neither government moved to resolve long-lasting Greek-Turkish disputes, which mostly involve marking maritime boundaries. As a result, even a measure ostensibly aimed at protecting the environment has reignited regional tensions.
The latest dispute was triggered by Turkey's designation of two marine parks in the Aegean Sea and eastern Mediterranean earlier this month. The park in the northeastern Aegean includes a protected area in the waters between the Greek islands of Lemnos and Samothrace. The southern park lies east of Rhodes and surrounds the Greek island of Kastellorizo.
For decades, Greece and Turkey have been at odds over the delineation of their maritime borders in the Aegean and the related economic rights, such as claims to natural resources like oil.
Greece's Foreign Ministry was quick to react to the announcement, calling the establishment of the parks "illegal." In a statement, it said the designation of Turkish marine parks in areas outside Turkey's territorial waters has no legal validity.
Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said at a Cabinet meeting earlier this week that he wanted to maintain good relations with neighboring countries. However, he stressed that "areas under Greek sovereignty are determined by international law" and that Greece is "always ready to defend them."
Competing to protect the Mediterranean?
For its part, Greece also announced two marine parks in 2025 — in the Ionian Islands and the southern Cyclades, both within Greek territorial waters. At the time, Turkey reacted in a clearly worded statement: "Unilateral actions should be avoided in closed or semi-closed seas such as the Aegean and the Mediterranean."
But Turkey has now declared its own marine parks — and without consulting Greece. Environmental protection appears to have been, at most, a secondary concern for the two countries in announcing their respective conservation parks. Instead, the move appears to be a new tactic for asserting dominance in the disputed maritime area — the latest chapter in a decades-long regional spat.
Greece believes Turkey sees the marine parks as a way to challenge the sovereignty of Greek islands. It fears the designation of the two parks is part of Turkey's revisionist "Mavi Vatan" doctrine, Turkish for "Blue Homeland."
Under the doctrine, Turkey lays claim to the exclusive economic zones of Greece and Cyprus — maritime areas in which a coastal state has special rights, including over fishing and the exploitation of natural resources. It also challenges the sovereignty of numerous Greek islands and islets.
Until now, the doctrine has largely remained theoretical and strategic in nature. It is now being advanced through legislative initiatives in Turkey's parliament, and Turkey intends to use the parks to formalize its claims to greater control over parts of the Aegean and eastern Mediterranean.
Greece invests in defense
Greece itself is content with the status quo in the Aegean but feels threatened by Turkey, which is significantly better armed. As a result, Greece has invested heavily in fighter jets, frigates, submarines and air defense systems.
After spending significantly less on arms imports for several years, Greece ranked 19th worldwide among the largest importers of major arms from 2021 to 2025, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.
Even as Athens builds new or closer alliances, Turkey is factored into decisions. In 2021, for example, the Greek government sent Patriot air defense missiles to Saudi Arabia, despite objections from the Greek opposition, to protect Saudi oil refineries from Houthi attacks — at a time when Riyadh and Ankara were at odds politically.
During a state visit with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Prime Minister Mitsotakis explicitly referred to Turkey's "destabilizing and counterproductive" role.
Relations between Ankara and Riyadh have since improved. In early August, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the Mecca Defense Pact, a major joint defense agreement.
An 'Iron Dome' for Greece
With Turkey in mind, Greece has also pursued strategic cooperation with Israel. Despite heavy criticism in Greece over the dire humanitarian situation in Gaza, Mitsotakis continues to maintain close ties with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
The Greek Defense Ministry is planning an air defense shield over the Aegean modeled on Israel's Iron Dome. The project, dubbed the "Achilles Shield," is designed to protect against all conceivable threats — including those from neighboring countries — and is expected to be fully operational by 2029.
For now, Mitsotakis continues to strike a conciliatory tone toward Turkey. But Greece is due to elect a new parliament by spring 2027 at the latest, and Mitsotakis may face growing pressure to take a tougher nationalist stance As the election approaches.

India's student-led Cockroach movement is taking its campaign for accountability to government schools, but its methods are meeting growing resistance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
09:04:00 UTC
18:04:00 KST

India's citizen-led school audits test limits of activism
August 30, 2026
The Indian activist movement dubbing itself the "Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)" shot to national prominence in May by leading weeks-long protests over a scandal involving highly competitive entrance exams.
The student-led campaign put the government under intense political pressure and ended with the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in July.
Now, the CJP is taking aim at India's government schools, organizing volunteer visits to classrooms, documenting conditions and demanding accountability for problems.
Launched on August 15, Independence Day in India, the campaign asks parents, students and volunteers to inspect schools and record basic facilities including toilets, drinking water, electricity, classroom furniture and school buildings. The CJP has said the findings will be used to pressure authorities to make improvements.
The initial target is to audit 100 rural government schools over two months. It has also proposed giving recognition to village leaders who improve their schools.
Unlike the first campaign, which was based on street protests, the school audits require a more sustained form of local activism. Volunteers are expected to work consistently at the local level, document conditions and follow up with officials, parents and communities.
The organization is dealing with different layers of the Indian administration. Responsibility for government schools is divided between state governments, local administrations and elected village bodies. The CJP is therefore set to tackle different rules and political interests across the country.
India has over a million government schools, according to Education Ministry data. They make up nearly 70% of all schools in the country but serve less than half of its 247 million schoolchildren.
CJP: 'We are not afraid'
That scale has given CJP a vast field for its campaign. But it has also brought a new set of challenges.
The authorities are raising questions regarding rules and locations for the CJP scrutiny, as well as safeguards when children are present.
The response is already varying from state to state. Some authorities have ordered their own inspections, while others have restricted access or taken police action against CJP volunteers.
Authorities in Maharashtra and Rajasthan states have objected to school visits carried out without permission.
In one case, a complaint by school authorities resulted in police action against CJP members after they entered the premises to conduct an audit.
In Rajasthan, restrictions have been imposed on outsiders entering government schools, as well as on filming, interviews and other forms of documentation. CJP volunteers in Rajasthan have also said they were attacked while inspecting a school.
"We are not afraid. We are seeking accountability from the government," said CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka.
Officials say schools are not open spaces
In the state of Uttar Pradesh, Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath has ordered officials to conduct on-the-spot checks of school facilities and directed police to register cases over what he called misleading videos about schools and colleges.
The CJP has said such measures undermine public scrutiny. Authorities have said schools are not open spaces for unauthorized inspections, particularly when children are present.
Vinita Gursahani Singh, managing trustee of We, The People campaign, which works on citizen empowerment, said the limits are set by law.
"Under the Right to Information Act, any citizen can inspect schools but you need to submit an application. And that makes sense as there has to be consideration for students and teaching," Singh told DW.
"All public scrutiny is legitimate. It is our job to scrutinize. But the scrutiny has to follow process. It has to be even-handed. What applies to one citizen must apply to all," she said.
Can activists serve as inspectors?
The CJP maintains government schools are publicly funded institutions and citizens have a legitimate right to ask how they are functioning.
Its volunteers use standardized audit forms to record conditions and send their findings to the CJP, which has said it will use the material to press local administrations to respond.
But critics question whether citizen activists can assume the role of inspectors. There are concerns about whether volunteers have the expertise to assess safety or infrastructure problems and how allegations posted on social media are verified.
Mohandas Pai, an education advocate, supports CJP's focus on government schools but disagrees with its methods.
"I like young people taking interest in school education. It's a broken system, and we need reforms," Pai told DW.
But he objected to large groups entering schools and questioning headmasters and children.
"You can't just barge into a school just because you think you are entitled to do it," Pai said, stressing that "children have to have a safe, secure environment."
Pai said the CJP should instead send small teams with permission, collect systematic data, publish regular reports and use the evidence to pressure governments.
CJP spokesperson Saurav Das rejected the argument that the campaign should rely on conventional channels, saying such approaches have failed to bring meaningful change.
Responding to Pai on X, he challenged him to join the next school visit and show the volunteers how it should be done.
Questions of student privacy
The audit campaign has also raised questions about privacy, consent and disruption of teaching when volunteers enter schools, film inside classrooms or question students.
However, Kavita Srivastava, president of the People's Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL) Rajasthan, opposes restrictions on outsiders entering schools and taking photos and videos in her state.
"Activists were visiting government schools to document their condition and demand accountability. Protecting children's privacy should not be used to prevent legitimate public scrutiny of government schools," Srivastava told DW.
A new role for the CJP
Activist Amrita Johri said the CJP's first campaign tapped into a longstanding accountability gap in India's examination system, which cost millions of young people time and money.
"The demand for accountability had popular resonance because there was no real response from the government," Johri told DW.
She backed the school audit campaign, saying public scrutiny should be welcomed.
"Public audits are an integral part of citizens' right to information and should be welcomed as an opportunity to fix accountability," she said. Johri added that the CJP needs to train volunteers, document problems and follow up with authorities to make the campaign effective.

Nepal floods revive Bihar’s annual nightmare: Why the state faces flooding every year
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
09:01:53 UTC
18:01:53 KST

The rivers that sustain the region for most of the year turn dangerous during the monsoon
NEW DELHI: Boats replacing cars on flooded roads, families moving to relief camps and swollen rivers spilling into villages. North Bihar is bracing for familiar scenes once again as floodwaters from Nepal move downstream.Floods have long been a part of life in northern Bihar. But a growing population and rapid urbanisation have made their impact more severe over the years.
The rivers that sustain the region for most of the year turn dangerous during the monsoon. And for people living here, there is little choice but to face the floods, rebuild and prepare for the cycle to repeat itself.Bihar minister Ramkripal Yadav said the state government is closely monitoring the flood threat in Bihar in view of the tragedy in Nepal."Bihar is adjacent to Nepal, and the water that has come from Nepal in the past has affected many areas of Bihar, leading to loss of life and property, destruction of crops and homes. The Bihar government and the chief minister himself are monitoring this," Yadav told ANI.He assured that the state government will extend every possible help to those affected."The Bihar government will provide every possible help. The flood victims of Bihar have the first right on Bihar's treasury, and it is secure for them.
The government will work," he added.
What was the trigger this time?
A glacial collapse at the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26 triggered a flash flood in Nepal that has claimed more than 600 lives.Analysis of satellite imagery indicated that a large mass of ice and rock may have fallen into the Lende Khola river, temporarily blocking its flow and creating a natural dam that later breached, sending floodwaters downstream.Due to the collapse, a large volume of ice and rock debris entered the Lende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi river in Nepal, generating a sudden surge that carried water, sediment and large boulders downstream.
The scale of the devastation can be gauged from the fact that twelve hydropower plants were reportedly knocked offline, dozens of bridges were swept away and the only road connecting the valley to the rest of Nepal was destroyed.Nature could not care less about political borders. And a flood that originated in Nepal will not stop at the border. From Nepal, the floodwaters will eventually move into north Bihar, before flowing into West Bengal and eventually Bangladesh, where they will empty into the sea.
Why does Bihar drown every year?
Speaking to The Times of India, IIT-trained civil engineer and flood expert Dinesh Mishra said Bihar's locational disadvantage is one of the reasons why it drowns every year in floods. He said the state is situated in such a way that water comes directly through the south-flowing rivers from Nepal."The first reason is Bihar's locational disadvantage. Bihar is situated in such a way that water comes directly from the mountains," Mishra said."All the rivers that enter Bihar from Nepal are south-flowing. So, the area north of the Ganga will inevitably remain waterlogged. And if it does not, there will be drought in the region," he added.
Rivers originating from the Himalayas, like Kosi, Gandak, Burhi Gandak and Bagmati, carry huge volumes of silt with them to Bihar. When the water level increases due to rain, these rivers overflow their banks.This makes Bihar India's most flood-prone state, with 76 per cent of the population in north Bihar living under the threat of floods.Bihar's disaster management authority classifies floods into four categories.
Class I refers to flash floods, which occur due to rainfall in Nepal, have a short lead time of around eight hours between forecast and flood, and recede quickly.
Class II refers to river floods, with a lead time of 24 hours and floodwaters that take a week or more to recede.
Class III refers to drainage congestion at river confluences, where the lead time exceeds 24 hours and the water lasts the entire monsoon season, receding only after about three months.
Class IV refers to permanently waterlogged areas.
This year, according to Bihar water resources department, the Gandak river has crossed the danger mark in Gopalganj, while the barrage at Valmikinagar released around 99,800 cusecs of water at 8 pm on Saturday.
"The water level of several rivers, including the Gandak, Kosi, Burhi Gandak and the Ganga, has been rising. Incessant rainfall in the catchment areas of Nepal has led to rivers touching or flowing above the danger level at several places," a senior official of the water resources department said.People in West Champaran, East Champaran, Sitamarhi and Muzaffarpur, besides Gopalganj, Saran and Vaishali, have also been facing heightened fears over the past three days following an unprecedented inflow of water from Nepal.Other than flooding, another concern is soil erosion along the banks of swollen rivers.
Embankments: Solution or part of the problem?
For over a century, embankments along rivers have been a major preventive measure against floods. Successive governments built these walls along river banks to prevent rivers from deviating from their course and protect settlements.However, Dinesh Mishra said these embankments are the root cause of the havoc wreaked by floods rather than being the solution."You build embankments basically to prevent river water from spilling out. But if floodwater that would naturally flow into the river is stopped, the water has nowhere to go," Mishra said.
"If it cannot return to the river, it will move into areas that were previously not affected by floods," he added.Mishra said Kosi once had space to spread and deposit its sediments, but embankments have now confined the river. With the sediments having nowhere to go, the riverbed has been rising, making the Kosi increasingly prone to overflowing."The river carries silt with it, and because of the embankments, the riverbed continues to rise," he said.Interestingly, Flood Atlas of Bihar, prepared by Isro along with the central and state governments, also says that "there must be a realisation that minimising the risk and damage from floods may be a more rational way of flood management rather than formulating structural measures along the dynamic rivers such as the Kosi."
Everybody loves a good flood
During the conversation, Mishra, however, rejected the notion that floods have always been a source of sorrow for Bihar. He said floods are also a time of celebration.He said farmers eagerly wait for floods because, as he put it, "a fresh layer of silt is deposited on the fields after floods, making the soil more fertile."He added that in the remote villages of north Bihar, people sometimes wait for floods because relief funds and the attention of politicians are also drawn towards villages where little development work has been done."People have been made this way. Earlier, they had clear SOPs to protect themselves during floods. But now, because they have become dependent on the government for relief, lives are lost," he said.
The traditions around floods
For generations, floods in north Bihar were not simply seen as a force to be feared. They were woven into the rhythm of life, with people learning to live alongside the rivers rather than trying to keep them at bay."Our ancestors knew this was a water-rich, flood-prone region. When they settled here, they must have done so with that understanding," Mishra said.
The relationship with the rivers was deeply personal. People revered them as mothers, and when the rains failed, women in villages would perform rituals to invoke the rivers and call for water.But when the floodwaters refused to recede, another ritual would follow. Women would gather with fruits, flowers, sandalwood, akshat and sindoor to persuade the river to leave.
The rivers were considered unmarried, Mishra said, and women would even "threaten" them with marriage if they refused to listen.These traditions show how closely floods have been tied to life in north Bihar for generations.
People did not always see the rivers only as a threat. They depended on them for water, fertile soil and agriculture, even as they feared the destruction that came when the rivers overflowed.That relationship continues even today. Every monsoon, the same rivers bring both relief and anxiety. And once the water recedes, people clean their homes, return to their fields and begin rebuilding knowing that the floods may return the next year.

Israel’s gasoline price will rise by 16 agorot to a record-equaling NIS 8.25 per liter overnight Monday
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
09:00:09 UTC
18:00:09 KST

Israeli gasoline prices to equal 2012 record after new increase
The maximum government-regulated price for a liter of self-service 95-octane unleaded gasoline will increase by 16 agorot to 8.25 shekels
Gasoline prices in Israel will rise again overnight Monday into Tuesday, bringing the cost of the most commonly used fuel to its highest recorded level in nearly 14 years.
The maximum government-regulated price for a liter of self-service 95-octane unleaded gasoline will increase by 16 agorot to 8.25 shekels, including value-added tax, the Ministry of Energy and Infrastructure’s Fuel and Gas Administration announced Sunday.
The new rate will equal the record set in September 2012, increasing pressure on motorists already facing elevated transportation and living costs.
Drivers who use full-service pumps will pay an additional 26 agorot per liter, up from the current 25-agorot surcharge. At a full-service station, the total regulated price will therefore reach 8.51 shekels per liter.
Bat-Sheva Abuhatzira, director of the Fuel and Gas Administration, attributed the increase to a combination of higher international gasoline prices, taxation changes and an updated marketing margin.
Global gasoline prices climbed by approximately 6% during the past month. The effect on Israeli consumers was partly softened by a roughly 3% decline in the value of the dollar, which reduced the local cost of fuel purchased on international markets.
Together, movements in the global gasoline market and the exchange rate added about 10 agorot to the price of each liter.
An inflation-linked adjustment to Israel’s fuel excise tax contributed another five agorot. The semiannual revision of the margin paid to fuel-marketing companies added a further one agora, bringing the total increase to 16 agorot.
The one-agora rise in the full-service surcharge was attributed in part to higher labor expenses following an increase in the minimum wage.
Israel updates its regulated gasoline price each month using several components, including international fuel costs, currency movements, taxes and marketing expenses. Although the weaker dollar provided some relief this month, it was not enough to offset the increase in global prices and domestic charges.

How China’s liquor heartland traded old spirits for new energy
Home to one of the nation’s legendary baijiu makers, Yibin is racing to reinvent itself as a hi-tech manufacturing hub – though stark challenges remain
Wuliangye, China’s second-largest liquor producer, is a household name. But Yibin, the lower-tier city in Sichuan province home to the famous baijiu maker, has long flown under the radar.
So when I received an invitation earlier this month for a media trip to Yibin, the first question that sprang to mind was: where exactly is it?
Tucked away behind the hills of western China, we had to fly to Chengdu, Sichuan’s capital, followed by a bus transfer. And when we finally arrived, local officials were keen to show us everything the city had to offer – except the liquor.
“Wuliangye is old-fashioned,” local cadres said.
What followed was a tour of a prefecture-level city trying hard to redefine itself: from a sleepy backwater into a manufacturing hub, with many of the costs typically associated with breakneck development.
One of the first things that caught our eye was a 288-metre (about 944 feet), 57-storey skyscraper rising from a prime waterfront plot with sweeping vistas of the Yangtze River. The building, one of the tallest in Sichuan, is expected to house the province’s first five-star Westin hotel in 2027 after its developer signed a contract with America’s Marriott International.

Scientists Create the Littlest Big Bang to Study the Universe's Origins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
09:00:00 UTC
18:00:00 KST

In the very first moments of the universe, matter didn’t exist as we know today. A millionth of a second or so after the big bang, the universe was a dense, hot soup scientists call quark-gluon plasma (QGP). For several years, particle colliders—which smash molecules together at nearly the speed of light—have been able to replicate this state, but often using heavy elements like lead.
Now, a recent experiment by the European Organization for Nuclear Research (also known as CERN from its French acronym) has demonstrated this plasma can be produced by much smaller collisions. Since there’s no longer an accessible natural source of this primordial sludge, these micro big bangs can help reveal what happened in the first few minutes of our universe.
First, a little context. Quarks are what make up protons and neutrons, which, in turn, are the building blocks of atoms and thus all matter. Meanwhile, gluons—as their name suggests—stick quarks together.
During the first microseconds of the universe, quarks and gluons were not yet confined within protons and neutrons but instead formed an extremely hot plasma. As the universe expanded, the matter cooled, and the quarks condensed into larger particles.
After decades of studying QGP in large nuclear collisions, physicists are now trying to understand the limits of this strange state of matter. In particular, they are exploring just how much they can scale down a collision and still observe a collection of particles that behaves like a drop of fluid.
According to a recent article in Physical Review Letters, CERN and an international team of collaborators were able to generate the substance using oxygen-16 and neon-20. Both are less than a tenth of the weight of a lead atom, which was previously considered one of the lightest elements capable of generating QGP.
“We have pushed the boundary for how small the atomic nuclei can be while still re-creating this primordial matter—what you could call a ‘little big bang.’ We now know more about the fundamental conditions required for matter to transition into this extreme state,” You Zhou, a researcher at the Niels Bohr Institute in the Netherlands and a coauthor of the study, explained in a press release.
The scientists found that, despite the small size of the oxygen and neon nuclei, the collisions produced signals consistent with the behavior they expected to find in QGP. For an instant, the generated matter appeared to expand collectively like a fluid before cooling and reverting to particles.
“Hopefully, this will help us better understand how the plasma behaved during the first moments of the universe—and how it later evolved into the forms of matter that everything around us is made of,” Zhou added.
This story originally appeared on WIRED en Español and has been translated from Spanish.

Lockheed Martin tests new JR3 rocket for HIMARS
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
08:59:01 UTC
17:59:01 KST

- Lockheed Martin conducted a second flight test of its JR3 training rocket at Yuma Proving Ground, firing rounds from a HIMARS launcher.
- The JR3 uses a reusable 24-round launch pod and is designed to replace the Army's current Reduced Range Practice Rocket.
Lockheed Martin fired multiple training rockets from a HIMARS launcher during a second flight test of its new Joint Reduced Range Rocket at Yuma Proving Ground, Arizona, the company said Friday.
The test measured range, trajectory, accuracy and the performance of the rocket’s marking payload, which allows crews to see where a round would have hit without using live ammunition. Lockheed Martin designed the JR3 to replace the Army’s current Reduced Range Practice Rocket, a training round used to simulate live-fire exercises at a lower cost and shorter range than a full combat rocket.
The JR3 fires from both the HIMARS and M270 Multiple Launch Rocket System. It comes packaged in a new 24-round launch pod, and the pod itself is designed to be reused rather than discarded after firing, which Lockheed Martin said lowers the cost of repeated training cycles.
“Our new training round offers a scalable, very affordable solution built on mature rocket motor technology,” said Dave Griser, vice president of Lockheed Martin Precision Fires Rockets. “With a 24-round rocket launch pod, our JR3 system meets the Army’s demand for higher training volume and lower cost without sacrificing performance.”
Lockheed Martin said the JR3 is built on established rocket motor technology rather than a new propulsion design, an approach the company said keeps the per-round cost low while still supporting repeatable, high-volume training. The reloadable launch tubes and reusable pods are central to that cost structure, according to the company.
The company said the JR3 would let launcher crews run realistic live-fire drills on training ranges with limited space, in day or night conditions, across multiple locations.
Lockheed Martin has scheduled another flight test later this year to continue validating the rocket’s performance. The company also said the JR3’s underlying architecture could carry over to future programs, including the Army’s Direct Support Fires Technology initiative, which is aimed at developing low-cost, mass-producible rockets.
This was the second flight test of the JR3 program.

Manhunt after fatal rave shooting in Switzerland
Swiss police were hunting at least one gunman who opened fire at the overnight rave party — a rare event in the Alpine nation despite relatively widespread gun ownership.
"For the moment, we have no reliable information regarding the perpetrators. We do not know whether it is a single person or several, nor whether they fled in a vehicle or on foot," police spokesman Bernhard Graser told reporters.

Police in Freiburg, in neighboring Germany, were also taking part in the manhunt, the German news agency dpa reported.
What else do we know about the Switzerland shooting?
According to Swiss newspaper Blick, the shots were fired before 3:00 a.m. local time (0100 GMT) during the annual Aarauer Rave.
The newspaper quoted police spokeswoman Vanessa Rumpold as saying that the shooting occurred at the Schachen race course where the techno party was being held.
Aarau has about 22,300 residents and is located about 40 kilometers (25 miles) west of Zürich.

U.S. Army’s newest tank prototype heads to 1st Cavalry Division
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
08:55:03 UTC
17:55:03 KST

- The U.S. Army's 1st Cavalry Division will test M1E3 Abrams and XM30 prototypes, according to the division's own social media announcement.
- The M1E3 is designed with a hybrid-electric drive, an autoloader and integrated protection in a lighter frame than current Abrams tanks.
The U.S. Army will send its M1E3 Abrams prototype to the 1st Cavalry Division for testing, the division confirmed in a social media post responding to an Army announcement about the next-generation tank.
The 1st Cavalry Division said it will receive both M1E3 prototypes and XM30 prototypes, testing the vehicles and providing feedback that will help shape the Army’s approach to future armored formations.
“And guess who gets to play with them first. The First Team will receive not only the M1E3 prototypes but also the XM30 prototypes to test, provide feedback on and to shape the future of Armored warfare,” the division wrote.
The Army’s announcement described the M1E3 as featuring a hybrid-electric drive, an autoloader and integrated protection systems built into a lighter frame than the current Abrams variants in service.
“The M1E3 Abrams represents a bold step forward in modern vehicle design, combining advanced protection, reduced weight, and a smaller logistical footprint to meet the challenges of tomorrow’s battlefield,” said Michelle Link, Deputy Capability Program Executive for Ground Combat Platforms.
The Army first showed the M1E3 publicly on January 14 at the Detroit Auto Show, presenting it as an early demonstrator built to test unmanned turret architecture, crew layout, digital systems and automation ahead of a planned M1A3 production tank. The design followed the Army’s earlier AbramsX concept demonstrator and reflects lessons the service says it drew from combat losses of donor Abrams tanks in Ukraine, where independent trackers and Ukrainian officials have reported significant losses among the 31 M1A1 tanks delivered, with estimates varying by source.
The most significant change from earlier Abrams variants is the unmanned turret. All three crew members, the commander, gunner and driver, are relocated into an armored crew capsule in the forward hull rather than sitting inside the turret itself, removing them from the tank’s most exposed section.
For targeting, the M1E3 uses the Leonardo DRS Stabilized Sight System, known as S3, as the commander’s panoramic sight, replacing the Safran PASEO system used on the earlier AbramsX demonstrator. The S3 is available in long-wave and mid-wave infrared variants and is also used on the Army’s M-LIDS counter-drone system.
Secondary armament comes from an EOS R400 Mk2 remote weapon station mounted atop the turret. In its displayed configuration, the station combines a 40mm Mk19 automatic grenade launcher, a 7.62mm machine gun and a launcher holding a single FGM-148 Javelin anti-tank missile. The R400 Mk2 is paired with an EchoGuard radar system for detecting and tracking small drones, giving the tank a built-in counter-UAS capability. Army representatives have said the weapon station’s loadout is modular and can be reconfigured depending on mission needs.
The Army has described the overall approach as built around a Modular Open Systems Architecture, intended to let new sensors, weapons and electronic warfare systems be added later through standardized interfaces rather than requiring a full redesign.
The Army has said four early M1E3 prototypes are planned, intended for testing with operational units to evaluate how the new features perform in practice, with serial production targeted for the end of the decade.
Separately, the XM30 program aims to replace the Bradley Infantry Fighting Vehicle, with General Dynamics Land Systems and American Rheinmetall Vehicles competing as finalists. General Dynamics delivered its XM30 Wolf prototype to the Army at Aberdeen Proving Ground last week.
The Army has not disclosed a specific delivery date for the M1E3 prototypes to the 1st Cavalry Division, based at Fort Cavazos, Texas, the total number of prototypes involved in this testing phase, or a timeline for when soldier feedback will inform further development of the design.

Most Swiss back stronger protection against heatwaves, survey finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
08:53:12 UTC
17:53:12 KST

Most Swiss back stronger protection against heatwaves, survey finds
A large majority of people in Switzerland are calling for better protection against heatwaves.
A survey by 20 Minuten and Tamedia, published on Sunday, found broad support for suspending work on building sites when temperatures reach 33°C and for installing air conditioning in public buildings. However, there was only narrow support for cancelling lessons during periods of extreme heat.
More
Sparse rainfall and heatwaves have put Switzerland on drought alert
There is overwhelming support for installing air conditioning in public buildings, particularly schools, care homes and hospitals, with 91% of those surveyed in favour. Support cuts across party lines, age groups and regions.
The Unia trade union’s call to suspend construction work when temperatures reach 33°C is also backed by a clear majority, with 81% in favour. Of those surveyed, 47% said yes outright and a further 34% said they were inclined to support the measure. Just 17% were opposed, including 6% who were strongly against it.
Support varies by gender. While 58% of women backed the proposal, the figure fell to 36% among men. A similar pattern was seen in relation to income, with lower-income respondents significantly more likely to support the measure.
More
Switzerland’s new energy challenge: keeping cool in a warming climate
Opinion is much more divided when it comes to school pupils. Should they be allowed to miss lessons once classroom temperatures reach 26°C? A slim majority of 51% say yes, while 47% are opposed. There is also a gender divide, with 57% of women backing the measure compared with 44% of men.
Air conditioning widely accepted
More broadly, 67% of respondents support wider use of air conditioning. Support increases with income.
A majority of respondents, 69%, also support relaxing cantonal planning rules for so-called split air-conditioning units, which consist of an indoor and an outdoor unit. Support for the move is particularly strong among men and among supporters of the Swiss People’s Party and the Radical-Liberal Party.
However, respondents do not necessarily want taxpayers to pick up the bill. Two-thirds, or 67%, oppose public subsidies for the installation of air conditioning in private homes.
The survey was conducted on August 19 and August 20 among 12,780 people across Switzerland in collaboration with the Leewas research institute. The margin of error was 1.4 percentage points.

NEW DELHI: India and Uzbekistan on Sunday agreed to deepen cooperation in trade and investment, digital connectivity, defence and energy as Prime Minister Narendra Modi held delegation-level talks with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev in Tashkent, with the two sides seeking to advance their strategic partnership and shared development goals.PM Modi, who is on a two-day state visit to Uzbekistan from August 29 to 30 at the invitation of Mirziyoyev, received a ceremonial welcome before the two leaders held talks on strengthening bilateral ties. The discussions focused on key areas of mutual interest and ways to advance the shared developmental visions of 'Viksit Bharat' and 'Yangi Uzbekistan', according to the Indian side.The talks came as India and Uzbekistan looked to build on the significant progress made in their strategic partnership in recent years. PM Modi had earlier said the relationship had witnessed significant advancement and expressed his desire to further deepen cooperation in key sectors.
PM Modi attends yoga session in Tashkent

It is bringing people and cultures together and strengthening people-to-people ties between India and Uzbekistan," the Ministry of External Affairs said in a post on X.
After the session, PM Modi said Uzbekistan had been a "proud participant" in the first-ever World Yogasana Championship held in Ahmedabad earlier this year. He also noted that some of the medal winners from the championship were present at the yoga session.
PM Modi's engagements in Uzbekistan

PM Modi to travel to Kyrgyzstan for SCO summit

The summit will mark the 25th anniversary of the SCO. PM Modi is expected to address the gathering and highlight India's priorities of "Security, Connectivity and Opportunity".He will also hold bilateral meetings with leaders of SCO member countries on the sidelines of the summit.PM Modi is further scheduled to attend the opening ceremony of the sixth World Nomad Games.The Uzbekistan visit is PM Modi's fourth trip to the Central Asian country and comes as New Delhi seeks to expand its engagement with the region through greater economic, strategic, energy and connectivity cooperation.

Niger says it regains control of airbase after soldiers mutiny
NIAMEY, Aug 30 - Niger's army regained control of a key military airbase on Sunday after it was attacked by mutinous soldiers a day earlier, the latest challenge to military ruler Abdourahamane Tiani as his government struggles to contain a jihadist insurgency.
The attack underscored tensions within Niger's armed forces, which have suffered repeated battlefield losses while fighting West Africa's al Qaeda and Islamic State affiliates.
Explosions and gunfire echoed across Niamey early on Saturday, including around the military airbase and the presidency. Three security sources told Reuters on Sunday that government forces had retaken the airbase after hours of fighting.
Residents said the capital appeared calm on Sunday, while aircraft circled overhead and authorities dismantled roadblocks erected during the unrest.
Located in the same complex as Niamey's civilian airport, the airbase is home to military aircraft and drones as well as a counter-terrorism unit of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES) which includes Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso.
Russian and Italian forces are also stationed there.
Africa Corps, a Kremlin-controlled paramilitary force, received a request for assistance in neutralising the mutineers in Niamey, Viktor Voropaev, the Russian ambassador to Niger, said on Saturday in an interview with TASS news agency.
Niger's presidential office said Algeria had also sent help in the form of four fighter jets, a transport aircraft and a refueling tanker delivered on Sunday.
Prior to Saturday's assault, the airbase had already been targeted twice this year - in January by the regional Islamic State affiliate and in June by the regional al Qaeda affiliate.
Niger state media said late Saturday that the attack involved "hundreds of disaffected soldiers" and that fighting lasted for several hours as forces loyal to military leader Tiani tried to regain control.
It aired footage purporting to show surrendering mutineers.
Reuters has not independently confirmed the state media report.
The Presidential Guard rallied to Tiani's defence, three security sources said. Tiani had not made any public appearances as of Sunday morning.
Niger, a West African nation rich in uranium, oil and gold resources, has been ruled by military officers since a July 2023 coup that ousted President Mohamed Bazoum.
SAHEL LEADERS STRUGGLE AGAINST JIHADISTS
Tiani, like his counterparts in Burkina Faso and Mali, has failed to make progress against jihadists.
The Islamic State affiliate has staged multiple deadly assaults on the military in southwest Niger, including one earlier this month that killed 18 soldiers.
The mutineers' operation involved soldiers based in Niamey as well as soldiers from the localities of Ouallam, Tera and Dosso, where the army has sustained heavy casualties.
Analysts and security sources say frustration with the government is mounting within frontline units, creating another vulnerability for Tiani beyond the insurgents themselves.
Since seizing power, Tiani's government has shifted away from Western partners, deepened ties with Russia and broken with the regional ECOWAS bloc.
The unrest comes as authorities tighten control over the uranium sector, having seized assets from France's Orano. Niger had been a key supplier of nuclear fuel to Europe, accounting for about 15% of Orano's uranium supply at full capacity. REUTERS

U.S. Army tests autonomous 257-foot vessel in Hawaii
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
08:46:00 UTC
17:46:00 KST

- Sea Machines Robotics added autonomous navigation to the 257-foot HOS Resolution vessel in nine days, then tested it with the U.S. Army in Hawaii.
- The test included an 18-hour autonomous transit from Pearl Harbor to Hawaii's Big Island using the company's SM300 autonomy package.
A commercial supply ship the length of a football field just spent nine days getting a robot brain installed, and then drove itself across open water in Hawaii with the U.S. Army watching.
The ship is called the HOS Resolution, a 257-foot (78-meter) offshore supply vessel normally used to haul equipment and supplies to oil rigs and other offshore operations. It’s owned and operated by a company called Hornbeck Offshore. This wasn’t some purpose-built robotic ship designed from the keel up. It’s a regular commercial vessel that a company called Sea Machines Robotics retrofitted with autonomous controls.
Here’s the part that stands out: Sea Machines says the whole conversion took nine days. That’s the time it took to bolt on the sensors, cameras, and computer systems needed to let the ship navigate and make decisions on its own, without a captain steering every move.
“HOS Resolution wasn’t built to be autonomous,” Sea Machines said in a statement. “Sea Machines added autonomous command and control to the existing commercial vessel in just nine days.”
Once the system was installed, the team put it to the test. The ship ran an 18-hour autonomous transit from Pearl Harbor to Hawaii’s Big Island, with the U.S. Army involved in the testing. Sea Machines didn’t say which specific Army unit or office was on hand, or what kind of military scenario the trip was meant to simulate.
The technology behind the conversion is called the SM300, which Sea Machines describes as a deployable package: essentially a kit of hardware and software that can be installed on an existing ship to give it autonomous capability, rather than requiring the military to design and build an entirely new type of vessel.
Building a brand-new class of autonomous ship from scratch can take years and cost enormous sums of money. If a company can instead take a ship that already exists, one that’s already been tested, already floats, already has a hull that works, and retrofit it with autonomy in a matter of days, that’s a much faster and cheaper way for the military to add more autonomous vessels to its fleet.
Sea Machines has worked on smaller autonomous vessel projects before, including some tied to U.S. Navy unmanned surface vessel programs. But the HOS Resolution, at 257 feet, is a considerably larger ship than what the company has previously converted, at least based on what’s been publicly disclosed.
What we don’t know yet: how much the conversion cost, whether the Army plans to keep testing with this specific ship, or how many more vessels Sea Machines might convert under this same approach going forward.

US diplomats urged to ask governments to deploy security forces for High Holy Days
In an instruction cable sent to US missions, American diplomats were asked to urge governments to deploy, when necessary, police forces, counterterrorism units, or even military personnel at synagogues and locations where prayers and holiday events will be held.

The official also referenced the executive order signed by US President Donald Trump at the beginning of his term, which states that it is US policy to fight antisemitism “with determination” and through all appropriate legal tools.

Iceland rejects EU membership plan in referendum, after almost all votes were counted
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
08:44:22 UTC
17:44:22 KST

Iceland has rejected the government's proposal to hold accession talks with the European Union, public broadcaster RUV reported on Sunday, with only a small number of votes left to count.
Based on the first 188,500 votes counted of an eligible 270,000 from Saturday's referendum, 52.5% were against the government's proposal to restart negotiations, while 47.5% were in favor, RUV reported. No information was available on turnout.
"Yes" campaigners said that joining the bloc could ease high interest rates and offer more security in a world unsettled by the war in Ukraine and US President Donald Trump's threats over another Arctic island, Greenland.
"No" campaigners argued EU membership would threaten the island's sovereignty and fishing waters.
"Today is our encounter with history," Iceland's former President Olafur Ragnar Grimsson, a campaigner against EU membership, said in a post on social media.
Old questions, new urgency
Iceland first applied to join the EU in 2009, amid a financial crisis that hit the country's small, exposed economy especially hard. Talks ended in 2013 when a Eurosceptic government shelved the process.
Renewed geopolitical turmoil has brought fresh urgency to an issue Icelanders have debated on and off for decades.
Foreign Minister Thorgerdur Katrin Gunnarsdottir, who has been backing 'yes', told Reuters last week that Saturday's vote boils down to a simple question: can Iceland still afford to stand apart in a world where old certainties are crumbling?
"The international order that underpinned our security and prosperity for decades is under serious pressure," she said. "In times like these, small nations need to think carefully about where they stand and who stands with them."

Details

Feature: Chinese training program boosts skills in Myanmar's garment industry
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
16:36:58 CST
17:36:58 KST

YANGON, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- A well-made garment starts with a well-made pattern. Nearly 40 garment industry professionals and students in Myanmar recently took part in a training course to improve their skills in pattern making and garment manufacturing.
Jointly organized by the Myanmar Garment Manufacturers Association (MGMA) and the Chinese Textile & Garment Association in Myanmar, the training was held in Yangon and led by instructors from the Changzhou Vocational Institute of Textile and Garment from east China's Jiangsu Province. It focused mainly on pattern making and sample development.
The six-day training, which concluded on Saturday, brought together factory owners, designers, garment workers and students from Yangon and Mandalay.
For Ma Yi Mon Khin, founder of Shwe Poe Mandalay Company, pattern making is the starting point of garment production.
"The first step in manufacturing a garment is the pattern. If the pattern is not right, the whole garment is not right," she said.
She traveled from Mandalay to Yangon to deepen her knowledge of pattern making. As a garment factory owner, she regularly reviews production reports and said that understanding the process would help her identify the causes of production problems and find ways to address them.
The training covered pattern making for jackets, skirts and trousers, as well as other aspects of garment production and ordering.
"The training is very beneficial because it can broaden the vision of participants working in the garment industry in Myanmar," said Su Su Paing, founder of Su Paing Co., Ltd.
Her company also sources fabrics from China, processes them in Myanmar and sells the finished products.
For 35-year-old designer Nang Kham Aung of Diamond Sea Sar Garment Co., Ltd., the training provided an opportunity to acquire new technical skills.
"This is the first time I have attended this kind of training. I learned about pattern making. It is beneficial for me," she said.
The course also included young people preparing to enter the garment industry. Among them was 22-year-old Thoon Sandar Wai, a student who is studying Chinese while developing practical skills in garment production.
"I joined the training as I am interested in garment manufacturing," she said.
She hopes to apply what she learned when she begins working, saying that her Chinese-language skills and knowledge of garment production could help her build a career in the industry.
According to data released by the Directorate of Investment and Company Administration, the manufacturing sector in Myanmar received the largest share of foreign direct investment during the 2025-2026 fiscal year, amounting to more than 245 million U.S. dollars. Myanmar's garment sector plays a pivotal role in the country's economic development.
The MGMA said Chinese investment has brought both capital and technology to the country's garment industry, while the sector relies on China for raw materials and accessories.
Against this backdrop, the association said it hoped cooperation with Chinese garment associations would continue through more technology-focused training programs, which it said would help local manufacturers and workers enhance their technical skills and competitiveness. ■

Ukraine Aims to Launch 1,000 Long-Range Drones Daily at Russian Targets
Ukraine is set to scale up its output of long-range aerial drones to 1,000 units per day, up from the current daily average of about 300 units.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy outlined this objective on August 28 following a meeting of the Supreme Commander-in-Chief's Staff, where officials discussed expanding air defenses and shielding the country from Russian strikes.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
President Zelenskyy noted that long-range operations are disrupting economic stability and supply networks across Russia, cutting into domestic petrol reserves and export volumes.
Expanding long-range capabilities is designed to increase economic pressure on Russia if it chooses to prolong Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine and decline peace talks.
Ukrainian officials also emphasized the need to accelerate the manufacturing of interceptor drones to counter jet-powered Shahed attack drones recently deployed in higher volumes.
Reuters reported in late August that Russian petrol production dropped to approximately 80,000 metric tons per day against an internal requirement of roughly 115,000 metric tons. The resulting shortfall led several regions across Russia to reintroduce restrictions on fuel sales.
Ukraine systematically targeted Russia's oil refineries, striking all 11 of the country's largest facilities to erode the Kremlin's financial foundation.
The campaign disabled over 40% of Russia's refining capacity, creating severe domestic fuel shortages and forcing Moscow to import petrol while selling discounted crude oil abroad.

Russia Plans Scenarios for Kyiv and Chernihiv Operations, Ukrainian Intelligence Says

In response, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine has developed defensive countermeasures and tactical responses for each potential scenario.
"I ask you to note: to plan and prepare. That is, indeed, several options were considered there. Accordingly, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine has developed possible options for response, defense, protection, and counteraction to these measures," Palisa said.
Ukrainian intelligence currently sees no indication that Russian forces are assembling offensive strike groups in those directions.
"The priority task for us is to prevent the creation of conditions for the Russians to be able to start any offensive actions at all," he added.
Ukrainian intelligence detected signs that Russia was preparing a new wave of mobilization immediately after the staged State Duma elections on September 21, 2026, likely in the first days of October.
The campaign was expected to involve between 300,000 and 500,000 new recruits. The underlying reason behind this politically costly step for Russian leader Vladimir Putin was the failure of Russia’s recruitment system, as the contract-based model that had sustained the Kremlin over the preceding two years was no longer keeping pace with battlefield losses.

Mystery military vehicle spotted in Japan sparks online debate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
08:34:58 UTC
17:34:58 KST

- Japanese social media users photographed a tarp-covered tracked vehicle being transported by truck this week, prompting online speculation about a new armored vehicle.
- No Japanese defense official has confirmed the vehicle's identity, and shared technical diagrams referenced online remain unofficial and unverified.
Something big and mysterious rolled down a Japanese road late last week, and the internet is obsessed with figuring out what it is.
A user on X posting under the name Yuzu snapped photos of a tracked military vehicle riding on a flatbed truck at night, completely wrapped in a yellow tarp. You could still make out the shape underneath: tank-like tracks, a boxy hull, the works. Yuzu’s caption was simple.
“Something amazing was running around,” Yuzu wrote.
That was enough to set off a small army of Japanese military watchers who spend their free time identifying vehicles from silhouettes and shadows.
One user, going by Future_Craft, started counting things. The vehicle has six road wheels on each side, which immediately rules out Japan’s Type 10 tank. There’s no engine bulge in the back, which rules out the Type 90 tank too. Based on the process of elimination, Future_Craft guessed it might be built on the Type 89 infantry fighting vehicle. But then something didn’t add up: the back of the side armor skirt looked cut away, with no foothold cutout where you’d normally expect one. Future_Craft’s reaction summed up the whole thread: a confused string of question marks and a joke about “X-Files” music.
Another user, posting as Beta, connected the dots to something more specific: a program referred to online as “loitering-type UAV countermeasure equipment,” essentially a vehicle meant to deal with loitering munitions, the slow, explosive-carrying drones that hover before diving into a target. Beta shared old-looking technical line drawings showing two versions of a tracked vehicle, one with a turret and cannon that looks like a proper armored fighting vehicle, and another that looks more like a support variant. Based on the width of what appears to be a radar mount in the drawings, Beta thinks the vehicle caught on camera matches the armored combat version.
A third user, THA BOS, pulled out a ruler, essentially. Comparing the leaked diagrams to Japan’s existing Type 89 and its “common tracked chassis” platform, this user noticed the spacing between road wheels looks stretched out, and the whole vehicle appears longer than what’s currently in service. Officially, though, it’s still classified as a modification of that same common chassis, not a brand new vehicle from scratch.
Here’s the honest answer, though: nobody actually knows for sure what this thing is. None of the diagrams being passed around online carry any official markings from Japan’s Ministry of Defense or its Acquisition, Technology and Logistics Agency. No Japanese defense official has said a word about it publicly. The “loitering-type UAV countermeasure equipment” name being used by online sleuths hasn’t been confirmed by anyone in an official capacity either.
So for now, it’s just a tarp, some grainy nighttime photos, and a very active group of amateur analysts trying to reverse-engineer Japan’s next combat vehicle from a truck bed.

Iceland rejects EU-accession talks in close-fought referendum
- Icelanders voted against reopening EU membership talks, prioritising control over fishing waters and sovereignty despite government support for joining.
- The referendum reflects long-standing debate intensified by geopolitical tensions and economic concerns like high inflation and interest rates.
- Opponents argue EU membership won't solve Iceland's problems, while supporters see it as a chance for economic stability and security in a turbulent world.
AI generated
REYKJAVIK – Icelanders voted to stay out of the European Union (EU), referendum results showed on Aug 30, as they rejected a government push to reopen membership talks and sided with those who said Iceland’s fishing waters were too important to risk.
The Arctic island of 400,000 people has debated whether to join the EU for well over a decade and had initially been narrowly expected to back holding membership talks, but opinion polls in August showed views had changed.
“This is a clear setback for Brussels,” an EU diplomat told Reuters, adding that the issues of fishing and independence had been decisive.
In the Aug 29 referendum, 52.8 per cent of ballots cast were against the government’s proposal to hold negotiations with Brussels, 47.2 per cent were in favour, and 82.5 per cent of eligible voters took part, public broadcaster RUV and other Icelandic media reported.
Out of six constituencies, only the two in central Reykjavik had a majority that voted in favour, while the rural areas and the Reykjavik suburbs voted against.
The government has framed membership as a shield against trade wars and Arctic rivalry and presented the referendum as a “now or never” moment. Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir said a “no” would end the debate for as long as her centre-left coalition was in power.
A government press conference is scheduled for 1pm local time (9pm Singapore time).
Decades of membership debate
In Brussels, some officials had voiced hopes a vote to join from Iceland could ease scepticism toward EU enlargement and strategically strengthen the bloc when Arctic security is in focus.
Iceland, a NATO member state but with no standing army of its own, also debated whether EU accession could boost the country’s security when US President Donald Trump has cast doubt on the US commitment to the military alliance.
Trump has also repeatedly said he wants to do a deal to acquire another Arctic island, Greenland.
But for some Icelanders, fishing was a sharper focus than security.
The industry is one of Iceland’s biggest, making up 15 per cent of gross domestic product in direct and indirect contributions, and some 40 per cent of export revenue, data shows.
Interest rates and the cost of living
The island nation first applied to join the EU in 2009 when a financial crisis hit the country’s small, exposed economy. A Eurosceptic government ended talks in 2013.
Ahead of the referendum, finances were again a central issue as Iceland has grappled with high inflation and interest rates.
Supporters of a “yes” vote said EU membership, and possibly adopting the euro, could bring relief. Iceland’s central bank interest rate is 8 per cent, compared with 2.25 per cent at the European Central Bank.
“It would not solve Iceland’s structural faults, but it could become a catalyst to a more healthy economy,” said chief economist Vilhjalmur Hilmarsson at Viska, one of Iceland’s largest labour unions.
Opposition leader Gudrun Hafsteinsdottir, who led the “no” campaign, said the economic case is overstated.
“These are not problems that Brussels will solve for us. These are problems that Icelandic politicians must solve,” she said.
Voter Ragnhildur Skarphedinsdottir, 70, said Iceland was managing well on its own and that she was voting “no”.
“By staying independent as we are, we look brightly to the future,” she said before casting her ballot in Reykjavik.
Under EU rules, fishing quotas are based on historical fishing patterns, among other factors. Some Icelandic officials have said Iceland would therefore retain control of its waters, since no EU country has fished there for decades.
Hafsteinsdottir disputed that. “I know that the European Union will come up with some promises of some flexibility, especially in the beginning, but we know that it will not be for good,” she said. REUTERS

Behind the Nepal-China border floods lie bad politics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
08:30:07 UTC
17:30:07 KST

Behind the Nepal-China border floods lie bad politics
While the solidarity on display in the wake of the disaster is commendable, the tragedy must not be viewed as an unpredictable, unpreventable act of nature
As the waters of the Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers recede, leaving behind mud, debris and damaged infrastructure, a familiar pattern is visible in Nepal. When disaster strikes, the country’s usual political divisions, cronyism and institutional mistrust give way, for a while, to real unity.
Across party lines, political leaders worked around the clock alongside security forces. Digital channels opened for the Prime Minister’s Disaster Relief Fund, a “one-door policy” was enforced to prevent duplication of relief efforts and telecoms operators made calls and internet free across affected areas. Diaspora communities and local volunteers stepped up alongside the state.
But a familiar governance pattern is at risk of taking hold again: treating this disaster as an unpredictable, unpreventable act of nature.
A natural event – glacier collapse, cloudburst, avalanche or wildfire – is a physical trigger. A disaster is something else. It is shaped by the human choices made around that trigger.
What was first reported as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake was, according to the US Geological Survey, a large mass of rock and ice breaking off a glaciated mountain in Langtang National Park, near the Tibet-Nepal border. The collapse released energy equivalent to a 5.2-magnitude earthquake, releasing a debris flow that travelled nearly 100km downstream.
An unstable lake formed by remaining ice blockages still sits upstream. Emergency readiness now means moving from reactive rescue to continuous, real-time monitoring and staged evacuation planning downstream.

Uzbekistan confirms delivery of Chinese J-10 fighter jets
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
08:19:38 UTC
17:19:38 KST

- Uzbek state television aired footage confirming delivery of Chengdu J-10CE fighter jets during 35th independence anniversary coverage.
- Uzbekistan is now the second foreign operator of the J-10CE after Pakistan, with a reported first batch of six aircraft.
Uzbekistan’s state television broadcast footage of a Chengdu J-10CE fighter jet on the ground during coverage of the country’s 35th independence anniversary celebrations, confirming for the first time that Uzbekistan has received the Chinese-made aircraft.
The footage aired on Uzbekistan 24, a state channel, and showed the jet taxiing on a runway. The first batch is reportedly six aircraft, based at Karshi-Khanabad airbase in southern Uzbekistan, though that basing detail has not been officially confirmed by Uzbek authorities.
The broadcast marks the first acknowledgment from Uzbekistan’s government that it has taken delivery of the J-10CE, following more than a year of unconfirmed reporting on the purchase. Uzbekistan is now the second foreign operator of the J-10CE, after Pakistan.
Researcher Andreas Rupprecht, who tracks Chinese military aviation, published a photograph in August that he described as likely the first clear image of a J-10CE belonging to the Uzbekistan Air Force.
“Likely the first clear(er) image of an Uzbekistan Air Force J-10CE,” Rupprecht wrote.
Uzbekistan had reportedly agreed to purchase 24 J-10CE fighters from China for around $1 billion, a deal that circulated in defense reporting since at least last year but was never officially confirmed by Tashkent before this week’s broadcast. Uzbekistan’s air force has relied on Soviet-era aircraft, including the MiG-29, making the J-10CE purchase a significant shift toward Chinese-made hardware.
The J-10CE is the export version of China’s single-engine, single-seat J-10C, built by Chengdu Aircraft Industry Group. The aircraft is a fourth-generation-plus multirole fighter equipped with an active electronically scanned array radar and capable of firing the PL-15E, a long-range, active radar-guided air-to-air missile with a publicly stated export range of around 145 kilometers (90 miles). The jet also carries the shorter-range PL-10 infrared-guided missile for close-in engagements and uses a fly-by-wire flight control system with canard-delta aerodynamics for high maneuverability.
The J-10C gained international attention following a brief conflict between India and Pakistan in May 2025, when Pakistan’s air force flew J-10Cs armed with PL-15 missiles in aerial engagements with Indian fighters. Pakistani officials claimed the J-10C was responsible for shooting down multiple Indian aircraft during that clash, including at least one Dassault Rafale, though India has not confirmed the extent of its own losses. The engagement was widely described as one of the first instances of Chinese-made fighters downing Western-made aircraft in real combat, and it significantly raised international interest in the J-10 family, including its export variant now delivered to Uzbekistan.
The Defence Blog first reported on the probable Uzbekistan contract in April 2025. Following that report, the Defense Industry Agency under Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Defense asked The Defence Blog to remove the article and delay further coverage.
“I would like to inform you that the given information does not reflect reality. Currently, negotiations are underway with several countries on this matter, and publishing such information may influence our discussions with other nations. We would be deeply grateful if you could postpone the article for some time. Once a final decision is made, we will notify you at your address,” a senior employee of the agency wrote at the time.
The agency did not issue any further statement confirming or denying the deal until this week’s state television broadcast. Uzbekistan’s government has still not published official details on the total number of aircraft delivered, the full delivery timeline, or the contract’s final value.
