• The US said it attacked Iranian rocket launchers on Larak Island on Sunday, with Iranian media reporting explosions and multiple casualties in the renewed strikes.
• Israel has launched fresh attacks in Gaza, killing at least one person and injuring several others in a strike in Deir al-Balah. The Israeli military claimed it killed a Hamas commander in yesterday's attack in Jabalia refugee camp.
• Fresh Israeli attacks have also been reported in southern Lebanon in violation of the fragile ceasefire deal.
• Iran's supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei has called on the Muslim world to unite against the US and Israel in a written message, six months after the start of the war.
•    Extremist settlers are continuing to rampage in the West Bank as pogroms against Palestinians intensify across the occupied territory. Attacks against Palestinian civilians have been reported in a dozen locations, including villages near Nablus and Ramallah, Masafer Yatta and Al-Mughayyir.
•    On Saturday, settlers attacked an American news crew near the besieged village of Qusra, drawing a rare condemnation from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. In Masafer Yatta, settlers kidnapped British activist Finn Joughin, whose whereabouts remain unknown.
 
Iran is attacking US forces stationed in Jordan, Fox News reporter Trey Yingst said on Sunday, citing a US source.
There has been no significant impact so far, the reporter's X post said, adding that nearly all incoming missiles "have been intercepted at this point."
The number of visible commodity vessels transiting the Strait of Hormuz dropped to five per day over the weekend, shipping data showed on Monday, as companies tread cautiously amid continued attacks on ships.
The actual number of ships passing the strait could be higher as some vessels have switched off their automatic identification system to evade attacks.
The US military has said it redirected 83 commercial ships, "disabled" three others and boarded two as part of the ongoing blockade against Iran as of 30 August.
The Trump administration plans to impose sanctions on another bank this week in an effort to clamp down on Iran transactions, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday.
Bessent spoke with The Associated Press ahead of Group of 20 meetings in Asheville, North Carolina, where he will meet individually with his counterparts from the world’s major and developing economies to encourage participation in the economic isolation of Iran.
"This is going to be financial violence if we have to," Bessent said in the interview. "We are showing people that we know who you are, you know who you are, and this has got to stop."
Bessent had recently announced a new campaign to push countries that still do business with the already heavily sanctioned Islamic Republic to sever their financial ties or face retaliation from the United States.
Lebanese media reports Israeli forces have launched phosphorus shells in Nabatiyeh el-Fawqa in southern Lebanon.
Syria's Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani hailed on Sunday the reopening of his country's embassy in the Libyan capital Tripoli, which had been closed for more than a decade.
Shaibani was welcomed by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah, who leads the UN-recognised administration in Tripoli, and held talks with Taher al-Baour, Libya's acting foreign minister.
"Today, this embassy returns to reaffirm the importance and value of the Syrian-Libyan relationship," Shaibani said.
Last year, a delegation from Damascus symbolically reopened the embassy, which was shut in 2012, but it did not immediately resume consular services.
Relations between the two countries had been upended by Syria's civil war and the chaos that followed the fall of longtime Libyan ruler Muammar Gaddafi.
Syria's new authorities took power in December 2024 when they ousted longtime ruler Bashar al-Assad after nearly 14 years of war.
"This embassy will handle the administrative follow-up for Syrians who took refuge in Libya during the years of war, at a time when there was no longer any diplomatic representation, since Tripoli had broken off relations with the former regime," Shaibani said.
According to Syria's state news agency SANA, the Syrian community in Libya is estimated at around 200,000 people.
Shaibani said the two countries "also agreed to strengthen security coordination to combat illegal immigration, as well as drugs and terrorist organisations".
Iran's Revolutionary Guards said a U.S. attack on Larak island on Sunday killed and wounded several Iranian fighters and civilians, and vowed to respond and punish those responsible, state broadcaster IRIB reported.
The Guards did not provide a precise casualty toll.
France is preparing for its presidential election in eight months, with analysts telling The New Arab that Palestine has become an increasingly important domestic litmus test in the battle for political power.
With President Emmanuel Macron constitutionally barred from seeking a third consecutive term, the 2027 race is more open than it has been in years.
From left-wing candidate Jean-Luc Melenchon, whose pro-Palestine rhetoric has helped bolster his support, to National Rally (RN) figures seeking closer ties with Israel, analysts said Palestine could emerge as not only a major foreign policy issue but also a defining electoral fault line during the campaign.
Read the full story here.
US forces struck Iranian rocket launchers on the Strait of Hormuz in first military action in weeks, US official says.
An explosion was heard near Iran's Larak Island, the Fars news agency reported Sunday, adding that the cause was unknown.
Earlier, Axios reported that US forces struck two Iranian launchers on Iran's Larak island: "Revolutionary Guard forces were observed preparing to launch rockets carrying sea mines toward the Strait of Hormuz," Axios reporter Barak Ravid quoted the official as saying.
A passenger ferry capsized and sank off Northern Cyprus Sunday, killing at least eight people and leaving more than a dozen missing, officials and media reports said, as police took the captain and seven crew members into custody.
Several rescued passengers told local media a blast had gone off at the bow of the ferry before it rolled over, and said the boat had an insufficient supply of life-vests.
The vessel capsized 6.5 kilometres (four miles) off the coast of Cyprus, shortly after leaving a Northern Cyprus port bound for Turkey's mainland.
On Sunday evening, four Palestinians were wounded by live bullets during an attack by settlers on the village of Al-Mughayyir, northeast of Ramallah.
The Palestinian Red Crescent said its teamns treated four people with live bullet injuries before hospitalising them.
Local sources added that Israeli forces also closed the only entrance to the village, amid a continued presence of soldiers and settlers there.
Syrian forces killed a former Assad-era commander during a security operation in Safita, east of Tartus, authorities said on Sunday, as the government intensifies its campaign against armed groups it says are linked to remnants of the former Assad regime.
Firas Abdul Karim Hammoud, known as "al-Khal", was the former commander of special forces in the unit once known as the 25th Division, the Syrian Interior Ministry said in a statement.
The ministry said Internal Security forces raided Hammoud’s hideout in the town of Safita in Tartus province after tracking his movements across several areas.
Two civilians were killed near the Druze-majority city of Sweida in southern Syria on Sunday, two local security sources told AFP, during suspected clashes between local armed groups and government forces.
The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights monitor reported the same death toll, adding that government forces and armed groups from the Druze minority group had been exchanging fire since Saturday night.
Tensions have been high in Sweida province since clashes between Druze and government-aligned forces last year led to some of the worst communal violence since the fall of longtime Syrian ruler Bashar al-Assad in 2024.
A Druze security source told AFP on condition of anonymity that a shell launched from a government-controlled area "targeted the outskirts of the city of Sweida, striking a tractor and killing two people on board, the driver and a woman who was with him".
Sweida city and other parts of the surrounding Druze-majority province are run by armed groups and are the last major areas outside the grasp of Syria's new Islamist authorities, who have been trying to unite the country after toppling Assad.
A tanker was struck by an unknown projectile while transiting inbound through the Strait of Hormuz on Saturday, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said on Sunday.
The incident occurred 12 nautical miles north of Oman's Khasab, UKMTO said in an advisory note, adding that no casualties or environmental impact were reported.
The United Arab Emirates and Egyptian central banks are coordinating on Banque Misr, they said on Sunday, after the US imposed sanctions on the bank's UAE branches over its alleged dealings with Iran.
The US Treasury on Friday said it was cutting off the bank's UAE operations from dollar transactions after accusing it of ties with Iran.
Banque Misr will take all necessary measures to conduct its business as usual, the central banks said in their joint statement.
US military officials have warned Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth that a prolonged war against Iran is unsustainable and jeopardising the military’s ability to respond to other threats around the world, the Washington Post has reported, citing anonymous sources.
In a 14 August report, army, navy and air force chiefs told Hegseth that the war has been "too much for too long" and is putting military readiness under strain.
Israeli forces have raided Qalandia refugee camp north of Jerusalem and the UNRWA-run Qalandia vocational training centre in East Jerusalem for the second time in a week, according to Palestinian news agency WAFA.
Security forces seized the UN-run centre on Tuesday and expelled dozens of staff, drawing international condemnation.
The Israeli military has claimed it killed a Hamas commander in today's drone strike in Deir al-Balah in central Gaza.
It identified him as Hussam Osama Hussein Nasir, who it said was a member of Hamas's military wing, the Al-Qassam Brigades.
Medics said two people were killed in the attack, including a man and a three-year-old boy.
Iraq sentenced a US-sanctioned oil official to seven years in prison after he was arrested as part of a government-led anti-corruption campaign, the country's anti-graft body said on Sunday.
Deputy oil minister for distribution affairs Ali al-Bahadli is among dozens of officials who were detained in June during anti-graft raids that took place in several areas, mostly in Baghdad's fortified Green Zone.
The Commission of Integrity said in a statement that an anti-corruption court sentenced Bahadli to seven years in prison for "illicit gains".
The ruling requires Bahadli to return to the state an amount equivalent to more than $20 million in ill-gotten gains, in addition to paying a fine of the same amount.
The United States imposed sanctions on Bahadli in May, accusing him of fraudulently mixing Iraqi and Iranian oil as part of a scheme to help Iran avoid sanctions.
Turkey will host Saudi Arabia and Pakistan for the first ministerial meeting of their new regional defence grouping on Monday, Turkish sources said Sunday.
The Mecca Joint Defence Agreement signed earlier this month commits the three countries to mutual defence in the event of any of them being attacked.
The pact came against a backdrop of war between the United States and Iran and attacks in the region from Tehran-backed Houthi rebels.
The meeting in Istanbul will set up a "political and defence strategic committee" involving foreign and defence ministers and military chiefs, Turkish foreign ministry sources said.
The agreement unites NATO's second-largest army, Turkey, with the Islamic world's only nuclear-armed state, Pakistan, and the leading Gulf power in Saudi Arabia.
Monday's meeting will be chaired by the Turkish foreign and defence ministers as well as the chief of the general staff.
Pakistan is sending Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar, along with the defence minister and the commander of the defence forces.
Saudi Arabia will be represented by its foreign minister, the defence minister and the chief of the general staff, Turkish sources said.
As well as international security, the participants plan to address boosting defence capabilities, the interoperability of their armed forces, and their cooperation in the defence industry, Ankara said.
The Israeli strike in Gaza's Deir al-Balah earlier this morning killed a three-year-old child and a man, according to local health officials.
Medics said the Israeli airstrike near a bakery killed one man, Hussam Nusair, a three-year-old boy, Tayyem Hamdan, and wounded several others.
Israel has killed at least five Palestinians in Gaza over the past 24 hours, according to Gaza's health ministry.
At least 1,318 people have been killed by Israeli forces since the "ceasefire" was supposed to come into effect in October, the ministry said in its daily bulletin.
The Israeli army has carried out a "massive" explosion in the border town of Houla in Lebanon's Marjayoun district, according to Lebanon’s National News Agency.
Israel's far-right national security minister on Sunday boasted of worsening conditions for Palestinian prisoners as he visited female inmates.
Two months before elections, Itamar Ben-Gvir posted a video in which a veiled woman, her face blurred out, said that prisoners had "extremely bad" conditions and "don't get any rights, and we have particular needs as women".
"We haven't bathed for three days and we haven't changed our underwear," she said, warning of the risk of disease.
Ben-Gvir responds approvingly as he compares the treatment to that of captives held for up to two years by Hamas and other fighters in Gaza following the 7 October 2023 attack.
"Our hostages had no shampoo and had no such conditions. I am proud that we have succeeded in reducing the terrorists' prison conditions to the bare minimum. The summer camps in the prisons are over," Ben Gvir said.
Militant settlers are continuing to rampage in the occupied West Bank as pogroms against Palestinians intensify across the territory. Attacks against Palestinian civilians were reported in a dozen locations on Sunday, including in villages near Nablus and Ramallah, Masafer Yatta and Al-Mughayyir.
Hundreds of settlers raided Islamic religious sites in the village of Awarta, southeast of Nablus, under the protection of Israeli forces.
Meanwhile, Israeli soldiers began destroying Palestinian-owned land in the town of Deir Ballut, in the central West Bank.

Iceland votes 'No' to further EU accession talks in tight result
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
08:09:25 UTC
17:09:25 KST

Iceland's relationship with Brussels will not fundamentally change. The country already participates in the European Economic Area and the passport-free Schengen zone, and both arrangements stay intact.
Iceland's "No" camp has narrowly won a referendum on whether to resume the country's suspended European Union membership negotiations, officials have confirmed.
The final result was close but decisive: "No" finished nearly 5.6% ahead of "Yes," a gap of just under 13,000 votes out of more than 225,000 cast — enough to settle the question, but far from a landslide.
Prime Minister Kristrún Frostadóttir used a post-result press conference to call for unity, urging the country to respect both sides of the debate.
"47% of the population was interested in it [restarting EU talks]. I think it is important that we go into the coming months and weeks and respect that point of view," she said.
Turnout reached 82.5%, one of the highest levels recorded in an Icelandic national vote, with well over half the country's roughly 400,000 residents turning out to cast a ballot on a decision that will shape Iceland's relationship with Europe for years to come.
Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir framed the turnout itself as one of the referendum's biggest takeaways.
"For me as Foreign Minister, it was incredibly good and nice that there was much more discussion about international affairs in society than before," she said.
The result exposed a sharp divide between Iceland's capital and its rural regions. Voters in Reykjavík North and Reykjavík South both backed "Yes" comfortably but that support evaporated outside the capital as the South, Northwest and Northeast constituencies all delivered emphatic "No" majorities.
The votes in order of the announcements were divided as follows:
Reykjavík North: Yes 57.5% - No 42.5%
Reykjavík South: Yes 54.5% - No 45.5%
South constituency: Yes 39.5% - No 60.5%
Northwest constituency: Yes 37.1% - No 62.9%
Northeast constituency: Yes: 38.8% No: 61.2%
Southwest constituency: Yes: 47.0% No: 53.0%
The "No" outcome will shelve the EU debate in Icelandic politics for at least two more years.
Speaking after casting her ballot Saturday, Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadóttir said the referendum campaign had "lifted discussions about the EU, about Iceland's place in the world, about our general geopolitical situation and status, to a higher level".
She had made no secret of her own preference for "Yes," but stressed the country would manage fine either way.
Frostadóttir had committed to shelving the EU membership question entirely for the remainder of her term — which runs until 2028 — if voters rejected reopening accession talks.
Her government had also indicated that, in a "No" scenario, it would leave the decision on whether to formally withdraw Iceland's EU membership application up to parliament, rather than deciding unilaterally.
Former president of Iceland, Ólafur Ragnar Grímsson, is against joining the EU and posted on X that the "nation has spoken".
The nation first sought EU membership after the 2009 financial crisis pushed its economy to the brink, but accession talks stalled in 2013 once a euroskeptic coalition took power.
Frostadóttir's current Social Democratic-led government revived the question this year, arguing that a more volatile international climate made it worth asking voters whether to pursue closer EU ties.
What impact will it have on EU relations?
Iceland's relationship with Brussels won't fundamentally change either way, though: the country already participates in the European Economic Area and the passport-free Schengen zone, and both arrangements stay intact.
The referendum itself carries no legal force, but the government has committed to abiding by whatever Icelanders decide.
Frostadóttir, Foreign Minister Þorgerður Katrín Gunnarsdóttir and Minister of Education and Children Inga Sæland have called a press conference for 3pm CET where the party leaders will discuss the result and take questions from the media.
Fisheries have long been the thorniest sticking point in Iceland's on-off relationship with Brussels — the country's fishing waters are central to its economy and identity, and it has resisted ceding control over stocks and quotas to the EU's Common Fisheries Policy.
Asked about the issue, EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said: "Iceland's unique specificities on fisheries and agriculture are well known. They would have to be carefully considered." She added: "I'm confident that, together with EU member states, we would find creative solutions."
How the night unfolded
Polls closed at 10 p.m. local time (00:00am CET), and the first partial results — drawn heavily from the capital, Reykjavik — showed "Yes" comfortably ahead, at nearly 58%. Pro-EU campaigners were cautiously optimistic in the early hours, pointing to strong urban turnout.
But as rural and coastal constituencies began reporting after midnight, the picture shifted sharply. Fishing communities where opposition to EU quota-sharing rules has run deep for over a decade, delivered "No" majorities above 65% in several districts. By 2 am CET, the national tally had narrowed to a near-even split.
The turning point came around 7am CET, when the northern agricultural region — traditionally a bellwether — reported a 60/40 split in favour of "No," pushing the national count into "No" territory for the first time. From there, the lead never fully reverted.
By late morning, all eyes were fixed on a single outstanding constituency: Southwest, the second-largest of Iceland's six, encompassing the commuter towns ringing the capital with some 79,000 registered voters.
It was the last piece of the count still to report, and the tightest battleground of the night.
The constituency had started dead even before "No" pulled ahead as counting progressed. At 11:30 CET, Southwest published its final tally, closing out the national count in favour of No.

23,000 bronzes, 14 years, 60 volumes: how China is mapping lost heritage held abroad
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
08:00:37 UTC
17:00:37 KST

23,000 bronzes, 14 years, 60 volumes: how China is mapping lost heritage held abroad
Peking University study reveals seven times more relics held overseas than previously thought, creating crucial evidence trail
In the quiet of a Peking University research room, shelves groan under the weight of 60 thick volumes. Stacked, they stand taller than an average human.
Inside their pages lie the details of more than 23,000 ancient Chinese bronze vessels, weapons, chariot fittings and ritual objects that left China’s shores long ago and now sit in museums, private collections and auction houses across nearly 30 countries.
Published in April by Shanghai Classics Publishing House, the Collection of Chinese Bronzes in Overseas Collections is the product of a painstaking 14-year investigation. It is also something more: an assembled toolkit for China’s intensifying campaign to reclaim cultural heritage lost to war, looting and smuggling, as well as an assertion of Beijing’s ambition to shape the global rules of repatriation.
“To create archives for the cultural relics, to preserve evidence for history,” said lead editor and historian Zhu Fenghan, a Boya Chair Professor at Peking University, capturing the project’s dual purpose in an article in the People’s Daily last week.
“We need to get a clear picture of our family assets and gain a more complete and comprehensive understanding of Chinese bronzes held overseas,” Zhu was quoted as saying.
The effort began in 2012, when China’s National Cultural Heritage Administration (NCHA) asked Peking University to map the true scale of the country’s dispersed bronzes, prompting a scholarly odyssey.
Team members criss-crossed more than 10 countries to visit more than 260 institutions, scan rare catalogues, trawl auction records and photograph objects that had rarely, if ever, been systematically recorded by Chinese researchers.

'Unsafe': Barnaby Joyce invokes disaster-hit Nepal to explain One Nation's refugee policy

In brief
- Questions remain over One Nation's refugee policy after MP Barnaby Joyce discussed it in an interview.
- Joyce did not confirm if the party would reduce Australia's existing humanitarian intake numbers.
One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce has suggested that Australia should not accept refugees from countries that the government deems unsafe for Australians to visit, invoking flood-hit Nepal as an example.
Appearing on News24 (formerly Sky News) on Sunday morning, Joyce was asked whether Australia's current humanitarian intake should be cut.
Joyce brought up Nepal, which is reeling from catastrophic mudslides and flash flooding that have killed nearly 700 people. More than 3,000 more are missing, including 42 Australians.
"The refugee program has got to work within a policy structure we've got," Joyce said.
"Remember, we've clearly stated that if an area, the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFAT) says it's too unsafe to go there, then it's unsafe to bring people from there and away from there, such as places in Nepal.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
"I presume that the Department of Foreign Affairs says it's not unsafe to go to Nepal, but I wouldn't be going there at the moment."
Asked whether One Nation would stop accepting people from Nepal if DFAT were to advise against travel there, Joyce said he wasn't clear on DFAT's current position on the country, but "I know the Nepalese community have a huge say in sections of our country in the workforce, but they do it within the visa category."
"If they do come in, they'll be within the NOM," he added, referring to net overseas migration.
People who arrive on humanitarian visas currently contribute to net overseas migration figures.
While natural disasters can make a country unsafe to visit, people displaced by disasters do not generally qualify as refugees on that basis alone.
DFAT's latest travel advice for Nepal encourages a "high degree of caution due to the risk of natural disasters and road accidents". For certain areas closer to the disaster-hit region, it advises Australians to reconsider their need to travel.
Pressed on whether One Nation was happy with the current annual humanitarian intake level of 20,000, Joyce repeated that "it fits within the NOM".
"That is our policy, and the refugee policy — it's not that it's dispensed — but you can't come from countries which are dangerous. Like if you can't go there, you shouldn't be coming here."
Reporting suggested this week that the government intended to slash Australia's humanitarian intake by a third, however, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said on Thursday that humanitarian placements would remain at 20,000.
On Sunday, Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek said that was a "permanent commitment".
What is One Nation's policy on refugees?
There has been ongoing confusion over the specifics of One Nation's broader immigration policy.
Last weekend, One Nation MP David Farley said his party's immigration target was "not too different" from Labor's, prompting party leader Pauline Hanson to reiterate that the policy was to reduce net overseas migration to 130,000.
That target would be achieved by reducing international students, temporary graduate visas, and a "much more targeted" skilled migration program, Hanson said. She did not mention the refugee intake.
Labor is yet to reveal its plan to reduce migration, but it previously set an official cap of 185,000 places on the permanent migration program.
On its website, One Nation says its immigration policy would refuse entry to migrants from nations known to foster extremist ideologies.
It also says it would withdraw Australia from the United Nations Refugee Convention "because Australia will not be dictated to by foreign organisations when deciding who we accept into our nation on humanitarian grounds."
SBS News has approached One Nation for clarity on its refugee policy.
What is the UN Refugee Convention?
No country has ever withdrawn from the Refugee Convention, which was adopted 75 years ago in the wake of World War Two.
The international treaty sets out who qualifies as a refugee and the protections that countries owe them.
It defines a refugee as someone who is outside their home country who has a well-founded fear of being persecuted based on factors including race, religion or political opinion.
Under the convention, countries must not return refugees to a place where they face serious threats to their life or freedom.
Australia is among 149 states that are parties to the convention and its 1967 Protocol, which effectively extended its protections beyond the immediate aftermath of the war.
The Refugee Convention does not set migration targets or require Australia to resettle a particular number of refugees each year.
The conversation in Australia comes amid broader international debate over refugee policy. In the United States, the Trump administration has expanded refugee protections for white South Africans while sharply cutting foreign aid that supports international refugee programs, including the UN's refugee agency, which relied heavily on US funding.

Iceland rejects EU accession talks in referendum

Unknown Publisher

Iceland rejects EU accession talks in referendum
The ‘No’ camp garnered 52.8 percent of the vote while the ‘Yes’ camp secured 47.2 percent, public broadcaster RUV reports.
Icelanders have rejected a government proposal to resume accession talks with the European Union, the public broadcaster RUV reports.
In a vote held on Saturday, 52.8 percent of Icelanders voted “no” while 47.2 percent voted “yes”, according to official results published by RUV on Sunday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Vote count under way in Iceland’s knife-edge EU referendum
- list 2 of 3Iceland rejects EU accession talks in referendum
- list 3 of 3Iceland votes in a tight race on whether to resume talks to join the EU
“The nation rejects accession negotiations with the EU,” RUV reported.
Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir said after the results that her administration will not move forward with the talks but Reykjavik will continue to strengthen its relationship with the European Economic Area (EEA).
Iceland joined the EEA in1994, giving Reykjavik access to the EU single market without being an EU member state.
The result deals a blow to Brussels, which had been eager to welcome a new wealthy member and had expressed a willingness to compromise with Reykjavík on fisheries and other thorny issues to facilitate its EU membership.
However, a European Commission spokesperson said in a statement that it respects the choice of the Icelandic people and the country remains a close partner of the EU.
Brussels had hoped to be able to present Icelandic membership as an example of positive enlargement that could also make it more palatable for member states to agree to take in less wealthy countries, such as Montenegro.
Iceland’s government had framed its membership plan as a “now or never” moment, and Frostadottir told voters in August that voting “no” would put all EU speculation aside.
“Yes” campaigners said joining the bloc could ease high interest rates and offer more security in a world unsettled by war in Ukraine and United States President Donald Trump’s rhetoric about annexing another Arctic island, neighbouring Greenland.
“No” campaigners said EU membership would threaten Iceland’s sovereignty and its fishing industry.
The industry was fiercely opposed to joining the bloc – 90 percent of its companies were against the idea – and the EU had tried to woo them with a conciliatory approach.
“Iceland’s unique specificities on fisheries and agriculture are well known. They would have to be carefully considered,” EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said.
“I’m confident that together with EU member states we would find creative solutions.”
Frostadottir pledged that if Iceland rejected the resumption of entry talks, the EU membership issue would not be put back on the political agenda during her mandate, which ends in 2028.
The government also said that in the event of a “no” vote, it would leave to parliament the question of whether to formally withdraw its EU membership application.
The small island in the North Atlantic is already closely linked to the EU as a member of the EEA and the free-movement Schengen zone, and those ties will remain unchanged.
While the referendum result is technically nonbinding, the government has promised to respect it.
Iceland first applied to join the EU in 2009 when a financial crisis hit the country. A eurosceptic government ended accession talks four years later.

C40 cities have built a framework for climate action, but which ones are actually delivering?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
07:50:33 UTC
16:50:33 KST

How C40 turns climate targets into city policy
The C40 Cities Climate Leadership Group brings together nearly 100 major cities around a shared approach to urban climate action. Founded in 2005, the network has evolved from a forum for mayors into a more structured system for setting targets, developing climate plans, reporting emissions, and sharing policy tools. Its importance lies in the framework it provides for turning a global climate objective into decisions made at municipal level.
That framework starts with the Climate Action Planning Framework (CAPF), which asks cities to align their climate strategies with the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C ambition. Cities are expected to establish emissions-reduction targets toward net zero by 2050, set interim goals for 2030, assess climate risks, address social equity, and integrate climate action into municipal planning and decision-making.
C40’s Deadline 2020 framework then attempted to translate those ambitions into city-level carbon trajectories, while its Climate Action Pathways work has assessed hundreds of possible interventions across buildings, energy, transportation, waste, and planning. The network’s Leadership Standards further formalize expectations around climate plans, delivery, mainstreaming, innovation, and collaboration.
This has turned climate action into something that reaches well beyond a city’s environmental department, shaping building regulations, transportation, land-use planning, public procurement, energy infrastructure, and municipal budgets. But C40’s policy framework only tells part of the story. The more useful measure is what happened on the ground, and, more specifically, which cities have actually reached peak emissions and continued to bring them down.
image © LI Xuejin
The cities that moved from targets to reductions
C40 has identified a group of cities that have already passed their emissions peak and are cutting greenhouse gas emissions. An earlier C40 analysis identified 27 cities that had peaked their emissions before 2012 and subsequently achieved sustained reductions, including Barcelona, Basel, Berlin, Boston, Chicago, Copenhagen, Heidelberg, London, Los Angeles, Madrid, Melbourne, Milan, Montréal, New Orleans, New York City, Oslo, Paris, Philadelphia, Portland, Rome, San Francisco, Stockholm, Sydney, Toronto, Vancouver, Warsaw and Washington, DC.
C40’s analysis found that the 27-city cohort reduced direct emissions by an average of around 2 percent per year after reaching peak emissions, while population and economic output continued to grow.
The trajectories are not identical, and neither are the policies behind them, though several patterns emerge.
Energy systems are one. Cities such as Copenhagen and Stockholm have reduced emissions through the decarbonization of district heating and electricity systems. Buildings are another, with increasingly stringent performance standards, benchmarking requirements and retrofit policies targeting the existing building stock. Transportation provides a third, with public transit, cycling infrastructure, vehicle regulation and electrification having become central tools for reducing urban emissions.
Copenhagen: large reductions, difficult final steps
Copenhagen is a good example of how far city-led climate action can go, and where it starts to run into harder limits. The Danish capital cut its territorial greenhouse gas emissions by around 80 percent between 2009 and 2022, with much of that progress coming from changes to its district heating system, renewable energy and long-term investment in cycling. These are not climate measures sitting apart from the city itself; they have reshaped how Copenhagen is heated, powered and navigated. But the last part has proved much harder. Copenhagen had set itself the goal of becoming carbon neutral by 2025, a target it ultimately did not meet. One of the sticking points was carbon capture at the Amager Bakke waste-to-energy facility. After major reductions in energy and transport emissions, technologies such as CCS became important for tackling the harder-to-remove remainder, but delivering them depended on financing and regulations beyond the city’s control. Copenhagen’s experience points to a familiar problem in urban decarbonization: the biggest reductions can come from changes a city can make itself, while the final ones may depend on infrastructure, money and decisions at another level of government.
image by Nick Karvounis
Oslo: when carbon becomes part of the city budget
Oslo has taken a different route, bringing climate targets into the city’s everyday budgeting process. Its Klimabudsjett, or Climate Budget, sets out emissions targets and measures alongside the city’s ordinary financial budget, giving municipal departments responsibility for specific reductions and tracking their progress over time.
The approach has been paired with practical changes across the city. Oslo has cut direct territorial emissions since 2009 and used its purchasing power to push fossil-free and zero-emission machinery on municipal construction projects. Electric vehicles and charging infrastructure have also become part of the city’s wider transition. But the harder reductions are proving more difficult. Oslo’s longer-term target depends in part on carbon capture at the Klemetsrud waste-to-energy plant, tying the city’s climate goals to a large and technically demanding infrastructure project, as well as the financing and construction time needed to deliver it. Oslo shows both the strength and the limits of putting climate action into the machinery of city government. A city can set the budget, change its procurement rules and push new infrastructure, but some of the biggest remaining emissions depend on projects and decisions beyond City Hall.
image by Andriy Oliynyk
Tokyo demonstrates another model of municipal climate action.
Tokyo offers a different approach, using regulation to tackle emissions from the city’s large buildings. In 2010, the Tokyo Metropolitan Government introduced its Tokyo Cap-and-Trade System, requiring large commercial and industrial facilities to meet mandatory emissions-reduction targets. Instead of relying mainly on voluntary action, the program sets facility-level baselines and requires emissions to be monitored and verified. What makes the system interesting is its treatment of buildings as part of a much larger energy system.
Tokyo uses regulation to push changes across a large part of the commercial building stock. That matters as cities turn their attention to existing buildings, where much of the energy demand is already locked in. Retrofitting heating, cooling and energy systems can affect thousands of buildings at once, making the accumulated impact far greater than that of individual new projects. Tokyo’s approach shows how regulation can work alongside design and construction, setting the conditions that push an entire sector in the same direction.
image via C40
The infrastructure behind the numbers
Across the C40 cities that have sustained emissions reductions, the changes are visible in the way cities are built and run, through cleaner electricity and district heating, tighter building standards, energy retrofits, expanded public transportation, cycling networks, low-emission zones and electric vehicles. Climate targets can sound abstract on paper, net zero by a certain year, or a percentage reduction from a baseline. In practice, they come down to much more familiar parts of urban life. Building codes determine what gets built. Transit networks shape how people move around the city. Low-emission zones change which vehicles can use its streets. Municipal procurement can create a market for electric construction equipment, while a climate budget can make individual departments responsible for delivering specific reductions. Looking across the C40 cities that have made measurable progress, one thing stands out: the targets tend to work when they are tied to the everyday decisions that shape the city.
C40 cities generally use the Global Protocol for Community-Scale Greenhouse Gas Emission Inventories (GPC) to track emissions produced within their boundaries. The system gives cities a common way to measure and compare emissions, but it leaves out some of the carbon associated with what those cities consume. A city can cut the emissions produced within its borders while still relying on materials, products and energy-intensive supply chains elsewhere. This can be particularly significant in cities with economies dominated by services, finance and other relatively low-emission activities.
C40’s own research found that the combined consumption footprint of 79 cities was substantially larger than their territorial emissions, with much of the difference coming from goods and supply chains outside the city. Construction is a good example. The emissions from producing cement, steel and other building materials are generated before those materials ever reach the site, so they do not necessarily appear in a city’s territorial inventory. A building can therefore look efficient once it is in operation while carrying a much larger carbon footprint from the materials used to construct it. There is a similar challenge when city inventories are compared with independent atmospheric measurements. Studies have found significant differences between self-reported inventories and atmospheric estimates in some cities, underlining how difficult it can be to pin emissions neatly to an administrative boundary.
image by Timo Volz
From ambition to evidence
C40 has given cities a shared framework for turning climate targets into policies, regulations and investment, but the cities that stand out are not necessarily those with the most ambitious targets. They are the ones where those targets have translated into changes on the ground and where emissions data shows that those changes are having an effect.
Copenhagen, Oslo and Tokyo offer three different approaches: changing the energy and transport systems, putting emissions into the municipal budget, and regulating the building stock. Each uses powers that already exist within city government to tackle a different part of the emissions problem.
The wider group of early-peaking C40 cities shows that emissions can fall while cities continue to grow. It also points to a harder phase ahead. As the easier reductions are made, cities have to deal with waste, industrial emissions, embodied carbon, national energy systems and supply chains that extend well beyond their boundaries. That makes the next test fairly straightforward: can cities keep cutting emissions as the remaining sources become harder to reach, and do the numbers still hold when their carbon footprint is measured beyond the city itself?
map of the C40 cities

Opposition parties call for early elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
07:43:00 UTC
16:43:00 KST

Opposition parties call for early elections
Riigikogu opposition parties Isamaa, Center and EKRE are calling for new elections to remove the Reform Party and Eesti 200 minority government from power.
The governing coalition lost its parliamentary majority three weeks ago when Eesti 200's Kalev Stoicescu and Reform's Meelis Kiili left their respective parties. The next Riigikogu elections will take place in March 2027.
On Sunday, the most popular opposition party, Isamaa, published a statement calling for a vote of no confidence in the government
"Isamaa proposes that all Riigikogu parties and independent MPs begin consultations to hold new, early Riigikogu elections without delay, as provided for in the Constitution," the statement said. "To initiate this, it would be appropriate, in accordance with the Constitution, to express no confidence in Kristen Michal's government."
Isamaa claimed Estonia will only be able to move forward if the government resigns.
"New elections are the beginning of restoring trust and an opportunity for honest feedback from citizens and for defining expectations for the future," it wrote.
On Saturday, the Center Party also called for early elections. It said the coalition's inability to govern the country poses a security risk.
Party Chairman Mihhail Kõlvart said the National Audit Office's latest report about the problems in the defense sector is evidence of the government's systemic failure.
"The current government has used defense spending to justify both unexpected tax increases and allowing the state budget to fall deeply into deficit, as well as people's worsening ability to cope," Kõlvart said.
"Now shortcomings have come to light that no country can afford in the current security situation. The large-scale disorder in national defense endangers the security of the entire country. The resignation of a few officials or ministers is no longer enough. The entire government must resign, and early elections must be called," he continued.
Kõlvart also said the latest economic forecasts show the "government has no substantive plan for reviving the economy and bringing the national debt under control" and that problems also exist in the education, energy and social sectors.
"The current government does not solve crises but postpones them and communicates a prettier version of reality. This is not leadership," he said.
Kõlvart said solutions cannot wait until the Riigikogu elections in March because Estonia is losing valuable time and solving the problems will become even more difficult.
This week, EKRE's board decided to send an appeal to all members of parliament proposing that Michal's minority government be removed as soon as possible.
The appeal sent by party Chairman Martin Helme states that Michal's government has long since lost the support of the majority of society and has now also lost the support of the majority in the Riigikogu.
"Support for the coalition parties has for some time been languishing at around a dozen percent, which is unprecedented in Estonia's history and abnormal in a democratic system," he wrote.
Helme proposes two alternatives to the Reform Party and Eesti 200 governing coalition.
"First, we form a so-called interim government until the elections, involving all political forces except the Reform Party and Eesti 200 and including, as extensively as possible, experts who do not participate in day-to-day politics. Such a government cannot and must not make important decisions or decisions with long-term consequences, but has one simple task: to take the country to elections without abusing the instruments of executive power in the knowledge that there is nothing left to lose," Helme said.
The second option would be early elections.
"In a situation where parliament is deadlocked, decision-making must be handed over as quickly as possible to the bearer of supreme power, namely the people. EKRE is prepared to participate constructively and with the common national interest in mind in implementing either of the two proposed options," Helme said.
SDE does not support early elections
The only opposition party not to call for new elections is the Social Democratic Party (SDE).
On Sunday, Social Democratic Party Chairman Lauri Läänemets said that although the Social Democrats do not support the current governing coalition, they will not support a vote of no confidence in the prime minister.
He said this would mean missing out on an election debate about Estonia's future.
"If we hold early elections, then that election debate will not take place. Then it will become an election along the lines of 'either the Reform Party or EKREIKE', and the Social Democrats believe that Estonia does not need EKREIKE," he said, using the acronym for the previous EKRE-Isamaa-Center coalition (2019-2021).
"We should choose a new path for Estonia in the Riigikogu elections, and that is why we do not support early elections that would take place around Christmas, where there would be no time for an election debate and the choice would be made purely so that EKREIKE could come to power. We do not think that is sensible," Läänemets said.
This article was updated to add comments from Lauri Läänemets.

1 in 5 food samples fails: Why so few cases end in conviction

1 in 5 food samples fails: Why so few cases end in conviction
Edited by: Ayush Pandey / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Aug 30, 2026, 13:12 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
Inadequate packaging can increase the risk of contamination
NEW DELHI: Nearly one in five food samples tested across India was found to be non-conforming in 2025-26, even as only 4.8% of food safety violations ended in convictions, highlighting gaps in enforcement and staffing across states, according to data analysed by Richa Gandhi.The share of non-conforming food samples has remained around 20% over the past five years, despite a steady rise in the number of samples tested. In 2025-26, authorities analysed 2,23,808 samples, of which 40,023 were found to be non-conforming.The proportion of non-conforming samples stood at 17.9% in 2025-26, down from 20.2% in 2024-25 and 19.8% in 2023-24. It had peaked at 25.1% in 2022-23.
Food safety checks expose widespread violations
At the same time, the conviction rate has gradually increased, rising from 2% in 2021-22 to 4.8% in 2025-26. However, monetary penalties remain the more common form of action against violators.
UP finds highest share of violations
Uttar Pradesh recorded the highest proportion of non-conforming samples among the states listed, with 52% of the nearly 40,000 samples tested in 2025-26 found to be non-conforming.The state analysed 39,519 samples and found 20,021 to be non-conforming.Haryana followed with 31%, while Jharkhand recorded 28%, Rajasthan 27%, Puducherry 22% and Himachal Pradesh 20%.
Enforcement gaps raise concerns over food safety
Tamil Nadu analysed the highest number of samples among the larger states, with nearly 45,000 tests, and also recorded the highest conviction rate among those states.Chandigarh recorded the highest conviction rate overall at 32.1%, followed by Tamil Nadu at 21.5%, Kerala at 17.7%, Haryana at 16% and Delhi at 14.7%.The data points to a sharp gap between the scale of food safety violations detected through testing and the number of cases that ultimately result in convictions.
Testing reveals gaps in India’s food safety system
Staff shortage adds to enforcement challenge
Shortages in food safety personnel are another major constraint on monitoring and enforcement.Bihar has the largest gap among the states listed, with 91 of its 105 sanctioned food safety posts vacant. Jharkhand has 74 vacancies against 77 sanctioned posts, while Chhattisgarh has 70 vacancies against 125 posts.
Shortages in food safety staff hamper monitoring and enforcement.
Andhra Pradesh has 68 vacancies out of 145 sanctioned posts, followed by Uttarakhand with 65 vacancies out of 57 sanctioned posts, according to the data.Haryana has 57 vacancies against 367 sanctioned posts, while Odisha has 57 vacancies against 147. Tripura has 52 vacancies against 23 sanctioned posts, Manipur 50 against 34 and Sikkim 50 against four.The staffing gaps limit the ability of state authorities to regularly inspect establishments, collect samples and pursue violations through the enforcement process.
Milk, dairy among frequently flagged foods
Milk and dairy products, ghee, spices, edible oils and sweets remain among the food categories frequently flagged in regulatory actions and recent cases.In one major case, ghee supplied for the preparation of Tirupati laddus came under scrutiny after samples failed quality tests amid allegations of adulteration with vegetable oils and animal fats.Milk and milk products such as paneer and khoya have also faced increased scrutiny. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India ordered a nationwide crackdown between September and October following cases involving alleged detergent and urea adulteration in Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra.
Milk and dairy products among food samples that continue to fail safety standards.
In Punjab, 47% of milk, cheese and dairy samples reportedly failed tests over a three-year period. Cheese was identified as particularly vulnerable to adulteration involving starch and chemical additives, with 255 of 531 samples failing tests in 2024-25 alone.
Spices such as turmeric and chilli powder have also been the subject of seizures over adulteration involving synthetic colours, wood dust and other unsafe fillers.Edible oils are another concern, with cheaper palm oil being used to adulterate more expensive oils such as groundnut and mustard oil.Sweets and khoya are also regularly identified as high-risk categories in FSSAI advisories during festive periods, when demand rises sharply.The figures underline the challenge facing India's food safety system: while testing has expanded and the detection of violations remains significant, limited staffing and the relatively low rate of convictions continue to constrain enforcement.

Flood warning notifications were issued to people's phones throughout Sunday morning as rescue workers tried to evacuate a main route connecting Kathmandu to one of the places most severely affected by Wednesday's devastating floods.
Authorities in Nepal have warned of potential new flooding on Sunday and advised people living in flood-affected districts to stay vigilant following an increase in the Bhotekoshi River's water level
Flood warning notifications were issued to people's phones throughout Sunday morning as rescue workers tried to evacuate a main route connecting Kathmandu to one of the places most severely affected by Wednesday's devastating floods.
In the town of Galchhi, a group of residents sought higher ground on a nearby bridge and watched as the river roared by.
People pointed to enormous rocks that had been washed downriver during the earlier floods, as others standing on a suspension bridge over the water were warned off with whistles.
The thick grey-brown muck that has covered entire communities in the worst-hit flood areas was visible along the river, with entire houses, cars, and farm tractors protruding from it. Parts of the rice terraces along the river were dropped into the river due to landslides.
Death toll rises above 800, with more than 3,000 missing
The latest updates on Sunday put the combined death toll in Nepal and Tibet at more than 800, with over 3,000 people still missing.
According to Nepal’s disaster agency, the death toll had climbed to 788 with 2,498 people missing, while Chinese authorities reported 16 deaths and 546 missing, including over a hundred Nepalis and people from over a dozen countries.
The latest warnings came after Chinese authorities informed their Nepalese counterparts of increased water flow upstream, Dharam Raj Uprety, chief executive of Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, told the Associated Press.
But residents of the flood-hit villages said they were struggling to make sense of near-constant alarms they’ve received since the initial floods.
“Sometimes they say a flood is coming, then we have to run again to higher ground, even at night. There is also rain,” said local resident Govind Shreshta. “It’s really difficult for me. I have a 72-year-old father and a 70-year-old mom. I must carry them, and I am exhausted. It’s going on like this for those who are still alive.”
Large concrete and smaller suspension bridges were destroyed, leaving communities on the other side of the river with less easy access.
“Those that are there are now stuck there. Those who are here are stuck here. It’s going to be very difficult,” said Sattan Singh Tamang, 47, who was working near a bridge when Wednesday’s the floods came.
Homes and businesses left intact after the flooding were still without electricity on Sunday, as twisted power line poles and wires lay tangled in the mud.
Prithivi Highway is a crucial supply route for food, fuel and other goods entering Kathmandu from other parts of the country. While most of the highway is operational, other parts still face repair challenges.

Iceland voters reject EU accession talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
07:42:00 UTC
16:42:00 KST

Iceland voters reject EU accession talks
Published August 30, 2026last updated August 30, 2026
Voters in Iceland have rejected a plan to restart accession talks with the European Union, final referendum results showed on Sunday.
The 'No' camp secured victory with 52.8% of the votes, while the 'Yes' camp garnered 47.2% support, the official count published by public broadcaster RUV showed.
The capital, Reykjavik, was the only area in the island nation of 400,000 people to support the referendum.
Some 270,000 Icelanders were eligible to vote, 82% of whom did so.
Iceland PM: 'Not a setback'
Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir, who backed the "yes" campaign, said she did not see her fellow citizens' vote as a defeat but as a fair democratic result.
"I don't see this as a setback. I see this as a victory for democracy," she said. "We had over 80% of the country participate in a matter like this."
She confirmed that her government was "not going forward with the accession talks this term" but that it would continue to strengthen its relationship with the European Economic Area.
"I don’t feel that there is bitterness," she said. "I know tempers run high for some people, but I have now spent time with a large group of people from all over the country and people are quite open to different outcomes."
Meanwhile, EU chief Antonio Costa told Frostadottir the bloc "fully respects the democratic choice" of the island's voters not to resume EU membership talks, according to a spokesperson.
"Iceland remains one of the EU's closest and most trusted partners," said the spokesperson for the European Council president.
Iceland opposition: 'This isn't the time'
The count through the night had the island nation on edge as the "Yes" campaign took an early lead, attributable largely to votes in the capital, Reykjavik, before results swung in favor of the opposition.
By dawn, only a few hundred votes separated the two camps before the gap grew as more ballots were tallied in rural areas of the country where opposition was greater.
"This isn't the time to go," one "No" voter, Daniel Bjarkason, told the Associated Press.
"Maybe in 10, 15, 20 years or more, we can take another look. But, for now, we're too divided and that's not a good look. Because it should be 70-30 'Yes' if we're going to [join the EU]."
Neck-and-neck vote after long debate
Iceland has spent the better part of two decades wrestling with the question of becoming a member of the bloc.
The Nordic country originally applied to join the EU in 2009 following the global financial crisis, which hit the country particularly hard.
Accession talks were suspended in 2013 after a euroskeptic government took office.
Iceland's current left-leaning government, elected in 2024, originally vowed to hold a referendum next year but brought the vote forward because of rising geopolitical tension over Russia's war in Ukraine and Greenland.
Fishing industry pulled weight
The decision puts to bed concerns among many voters that joining the bloc would undermine Iceland's sovereignty, with fishing rights a major concern.
The fisheries sector has been fiercely opposed to joining the bloc, with 90% of industry players against the idea.
The result is a disappointment to Brussels, which had appeared willing to compromise on thorny issues, including fishing and farming, to facilitate Iceland's accession.

The toxic waste of the Gaza war has reached Israel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
07:41:08 UTC
16:41:08 KST

Toxic waste of war on Gaza reached Israel
The Israeli government cannot insulate its citizens from the impact of the ecocide it wrought onto the strip.
Earlier this month, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and representatives of the Board of Peace agreed to set up a working group on sanitation and public health affecting both Israel and Gaza. Its membership and detailed operating structure are yet to be made public.
It appears it has finally dawned on the Israeli authorities that the consequences of the unrelenting ecocidal destruction of Gaza were eventually going to hit Israel. The toxic leftovers of war – untreated sewage and contaminated rubble – are now a problem for Israeli public health as well.
Gaza shares the Mediterranean, coastal ecosystems and coastal aquifers with Israel. The destruction of its electric power and sanitation infrastructure forces over 100,000 cubic metres of raw, untreated sewage into the Mediterranean Sea or on land every day. Because in this part of the Mediterranean currents move primarily from south to north, this waste is carried straight up the coast into Israeli waters.
The Ashkelon desalination plant in southern Israel has been forced to shut down multiple times due to high faecal bacteria contamination from Gaza’s wastewater. Raw sewage also triggers toxic algae blooms blocking and damaging desalination filtration systems, as well as creating dead zones where fishing would normally happen.
Wastewater toxins, heavy metals and pathogens are absorbed by local marine life. Because fish migrate across maritime boundaries, contaminated seafood poses a direct health hazard to Palestinian as well as Israeli consumers. Raw sewage carries the same pathogens afflicting Gaza into the shared marine environment. Its northward drift directly impacts Israeli coastal cities.
Although pathogens can persist and migrate under certain conditions, pathogen contaminated groundwater is unlikely to feed into Israeli municipal water supplies, but can still affect the shared aquifer and surrounding environment.
Salts and other chemical contaminants can travel much farther and are often a bigger long-term aquifer concern. They can contaminate a shared groundwater system and reduce the quality and usability of the aquifer over time for irrigation, agriculture and drinking.
Israel has recently also begun moving some of the estimated 60 million tonnes of rubble from Gaza into undisclosed locations inside Israel and the West Bank, potentially transferring the pollutants in that rubble directly to disposal or storage sites. In recent weeks, Euro-Med Monitor tracked some 100 Israeli trucks daily leaving the Gaza Strip with debris.
Transferred pollutants may include heavy metals, such as lead, mercury, cadmium and traces of other metals or residues from specialised munitions, as well as white phosphorus particulates, unspent explosives, industrial chemicals, and widespread asbestos fibres from pulverised older buildings. Heavy metals present in dust and rubble may exhibit carcinogenic, mutagenic, teratogenic, neurotoxic, nephrotoxic and bioaccumulative properties, posing long-term human health and environmental risks.
The rubble also contains biological matter, pathogens and fluids from decomposing human remains and accumulated organic waste, as well as insects, rodents, and other disease vectors. Airborne transmission of hazardous dust particles, asbestos fibres and particulate matter degrades the quality of the air while hidden unexploded ordnance in the debris can cause a detonation risk and soil toxicity.
When managing highly contaminated disaster debris, international agencies such as the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) and regional environmental authorities like the Gaza Debris Management Working Group (DMWG) stipulate transfers must follow strict protocols and operational procedures to isolate hazards, including an immediate freeze on all operations if human remains are detected. Moving these materials across borders or jurisdictions should also trigger legal frameworks and rigid groundwater protection standards.
Critics have pointed out that bulldozing sites that contain mass graves is destroying key evidence of genocidal crimes. But apart from that, this transfer of debris in disregard of international rules and regulations is putting at risk the health of people around collection and disposal sites.
If the aim of this structural disparity is to keep Israeli groundwater zones tightly protected and shift the long-term burden of aquifer and soil pollution onto Palestinian communities in the West Bank, it ignores the risks to the Israeli transfer personnel and to all people living there, which includes 700,000 illegal settlers.
This is not a problem that the genocidal war created. Environmental groups such as EcoPeace have long warned that the shared environment creates total interdependence, meaning humanitarian and sanitation crises in Gaza directly compromise Israel’s public health.
Back in 1990, the former Jerusalem Mayor Teddy Kollek candidly admitted that his administration had done little for East Jerusalem beyond extending basic water and sewage lines out of fear that cholera outbreaks in neglected Arab neighbourhoods would spread to West Jerusalem.
Even if Israel is morally incapable of meeting its human rights responsibilities as occupiers to solve the sanitation crisis, it should understand that if it does not strictly follow environmental protocols, its own population will endure the same consequences as the Palestinians whose welfare it callously and criminally disregards.

Nepal rescuers drill into tunnels in bid to reach trapped workers
Nepali army joins flood rescue efforts at hydroelectric facilities where workers are thought to be trapped in tunnels.
Nepali rescuers seeking to reach hydropower workers believed trapped in tunnels swamped by flood debris have resumed work after rain and rising river waters hampered efforts.
Nepal’s government says more than 100 workers may still be alive and trapped inside multiple tunnels at hydropower projects, with key rescue efforts focused on the Trishuli 3A and 3B sites.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Chinese rescuers race to reach mudslide survivors in Nepal-China border
- list 2 of 3Anger mounts in Nepal over the government’s response to flash flood
- list 3 of 3Isolated by raging floodwaters, Nepal’s miracle home amid the devastation
Huge flash floods triggered on Wednesday when part of a glacier collapsed near Nepal’s border with Tibet have left at least 750 people dead and more than 3,000 missing.
Nepal’s National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority says there are 933 hydropower workers among the missing.
At Trishuli 3A in Nepal’s Rasuwa District on Saturday evening, army rescue teams using drills broke through into the upper part of a mud-swamped tunnel and began pumping air as well as sending in a camera.
But overnight rain and rising river waters hampered efforts early on Sunday, filling the excavation area with water before conditions eased.
“As the floodwaters have receded, the team has resumed efforts to locate the tunnel entrance using drilling machines, excavators, hydraulic cutters and other equipment,” said a Nepal Army statement on Sunday.
Al Jazeera’s Minelle Fernandez, reporting from the Nepalese capital, Kathmandu, said the government has requested specialist help from India and China to “fill gaps” in its rescue operations.
“The government is trying to give it its best shot, bringing in these experts to see if there is any way or means of bringing out anyone who is still alive,” she said.
The catastrophe on Wednesday was triggered when part of a glacier at roughly 5,200 metres high in the Himalayas collapsed, plunging about 1,200 metres and gathering rock and debris before slamming into the Lende River.
The resulting surge swept south through Nepal’s Rasuwa, Nuwakot and Dhading districts, at one point raising the Trishuli River by nine metres in 30 minutes. The US Geological Survey revised its initial finding of an earthquake trigger, concluding the seismic signal instead came from the landslide itself.
Al Jazeera’s Jessica Washington, reporting from Dhading, said the river had receded on Sunday, but the current remained strong.
She said the floodwaters had destroyed many homes, leaving behind only the foundations. Those still standing are “in a state of complete disrepair,” she said.
“Speaking to some residents, this [disaster] represents not only the destruction of their homes, but their livelihoods as well because many of the residents told us that they had small stores and small businesses in the bottom floors of their homes and all of their products – everything – has been completely washed away.”
Nepal’s National Disaster Management Authority said on Sunday that 734 bodies had been recovered. The number of missing on the Nepalese side of the border is at least 2,498.
Chinese authorities have reported that the death toll in Tibet has increased to 16, with 546 people missing. Al Jazeera’s Katrina Yu, reporting from Beijing, said 261 foreigners from 23 countries are among those unaccounted for.
Countries pledge support
International aid has arrived from the United Nations, the Red Cross Federation, Australia, India, South Korea and the United States.
The US and Canada said they would provide $3.6m each in humanitarian aid. The United Kingdom has offered $6.8m in aid, while the UN released $2.5m in emergency funding.
On Friday, the European Union pledged $2.3m and the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) said it had allocated more than $1m and launched an emergency appeal for $31m.
Al Jazeera’s Samer Allawi said authorities “have not yet moved to the second phase of relief operations, which includes humanitarian assistance and reopening roads”, because of “the rugged terrain and the lack of sufficient resources”.
He said that Nepal’s finance minister estimated losses from the disaster at “more than $4bn”, while warnings remain in place over possible flooding along rivers in northern Nepal.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The land-based Harpoon Coastal Defense System (HCDS) successfully hit a target vessel during a developmental test at the Point Mugu Sea Range in California in July, the US Navy said Friday.

Captain Sarah Abbott, Precision Strike Weapons program manager, said, “The flawless execution of this test is a direct testament to the unparalleled expertise and relentless dedication demonstrated by the entire team.”
The Harpoon missile was launched from land and successfully hit a target ship in nearshore waters, according to the Navy. The system is designed to provide land-based anti-ship defense, using the proven Harpoon missile to protect key coastal areas and sea routes, it said.

A Littoral Combat Command was established in July, incorporating the Navy’s mobile radar units, missile vehicle units, and unmanned aerial vehicle forces under a new operational structure.
The command will rely on Taiwan’s domestically produced Hsiung Feng-series anti-ship missiles and the HCDS to bolster coastal defense.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — SEMICON Taiwan 2026, one of the global semiconductor industry’s flagship annual events, is expected to attract more than 100,000 professionals from 65 countries when its exhibition opens Wednesday at the Nangang Exhibition Center.
The event will feature more than 1,300 exhibitors and 4,300 booths, both record highs. The event is part of International Semiconductor Week. The number of country pavilions has also reached a record 18, while the number of booths in the Global Pavilion has grown more than 250% since the program began, per a SEMICON press release.
AI and high-performance computing are driving demand for more advanced semiconductor manufacturing and packaging. SEMICON Taiwan will focus on advanced process nodes, advanced packaging, smart manufacturing, and ecosystem collaboration.
Advanced packaging is becoming increasingly important as AI chip packages grow larger and require more computing power and bandwidth. Technologies attracting attention include fan-out panel-level packaging (FOPLP) and TSMC’s chip-on-panel-on-substrate technology (CoPoS).
TrendForce reported in June that TSMC has standardized its CoPoS development around a 310-by-310-millimeter panel format, with pilot production targeted for 2027 and mass production planned for the second half of 2028.
Panel-level packaging can improve material utilization and production efficiency compared with conventional wafer-level approaches. TrendForce expects FOPLP to become an increasingly important area of competition as chipmakers and packaging companies seek ways to accommodate larger AI packages.
Taiwanese companies including TSMC, ASE Technology Holding Co., Powertech Technology Inc., and display manufacturers Innolux Corp. and AUO Corp. are developing panel-level packaging technologies, while international companies are also pursuing FOPLP, per CNA.
Powertech is preparing for FOPLP mass production by mid-2027, with AMD and Broadcom reportedly having booked most of its planned capacity. ASE is also developing panel-level packaging, while Innolux has established a production line for FOPLP applications.
The technology is expected to play an increasingly important role in applications ranging from power management and consumer electronics to AI accelerators and high-performance computing. SEMICON Taiwan 2026 will also feature dedicated zones for silicon photonics, high-bandwidth memory, quantum technology, and other emerging semiconductor technologies.

The investment marks HubX’s first external funding. The company has developed more than 40 mobile and web applications, including Nova, Wiser, DaVinci and Lotus Flow, and has reached more than 600 million users in over 190 countries.
Türkiye is now home to eight unicorns: Peak Games, Getir, Dream Games, Trendyol, Hepsiburada, Insider, Loom and, most recently, HubX. These companies have achieved unicorn status by surpassing the $1 billion valuation threshold.
The Turcorn 100 Program, launched by the Industry and Technology Ministry in 2022, aims to help create new billion-dollar companies in Türkiye.
The program supports technology-focused startups that have successfully passed the early-stage phase, possess strong growth potential and aim to expand into global markets.
The number of candidate startups in the Turcorn 100 Program reached 43 in the first half of the year. This represented nearly a twofold increase in 15 months from 23 startups in the program in March 2025.
The initiative aims to produce 100 Turcorns from Türkiye by 2030, increase the number of technology startups in the country to 100,000 and raise the combined valuation of Turkish unicorns to more than $100 billion.

The struggle for power in Iran could determine when the war with the United States will end - CNN

The struggle for power in Iran could determine when the war with the United States will end - CNN
Kyiv • UNN
Iranian authorities are divided over a deal with the United States: pragmatists are calling for negotiations, while the hardline faction wants to continue the confrontation.
A confrontation is intensifying within Iran's leadership between those who support concluding a deal with the United States as soon as possible and representatives of the hard-line faction who advocate continuing the standoff. The outcome of this internal struggle could determine when and under what conditions the war with the United States and Israel will end, UNN reports, citing CNN.
Details
According to the television network, six months after the start of the war, two camps have effectively formed within Iran's leadership, assessing the country's further strategy differently.
The first includes Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, parliament speaker and negotiator Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, as well as Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi. They advocate Tehran using the current situation to reach an agreement with the United States while Iran, in their view, can still negotiate from a relatively strong position. Supporters of this approach point to the worsening economic situation, the consequences of sanctions and the naval blockade, damage to infrastructure, and the population's war fatigue.
Representatives of the hard-line conservative wing, including part of the leadership of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and ultraconservative forces, take a different position. They believe Iran should not rush into an agreement with Washington, since the country has managed to withstand six months of war and preserve its main governing institutions. In their calculation, prolonging the conflict could increase the United States' economic and political costs to such an extent that the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump would be forced to soften its demands.
The hard-line supporters' position was strengthened by recent personnel appointments in Iran's security structures. In particular, former IRGC commander Mohsen Rezaei became secretary of the Supreme National Security Council. He put forward a number of conditions to the United States for ending the confrontation, including lifting the sanctions and blockade, unfreezing Iranian assets, and ending U.S. military operations.
At the same time, the final decision on Iran's strategic course is expected to depend on Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. However, since coming to power, he has made virtually no public appearances. Reuters previously reported, citing Iranian officials, that Khamenei sustained serious injuries during the first strikes of the war and is running the country from a shelter.
Against this backdrop, Western media report, the IRGC's influence has grown significantly. The American side also doubts that Iran's civilian representatives taking part in diplomatic contacts can independently guarantee the implementation of a potential agreement without the support of the military leadership.
Economic pressure
The situation is complicated by the deterioration of Iran's economic position. According to data cited by Reuters, annual inflation in the country reached about 66% in July, while food prices rose significantly. Foreign trade is also declining amid sanctions and restrictions on maritime transport. The economic situation itself is one of the main arguments made by supporters of a swift end to the war. Their opponents, by contrast, believe that a public display of weakness will only encourage the United States to increase pressure.
One of the central issues in a potential agreement remains the Strait of Hormuz, through which a significant share of global oil and liquefied natural gas supplies passed before the war. Iran uses control over shipping in the strait as one of its main levers of pressure. Washington insists on restoring freedom of navigation, while Tehran links this to the lifting of the American blockade and sanctions.
According to CNN, the outcome of the struggle between the pragmatic and hard-line wings of Iran's authorities could become one of the key factors determining the duration of the war.
Supporters of an agreement believe Iran should take advantage of the opportunity to conclude a deal before the economic situation deteriorates further. Their opponents calculate that time will work against the United States and force Washington to make concessions.
To remind
A few days earlier, President Donald Trump said that the United States was not holding negotiations with Iran, as Washington was focusing on economically punishing Tehran, promising to punish countries that do business with the Islamic Republic.
