A manhunt is under way in Switzerland after a 22-year-old woman was killed and five people were injured, some seriously, in a shooting at a rave in the northern town of Aarau, local police have said.
In the attack in the early hours of Sunday at a techno party at a covered horse-racing track, an Italian woman died from her injuries at the scene, authorities said. All those caught up in the shooting were residents of Switzerland and in their 20s.
Police appealed to the public for any images of the incident and said large areas of the town had been cordoned off in the search for one or more attackers.

A 34-year-old witness who asked for anonymity said he heard shots shortly after the music stopped at 2.30am on Sunday, which he initially mistook for fireworks.
Some took cover behind a DJ booth and one woman hid behind a refrigerator but was hit in the back by a bullet and bled to death despite efforts to revive her, he said.
“It’s just incredibly tragic. She was young,” he said. “That something like this could happen in Aarau, at a local event, is simply unimaginable. I still can’t really process it.”
As a precaution police have increased their presence beyond the town – which is about 50km west of Zurich and 30km south of the German border – but Graser said there were indications the shooter or shooters were no longer in the immediate area.
“But we still have a lot of police here in the area, in the town of Aarau, in the whole state, to make sure that we could get them if they’re still around,” he said.
Reuters footage showed armed officers patrolling the area, police convoys moving through the streets and armoured vehicles parked near the crime scene.
Organisers of the annual rave said they were shocked and heartbroken by the incident. “A rave should always be a place of joy and love, never a place where people are killed, injured, or left in fear,” they said.
Switzerland has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in Europe although violent shootings are rare and it approved tighter gun control rules in 2019.

15:40:35 KST

Lionel Messi scored four goals in a Major League Soccer match for the first time in his career to help host Inter Miami snap a five-game winless skid across all competitions with a 7-1 rout of Montreal on Saturday night.
Messi broke a 1-1 tie shortly before halftime, added a second goal in the 52nd minute, a third in the 83rd minute, and a fourth on a free kick in the sixth minute of second-half stoppage time. Messi has 18 goals this season and passed Dallas' Petar Musa (16) for the lead in the MLS Golden Boot race. Musa and Dallas visit St. Louis City SC on Sunday.
It was also the ninth time in Messi's pro career that he's scored four or more goals in a match.
Inter Miami (12-4-6, 42 points) secured a needed three points while Montreal (5-11-6, 21 points) had a four-game unbeaten streak in league play snapped.
Casemiro, Luis Suarez, and rookie Alexander Shaw each also scored one goal.
Assistant coach Perez leads match after Hoyos suspension
Inter Miami assistant coach Rafael Perez coached the match with Guillermo Hoyos watching from a skybox at the stadium. Hoyos was suspended for the match for violating the league's Late Kickoff Policy multiple times in recent matches. Hoyos will soon be replaced by Argentine Kily Gonzalez, who was hired this week but is waiting for the necessary paperwork to clear so he can join the team in the United States.
Casemiro headed home a ball off a corner kick by Telasco Segovia to open the scoring in the 20th minute.
Montreal leveled the match in the 37th minute when Fabian Herbers scored his first goal of the season. Noah Streit took a long ball inside the 18-yard box and swung it to the top and just outside the box to Herbers, who then fired a shot past Miami keeper Dayne St. Clair.
It was the 21st goal of Herbers' career.
Messi answered quickly in the 40th minute, angling a free kick just inside the near post that Montreal goalkeeper Thomas Gillier was unable to deflect.
Messi's second goal was a masterpiece, as he wove his way among three defenders and fired a shot past Gillier. Suarez's goal in the 80th minute came on a counterattack, as did Shaw's, which he scored in the 89th minute of just his third career MLS match.

Angola Is Emerging as One of Africa’s Most Important Gateways to the Asia-Pacific
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
06:33:00 UTC
15:33:00 KST

Angola’s city of Lobito, resting behind a natural harbor on the Western side of Africa, is becoming a major industrial port city. It is the second largest port along Angola’s coast, and it has grown steadily over the course of the last two decades, strategically placed as the head point of the internationally funded Lobito Corridor. The story of its success has not been straightforward. The Benguela Railway runs from Lobito into the heart of Africa, bearing critical minerals like cobalt and copper from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zambia. But Angola’s export wealth has only recently turned towards minerals and, in the past, it focused on oil exports from terminals and offshore reserves at Cabinda and Luanda. Oil markets are volatile, and lower global oil prices in 2014 plunged Angola into a severe economic depression, shaking its energy resource-driven economy and paving the way for the diversified market that is developing across Angola today. It is a market uniquely expanding into global trade, and it will be critical for Asia-Pacific energy supplies and trade links in the long run.
Angola has now paid back the majority of its infrastructural loans to China, bringing the peak of total borrowing from $45 billion in 2000 to roughly $12 billion today. Angola has steadily repaid its debt without restructuring, paying off more than necessary during its payment cycles, and showcasing an ‘Angola Model’ of using oil-backed loans which have become uniquely favorable positions in the midst of recent rises in global oil prices. For development loans where oil revenues do not contribute to repayment, Angola has found unique opportunities to readjust repayment plans for fiscal sustainability. For example, the country announced a “debt-for-education” swap with the World Bank’s Multilateral Investment Guarantee Agency in March of this year. The deal converts debt repayments into investments in education. The savings on interest will be fully applied to an educational program that spans all 21 provinces, aiming to empower girls’ school attendance, human capital, and access to education. The $400 million agreement was finalized in late July, with disbursements to over thirty schools beginning immediately, impacting over 32,000 students.
The debt restructuring is a novel way to continue development even after loans have served their infrastructural purposes, and it represents Angola’s fiscal responsibility, ambitiously aimed at diversifying its own economy. Angola has also stepped up on the world stage. The crisis in the Gulf, which has strangled energy supplies for much of Asia, turned out to become a major opportunity for Angola. For example, President João Lourenço inaugurated a major aluminum plant in Bengo Province in January. That factory now puts out 240 tons of ingots daily, pouring into the 9 percent gap in supplies caused by the closure of Hormuz. Furthermore, Angola’s natural gas reserves are contributing to $2 billion in new investments for an Ammonia-Urea complex, one that, when it opens in 2027, will produce roughly 4,000 tons of fertilizer per day. Angolan trade is not only expanding into novel markets, but traditional markets are also tapping into its supply. Australia, Vietnam, and Hong Kong are likely candidates to increase imports from Angola. The oil sector dominates these new networks; however, they lead to expanded cooperation along the supply chain, especially as Angolan markets build out more value-added industry. These emerging links are particularly significant for the Asia-Pacific, where demand for energy and industrial inputs is reshaping supply chains.
In the case of Vietnam, Prime Minister Lê Minh Hưng suggested that cooperation with Angola needed to accelerate, considering Angola’s recent role as Chair of the African Union. He noted, furthermore, that Vietnam would function as Angola’s gateway into ASEAN, seeking multi-layered market integration that can expand beyond bilateral relations. As for other partnerships, China stands out as Angola’s second largest African partner, mostly due to oil exports. South Korea has, like Vietnam, called for new approaches to the Angolan relationship, partly as a response to prioritizing new oil and LNG supply chains following the Gulf crisis. The expansion of the Lobito Corridor is the largest factor in Angola’s new relationships with Asia, and it is expected to be a major driver for diversification across Angola’s and all of Africa’s global trade links. For the Asia-Pacific, this creates a potential bridge between African critical minerals and energy resources and Asian manufacturing, technology, and consumer markets. For the Lobito Corridor specifically, a Memorandum of Understanding between the European Union, United States, and the African Development Bank has already opened the door to significant investment, including cooperation with partners in the East.
President João Lourenço’s leadership has further encouraged economic reforms aimed at improving transparency, strengthening institutions and encouraging private sector growth, each aimed at solidifying and securing international investment interests. Angola’s investment promotion agency has received hundreds of proposals across sectors ranging from agriculture to logistics, manufacturing and tourism. The uptick in economic potential comes as a recognition of Angola’s fiscal stability and its appealing supply of natural resources and strategic geography. The Lobito Corridor makes inland investment possible as well, finally overcoming many of the infrastructure bottlenecks that plagued exports. Minerals flowing from Zambia and the DRC are critical to the world, for low-carbon energy technologies, advanced electronics, and battery storage systems. For Asian economies seeking to diversify critical-mineral supply chains, the corridor offers a potentially important alternative route into Africa’s resource base.
These materials pair with Angola’s existing energy exports, and hydrocarbons still represent a substantial share of GDP; however, policymakers in Luanda are actively sorting out a new model. Alongside oil, natural gas is playing a growing role as a transitional resource, supporting power generation and industrial development while helping to diversify the energy mix. The national energy company Sonangol is also pursuing plans to expand refining capacity, including building a large plant near Lobito. Increasing domestic processing will reduce the reliance on imported fuels while creating skilled jobs and strengthening Angola’s industrial base. Hydropower helps to power this transition domestically, where significant river systems and existing large-scale dams provide plentiful electricity generation for industrialization while improving energy reliability. In a region where power constraints often limit economic activity, renewable energy sources provide the foundation for sustained growth while aligning with a plethora of global efforts aimed at reducing carbon emissions. A resilient energy supply is a necessity for the expansion of cooperation with partners like those in South Korea or Vietnam, as well as for deeper integration with wider Asia-Pacific supply chains.
A stronger Angolan economy, with reliable power and a trustworthy government, will support stability across southern and central Africa by improving trade routes, expanding economic opportunity, and strengthening regional cooperation. The benefits, however, will spread far beyond national borders. None of this means Angola’s challenges have disappeared. Diversifying the economy long dependent on oil takes time, and building institutions that encourage sustained private investment requires persistence and the political will. It requires international trust-building and newfound cooperation with partners like those ready for business in ASEAN. Infrastructure projects like the Lobito Corridor will go a long way, and so will diplomatic agreements, but innovative development financing may go even further as it sows the seeds for a future generation of builders and leaders for a stronger Angola. In many ways, Angola’s debt refinancing through the World Bank substantiates Angola’s economic ambitions in the Asia Pacific and elsewhere. For Asia-Pacific policymakers and investors, Angola’s trajectory offers a case study in how infrastructure, energy diversification, and development finance can reshape a country’s role in global supply chains.

Martin Mölder: The average voter gets what they want from the presidential election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

Martin Mölder: The average voter gets what they want from the presidential election
If direct presidential elections were held, the result would likely also be that Ülle Madise becomes president, notes Martin Mölder.
It appears that the process of finding a new president has now concluded. Ülle Madise, the Chancellor of Justice, has been submitted to the Riigikogu as the sole candidate with 75 supporting signatures, and it is very likely that the Riigikogu will confirm her as the new president.
There are probably no surprises left, but in politics one can never be certain until things are officially decided. So we will wait for next week and then see. Until then, we can look back at the process a bit and assess what actually happened. Some steps and decisions were logical, but some inevitably remain at least somewhat unclear.
The very first move in this process was made by EKRE already in early May, stating directly and explicitly that their presidential candidate is Mart Helme. With this, they essentially signaled that they would not participate in the process of finding a president in the Riigikogu, since it was highly unlikely that any other party would support Mart Helme's candidacy.
EKRE itself does not have enough seats in the Riigikogu to nominate its own candidate. That privilege currently belongs only to the Reform Party, which approached the entire process very calmly and did not rush. And other parties did not hurry much either. Summer passed quietly. Against this backdrop, several "candidate‑candidates" were active — people who essentially put themselves forward without any party directly backing them.
Riho Ühtegi, one of these candidate‑candidates and perhaps the main figure who could have clearly appealed to more conservative politicians and voters, withdrew in early August due to health reasons. A few days later, university rectors proposed Tallinn University of Technology rector Tiit Land as a candidate‑candidate. In fact, Tiit Land had already been mentioned as a candidate‑candidate in mid‑July by Reform Party founding member Neinar Seli.
Parallel to this, Ülle Madise — who had for some time been considered a possible candidate‑candidate — indicated that if she received sufficient support, she would be willing to run for president. The governing parties and the Social Democrats began aligning behind her.
Ülle Madise announced her willingness to run for president on 17 August. The day after, a poll commissioned by Delfi and conducted by Turu‑uuringute AS in early August was published, showing that 32 percent of voters — among those who had a preference — supported her as president. Support for other candidate‑candidates was significantly lower.
The support of the governing parties and the Social Democrats for Madise was strong, but not enough to elect a president in the Riigikogu. And although there were other candidate‑candidates, in the end the attention focused on Tiit Land alongside Madise.
This likely benefited Madise's chances of being elected, because a candidate who defines themselves as a liberal and strongly supports the green transition is not someone who would genuinely appeal to more conservative MPs — for example, from Isamaa or the Center Party. If the alternative to Ülle Madise is Tiit Land, then for some MPs Madise may seem a much more suitable candidate than she otherwise would. The situation would likely have been very different if the alternative had been Riho Ühtegi.
Thus, it is logical why Isamaa ultimately decided to support Madise. It remains at least partly unclear why the Center Party was and remained behind Tiit Land.
Both the Center Party and EKRE have, in a sense, stayed outside this process in the Riigikogu. Both parties have long supported the idea that the president should not be chosen through the Riigikogu, but by the Estonian electorate. Direct elections have also always been the preference of a very large share of Estonian citizens. According to the latest Norstat and Institute of Societal Studies poll (19–20 August), 70 percent of voters support direct elections.
In addition to wanting to elect the president directly, citizens are also dissatisfied with the current process. According to the Institute of Societal Studies, 59 percent of voters are unhappy with the presidential election process. And no wonder. The dynamics of finding a president — why someone ran or did not run, or who supported whom and why — inevitably remain opaque to the public.
When decisions are made in party backrooms and the president is essentially chosen before the Riigikogu even votes, this dissatisfaction is not surprising.
At the same time, this process paradoxically produces a result that currently aligns very well with voter preferences.
As of 20 August, more Estonian citizens supported electing Ülle Madise as president (43 percent) than opposed it (36 percent). And it was clear that parties acted in line with their voters' preferences. Madise's election was supported by 83 percent of Reform Party voters, 69 percent of Social Democratic voters, and 57 percent of Isamaa voters. Fifty percent of Center Party voters and 79 percent of EKRE voters did not support her election.
It seems that the Estonian electorate, on average, is now getting the president they most know how to want. If direct presidential elections were held with the same candidates who remained in the final selection now, the result would likely also be that Ülle Madise becomes president.
If Estonia truly had direct presidential elections, this would mean that the nomination process would not be controlled by parties. In that case, the pool of candidates — and therefore the final result — would likely be different.
--
Editor: Kaupo Meiel, Argo Ideon

The war with Iran will not be won through airstrikes, so what's left? - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
06:21:51 UTC
15:21:51 KST

The Pentagon reportedly asked outside analysts this month for creative ideas on Iran. That request itself is worth paying attention to. Over 180 days into a war that produced the most intensive American air campaign since Iraq in 2003, the CIA has now confirmed what the strike data was already reflecting.
First, Iran's military capacity did not collapse. Second, air power resolved neither the institutional problem nor the negotiating problem. Third, the Pentagon still lacks the tools needed to end the war with the Islamic Republic.
Three moves remain available and must be calculated within the Pentagon and the American administration.
Congressional recognition of Iranian minority independence
Iran is not a nation-state in the conventional sense of the word. At its core, it is a Persian majority governing four other large national minorities with distinct languages and cultural identities. Some of these communities have longstanding autonomy or independent movements, which the Iranian government has worked to suppress by monitoring them or, in some cases, confronting them militarily.
The four minority groups in Iran consist of the Kurds in the western Kurdistan province of Iran and surrounding regions; Ahwazi Arabs in Khuzestan, sitting on top of Iran's oil; the Baluchis in the southeast; and the Azeris in the northwest. Together, these populations account for approximately 50% of Iran's over 90 million citizens.
Hypothetically, a unanimous resolution passed by the US Congress recognizing the sovereign independence of the Iranian Kurdistan, Ahwaz, and Baluchistan people would do something no airstrike can do. It would change the internal calculation of every ministry official, every IRGC provincial commander, every Basij unit, and every Iranian citizen calculating whether the regime survives the year. It would do this at zero kinetic cost and maximum pressure - something no economic warfare can achieve.
Such a move is not without precedent.
The Kurds living in Iran declared independence in the 1940s. They had an independent state that existed for one year before the Soviets withdrew their support and the Kurdish Republic collapsed in Mahabad. In 2017, the Kurdistan Region in Iraq launched an independence referendum. Meanwhile, the Ahwazi liberation movement has been active for decades, and the sustained Baluchi insurgency in Sistan and Baluchistan all provide organizational infrastructure that congressional recognition would legitimize and further empower.
Sure, Turkey will object, and Iraq likely will as well. But that is the point.
Recognizing these states would force a choice on Tehran that airstrikes have not. It would change course on its nuclear program, its network of regional proxies and other forward defenses, and its posture in the Strait of Hormuz. Otherwise, Iran would risk seeing the country break into smaller states that look increasingly toward the Gulf and the West rather than toward Tehran.
Partition would signal that the war has moved past regime change as a coherent objective. Regime change assumes the same territorial container with different management. This unbundles the container.
America must follow through and not abandon these minorities again.
Economic enlistment for indebted military-age Americans
The narrative war on the domestic American front has already failed. The Pentagon has not been able to sell this war to the American public because the war has been rhetorically fused with Israel's operations in Gaza, and the American public rejects the fusion.
Recruitment numbers are running below what a ground invasion of Iran would require. Estimates for a successful ground campaign against Iran's 31 provincial commands and its Mosaic Defense Doctrine run between 750 thousand and 1.5 million American troops. The current active US Army stands at roughly 452 thousand. The math does not work, obviously.
Based on American history, however, there is a path forward. Not conscription or a draft in a world war-era sense, but enlistment through a “debt forgiveness program.”
The average American aged 18 to 34 carries more than $40 thousand in non-mortgage debt across student loans, credit card balances, auto loans, and personal loans, with some estimates go as high as $100 thousand.
This is the cohort the Pentagon needs. A federally administered debt-forgiveness enlistment program that fully discharges student loan, credit card, and loan balances after 24 or 36 months of service, and extends the GI Bill, would produce voluntary enlistment at scale.
This is not theoretical.
It is the American state doing what the American state has always done when it needed staff it could not otherwise generate. World War II offered the GI Bill. Vietnam offered college deferments. The post 9/11 wars offered signing bonuses and citizenship pathways. The Iran war will need to offer debt relief. The economics of the indebted American 20-and 30-something make this the most efficient conversion mechanism available to the Pentagon and the Trump administration.
The moral reading on this is uncomfortable. But states generate the soldiers they need through the incentives that work on the population they have.
A Washington-to-Beijing agreement on Iranian oil
China’s President Xi Jinping's visit to the United States this year creates a window that has not existed at any prior point in this conflict. The bilateral agenda will include trade, semiconductors, Taiwan, and the South China Sea. It should and most likely will include the Iran file.
The frame is transactional. China's current exposure to Iranian oil, the Belt and Road Initiative, and Gwadar Port infrastructure is protected under only one scenario:. A Washington-to-Beijing understanding that guarantees Chinese access to Iranian oil under a post-conflict governance arrangement, in exchange for China withdrawing diplomatic and material support to Tehran. Beijing gets its supply insulated. Washington gets Tehran's most consequential strategic partner off the board.
The counter-trade is Taiwan. Beijing has wanted a public American recalibration on Taiwan for two decades. Whether Washington and Trump are willing to offer that, and at what depth, is the negotiation. But the negotiation is available for the first time in a way it has not been before, because Iran has finally created a scenario in which both capitals have overlapping interests strong enough to overcome their structural competition.
This signals that the Iran war is now large enough to reorder the primary rivalry of the 21st century. China calculated correctly during the kinetic phase. It provided sanctions-blocking cover and diplomatic protection because the cost of doing so was low. The cost is now rising. Beijing will listen to a deal it would have refused six months ago.
Where this lands
None of these three moves solve the Iran problem alone. Together, they might resolve it. Partition breaks the state morally, politically, psychologically, and undermines Iran’s authority on its own soil. Debt-driven enlistment provides the force to enforce the partition if Iran does not capitulate during that phase. A Beijing deal removes the external protection that has kept the Iranian government standing.
While the kinetic phase of this war is over, the strategic phase is just starting.
The tools that win the strategic phase have almost nothing to do with what the F-35s and B-2s have been doing for the last six months. They have to do with legislative action, domestic economic policy, and great power negotiation.
The Pentagon asked for creative ideas. Here are three. The real question is whether Washington has the political stomach to execute any of them. My read is that the administration will attempt all three in some sequence, and that the sequence will start with the China deal because it is the lowest-cost and highest-leverage of the three.
The Iran war does not end at the point that a ceasefire is signed. It ends when Iranian institutional coherence is broken. Six months of airstrikes did not do that. Three quiet moves in Washington might.

'I was a wreck': Popyrin bares his soul before US Open bid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
06:15:44 UTC
15:15:44 KST

In short:
Australia's Alexei Popyrin is working with F1 driver Oscar Piastri's mindset coach Emma Murray as he prepares for his latest US Open campaign.
Popyrin slipped as far as number 139 in the rankings, but has received a wildcard to this year's tournament.
What's next?
Popyrin will play former US Open semi-finalist Grigor Dimitrov in round one at Flushing Meadows.
Alexei Popyrin hit rock bottom when he feared he wouldn't enjoy even his own wedding next month.
From the giddy high of taking down Novak Djokovic at the 2024 US Open, Popyrin needed a wildcard into this year's New York grand slam after slumping to as low as number 139 in the rankings last month.
He knew then he needed professional help.
The fallen Australian tennis star turned to Oscar Piastri's esteemed mindset coach and credits Emma Murray for helping him find contentment again. To a point.
"It's not easy," Popyrin said in a raw interview ahead of his first-round Open date with former semi-finalist turned 2026 qualifier Grigor Dimitrov.
"A lot of that is what was eating at me, thinking about things, searching for that feeling of being at the career-high rankings, of playing at that level, and it becomes a kind of an unhealthy obsession.
"It becomes a really negative and bad balance between you and tennis and it's what was really not helping me and it was the main culprit in what has been happening over the last few months.
"I needed to change that and I needed to change just the whole way I look at tennis as a whole, and it's still a work in progress and it's not going to be a quick fix over one or two weeks."
Popyrin took his first mental-health break after Wimbledon last year before needing another reset following a straight-sets first-round loss at the All England Club six weeks ago to Jiri Lehecka.
"After Wimbledon, I was a wreck," said the former French Open junior champion.
"I used to — well, I still do — every time I lose, I think I don't deserve to have fun. After, I think I don't deserve to be happy.
"I was worried that I wouldn't enjoy my wedding because of my tennis, and when I had that thought for the first time I was like, 'OK, something is really, really wrong and I've really got to take some time and figure things out.'"
The 27-year-old one-time world number 19 has been working with Murray for only a short time, but already the high-performance emotional regulator is making progress.
"I'm trying to not associate my results with how I feel as a person," Popyrin said.
"I'm trying to look at it in a way that it's just a journey that I'm on. Where I am is where I am and what I have to do is just continue trusting the process that I'm on.
"I've stuck with the same team and I haven't changed anything. I believe in the guys. I believe in myself. I believe that everything is just mental for me.
"And if I'm able to make those changes up in my head, then I'm able to not only get to where I am, but I believe I can go further.
"I've got to kind of start from scratch, which is never easy. It's something I have done before, but it's even harder for me to do that because of where I have been and what I have done and what I have achieved.
"But it's important for me if I want to continue playing tennis that I get through this, and the way I get through this is continuing on the trajectory that I have been the last month."
AAP

Swiss police report 'several victims' in Aarau shooting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
06:12:00 UTC
15:12:00 KST

Manhunt underway after woman killed in Swiss rave shooting
Published August 30, 2026last updated August 30, 2026
A 22-year-old woman has died after a shooting at a rave in Aarau, near Zürich, Switzerland, police said Sunday.
The woman was an Italian national, Italy's Foreign Ministry said in a statement.
Five other people, aged between 24 and 27, were wounded in the incident, some of them seriously, according to local police.
Manhunt after fatal rave shooting in Switzerland
Swiss police were hunting at least one gunman who opened fire at the overnight rave party — a rare event in the Alpine nation despite relatively widespread gun ownership.
"For the moment, we have no reliable information regarding the perpetrators. We do not know whether it is a single person or several, nor whether they fled in a vehicle or on foot," police spokesman Bernhard Graser told reporters.
"Certain elements suggest they may no longer be in the area, but we have still deployed a significant police presence in the region ... so that we can arrest them if they are still there," he added.
Officers urged people to stay away from the area, and asked for any videos or images of the incident.
Police in Freiburg, in neighboring Germany, were also taking part in the manhunt, the German news agency dpa reported.
What else do we know about the Switzerland shooting?
According to Swiss newspaper Blick, the shots were fired before 3:00 a.m. local time (0100 GMT) during the annual Aarauer Rave.
The newspaper quoted police spokeswoman Vanessa Rumpold as saying that the shooting occurred at the Schachen race course where the techno party was being held.
Aarau has about 22,300 residents and is located about 40 kilometers (25 miles) west of Zürich.

Feature: A narrow escape, a lost home -- Nepal survivors recount terrifying mudslide
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
14:04:47 CST
15:04:47 KST

This photo taken with a mobile phone shows mudslide-affected residents cleaning up their belongings in Devighat in Nuwakot, Nepal, Aug. 29, 2026. As of 9 a.m. local time on Sunday, 734 bodies had been recovered from mudslide-hit areas, with 2,498 people still missing, according to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority. (Xinhua/Zhao Manjun)
NUWAKOT, Nepal, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- For Santosh Thapa, his family was lucky when a devastating mudslide hit Devighat in Nuwakot in central Nepal; all his relatives managed to escape the disaster, leaving their belongings behind as mud gushed down.
It was a narrow escape, Thapa said. Although he was in Kathmandu at that time, his affected relatives told him the whole story.
"They first heard a terrifyingly loud noise, and then saw floodwater mixed with mud rushing toward them quickly. Realizing the danger, they became very panicked and immediately fled on a motorcycle. They probably had only one or two minutes to escape -- if they had had to go on foot, they might not have made it in time. They took almost nothing with them when they fled," the young man told Xinhua on Saturday while helping his uncle and aunt clear out the things left at the house.
Thapa said his grandfather runs a shop on the ground floor of the house, but now it is completely buried in mud. The first and second floors were all affected by the mudslide, indicating that the mud flowed as high as about nine meters when it struck the area. The house, shop, merchandise, and household items were largely destroyed, and most of what the family had accumulated over the years was lost, he said.
According to Thapa, there are about 300 households in the area, but only elders stay in the village, and their children live in Kathmandu, so the actual number of people in the village at the time of the mudslide cannot be accurately estimated, and the numbers of casualties and missing persons have still not been fully tallied. He said that when he arrived at the scene, he saw two victims' bodies with his own eyes -- one of them seemed to be a friend from his sixth-grade year.
A few kilometers upstream of the Trishuli River from Devighat, the scenario in the main town of Bidur is also heartbreaking. The once bustling street of Trishuli Bazar had almost disappeared and was covered with thick grey mud. Bridges crossing the Trishuli River connecting both sides of the town were washed away, leaving some villagers unable to return home.
Some survivors returning to check on their homes after the disaster walked across the land covered in mud. With every step, their legs sank into the soft, knee-deep mud. All they could pull out were their mud-caked feet -- their shoes were sucked deep into the mud. Some simply gave up and trudged barefoot through the mire.
Aravindra Gupta has been living in the area for 25 years and ran a vegetable shop in the bazaar. "I was sitting outside my shop when the mudslide arrived," he recalled. Pointing at a vacant place alongside the river, he said his shop was there, but the mudslide swept everything away.
Gupta, who now stays in his friend's place, came from India at the age of 1. "I have already spent 25 years of my life here. I was only one year old when I came here. So, why would I go to India? I will stay here, but what can I do? What am I supposed to do? That's what I'm thinking about now," the 26-year-old said, perplexed.
At a nearby military camp being used as a transfer station for disaster victims, helicopters shuttled back and forth between the disaster zone and the camp, transporting the wounded and stranded survivors. Outside the camp, family members of those still unaccounted for waited desperately for the military to release the names of each new batch of arrivals, hoping to hear a name they recognized. Many had been waiting here for three or four days, but still had received no news at all.
A local reporter told Xinhua on Saturday that it was currently the fourth day since the flood occurred. From what he can summarize, the situation has not normalized yet. Rescue operations are ongoing, but rescuers face extreme difficulty reaching the exact locations, as road connections and critical bridges have been swept away in multiple places, severely obstructing rescue logistics.
There is a complete breakdown of telecommunications networks, and electricity has not been restored properly in the affected areas, he said, adding that official figures of casualties are not yet confirmed, but unofficial reports indicate more.
As of 9 a.m. local time on Sunday, 734 bodies had been recovered from mudslide-hit areas, with 2,498 people still missing, according to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority.
In the affected valley areas, the temperature is high and the air is humid. The World Health Organization (WHO) has warned of the risk of disease. "As always, when we have a disaster of this scale and we have displacement, overcrowding, and we may have disruption of water, sanitation and health services, and that can increase the risk of infectious diseases," said a UN report, citing WHO spokesperson Tarik Jasarevic.
Thapa told Xinhua that although local people have been provided with food, temporary shelter, and medicine, he is concerned that the hot weather poses a risk of infectious diseases in the disaster-hit areas.
Many dead animals from the mudslide have not yet been found or promptly removed. If the human remains and animal carcasses are not properly disposed of, bacteria could multiply quickly and cause infections, he said.
"Searching for the missing and clearing away the dead are important; it is also necessary to protect the survivors and promptly carry out sanitation, epidemic prevention, and environmental cleanup work," he said. ■

Factbox: Latest relief and rescue progress at mudslide-hit border port in China's Xizang
China

A press conference is held by the information office of the Xizang regional government to brief the rescue and relief efforts after a mudslide struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in the autonomous region, in Xigaze, southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region, Aug. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Tenzing Nima Qadhup)
BEIJING, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- A fast-moving chain mudslide, triggered by a high-altitude glacier collapse on the Nepali side, struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Aug. 26, causing heavy casualties and leaving many missing.
Chinese rescuers immediately launched an all-out effort to reach the mudslide-hit port area and search for the missing. Here is what we know about the deadly mudslide and the latest rescue and relief progress there:
-- Sixteen people have been confirmed dead and 546 others remain missing as of 6 p.m. Saturday, according to the regional government.
-- A total of 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries have been identified as unaccounted for after the mudslide. The figure was announced on Sunday morning at a press conference held by the information office of the regional government, following a joint search and cross-checking of information by foreign affairs, public security, culture and tourism, and emergency management authorities.
-- During his phone conversation with Nepali Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal on Saturday, Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said that China attaches great importance to the disaster, which also caused heavy casualties and left many missing in Nepal. Wang said that while urgently carrying out rescue and relief efforts on its own side, China extended a helping hand at the earliest opportunity and supported Nepal in its emergency disaster relief efforts.
-- A total of 2,141 Chinese rescuers have joined the mission, according to the update by the region's emergency management department on early Saturday morning. Excavators were busy repairing a key road to facilitate entry into the port. A total length of 2.6 km of road section had been restored, leaving 1.7 kilometers to go before reaching Gyirong Port by around 1 p.m. Saturday.
-- All civilian vehicles and personnel are prohibited from traveling toward Gyirong Township, with immediate effect, according to a notice issued on Saturday by the local traffic police. The notice specified that only authorized special-purpose vehicles for emergency rescue, disaster relief, and material support are permitted to pass with valid permits. The restrictions will remain in place until further notice.
-- China's Ministry of Emergency Management on Saturday dispatched five Chinese tunnel experts to Nepal to support rescue efforts at a hydropower plant tunnel, at the request of the Nepali government.
-- Three sets of portable automatic weather stations have been deployed to provide targeted weather support for restoring road access, search and rescue operations, drone flights and surveying a barrier lake, the China Meteorological Administration said Saturday.
-- The National Cryosphere Desert Data Center has provided 53 service datasets, with a total data volume of roughly 85 GB, available for download and use by relevant emergency response, rescue and research institutions.
-- The National Earth Observation Data Center has compiled remote sensing data resources from civilian and commercial satellites, with a total data volume exceeding 20 GB. The data is provided to support post-disaster road damage assessment, building collapse identification, and secondary disaster monitoring. ■

New Tallinn tram line to launch on September 1
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
06:03:00 UTC
15:03:00 KST

New Tallinn tram line to launch on September 1
Public transport in Tallinn will switch to autumn-winter timetables with more frequent departures from September 1, and a new tram line will begin operating.
From the start of the new school year, tram T6 will begin operating on the Kopli–Suur-Paala route.
Timetable changes also affect buses and trolleybuses.
Parents are advised to check their child's route to school and suitable public transport connections before the start of the school year.
Tallinn City Council said, if possible, it is worth travelling the route to school with a child by public transport before September 1 so that the route, stops and any transfers are familiar. It is also worth checking the new timetables before the first day of school, as a familiar route or departure time may have changed.
Deputy Mayor Joel Jesse said all road users should allow more time than usual for their journeys during the first weeks of September.
"The start of the school year noticeably changes Tallinn's traffic picture – there are once again more cars, public transport users and children on the streets, many of whom are only getting used to their route to school and travelling independently. We ask everyone to be attentive and considerate of one another," Jesse said.
Several construction projects are also continuing throughout the autumn, which is expected to lead to traffic jams in the capital.
Up-to-date timetables, routes and stops can be viewed at transport.tallinn.ee.

War update: 221 clashes along front line over past day, fiercest fighting in Pokrovsk, Kostiantynivka sectors
According to Ukrinform, this was reported by the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Facebook in an operational update as of 8:00 on Sunday, August 30.
Yesterday, Russian forces launched four missile strikes using five missiles and carried out 79 airstrikes, dropping 292 guided aerial bombs. In addition, Russian forces deployed 11,357 kamikaze drones and carried out 3,138 shelling attacks on settlements and Ukrainian military positions, including 60 using multiple launch rocket systems.
The enemy shelled, among other locations, the settlements of Neskuchne, Korenok, Potapivka, Mala Korchakivka, Volfyne, Atynske, Sopych, Bachivsk, and Tovstodubove in the Sumy region, as well as Liskivshchyna in the Chernihiv region.
Ukraine’s Air Force, missile forces and artillery struck 14 clusters of Russian personnel, seven artillery systems, six UAV control posts and three other important enemy targets.
In the Northern Slobozhanshchyna and Kursk sectors, five combat engagements were recorded. Russian forces carried out 167 attacks on Ukrainian positions and settlements and conducted two airstrikes using five guided aerial bombs.
In the Southern Slobozhanshchyna sector, Ukrainian units repelled 10 Russian attacks. The enemy attempted to advance toward Lyman, Hrafskе, Chuhunivka, Ozerne, and Khatnie, as well as near Starytsia.
In the Kupiansk sector, Russian forces launched two offensive actions toward Radkivka and Podoly.
Attempts to break through Ukrainian defenses were repelled in the Lyman sector, where Russian forces attacked nine times near Novoselivka and Cherneshchyna as well as near Lyman and Dibrova.
In the Sloviansk sector, Russian forces launched eight assaults near Kryva Luka, Riznykivka, and Zakitne as well as toward Orikhuvatka.
No Russian assault operations were recorded in the Kramatorsk sector.
In the Kostiantynivka sector, 31 Russian attacks were recorded. The enemy launched assaults near Kostiantynivka, Illinivka, Novoselivka, Rusyn Yar, Toretskе, and Sofiivka, as well as toward Mykolaipillia and Kucheriv Yar.
The enemy carried out 30 attacks in the Pokrovsk sector. Russian forces attempted to advance toward Bilytske, Shevchenko, Novohryshyne, Vasylivka, Serhiivka, Novopidhorodnie, and Novyi Donbas, as well as near Udachne, Orikhove and Novomykolaivka.
In the Oleksandrivka sector, Russian forces launched four attacks toward Berezove.
In the Huliaipole sector, Russian forces attacked Ukrainian defensive positions 10 times. The enemy attempted to advance toward Vozdvyzhivka, Huliaipilske, Charivne, Novoselivka, Kalynivske, Nove Zaporizhzhia, and Maliivka.
In the Orikhiv sector, Ukrainian defenders stopped three Russian attempts to advance near Pavlivka and Mala Tokmachka.
No Russian assault operations were recorded in the Dnipro River sector.
No signs of Russian forces forming offensive groupings were detected in the Volyn and Polissia sectors.
As reported by Ukrinform, total Russian combat losses since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine on February 24, 2022, through August 30, 2026, have reached approximately 1,486,600 personnel, including 1,400 over the past 24 hours.

MOSCOW, August 30. /TASS/. Among French mercenaries fighting on the side of the Ukrainian military, 35% are neo-Nazis, Laurent Brayard, a French expert, historian, and military correspondent working in the Donbass, told TASS.
"France has a very high proportion of neo-Nazis, neo-fascists, and, in general, members of this ultra-nationalist, supremacist movement and so on [fighting on the Ukrainian side]: 35%, which is enormous," he noted.
The expert clarified that this figure differs from the overall trend within the Ukrainian armed forces. "Whereas for the entire contingent [of foreign mercenaries in the Ukrainian military], I have information indicating that about 10-12% are neo-Nazis," he added.
According to Brayard, "France, unfortunately, is the leading country in Western Europe supplying mercenaries.".

Tuscany’s treasured islands: five to explore
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
06:00:49 UTC
15:00:49 KST

Scattered between the Tuscan coast and Corsica, the seven islands of the Tuscan archipelago offer a striking contrast to mainland Tuscany. All are part of a protected national park, but each has its own character – some are lively, others tiny and sparsely inhabited. Montecristo and Gorgona are only accessible via strictly limited guided tours, but here’s a brief guide to the highlights of the other five.
Elba: the all-year-rounder
As Italy’s third-largest island, and with a year-round community, Elba is the archipelago’s main tourist hub, blending Napoleonic history with rugged landscapes, lively seaside towns and fine beaches. It is famous for Napoleon’s brief 1814 exile at the Palazzina dei Mulini, but its history runs much deeper, with 16th-century Medici fortifications to defend against pirate raids around the coast, and medieval hill towns, some standing on sites occupied since Roman times, inland.
Beach lovers tend to divide between the white-pebble coves of Sansone and Capo Bianco near the largest town, Portoferraio, in the north, and the golden sands of Fetovaia and Cavoli in the south-west beneath Monte Capanne. Marina di Campo on the south coast is a favourite for watersports, and windsurfing and sailing schools are popular in many resorts, from Procchio in the north to Lacona in the south.
Hikers can explore the 36-mile (58km) Grande Traversata Elbana, crossing the island from Cavo in the north-east to Pomonte or Patresi on the west coast, passing along mountain ridges and through traditional villages. Usually completed in three or four days, it’s best tackled in spring or autumn.
Where to eat: In Portoferraio, Ristorante da Gianni is a favourite for handmade pasta, seafood and traditional cuisine. Try the house speciality, orecchiette with prawns and courgettes. In Marina di Campo, Da Piero serves seafood-focused dishes right on the beach. 
Where to stay: Near Fetovaia, Hotel Montemerlo (doubles from about £88 B&B) offers a relaxed, eco-conscious stay among olive groves. In Marina di Campo, Hotel Punto Verde (doubles from about £90 B&B) is a charming family-run hotel near the beach. On the west coast Hotel Gallo Nero (doubles from £79) is a family-run hotel overlooking Capo Sant’Andrea Bay. In an 18th-century building in Portoferraio’s historic centre, Indarsena (doubles from £86 B&B) is 10 minutes’ walk from several beaches.
Getting there: Ferries from Piombino to Portoferraio take about an hour with Toremar, Moby or Blu Navy. 
Giglio: the charming isle
At just 21 sq km, Giglio is small but has three villages, secluded coves, an extensive coastline and a landscape of historic terraced vineyards. Access for private vehicles is heavily restricted during August, with exceptions for longer stays, which helps preserve its peaceful atmosphere, while buses and taxis link the harbour, villages and beaches, so a car-free holiday is easy.
From Giglio Porto, trails lead to hidden coves and hilltop viewpoints, while the medieval lanes of Giglio Castello, a fortified 12th-century hilltop village, are perfect for an aperitivo and an evening stroll.
Beaches have distinct characters. Campese, on the north-west coast, is the largest, with reddish-gold sand and views of the 16th-century Torre del Campese. Cannelle, in the east, offers pale sand and crystalline water, while farther north, Arenella combines golden sand, granite boulders and clear water for snorkelling.
Where to eat: In Giglio Porto, Ristorante Doria is a seafood favourite with a sea-view terrace (try spaghetti alla chitarra with sea urchin and toasted breadcrumbs). In Campese, Da Zio Meino offers cucina povera (peasant cooking) such as pancotti di mare and spaghetti alle vongole e alla bottarga (with clams and cured mullet roe).
Where to stay: On a hillside overlooking Giglio Porto, B&B La Vela (doubles from £87 B&B) is a small guesthouse with maritime-themed interiors. On a headland above Campese Bay, Le Poste di Simplicio (doubles from £100 B&B) is a family-run B&B with sweeping sea views.
Getting there: Toremar or Maregiglio ferries run from Porto Santo Stefano to Giglio Porto in about an hour.
Capraia: a wild hikers’ paradise
Located just over 20 miles (33km) north-west of Elba, Capraia is one of the archipelago’s most remote islands. Largely car-free, with few roads, it is best explored on foot along mule tracks winding between sea cliffs, hidden coves and 16th-century Genoese fortifications, although taxi boats and a bus provide limited transport.
Highlights include the red rock formations of Cala Rossa, the Genoese fortress of San Giorgio and the 16th-century Torre dello Zenòbito.
Beaches are few, but swimmers can cool off at Cala San Francesco, hike to Cala del Ceppo and Cala dello Zurletto, or take a taxi boat to Spiaggia della Mortola, one of the few sandy stretches.
Where to eat: In the main village, the fixed menu at Il Carabottino changes according to what the local fishers happen to bring ashore, while Il Pigghiolo takes a more contemporary approach, reworking island flavours in dishes such as squid parmigiana and cod croquette.
Where to stay: Accommodation is limited, but La Mandola Eco Hostel (doubles from £70 room-only) near the port is a restorative basecamp for walkers, beachgoers and divers, with a sheltered saltwater pool. In Capraia village, Il Saracino Boutique Suites is a small, characterful retreat with sea views (doubles from £130 B&B).
Getting there: The ferry from Livorno takes 1 hour 45 minutes with Toremar.
Pianosa: the protected isle
Daily visitor numbers to Pianosa are restricted, helping preserve the island’s fragile environment and tranquil atmosphere. You can either buy a ticket on the limited ferry service or join an authorised guided excursion.
Roman remains (including early Christian catacombs) and abandoned prison buildings from when the island served as a penal colony offer glimpses of its history. And the restored Casa dell’Agronomo and Museo delle Scienze Geologiche e Archeologiche explore its agricultural, geological and archaeological heritage.
Guided walks, cycling and kayak excursions are among the best ways to explore. Swimming is restricted to Cala Giovanna, an easy walk from the small port and historic village, to help safeguard the marine ecosystem.
Where to eat: Da Brunello in the small harbour village is Pianosa’s only cafe/restaurant, with a focus on fresh fish and vegetables grown on the island.
Where to stay: Close to the cafe and run by the same management, the island’s only accommodation, Albergo Milena (doubles from £95 half-board) offers simple rooms in a historic building. 
Getting there: There are authorised excursions from Elba with Acquavision (45 minutes), and limited Toremar ferry services run from Piombino to Pianosa (about three hours).
Giannutri: the roadless retreat
While Elba hums with holidaymakers and Vespas, this tiny, car-free limestone crescent, where scent-heavy macchia slopes into ink-blue waters, offers a radical detox from modern life.
With only one restaurant-cafe, which also functions as a small grocery shop, day trippers are advised to bring their own water and lunch. Most people swim at Cala Spalmatoio and Cala Maestra, while much of the coastline forms part of a protected marine reserve renowned for its diving and snorkelling. A guided tour of a Roman villa linked to the Domitii Ahenobarbi family is a must.
Where to eat: La Vela Giannutri, the island’s only dining option, focuses on seafood dishes, from tuna tartare to spaghetti alle vongole.
Where to stay: Accommodation is limited to the family-run A Casa Diana (doubles from £123 B&B), with simple rooms and sea views, and a scattering of holiday rentals.
Getting there: Maregiglio runs ferries from Porto Santo Stefano, or there are seasonal excursion boats (taking about an hour). In summer, Maregiglio also operates excursions and mini-cruises between Giglio and Giannutri.

South West Water has worst environmental record in England, analysis shows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
06:00:48 UTC
15:00:48 KST

South West Water is doing more harm to the environment than any other water company in England, according to new analysis, with more sewage discharged in Devon, Cornwall, Dorset and Somerset than anywhere else.
Friends of the Earth analysed water companies’ environmental performance in six categories: sewage spills, water quality at bathing sites, pollution incidents or warnings at bathing sites, severity of sewage pollution at bathing sites, the percentage of rivers rated below the standard for good ecological health, and the affordability of bills.
South West Water, which operates across Devon, Cornwall and parts of Dorset and Somerset, was among the top three worst performers in four out of the six categories.
The water company had the highest total duration of sewage spill events since 2024, averaging 574,323 hours annually. Severn Trent and Yorkshire Water came second and third respectively but were outstripped by South West Water, by almost 200,000 spill hours.
South West Water’s designated bathing sites also recorded the most pollution incidents and warnings, with 666 recorded in 2025 alone.
There are 157 official bathing sites in South West Water’s catchment. If a site is designated, the Environment Agency will monitor water quality during the bathing season to protect people’s health.
A spokesperson for the company said: “We manage more than a third of England’s designated bathing waters, so improving water quality is a huge priority for us. We’re already seeing progress, with storm overflow spills down 17% and spill duration down 25% over the past year, despite significantly higher rainfall across the region. We’re also on track to meet new Environment Act bathing water standards by 2030, five years ahead of the national deadline, showing the impact of record investment across the south-west.”
Alongside this poor environmental performance, Friends of the Earth said South West Water’s roughly 1.8 million customers faced some of the highest water bills at £726 annually. Since 2024, they have had the second biggest increase in England, with bills rising by 39%.
Southern Water is responsible for the most expensive water bills in England and the biggest increase since 2024, with £281 added to the average bill in that period.
Kierra Box, a water campaigner at Friends of the Earth, is calling on the government to bring forward a robust clean water bill that sets out a “meaningful plan for restoring the health of the UK’s rivers and seas”.
She said: “People have had enough of hearing ministers say they’ll fix the problem, only to bring in measures that superficially address the issue. If we’re to end the sewage scandal once and for all, we must see the government committing to a complete overhaul of our water system.”
A Defra spokesperson said: “It is totally unacceptable that some water companies are failing to deliver value for money for customers and polluting our rivers, lakes and seas.
“The government recognises that we need to build on our reforms which banned bonuses so our water system works for the public. That’s why we are driving forward the biggest overhaul of the water sector in a generation, with new legislation to give the public more control and help keep bills as low as possible.”
Friends of the Earth is also calling on the government to nationalise water companies. Sources recently told the Guardian that the prime minister, Andy Burnham, was considering ripping up insolvency laws to make it easier to bring key utilities such as water companies under public control. However, the Times reported that Burnham had shelved plans to put Thames Water into administration amid concerns about the cost and the legal risk involved.
Defra said Thames Water remained financially stable, but the government stood “ready for all eventualities, including applying for a special administration regime if that were to become necessary”.
A Water UK spokesperson said: “No sewage spill is ever acceptable, and we are working to end them as fast as we physically can. That’s why we are tripling investment over the next five years to halve spills from storm overflows and upgrade the capacity of 1,700 wastewater treatment works.”

On long road back from Brexit, north-east’s recovery rides on survival of Nissan’s ‘shining star’ plant
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
06:00:48 UTC
15:00:48 KST

In a factory in Gateshead, engineers carefully wind metal wires around iron cores to go in electric motors. Here, workers produce a smaller “pancake motor”, which generates higher torque than conventional versions for supercars or construction equipment.
These workers form part of north-east England’s automotive industry, which has experienced a long line of political disruptions, from Margaret Thatcher’s efforts to attract international investment, through Brexit and now Andy Burnham’s reindustrialisation strategy.
Across the Gateshead factory, which is owned by Turntide, more people are readying tools to assemble 2.5-tonne prototype battery packs for Hitachi’s hybrid trains, also to be built in the north-east.
The busy factory is just one example of the ripples that have spread out from the centre of the area’s automotive industry, the Sunderland car factory 15 minutes down the road owned by Japan’s Nissan.
Turntide’s business would not be here without its bigger automotive neighbour. Hyperdrive, one of the businesses combined into US-owned Turntide, secured its first batteries from a factory supplying Nissan. The smaller company shows why governments court big manufacturers: they bring stable jobs and can also spark growth in the local economy.
Yet the situation is not so positive across the local industry. Four decades after opening in 1986, Nissan’s underutilised Sunderland plant is hoping to build cars for China’s Chery. The deal, which is still not confirmed, came at just the right time for Sunderland’s workers, with the plant operating at barely half its capacity and facing a series of Brexit threats to its export-led model.
The Nissan factory opened as the keystone of Thatcher’s investment drive. In Sunderland those efforts are mostly seen as a success: the first Bluebird from the plant takes pride of place in the city’s museum. The factory produced 507,000 cars in 2016, just shy of the 510,000 made in 2012, and it was seen as the carmaker’s most efficient plant internationally.
Andy Palmer, who was Nissan’s global chief operating officer before leaving to lead Aston Martin in 2014, said the plant was “the shining star globally for Nissan in the manufacturing world”.
Yet it still had to fight to survive. Nissan closed its other European plant in Spain in 2020 (later selling it to Chery). That survival was “no mean feat”, Palmer said, and came “in spite of everything else” that it had to deal with.
Brexit threats
The list of challenges faced by the global car industry over the past decade is long, with the pandemic and subsequent supply chain chaos, increased protectionism and the rise of Chinese competitors – all while finding cash to invest heavily in electric technology. But Sunderland’s automotive industry in particular became a symbol of a difficulty specific to Britain’s companies: Brexit.
The Brexit vote triggered a decade of political turmoil in the UK, and huge uncertainty for carmakers over whether the Conservative government would pursue a “no deal” exit that would have led to the overnight imposition of tariffs on the UK’s largest export market. Nissan was eventually granted £61m in secret state aid to invest in new models, followed by another £101m in late 2022.
The no deal outcome – seen as a catastrophe by most exporters – was averted but car exporters still have to cope with twin Brexit threats this year. The first is from EU rules of origin that say electric cars made in Britain must contain batteries made in the UK or EU to avoid paying tariffs, and vice versa. The rules were included in the 2020 Brexit deal to spur manufacturers to secure British and EU batteries rather than relying on Chinese imports. However, many of the battery projects have collapsed, leaving the industry short of European supply.
Nissan sources batteries from the next-door gigafactory run by Chinese-owned AESC, but the rules also require crucial cathode materials inside the cells to be sourced from Europe. That may prove too hard, so the automotive industry in the UK and EU is pushing for the latter to extend the rules of origin deadline for a second time. But some industry insiders do not expect an extension until as late as December, as the EU uses it for leverage in negotiations.
The second threat is from the EU’s separate Industrial Accelerator Act that will limit public procurement and subsidies to cars “made in EU” in an effort to protect carmakers from China. Factories in Britain will be locked out under the current draft. British and EU companies (who own most of the UK’s car factories) have called for the UK to be included in the rules. Nissan, which declined a request for an interview, has privately warned the government that Sunderland’s future was at risk.
“It’s not a slam dunk that Nissan will survive,” Palmer said. “If made in Europe excludes the UK then I think it’s existential for Sunderland. Sunderland will die.”
David Bailey, a professor of business economics at the University of Birmingham, said: “Brexit keeps bringing up these uncertainties. The world is changing, and the EU responds to that, and that affects the UK.”
Electric shocks
The big carmakers in the UK are also lobbying hard on another issue the government is considering: watering down electric vehicle targets, known as the zero emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate. The existing rules mean battery cars make up 80% of sales from high-volume manufacturers, but Burnham’s government this month announced the new target could be as low as 50%.
Nissan was an electric pioneer and has invested heavily to build its new electric Leaf and Juke crossover SUV models. Yet the company will welcome lower targets after reportedly shelving development of an electric Qashqai, wary of lower-than-expected demand for battery cars around the world. It has also set its sights on selling new petrol cars beyond 2035, when they are due to be banned.
Some analysts believe carmakers trying to delay the shift to electric are signing their own death warrants by ceding the market to Chinese competitors. Colin Walker, the head of transport at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit, a thinktank, said: “Embracing this new technology represents the best chance that manufacturers have to survive and thrive in an electrified world. Pushing increasingly obsolescent technologies will only hasten their demise and would be a recipe for factory closures and mass redundancies.”
A Nissan spokesperson said it was “committed to a fully electric future” and that the mandate “must align with real-life consumer EV demand to ensure a gradual transition to full zero-emission vehicle sales while supporting the competitiveness of UK automotive manufacturing”.
Nissan is undergoing a painful restructuring process worldwide, with the chief executive, Ivan Espinosa, closing seven factories and cutting 20,000 jobs.
If confirmed, Nissan will build cars for Chery, a part-state-owned Chinese carmaker that also makes the Omoda and Jaecoo brands. Nissan would still own the plant and employ the workers and would be able to use its spare capacity – it only managed 273,000 cars in 2025.
Some experts think there is little chance of Chery confirming the deal if the Brexit issues are not resolved. Yet the Unite union is pleased, arguing it would keep volumes up, thus preserving jobs.
For Turntide, the north-east of England still offers what it needs to try to grow its business. David Orgill, Turntide’s vice-president of global operations, said: “Why not here? Why not in the north of England? The supply chain is fantastic up here.”
Turntide’s US parent company, backed by Bill Gates’s Breakthrough Energy Ventures, BMW and Amazon, combined three UK businesses with the aim of expanding sales. It is expecting surging demand for its pancake motors (which are known as axial flux motors because of the different arrangement of their internal magnets). Based on talks with carmakers and construction equipment companies, it wants to expand production to 12,000 motors a year by 2028.
“We’re expecting to grow significantly in the next 18 months,” Orgill said. “We’re actually able to pull back a lot of the capability and manufacturing back into the UK.”
The survival and success of the Nissan plant is seen as politically crucial in the north-east and at Westminster, which partly explains why the government is indeed preparing to weaken the mandate further.
Kim McGuinness, the Labour mayor for the north-east, said Nissan was a key part of the region’s economic plans. She said that despite the political disaffection, Sunderland was thriving, with significant investment in improving the city centre, as well as extra public transport, such as extending a metro line from the city (which lies to Nissan’s east) to Washington, the town to Nissan’s west.
“In the north-east, we all know that factory is absolutely fundamental to our regional economy, but also [to] the position of the country in the automotive industry,” she said, adding that it acted as an anchor for the broader supply chain. “This is what the north-east does very well – that clustering effect”.
McGuinness is hopeful that devolution will help to attract more manufacturing jobs and assuage the “left behind” feeling that drove the Brexit vote and the subsequent rise of Nigel Farage’s Reform UK party, which won control of Sunderland council in May’s local elections. The Reform branch in Sunderland did not respond to requests for an interview.
McGuinness said: “People like me can give local residents more say. I believe that is the way that we combat Reform.”
Even if the Chery deal is confirmed, the north-east’s automotive industry faces a long road to get back to its heyday when Nissan was producing half a million cars. Yet it has got through tricky situations before.
“I admire the plant for surviving,” said Prof Colin Herron, an automotive expert at Newcastle University. “The resilience of the people at that factory is incredible. Now they’re entering a new phase.”

Humanitarian crisis worsening in refuge for civilians fleeing Sudan’s civil war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
06:00:48 UTC
15:00:48 KST

Humanitarian conditions in the Sudanese city of El Obeid and two camps on its outskirts are dire and deteriorating, according to people on the ground, as civilians displaced by fighting between the Sudanese Armed Forces and Rapid Support Forces (RSF) militia continue to pour in from the surrounding countryside.
The UN says more than 15,000 families have arrived since mid-July, joining more than 200,000 people who arrived in the first half of the year, according to government figures cited by Save the Children.
“The situation is very harsh and is deteriorating as El Obeid is receiving IDPs [internally displaced people] on a daily basis … The city is shockingly overcrowded,” said Maryam, a humanitarian volunteer whose name has been changed for her safety.
The new arrivals came on foot, carrying almost nothing, she said. “They also suffer from a shortage of food and they definitely arrive traumatised.”
The city, the capital of North Kordofan province, was home to around half a million people before the war broke out more than three years ago.
While many of the new arrivals have been absorbed into the city, tens of thousands are living in two main tented camps. According to analysis of satellite data by the Yale Humanitarian Research Lab, 800 new tents appeared in one of the camps between 4 and 25 August.
“During my visit, I saw 450 arrivals coming from the surrounding villages just that morning,” said Paul Byars, the Sudan country director for the Danish Refugee Council, who was in El Obeid last week. “The authorities’ estimates are correct, that 85% of them are women and children. Most of the men are staying behind because this is the only time for farming.”
Civil war erupted in Sudan’s capital, Khartoum, about 250 miles (400km) north-east of El Obeid, on 15 April 2023, when a power struggle between the armed forces and RSF descended into open conflict.
Since then, about 11.3 million people have been displaced, more than a fifth of the population. Some parts of the country, including El Obeid and surrounding areas, are at risk of famine.
Estimates of the number of people killed in the war range from tens to hundreds of thousands. More than 10,000 people are thought to have been massacred by the RSF in El Fasher over two days when they seized the city in Sudan’s western Darfur region in October 2025 after an 18-month siege.
A surge in RSF drone strikes on El Obeid and nearby areas in June led the UN to warn that the city could face a repeat of what happened in El Fasher.
The number of strikes has since fallen. The armed forces also recaptured a key road leading north to Khartoum in late July, which at least partly lifted the threat of besiegement. However, drones are still killing and injuring civilians, while violence rages in the surrounding districts, pushing people to the city.
Recently, volunteers in El Obeid had noticed more “double-tap” drone strikes, where a second drone follows the first, hitting rescuers at the scene, Maryam said. “It is hard, so hard, living with this, hearing the sound of a drone hitting somewhere,” she said. “It’s very disturbing.”
Sudan’s civil war has become dominated by drones, accounting for half of all violent incidents, up from 4% at the start of the war, said Nohad Eltayeb, who monitors Sudan for Acled, a conflict tracking group.
Both sides used drones, but the RSF’s usage had become more volatile since the US war with Iran began to interrupt supply lines in February, she said. “They rely on fewer, very targeted strikes.”
So far this year, there have been 322 incidents of violence affecting civilians in the wider Kordofan region, compared with 388 for the whole of 2025, according to Acled data. While the RSF was responsible for half of those, the SAF has also killed and injured civilians. On 10 August, armed forces and an allied militia killed five civilians and injured 10 about 60 miles north-east of El Obeid, according to Emergency Lawyers, a non-governmental group.
With the threats to delivery trucks, food prices have rocketed. In north Kordofan in July, according to World Food Programme data, a litre of groundnut oil cost 17,000 Sudanese pounds (£21), up from 13,000 in June and 7,700 a year ago. The prices of wheat flour and goat and sheep meat have also more than doubled in the last year.
Meanwhile, El Obeid’s power and water infrastructure still has not fully recovered from RSF drone strikes in June.
“The main problem is the big [water] source that is in the north of the city has been severely damaged and it has not been repaired,” said Esperanza Santos, an emergency coordinator in Sudan for Médecins Sans Frontières. “The water pipes in the city have [also] been impacted. So mostly, both in the city – for example, in the hospital – and also in the IDP camps, they are relying on water trucking and it’s not enough.”
Conditions in the camps were poor too, Santos said. “In terms of sanitation, it’s very, very bad. It’s not enough. The ratio of latrines per person is impossible – there are more than 100 people for a latrine. So basically there is open defecation.”
Maryam said she and her fellow local volunteers remained committed, despite the difficulties. “The situation is deteriorating, but we are trying to stay together, to stay strong in the face of the drone attacks and the influx of IDPs … We are living with this and we hope things will become better.”

Will Hong Kong see fewer creditor-led commercial property sales as assets stabilise?
City’s office and retail property segments have been mired in a multi-year slump that has triggered loan defaults
Financial distress in Hong Kong’s commercial property market has moderated but not been completely eliminated, analysts say, with highly leveraged asset owners still expected to find refinancing their loans a challenge.
The city’s office and retail property segments have been mired in a multi-year slump, with new supply outstripping demand in recent years as consumption slowed and interest rates surged, triggering loan defaults.
“We do not expect defaults will increase noticeably from this time point, with transaction activity remaining relatively resilient, and much of the valuation correction has already been reflected in pricing,” said Thomas Chak, head of capital markets and investment services at Colliers Hong Kong.
“Banks, however, continue to release distressed assets, and mortgagee sales remain an important source of transaction activity in order to recover cash and take advantage of the relatively more liquid market this year.”
In the first half of the year, Hong Kong saw HK$22.3 billion (US$2.84 billion) worth of non-residential property transactions above HK$50 million, up 120 per cent from the same period last year, with offices accounting for more than two-thirds or HK$15.1 billion, Savills added.

Drilling of wells in joint Balal field enters new phase
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
