14:09:07 KST

China on Sunday said 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries were missing on the Tibetan side of a border crossing with Nepal following a mudslide that tore through the Himalayan region, while the death toll in Tibet has reached 16 people.
Officials from China's Tibet Autonomous Region said at a press conference that the highest number of missing foreigners was from Nepal at 104, while 49 Indian, 33 Latvian, 18 American, and 15 British citizens were also unaccounted for. They said authorities in Beijing have notified foreign missions.
The nationality breakdown was the first from the Chinese side since the collapse of a glacier on Wednesday unleashed a torrent of ice, rock, mud and debris down Himalayan rivers.
Authorities said 16 people had died in Gyirong County as of Saturday evening and that 546 were missing.
In Nepal, the disaster authority said at least 675 people were killed on its side of the border, 2,498 are missing, and 7,514 have been rescued.
Risk of further flooding persists as rescue efforts continue
Local police told Reuters that residents and rescue workers have moved to higher ground after the water level in the nearby Trishuli River rose over the past few hours, underscoring the risk of further flooding even as rescue efforts continue.
The disaster was "caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming," Chinese state broadcaster CCTV reported on Sunday, saying it is a "new and prominent feature of cryosphere disasters" on the Tibetan plateau.
It took six to seven minutes for the mudslide from the Nepalese side to reach the Gyirong border crossing, CCTV reported, citing the findings of Chinese scientists.
Surveillance footage from the crossing showed torrents of water and debris engulfing buildings while people tried to flee.
China mobilizes over 2,100 emergency rescue workers for mudslide relief
China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi told his Nepalese counterpart in a Saturday telephone call that the mudslide was their "most severe cross-border disaster" in recent years, and that rescue operations were of unprecedented difficulty and complexity, CCTV reported.
China has mobilized over 2,100 emergency rescue workers and allocated at least 220 million yuan ($32.7 million) to support relief efforts. It is also providing emergency cash aid, disaster relief supplies, satellite and hydrological data, and tunnel rescue experts to Nepal, the state broadcaster said.
The countries are working together to identify missing citizens and foreign nationals, as well as strengthening cooperation in disaster prevention and mitigation, and climate-change response, CCTV reported.
More than 90,000 people are likely to have been affected by the disaster, the Red Cross estimated.

Kismet, London SE1: ‘The sort of beans that make you want to move to the sun’ – restaurant review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
05:00:48 UTC
14:00:48 KST

A Turkish-Cypriot meyhane, which translates roughly as “wine house”, has slotted in upstairs at the Globe Tavern in Borough Market, south London. Any cab driver worth his salt will bend your ear over the fact that this is “where Bridget Jones lives”, which might be a bit confusing if you’ve booked in to eat kuzu şiş (lamb neck kebabs) and to knock back a couple of rakis with a fermented turnip juice chaser.
That Bridget Jones trivia, by the way, is completely true: the upstairs space at the Globe was used as the heroine’s gaff in that famous film franchise. Now, however, when you climb the staircase up to Kismet, an old, slightly eerie and flickering TV by the restaurant entrance begins to tell a very different tale. This is chef Keiran Mustafa’s very personal tribute to his family’s homeland and the community they built in London. Mustafa was the opening head chef at BiBi, to my mind one of the best restaurants in London, and before that he worked at industry stalwarts Chez Bruce and the Harwood Arms.
Mustafa’s partner in this new venture is Dom Hamdy, the smart-cookie restaurateur behind Crispin, Bistro Freddie and Canal. The result is structured and very chic bedlam that’s lovable and edgy in equal measure. On a midweek lunchtime not long after opening, chaotic Turkish jazz gives way to Turkish techno on the speakers as the grill in the open kitchen roars and glasses of Karmen’s Diren white wine at £8 a pop slide down rather too easily for the lunchtime crowd. Mustafa tells us that our table is where the weekly live music sets up. I haven’t sat that close to a PA since I was on a cross-channel ferry eating chips beside the bingo caller, and I’m sure that Kismet in full swing will be just as choppy.
The dining space is split into two rooms, all dark wood and white tablecloths, with lace over the windows and walls the colour of a 70-a-day Rothmans smoker’s lounge. Those walls are also festooned with Mustafa’s childhood photos, including one of his mum as a waitress in a long-gone restaurant.
The menu, meanwhile, is soothing, filling and hearty, with all manner of Turkish favourites. There’s girit ezme, or white cheese with walnut, dill and mint, and sigara boregi (feta rolled up in yufka pastry and deep-fried). There’s a grill, too, of course, blasting out the fragrant smells of beef and lamb köfte and tavuk şiş (chicken thigh kebab). The cooking leans heavily, if not decadently, on lashings of strained yoghurt, chilli butter, good olive oil and tahini – six of the nine cold meze are built on one or other of them. But don’t expect a great deal of spicy heat because this is more about comfort and coddling. Kick back with a basket of warm, pillowy bread that’s begging to be pulled through some atom (strained yoghurt) in a red pool of chilli butter.
In fact, that very humble-sounding atom with bread might well be one of the best things being served anywhere in Borough Market right now. I ate two whole baskets to myself, which finally killed off my ambition to be Victoria’s Secret’s most elderly thong model. Damn it, give me warm carbs. We ate monkfish straight off the mangal, which at £30 is the most expensive dish on the menu (the meze start at £6). To begin with, I was a little concerned that we’d never finish it and it would be a huge waste of fish, but no, it’s properly great: expertly grilled, succulent, and served with yet more yoghurt and chilli butter. The lamb neck kuzu şiş was likewise incredibly juicy, and we ate it with hand-cut fried potatoes that were unmistakably shallow-fried – proper staying-at-your-gran’s-house chips. Braised green beans were soft but fibrous, beautifully seasoned and the sort of beans that make you want to sell your house and move to the sun whenever you’re on holiday. A £14 plate of fried liver with onion salad lent some iron to proceedings, with a side of velvety and not-remotely bitter braised swiss chard.
Over tiny glasses of tea and glossy, teeth-chatteringly sweet pistachio baklava, we picked at a pistachio ice-cream that was much, much less sweet than the pastries, and therefore balanced them beautifully. You must order both, and we asked for the bill without an ounce of regret for our overindulgence.
 Kismet will not make my confused definition of a meyhane any easier, nor will the Turkish-Cypriot community be in full agreement over whether it’s at all like one in Istanbul, either. What’s undeniable, however, is that Mustafa and Hamdy have come up with something that’s unique in its own right: the first genuinely cool, weird thing to have happened in Borough for ages. They’re only signed up to be here for a year, so go before that telly gets turned off.
- 
  Kismet Upstairs at The Globe Tavern, 8 Bedale Street, London SE1 (no phone). Open lunch Weds-Sun noon-2.30pm (3pm Sun); dinner Tues-Sat 5-10pm (9.30pm Tues & Weds). From about £40 a head à la carte, plus drinks and service

The president and the penthouse: how Madrid’s government spent €6.3m on a temporary ‘office’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
05:00:48 UTC
14:00:48 KST

The outspoken rightwing leader of the Madrid region is under growing pressure to explain why her government spent €6.3m (£5.4m) on a residential penthouse purportedly to serve as a temporary workspace while her offices were being renovated.
Isabel Díaz Ayuso, a prominent member of Spain’s opposition conservative People’s party (PP), has been the president of the Madrid region since 2019.
In that time, she has forged a reputation as a politician who prides herself on speaking her mind – and on being a thorn in the side of the country’s socialist prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, whose family and government have been mired in graft allegations for the past two years.
Although Ayuso has frequently accused Sánchez and his Spanish Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE) of being corrupt, she and her administration now face growing calls to provide a transparent explanation for the purchase of the penthouse.
El País reported at the end of July that the Madrid regional government had bought the penthouse in the well-heeled Chamberí neighbourhood of the Spanish capital in April. A spokesperson told the paper the property had been acquired for Ayuso to use while her offices in the Real Casa de Correos – the seat of the regional government – were being renovated. The spokesperson did not respond to questions about the price of the flat, nor whether Ayuso intended to live in it.
It later emerged that the flat cost €6.3m and planning laws meant it could only be used for residential purposes, not as an office. El País reported this week that Ayuso’s government had stipulated that the property it wanted should be “between 250 and 400 square metres and have a large terrace” – the latter being an odd requirement for an office.
The Madrid president lives with her partner, Alberto González Amador, a businessman who recently put two of the flats they have shared up for sale. González Amador is awaiting trial on charges of tax fraud and falsifying documents. He denies the charges.
Ayuso initially dismissed the revelations as a “smear campaign”, insisting the penthouse was not bought for her to live in but as a venue for “institutional meetings”. She also said she hadn’t had “the faintest idea” about the purchase.
The regional government has subsequently announced that the flat will be sold and the proceeds donated to the victims of this summer’s wildfires near Madrid.
Ayuso recently told reporters she considered the matter closed, saying in her trademark colourful language: “Está en venta, chao pescao”, which roughly translates as: “It’s up for sale, so see you later, alligator”.
The soundbite has elicited comparisons with the time she was caught in congress describing Sánchez as a “hijo de puta” (“son of a bitch”), only to claim she had been misheard and had actually said: “Me gusta la fruta” (“I like fruit”). It has become one of her most well-known pronouncements, along with her electoral slogan of “communism or freedom”.
However, the row over the flat refuses to die down. A judge in Madrid is investigating five separate complaints relating to its purchase and Ayuso’s own boss has said there were still questions to answer. In an interview last week, the PP leader, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, said that while he was satisfied with her explanations, the relevant department in the regional government “ought to explain why a property that can’t be used as an office was bought”.
Feijóo said Ayuso’s team had told him in April that they were looking for temporary offices. That acknowledgment appears to be at odds with Ayuso’s insistence she was ignorant of the purchase.
Her opponents have seized on the row, with the central government dismissing her explanations as “patently insufficient and patently worrying”, and calling for her to resign.
“So they were looking for ‘temporary offices’ and they got in touch with an estate agent who specialises in luxury properties (not offices) and they requested something that was between 250 square metres and 400 square metres and which had that vital feature any administrative office requires – a big terrace,” said one PSOE councillor in the Madrid town of Móstoles. “See you later, alligator … but with a terrace.”
Pablo Simón, a political scientist at the Carlos III University of Madrid, said the “lack of clear explanations” over the purchase, combined with the judge’s investigation, had left Ayuso in a difficult predicament.
“From a political perspective, I think this has hurt her, because ultimately it’s a very cross-cutting issue that has generated criticism from both the left and the right,” he said.
Simón said while the current “wear and tear” was unlikely to prevent Ayuso winning another term at next year’s regional election, it could result in the loss of her absolute majority and force her to strike a deal with the far-right Vox party to remain in government.

Arms and the £5m man: Farage megadonor Christopher Harborne’s military empire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
05:00:47 UTC
14:00:47 KST

As he struggles with questions about the millions he has received from the billionaire Christopher Harborne, Nigel Farage has made no secret of his enthusiastic support for the industry that made part of his benefactor’s fortune – cryptocurrency. The Reform UK leader even urged the governor of the Bank of England to drop a crypto policy that may be costly for Harborne.
But another element of Harborne’s business interests could prove still more consequential if it shapes Farage’s positions. There appears to be no precedent for a major UK donor who is so entwined with the military.
The Guardian’s ongoing investigation into the origins of Harborne’s riches and whether his donations inform Farage’s agenda has established the Thailand-based tycoon’s global web of commercial interests in the arms industry and military contracts. Among Harborne’s business collaborators are a striking number of former army officers, air force pilots, military officials and even, it seems, a former MI6 officer.
Described by his lawyers as an “intensely private” man, Harborne’s military interests reveal another side to the proprietor of a wellness sanctuary on a paradise island off Thailand.
A businessman who works with Harborne’s jet fuel venture describes it as a top supplier to US military operations worldwide, “strengthened by former US Department of Defense specialists and retired US military pilots, bringing decades of operational and strategic expertise to every mission”.
And Harborne is the biggest shareholder in what was once the research arm of the UK military, now a private company developing autonomous weapons.
At a moment when one of the biggest questions political leaders face is how much of the state’s resources to divert to military spending, Farage’s reliance on Harborne’s money presents a potential conflict of interest. Harborne has given Reform two-thirds of its funding, plus a £5m undeclared gift to Farage that the MPs’ watchdog is investigating.
Sam Power, a political funding expert at the University of Bristol, said: “It doesn’t necessarily follow that Reform will have policies that will benefit Harborne’s interests in the military-industrial complex. But it warrants a spotlight. It will be interesting if Reform’s policies start aligning with Christopher Harborne in this area as they have in cryptocurrency.”
Harborne’s lawyers at the London firm Schillings said: “The policies or positions Mr Farage may choose to adopt are a matter for Mr Farage and the Reform party. Our client’s commercial interests are unconnected in any way whatsoever with his political affiliations.”
Harborne’s military beginnings
After private school, Cambridge and stints at the McKinsey management consultancy and PepsiCo, Harborne moved to Thailand in the 1990s, made money in the markets, and set up on his own.
In 2006, he loaned £1.6m to a company called Subsea Resources, whose deep-sea operations were designed to salvage metal and artefacts from sunken shipwrecks and retrieve lost aircraft for governments. His loans “were made on an informal basis without legal documentation”, the company’s filing says, and he then exchanged them for shares, becoming a director in December 2006.
Subsea Resources only had five directors. Another, who joined on the same day as Harborne, was David Charters. His official filing said he was a Foreign Office veteran. That styling is frequently used for those who were, in fact, officers of the UK’s Secret Intelligence Service, or MI6. A description of Charters at a security conference years later called him “a former MI6 intelligence officer”.
That was not Subsea Resources’ only apparent connection to the UK’s defence establishment. When Harborne gave up his board seat months later, his replacement was Tim McClement, a recently retired Royal Navy vice-admiral whose exploits included sinking the Belgrano while a submariner in the Falklands war.
Harborne was at the time setting up a venture of his own, AML Global, which has become a major military contractor. At the outset, there were connections to the armed forces, Thai corporate documents indicate. A fellow British director of a company that would go on to be part of AML Global, Arthur Napolitano, had proceeded from officer training at Sandhurst to the Queen’s Dragoon Guards. He later served in the Sultan of Oman’s land forces, a corporate biography says.
The new venture was close to Harborne’s heart. “Many of his business activities and investments flow from his passion for aviation,” say lawyers for Harborne, a licensed pilot who once crashed a light aircraft in residential Hampshire. AML Global is one of them. It brokers jet fuel, arranging for supplies to reach clients on whatever far-flung tarmac they wish to fill up their private jets.
AML sourced fuel in North America, Europe, Asia and Russia, according to a 2006 article in the industry press. It has, Harborne’s lawyers say, “grown into a worldwide leader in its industry with a comprehensive fuel supply network that maintains over 1,200 locations worldwide”. They add that AML Global no longer arranges the supply of jet fuel produced in Russia.
At first, the clients were civilians. In time, AML Global started to supply the organisation that consumes more fossil fuels than any other: the American military.
AML Global Pentagon contracts
The LinkedIn profile for Scott Elder, AML Global’s vice-president, records that he was a colonel in the US air force. Another entry on an earlier profile said he worked at the US embassy in Bangkok from 1996 (the year Harborne arrived) to 2011 (the year Harborne took Thai citizenship), and was a “host nation liaison” for the Pentagon.
Shortly after his time with the US government appears to have ended, Elder joined AML Global, and by the following year, 2013, AML Global was receiving Pentagon contracts for jet fuel. They started with $4,000 for a shipment to the Philippines and stayed small for years.
In 2017, Elder told his school alumni newsletter he had “decided to quit his day job and dedicate his life to the study of the Champa Kingdom (Vietnam)”. But instead he stuck with Harborne, and AML Global’s military income boomed.
Late in Donald Trump’s first term, AML Global’s US military contracts started to surge, reaching tens of millions annually. They total more than $140m in the years since, according to published US government data.
While AML Global issues few statements, publicity material by its Northern Irish partner, Jet Assist, says no other company supplies the US military with jet fuel in more places beyond its borders – 62 by the end of 2025. The material trumpeted AML Global’s recruitment of US military personnel and envisaged its role in “future US, UK and allied military deployments into Europe”.
AML Global’s $140m from the Pentagon may not be a big share of the billions it spends each year on fuel but Harborne is trusted to supply the American armed forces in strategic locations, from Europe’s frontier with Russia, to the Middle East, a South Pacific outpost and Asian allies threatened by China.
“The government vets these companies,” says Jerry McGinn, a military procurement expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies thinktank in Washington. “They take this very seriously.”
According to documents obtained by the International Consortium of Investigative Journalists, bankers filed an alert with US authorities in 2014 saying they had been “unable to identify the economic, business or lawful purpose” for large payments Harborne made related to crypto dealings under his Thai name, Chakrit Sakunkrit. But such suspicious activity reports are evidence of concern, not wrongdoing. Harborne denies any, and the Pentagon evidently sees him as a trusted supplier.
A growing stake in Britain’s defence industry
In the UK’s military-industrial base, Harborne occupies an even more sensitive position – one he has expanded dramatically since becoming an influential donor.
In 2022, while he was solidifying his position as one of the most influential political financiers by following his payments to Farage’s party with others to Boris Johnson’s Conservatives, he started building a stake in QinetiQ.
QinetiQ used to be the Ministry of Defence’s research arm. It was privatised under Tony Blair and, under MoD contracts, remains integral to the UK’s war-fighting capabilities. It runs Hebridean missile-launch sites, develops stealth capabilities for nuclear submarines, maintains the Royal Air Force’s Typhoon fighter jets, and is building the drones and robots that are redefining warfare.
Harborne, whose ancestor RC Sherriff feted the invention of the bouncing bomb in his wartime drama The Dam Busters, is now QinetiQ’s biggest shareholder, with a 15% stake worth about £400m. And his military tech investments have been proliferating.
In March, he bought a stake in a company set up by a former Royal Marines reservist to develop “Iron Man” suits for combatants. That came after he acquired shares in a rival to Starlink, the satellite service that has given Elon Musk the power to influence the course of conflicts such as Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
And Harborne’s military connections are not confined to the west. They appear to extend to Thailand, which granted him citizenship in 2011 and whose armed forces loom over civilian life.
Paul Chambers, a leading expert on the Thai military who left the country last year under pressure from the army, says Harborne maintains a business relationship with the armed forces there through AML Global and Sherriff Global Group, which appears to run Harborne’s fleet of private jets.
“The Royal Thai Air Force interacts with these firms for global logistical support, international flight operations, and overall air transport administration,” says Chambers, now a lecturer at the University of Oklahoma. Neither Harborne’s lawyers nor the Thai air force answered questions about this.
Donations and Reform’s defence policy
Harborne has lately begun to intervene personally in the big military questions of the day.
Last year, the Guardian revealed that he accompanied Johnson on a September 2023 visit to Ukraine after giving the former Tory prime minister £1m. Jamie Shawyer, a Gulfstream pilot who has worked on Harborne’s aviation ventures for 20 years, appears to have flown the pair to Poland, from where they proceeded overland to Kyiv.
Harborne later said in an interview with the Daily Telegraph that Johnson arranged for him to meet Volodymyr Zelenskyy and that he told Ukraine’s president: “I’m absolutely passionate that Europe has to defend itself.”
By June 2024, when Reform launched its general election manifesto, Harborne had switched his largesse back to Farage, handing him a £5m gift. Both insist it was “unconditional”, and Farage decided he did not need to declare it after he won a seat.
The manifesto committed Reform to increasing defence spending and to introducing “incentives and tax breaks to boost the UK defence industry”. It said it would “improve equipment self-sufficiency and manufacture world-class products for export”, and set up a “Joint Acquisition Corp” that would “ensure world-class procurement”.
These policies seem likely to benefit QinetiQ and perhaps other Harborne military interests.
Farage says Harborne asks for nothing in exchange for his donations. Yet just as Farage has championed Tether, the crypto firm Harborne part-owns, he has saluted his benefactor’s military interests.
“Christopher Harborne is an immensely successful man,” Farage told the Triggernometry podcast in July. “They all say crypto, but actually that is but a part of what this guy does. I think there are some things that are known in public, such as his big stake that he holds in QinetiQ, the defence technology company. I think he probably owns the biggest jet refuelling operation in the world, plus his crypto investments.”
And Farage has struck militaristic positions.
When Trump bombed Iran, he urged Keir Starmer to have British forces join the campaign.
After Trump expressed disquiet with British plans to give Mauritius control of the Chagos Islands, home to a US-UK military base, Farage boarded one of Harborne’s private jets and flew to the region in protest. Richard Tice, Reform’s deputy leader, has said his party would rip up the deal if it takes power.
A Reform spokesperson said Harborne had not discussed defence spending, defence policy or foreign policy with Farage or party officials and denied that its megadonor’s military business interests gave Reform a conflict of interest on defence spending policy.
Harborne’s lawyers added that he “has not sought to influence any politician to support any of his commercial business interests”.

‘You’re at war when you get attacked’: Mark Carney shows combative nature in face-off with Trump
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
05:00:46 UTC
14:00:46 KST

Mark Carney stood before a walnut-veneered lectern, his face drawn tight, as he announced that talks with Canada’s biggest trading partner had collapsed. “Last spring, I warned that America is trying to break us so that they can own us,” he said. “And I promised: that will never, ever happen. We are keeping that promise.”
For years, the former central bank governor had worked hard to calm markets. Now, he was asking Canadians to accept uncertainty and confrontation.
Near the end of the press conference last Saturday, a reporter made reference to the sombre, combative tone of the speech: “Why does it feel like today Mark Carney is going to war?”
The prime minister paused.
“We were attacked. You’re at war when you get attacked,” he said. “We got attacked.”
The unlikely transformation of an economist and central banker with no prior electoral experience into a powerful global politician has bucked precedent and expectations. But Carney has settled into the role he warned was necessary for the country, that of a wartime leader standing up to an erratic and vindictive adversary who seems hellbent on subjugating Canada.
After trade negotiations with the US broke down, the two sides traded recriminations and made good on threats to impose new tariffs on each other. In his latest act of petty antagonism, Trump signed an executive order on Thursday directing the US federal government to rename Lake Ontario as “Lake America”.
But Carney, in walking away from the proposed deal, did what few other leaders have done: dared Trump and the US to test his nation’s resolve.
“We cannot accept what they have offered, and we will not give what they have asked,” he said.
‘He was pretty doggedly determined’
For those who have worked with the demanding – and, at times, temperamental – central banker, such a calculated refusal to accede to a bad deal comes as little surprise.
Carney was raised in Canada’s western prairies, and his story – of an outsider gradually working his way into, and eventually reshaping, powerful institutions – offers clues to a man unwilling to accept the terms set by others.
“He was pretty doggedly determined,” said one person who worked alongside Carney when he was serving as UN special envoy for climate action in 2021.
When trying to convince banks to sign up to climate pledges, Carney could turn on the charm. “He was pretty diplomatic, when dealing with people that he knows he’s got to influence,” his former colleague said.
But it has been no shock to see Carney standing up to Trump on the world stage. “It doesn’t surprise me … and I think it’s because of that determination and that unwillingness to back down.”
Carney was not always so sure-footed. When he was handpicked as governor of the Bank of England in 2013 by the then UK chancellor, George Osborne, Carney’s hard-driving approach was not a natural fit with the venerable institution in London’s Square Mile. When he arrived, it still had pink-uniformed, top hatted guards at the entrance.
The traits acquired during his days at Goldman Sachs have continued into his tenure as prime minister. He remains an early riser, a dedicated runner and demands that ministers know their files front to back, according to those who work with him. Media have also reported that staff are expected to dress in formal business attire and documents are to be written using British spelling – to the frustration of Canadian linguists.
While Carney’s career in a string of powerful institutions reflects a sharp, analytical mind, his tenure at the Bank of England telegraphed that the wonkish economist was also willing to become political when necessary.
When Carney overhauled the Bank’s communications strategy, introducing “forward guidance” to show its thinking about future interest rates, it was not immediately embraced as a success.
The senior Labour MP Pat McFadden – now a cabinet minister – accused the Bank under Carney of baffling investors and the public with mixed messages about the future of interest rates.
In October 2015, with the referendum looming on whether Britain should leave the European Union, Carney used a speech at Oxford University to underline the benefits to the UK of the “economic and financial openness” that came with membership.
With the eurozone debt crisis a recent memory, Carney also highlighted the increased risk of financial instability that membership of the EU implied; but Brexiters seized on his positive comments as an unwarranted intervention in a highly politicised topic.
The row deepened when Carney suggested Brexit might plunge the UK into recession. Bernard Jenkin, the Conservative director of the leave campaign wrote to the governor, urging him to butt out.
Carney’s reply displayed the same relish for a fight that has been evident in his handling of Trump. “Dear Mr Jenkin,” his letter began, “I am responding to your letter to dispel immediately the numerous and substantial misconceptions it contained.” He went on to accuse the veteran MP of “a fundamental misunderstanding of central bank independence as enshrined in statute”.
In the event, there was no Brexit recession, something many economists attributed partly to the Bank’s robust response, including rapid interest rate cuts and quantitative easing (the emergency bond-buying scheme used during the global financial crisis).
Charles Randell spent five years on the board of the Prudential Regulation Authority, which Carney chaired after becoming Bank of England governor. “I’m sure if you ring around enough people who worked with him at the Bank, you’ll find people who will say that he had his shortcomings,” Randall said. “But with time to reflect on my experience … he’s one of the most impressive people I’ve ever worked with.”
Randell, who was then the chair of the Financial Conduct Authority, said that even behind the scenes, Carney was a “very serious person, very analytical, very driven” and “very careful about how he communicates”.
“On the morning after the Brexit vote in 2016 … he went in front of the cameras to reassure financial markets that the Bank was ready to deal with any of the consequences of that decision,” he said. “It was a masterpiece in strategic messaging.”
‘Compliance will not buy safety’
Joseph Steinberg, a professor of economics at the University of Toronto, said that while during the Brexit debate, Carney “did not shy away from trying to tell kind of the hard economic truths”, he had not spoken much about the economics of the current US trade war.
“In public, he is leaning pretty heavily on the sovereignty angle. It is clear that he privately is probably thinking about the cold, hard economics of an incredibly tenuous situation.”
Carney’s decision to retaliate against the US has caused some economists, including Steinberg, to point out that Canada will take a far more painful blow than the US.
For the first time in his career Carney is fully beholden to a wary public, a reality that underscores the clashing of two personalities: the technocrat who understands the economics, and the politician who must contend with the political costs of compromise.
“At the moment, Canadians are likely to be extraordinarily intolerant of making any kind of concessions to the US whatsoever, even if they are in our economic best interest,” he said.
In January, Carney warned people at Davos that “compliance will not buy safety” in a world increasingly dominated by hegemonic powers. While it never mentioned Trump, his speech was seen as a thinly veiled critique of the US president’s aim to abandon longstanding alliances and reshape the world to his advantage.
One of Carney’s prescriptions – forging deep relations with like-minded “middle powers” and restructuring to lessen reliance on former allies – has already taken shape in Canada, at a speed and degree to which the pollster David Coletto described as a “wartime-footing government without a war”.
“It’s a government organised around an external threat that’s willing to suspend its own party’s orthodoxies, centralise power to move fast, and measure itself in outcomes rather than values,” he wrote.
Carney abandoned many of the policies of his predecessor Justin Trudeau, including his carbon and electric vehicle mandates. He has also fast-tracked large projects, including an oil pipeline, and invested tens of billions more into defence.
“The public has hardly blinked,” Coletto said in an interview. “Mark Carney’s approval rating has just sustained itself through this entire period.”
“When [Carney] first became prime minister, I was sceptical that a central banker would be able to respond to public opinion because that is the opposite of their job,” he said. “But I’ve been surprised with his nuanced read of the country. He’s been adept at being not just politically effective but in holding his support together through a trying time. This suggests there’s little value in underestimating his political instincts.”
Polling shows that Carney remains the leader Canadians trust most to steer the country through economic uncertainty. But the prime minister has also embraced a role that would once have seemed almost incongruous: asking a country vastly smaller and less powerful than its neighbour to stand its ground.
He said in his recent address: “Canadians don’t submit to the weather – we thrive in it. We don’t wait to see which way the wind is blowing. Or surrender ourselves to the waves to be storm-tossed by events.
“We set our own course. We make our own weather. In Canada, we are masters in our own home, from coast to coast to coast.”

Which cities are the most expensive to buy an apartment in Europe?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
05:00:43 UTC
14:00:43 KST

The price per square metre of buying an apartment in city centres differs widely across Europe. Among the five largest European economies, only two have their capital cities in the top 10 most expensive list.
Housing is a major issue across Europe. The problem is not just availability, but affordability too, with housing being particularly expensive in capital cities, major urban areas and tourist destinations.
House prices and rents vary significantly across Europe. So, which countries and cities are the most expensive for buying a house or flat in 2026? How much does a square metre cost? And how much is needed to buy an apartment in a city centre?
The "Mapping the World’s Prices 2026" report, published by Deutsche Bank Research Institute, compares the price per square metre of buying an apartment in the city centre across 69 cities, 28 of them in Europe.
Switzerland is the most expensive country to buy a house
Two Swiss cities rank at the top, making Switzerland the most expensive country to buy real estate in city centres. The price per square metre for an apartment is €22,910 in Zurich and €19,439 in Geneva.
For an 80-square-metre apartment, that would mean a price of around €1,833,000 in Zurich and €1,555,000 in Geneva.
London ranks third at €17,241 (£14,782) per square metre. So, an apartment of this size would cost around €1,379,000, or £1,183,000.
London is 35% more expensive than Paris
While Paris comes next, real estate in the French capital is comparatively cheaper than in London. The price per square metre is €12,771. Buying an apartment in London city centre is around 35% more expensive than in Paris.
Vienna completes the top five, with a price of €12,483 per square metre.
Only two cities in the top five are from Europe’s largest economies: London in the UK and Paris in France.
The most expensive city in Germany is Munich at €11,435 per square metre.
Luxembourg (€11,011), Copenhagen (€10,191), Stockholm (€10,037) and Oslo (€9,785) are also in the top 10. The price falls below the €10,000 mark in the Norwegian capital.
Three Nordic cities are in the top 10 while Helsinki ranks 13th at €8,431 per square metre.
Milan and Amsterdam are just above the Finnish capital at €9,378 and €9,273 per square metre respectively.
Prague is pricier than Madrid and Berlin
Prague is more expensive than the Spanish and German capitals. The price per square metre to buy an apartment in the city centre is €8,352.
This compares with €7,831 in Madrid and €7,613 in Berlin. Rome follows at €7,328 per square metre.
It is still above 7,000 levels in Dublin (€7,185) and Frankfurt (€7,162)while it is over 6,000 in Lisbon (€6,636) and Barcelona (€6,485).
Cheapest cities: Istanbul and Athens
Istanbul is the cheapest European city on the list at €2,646 per square metre, followed by the capital of neighbouring Greece, Athens, at €3,442.
Brussels, the EU capital, is also among the cheapest cities, ranking third from the bottom. The price per square metre to buy an apartment there is €4,380.
Birmingham in the UK (€4,671) is also below the €5,000 mark, while Budapest (€5,243), Warsaw (€5,443) and Edinburgh (€5,708) are above this level.
The simple average across the 28 cities is €9,090 per square metre.
Based on this, the cost of an 80-square-metre apartment exceeds €1 million in only four cities. Zurich is actually close to €2 million, while Geneva is above €1.5 million.
The average price for an 80-square-metre apartment across the list would be around €727,000.
Hong Kong is the most expensive, Cairo the cheapest
Among all 69 cities in the report, Hong Kong is the most expensive, at €23,790 per square metre, followed by Zurich (€22,910) and Seoul (€21,897).
The cheapest cities are Cairo (€784) and Johannesburg (€913), both below the €1,000 mark.
The figures in the report are based on data from Numbeo and Deutsche Bank. They were converted into euros using the ECB’s average exchange rates for the first half of 2026.

Europe’s scorching summer has ‘charged’ the Mediterranean Sea. What weather will September bring?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
05:00:25 UTC
14:00:25 KST

Weather forecasters have warned that parts of Europe will be entering “flash-flood season” following a blistering summer.
Europe’s blistering summer was a “grim illustration” of human-caused climate change.
That’s what the European Commission said in June, when much of the continent was already baking under its third heatwave of the year.
July and August provided little relief, bringing with them extreme heat scientists say would have been “virtually impossible” if it weren’t for the burning of fossil fuels.
Scorching temperatures and scant rainfall cast huge swathes of Europe into drought, paving the way for deadly wildfires that ravaged Spain, Portugal, France, Greece and Türkiye – burning thousands of hectares and resulting in the biggest evacuation effort since the Second World War.
But with September just around the corner, are things finally about to cool down?
Europe’s September weather outlook
Data from global weather forecasting platform WFY24 shows that the first week of September will stay warm across the Mediterranean, with daily highs averaging around 35°C in Rome, 34°C in Athens and 33°C in Madrid.
That’s around 6-8°C above the seasonal average for early September, suggesting that Europe’s extreme summers are starting to expand.
However, Northern Europe is showing much more “cool and unsettled” conditions, with highs of just 21°C in Berlin and 20°C in London. Heavy rain and thunderstorms have already broken the heat and quenched parched soils in parts of the UK, Germany and France.
But the Mediterranean is in for the steepest increase in rainfall.
“September and October are the Mediterranean’s flash-flood season: the sea is at its annual warmest after three months of heating and the first cold troughs arrive overhead,” Ioanna Vergini, founder of WFY24 tells Euronews Earth.
The contrast, she explains, spins up the destructive weather system known in Spain as a DANA (Depresión Aislada en Niveles) – a high-altitude isolated depression or ‘cold drop’..
“That’s what produced Valencia’s deadly floods in October 2024 and Genoa’s repeat events,” Vergini adds. “A hot summer loads it, because the sea is the fuel and it has spent the summer charging.”
Every year, rainfall in Valencia rises from an average of 18mm in August to 47mm in September. It’s the same in Palma (21mm to 55mm) and Palermo (15mm to 42mm), while northern European cities like Berlin, Warsaw and Stockholm tend to experience slightly less rain in September than August. These figures are based on normal seasonal averages, however, and not a weather forecast.
Will El Niño hit Europe this September?
Media coverage on the weather is currently being dominated by El Niño, which experts have warned could be the “strongest in living history” this year.
The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) warns that the weather phenomenon, which occurs when sea temperatures in the Eastern Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, continues to “intensify steadily” and is expected to “dominate climate patterns” over the next couple of months.
El Niño events push up global temperatures, paving the way for more frequent bouts of extreme weather. However, these effects are mainly felt in the tropics.
South America, the southern US, East Africa and Central Asia have all experienced increased flood risks during previous El Niños, while droughts and wildfire risk rises across parts of Australia, northern parts of South America and in certain Asian countries like Indonesia.
Despite reports linking Europe’s scorching summer to this year’s El Niño, experts have reiterated the fact that climate change is to blame.
“This summer we have experienced heatwaves across Europe reminding us of the effects of climate change,” says Professor Stephen Belcher, the UK Met Office’s Chief of Science and Technology.
“This large El Niño is a reminder that natural variations in the climate system are also at play, adding to the stresses of climate change.”
In Europe, El Niño’s impacts are much more indirect and tend to be less severe.
According to the UK Met office, the influence of El Niño may start to increase the chances of “wetter, stormier conditions” for northwest Europe in the coming autumn and early winter.
The European Commission states that an El Niño could also make Europe’s autumn temperatures “warmer-than-normal”, with that warmth building towards next spring. It’s why scientists fear that 2027 is gearing up to be the hottest year globally on record.

Events in Qatar worth travelling for: What’s coming up in 2026-2027?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
05:00:08 UTC
14:00:08 KST

From music concerts and motorsport to cultural festivals and design exhibitions, here’s what’s on the Qatar calendar this autumn and winter.
Qatar’s calendar is action-packed with concerts, motorsport, football and cultural festivals among the highlights in Doha and beyond between September 2026 and March 2027.
The FIFA Under-17 World Cup will return to the Gulf nation, alongside the Formula 1 Qatar Airways Qatar Grand Prix, the MotoGP Qatar Airways Grand Prix and live performances from global stars including John Legend and Hans Zimmer.
The season will also include heritage exhibitions, design showcases and food festivals.
Here are the key events taking place in Qatar this autumn and winter...
8-12 September 2026: S'hail – Katara International Hunting & Falcons Exhibition
The 10th edition of S'hail, the Katara International Hunting and Falcons Exhibition, will take place at Katara Cultural Village. The event brings together falconry and hunting specialists, outdoor equipment brands and Qatari heritage groups.
Since launching in 2017, it has grown into a regional showcase, now drawing more than 260 exhibitors from more than 20 countries.
The exhibition includes falcon auctions, live demonstrations and workshops on falconry heritage.
10 September 2026: John Legend live
Award-winning singer-songwriter John Legend will perform at the Qatar National Convention Centre (QNCC) in Doha.
Known for hits including "All of Me" and "Ordinary People”, Legend has built a career spanning soul, gospel and pop over two decades.
He is a 13-time Grammy winner and one of the few artists to achieve “EGOT” status for winning Emmy, Grammy, Oscar, and Tony awards.
Titled "An Evening of Songs & Stories”, the show will feature stripped-back renditions of his hits. Tickets start from QAR195 (€46).
28 September to 3 October 2026: Doha Jewellery and Watches Exhibition
Organised by Qatar Tourism and Visit Qatar, the Doha Jewellery and Watches Exhibition (DJWE) is set to take place at the Doha Exhibition and Convention Centre (DECC).
Spanning more than 33,000 square metres, the event typically draws around 30,000 visitors from more than 175 countries.
DJWE brings together leading local and international jewellery and watch brands, alongside talks, workshops and networking sessions for industry professionals. Admission is free.
16 October 2026: Angham live in Doha
Egyptian singer Angham, known as "the Voice of Egypt”, will perform at Al Mayassa Theatre, part of the Qatar National Convention Centre (QNCC).
She has built a career in Arabic-language pop spanning nearly four decades, with hits including "Sidi Wesalak" and "Omry Maak”.
Her 2007 album "Kolma N'arrab" sold more than 500,000 copies across the Middle East, earning platinum certification. And in 2025, she became the first Egyptian female artist to perform at London's Royal Albert Hall.
4-7 November 2026: Qatar Boat Show
The third edition of the Qatar Boat Show will be held at Old Doha Port, featuring superyachts and displays from marine brands.
Launched in 2024, the event's most recent edition drew more than 27,000 visitors from 105 countries and showcased more than 65 boats and marine vessels worth a combined QAR880 million (€207.2 million).
The show also features watersports and activities including jet skiing, kite surfing and paddleboarding.
5 November 2026 to 31 January 2027: Design Doha Biennial
The second edition of Design Doha, a design biennial for the MENASA region, will be held at venues across Qatar’s capital.
The event includes exhibitions, talks and installations in 16 design disciplines, from architecture to textiles and crafts.
Its headline exhibition, "Arab Design Now", will be curated by Noura Al Sayeh and feature work from 81 designers.
The Design Doha Prize will also be awarded, recognising work across four categories: craft, product design, furniture design and emerging talent.
6 November 2026: Hans Zimmer live
The celebrated German film composer and music producer is set to perform "Hans Zimmer Live: The Next Level" at the 974 Stadium Precinct in Doha.
Known for scores including "The Lion King", "Gladiator", "Inception", "Interstellar" and "Dune", Zimmer has composed music for more than 150 films and other productions. He has also won two Academy Awards, five Grammys and three Golden Globes.
The show features Zimmer performing with a 19-piece band. Tickets start from QAR95 (€23).
6-8 November 2026: MotoGP Qatar Airways Grand Prix
The MotoGP Qatar Airways Grand Prix returns to Lusail International Circuit in November. The circuit hosted its first MotoGP race in 2004, while Qatar became the championship's first night race when the grand prix was held under floodlights in 2008. A three-day adult ticket costs QAR200 (€48).
19 November to 13 December 2026: FIFA Under-17 World Cup
Qatar will again host the FIFA U-17 World Cup, the second of five consecutive editions awarded to the country between 2025 and 2029.
Showcasing the future stars of world football, the tournament features 48 national teams after the format expanded for the first time in 2025.
Matches will take place across venues in the Aspire Zone Competition Complex, with the final staged at Khalifa International Stadium.
The 2025 edition drew more than 100,000 spectators, with Portugal beating Austria 1-0 in the final.
27-29 November 2026: Formula 1 Qatar Airways Qatar Grand Prix
Lusail International Circuit will host the Formula 1 Qatar Airways Qatar Grand Prix, part of a 10-year agreement running from 2023 to 2032. Qatar first joined the Formula 1 calendar in 2021.
The 2025 edition drew an attendance of more than 162,000, and unlike previous years, the 2026 weekend will not include a Sprint format. General admission tickets start from QAR600 (€144).
18 December 2026: Qatar National Day
Qatar marks its National Day on 18 December, commemorating the country's unification under founder Sheikh Jassim bin Mohammed Al Thani in 1878. The day was established as an annual public holiday in 2007.
Celebrations traditionally include the Darb Al Saai heritage festival and events on the Doha Corniche, including military displays and fireworks. Entry to the festivities is free.
13-23 January 2027: Qatar International Food Festival
Qatar International Food Festival (QIFF) returns to Lusail Stadium Precinct, following its most attended edition yet in 2026, which drew 490,000 visitors over 10 days at 974 Stadium.
The 2026 edition featured 200 local vendors and 46 international vendors, alongside more than 50 chefs leading live cooking demonstrations and workshops.
The festival includes family-friendly attractions such as the "Dinner in the Sky" experience, suspended 40 metres above ground. Entry to the festival is free.
February 2027 (dates TBC): WTA and ATP tennis
Doha will host WTA and ATP tennis tournaments at the Khalifa International Tennis and Squash Complex, typically held in consecutive weeks each February.

Renovations threaten Kaunas’ beloved Courtyard Gallery
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Some of the artworks that make up Kaunas’ renowned Courtyard Gallery could disappear under a new layer of plaster and paint as renovation work begins on the building that houses them.
The gallery, located on Ožeškienės Street in central Kaunas, was launched 14 years ago by artist Vytenis Jakas. Its murals tell the story of the Jewish community that lived in the courtyard before World War Two.
Scaffolding now surrounds one of the gallery’s walls as preparations begin to renovate the building. Under the current plan, the murals will be covered.
“This is a heritage site that cannot be destroyed. This would be outright vandalism,” Jakas said.
The dispute escalated even before renovation work began. Police are investigating possible vandalism after witnesses reported seeing a resident of the building damaging the artworks with a hammer.
Kaunas resident Darius Pečiulionis said he saw a man striking the wall with a chisel and hammer.
“I approached him and asked, ‘Why did you do that?’ He said in broken Lithuanian, ‘I am a resident. I don’t like this. The renovation has to be done here,’” Pečiulionis said.
One of the damaged features was a QR code that provided information about the history depicted in the artwork in Lithuanian and English, Jakas said.
The Courtyard Gallery is one of Kaunas’ most visited attractions. Tour guide Nomeda Balasevičiūtė said visitors are often struck by the artwork.
“They are amazed. Everyone falls silent when they walk through here. They say they take photos, even people who don’t usually take photos in this courtyard,” she said.
Residents may be bothered by constant tourist flows taking snapshots, but numerous signs warn them to be quiet and respect people’s right to peace. By now, most of the locals have become accustomed to tourists visiting the courtyard and viewing the artworks.
Jakas says he has proposed a solution that would allow the renovation to proceed while preserving the murals. He offered to repair the lower section of the wall with murals himself, at no cost to the building's residents.
“I want to repair the entire lower part myself. We wouldn't take a single euro from them; they would save money,” he said.
The building is located in a cultural heritage zone, and the Kaunas municipality is helping finance part of the renovation. But the artworks on the building’s wall were never formally authorised, and the owners did not give their consent for them to be installed.
That leaves municipal officials with limited legal means to prevent their removal.
“We are all hostages of this situation. The paintings were installed without asking anyone, on the artist's initiative, so somehow we don’t have the instruments to protect them,” said Saulius Rimas, head of the Kaunas municipality's Heritage Protection Division.
At the same time, the municipality has acknowledged the value of the artworks.
“We have said that we see the meaning in these artworks. They are not bad,” Rimas said.
The municipality and the building’s administrator have suggested alternatives that would allow both the facade to be renovated and the artworks to be preserved. But the building’s owners have so far rejected them.
Two-thirds of the 13 owners have voted to renovate the entire wall, according to the building administrator.
“If there were other decisions, there would be other solutions. As things stand today, the solution is to repair the building’s facade without preserving the art installations,” said Marijus Zaborskas, head of Kaunas Butų Ūkis, the building administrator.
The renovation plan could still be changed if the residents approve an alternative, Zaborskas said. But time is running short: Work on the building’s facade and roof is scheduled to be completed in September.

WhatsApp chat used to launder cash for crime and extremism
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
05:59:56 BST
13:59:56 KST

WhatsApp chat used to launder cash for crime and extremism
- Published
A WhatsApp group chat was used to launder hundreds of millions of euros in cash around the world, funding organised crime and extremism with no paper trail, an investigation by European broadcasters has found.
The 532-member group chat, called "Traders of Greater Europe", was used to arrange cash transfers across borders for their clients, including to UK cities such as Birmingham and London.
In one case, payments from Brussels went to militants from the Islamic State group (IS) in Syria.
The European Broadcasting Union (EBU) investigative journalism network, external, which includes the BBC, also found wider evidence of similar cash transfer systems being used in people smuggling and drug trafficking.
The group chat, which contained more than 82,000 messages sent between late February and December 2022, was first uncovered by Belgian investigating magistrate Vincent Guerra. An investigating magistrate is a judge who examines evidence in complex cases before trial and makes a recommendation about whether they should proceed.
Guerra said the number of transactions was "staggering" and the network covered "the entire planet". The case began as an investigation into terror financing, but "it became just a drop in the ocean of transactions", he said.
Members of the group chat sent messages in Arabic to each other to set up cash payments using the ancient hawala transfer system. Hawala involves a network of trusted money brokers who can arrange for funds to be sent around the world without any electronic record or physical transport of bank notes.
The system involves an agreement between two brokers, known as hawaladars, in different locations. One of the hawaladars is paid a sum of cash and the other agrees to supply the same sum, minus commission, to the recipient. The hawaladars agree to settle up all their transactions between themselves at a later date.
Hawala transfers are frequently used for legitimate purposes, such as immigrant workers sending funds home to support their families in countries with limited access to banks.
But criminals can also take advantage of hawala transfers to avoid the Swift system used for most international money transfers, where banks typically flag large transactions outside the normal course of business and are required to report any suspicious activity.
The Traders of Greater Europe group was reserved for transactions over €5,000 (£4,279) and payments were often much larger. There is no indication that all those participating in the group were involved in handling criminal funds.
Hawala is illegal in many countries, including most of the EU, but is legal in the UK as long as the brokers are registered with Revenue and Customs (HMRC).
The cache of WhatsApp messages was obtained by the EBU following a 2024 court case in Belgium which convicted six money launderers, including Abu Adam, the head of the network in Brussels, and his number two, Abu Ahmed.
Belgian police had discovered evidence that the defendants had been sending money to IS, which was intended to help the wives of militants escape from detention camps in Syria. When they arrested Abu Adam, they discovered the Traders of Greater Europe group chat on his phone.
Guerra said it was like "hitting the jackpot", uncovering the inner workings of a vast, underground system. The phone also contained 6,000 photos of €5 notes showing the serial numbers and 6,000 photos of identity cards. These details are often used as unique identifying codes in hawala transactions, and the total number of notes and ID cards suggest Abu Adam had processed at least 12,000 transactions, Guerra said.
"This isn't just amateur work; it's professional, and at a level we could never have imagined," he said. "They're bankers with no government oversight."
The EBU also found further gangs across Europe using the hawala system for criminal activity. One former money launderer previously involved in European hawala networks, whom we are calling Frank, told the EBU he had been involved in transactions totalling several hundred million euros.
His first introduction to the hawala system had been at an office in a small town outside Rotterdam, he said. There, five or six messengers had arrived with money in about an hour and a half, transferring at least a million euros, he estimated.
"What I found out later is that it's not just about money. It's about the financing of terror. It's about drug trafficking. It's about prostitution and all sorts of other crap, to put it nicely," he said.
Cases in Austria have also revealed how the hawala system is bound up with people smuggling and violence.
In one case investigated by Austrian broadcaster ORF, part of the EBU network, Austrian police raided what they called "the biggest hawala office in Vienna". It was run from a kebab restaurant on a busy thoroughfare and which authorities say was used to make payments for people smuggling.
Two Syrian brothers who ran the operation were charged with human trafficking, as well as torturing and raping a courier who had lost €350,000 (£300,000), saying he had been robbed. They were convicted last year and sentenced to 18 and 8 years in prison respectively.
Austrian police and Europol also recently dismantled another people-smuggling ring financed through hawala, which officials said had transported about 100,000 people into Europe over 18 months.
Gerald Tatzgern, who leads human-trafficking investigations at Austria's Criminal Intelligence Service, the BK, told ORF that torture was a reality of people smuggling and was also used to maximise profits.
He said: "Videos of the torture are then sent to the families, saying that if they don't send another €1,000 or several thousand euros, then the person concerned - your son, your brother, your father - will suffer."
Payments to stop the torture were demanded through the hawala system, he said.
Police commander and Europol liaison officer Quentin Mugg, who has led a number of money-laundering investigations, said the hawala system was "the primary money-laundering channel for organised crime".
"Whether the money comes from migrant smuggling, human trafficking, pimping, a grandmother's savings sent as a birthday present to her son, or a Malian working in France who wants to support his family, [the hawaladars] couldn't care less," he said. "And they'll apply their rates."

Needle-toting cockroaches could be deployed by search-and-rescue teams for lifesaving injections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
04:51:53 UTC
13:51:53 KST

A swarm of giant cockroaches may sound like the stuff of nightmares, but Australian researchers say the insects could one day be used by search-and-rescue teams to deliver lifesaving drugs to people trapped after disasters.
Scientists from the University of Queensland and the University of New South Wales have developed paramedic cyborg cockroaches, dubbed "paraborgs," equipped with miniature injection devices and cameras.
They hope the insects could help keep victims of earthquakes and building collapses alive by providing basic medical assistance in narrow, debris-filled spaces before rescuers arrive.
"A lot of people might not like the sight of a giant cockroach scurrying towards them, but if you're trapped in rubble or stuck in a cave and need help, it could make a real difference between life and death," said PhD candidate Hai Nhan Le, co-author of the study published in the journal Advanced Science.
Research teams fitted North Queensland giant burrowing cockroaches, the heaviest cockroach species in the world that measure up to 8.5 centimeters, with backpacks containing syringe cylinders and cameras.
Scientists hijack cockroach nervous systems for steering
The study said the research went beyond earlier work on cyborg insects, which has focused only on using them to locate victims rather than treat them.
Researchers used real cockroaches because no robot could match their agility, resilience, and low power requirements.
Implanted electrodes let operators stimulate the insects' nervous systems and steer them.
"We start with anesthetizing the insect, immobilizing them so that we make sure that they cannot feel anything during the implementation process," said biorobotics engineer and study co-author Thang Vo-Doan.
"Once we implant an electrode into the insect, we can apply a small electrical signal to activate or stimulate the nerve system so that they can respond to our command."
The study used one "observer" cockroach equipped with a camera to locate targets for operators, and a second cockroach carrying the drugs to be remotely triggered.
The study recorded a 100% success rate in reaching designated checkpoints during tests and an overall drug-delivery success rate of 72%.
When the injection was launched from within 15 centimeters of a target, success rates rose to as high as 95%.
Swarms of cockroaches could aid in locating disaster victims
Such a system could eventually be used to stabilize victims in situations where minutes mattered, including snakebite emergencies and severe allergic reactions, the study said.
"In the future we want to have maybe a swarm of (cockroaches) go deep into collapsed structure... we need to have a network of many of them, so that we can easily find the victim as soon as possible," Vo-Doan said.
The experiments used silicone targets and pig skin under controlled laboratory conditions.
The study said further testing would be needed to address challenges operators would face in real-world applications, including complex terrain, signal loss in collapsed structures, and injection safety.
Ethical guidelines for research on insects are not yet standardized, but the cockroaches were kept in a "suitable living environment" and fed dry gum leaves and apples, the study said.

Seeing beyond the barriers and shapes, encouraging viewers to perceive space in the most unexpected places – that’s Noma Bar.
Born Avinoam Bernstein in 1973 in Afula, Bar is one of the world’s most awarded and recognized illustrators.
His distinctive visual language is known for its minimalism, use of negative space, humor, and bold flat colors. In his interview with the Magazine, to show an example of negative space, he picked up his phone and pointed out the space between his fingers and the phone.
Bar has been drawing since a young age, often weaving satire into his work. At age nine, he drew a picture of his rich neighbor with financial graphs instead of teeth.
At the age of 17, during the First Gulf War, sitting in a shelter and reading about Saddam Hussein and chemical weapons, he noticed a resemblance between the radiation symbol and Hussein’s face. He created his portrait. Years later, after graduating in visual communication from the Bezalel Academy of Arts and Design in Jerusalem and moving to London in 2000, he recreated this iconic image as a postcard. It opened the door to his career.
Over the past 25 years, his work has appeared on the covers of leading newspapers and magazines, including The New Yorker, The Guardian, The New York Times, The Economist, and Time Out. His illustrations have also appeared on the covers of best-selling novels by Margaret Atwood and Haruki Murakami, and anchored major campaigns for cultural institutions and global brands such as Apple, Coca-Cola, Mercedes-Benz, the Victoria and Albert Museum, and Netflix.
Throughout his career, he has also not shied away from addressing political issues and opinions; however, his solo exhibition in Tel Aviv, which opened on August 5, is not focused on this.
After spending half of his life in London, he brings a wide range of his works back to Israel, presenting illustrations, two- and three-dimensional prints, animation, sculpture, and installation in his first solo museum exhibition, “Look Again” (Hebrew name: “Mitzad sheni” [lit., From the Other Side]), at The Tel Aviv Museum of Art.
The exhibition attracts both adults and families with children.
How does it feel to show your art in Israel?
It’s exciting! It’s the first time seeing my work in Hebrew. I’ve seen it in English, French, German, Dutch, and Japanese, so suddenly seeing my work next to the Hebrew letters is amazing, and it’s good to be here.
“Mitzad Sheni” in Hebrew and “Look Again” in English, the exhibition (curated by Yuval Saar) at the Tel Aviv Museum of Art is your first solo museum exhibition, right?
I’ve participated in group exhibitions in various museums, but yes, this is the proper solo museum exhibition.
I’ve seen it twice now, and my initial thoughts were: first, the colors – they’re fun; and second, I felt a bit like I was taking a major psychological test. A Rorschach test, or looking at Edgar Rubin’s vase.
It also reminded me of the famous, ambiguous image of an old woman and a young woman from a 19th-century postcard, popularized in 1915 by William Ely Hill as “My Wife and My Mother-in-Law.” Later, this image was also used in psychology. Do you base your work on psychology?
No, it doesn’t come from there; it’s actually [rooted in] typography and negative space, a term in design and architecture. [Negative space] is the space between. Every architecture or design student studies it because it’s very important to understand the gap between buildings and how to make the most of space; for designers as well. In illustration, which is my area, you don’t see it a lot.
I’m coming from design, less from the Gestalt theories. But over the years, it really developed to that, without talking about the Rubin vase, that there is something there about two sides. I think it’s in my biography. Obviously, coming from here, from Afula, a place where Arabs and Jews live next to each other, had an impact.
You explore positive and negative space in your illustrations. Does it also relate to your life? You spent half of your life in Israel, and half in England. Which is the negative?
I don’t think it’s clear what’s positive or negative. I see them as two sides that complete each other, and when I’m here I miss there; when I’m there I miss here. I think it’s the constant striving for something or for an ideal place.
Yet back in Israel, you worked as a graphic designer at the Channel 2 news desk.
For two years, it was a part-time job, from 5 a.m. to 9 a.m. And afterward, I used to go to the Bezalel Academy. I learned a lot about how to work fast and how to work in journalism.
These tools helped me when I came to the UK to become an illustrator for a weekly column for The Guardian. Speed was necessary there.
What made you move to the UK?
When my wife and I were in our second year of studies (at Bezalel), [we visited London] and went to a shop in Covent Garden, a three-story bookshop dedicated solely to graphic design and illustration! We’d never seen anything like that. That was before the Internet; all the knowledge was in books and magazines. We spent three days there, just looking and buying books. We realized that there was an interesting scene in London.
Did you intend to stay?
It was a gamble. Let’s see what’s going to happen. But I found a job very quickly, and they sorted out a visa because they really liked my work.
I started working as a graphic designer in a design agency, and at night I used to do illustrations and send my work to magazines and newspapers.
Did you always know you wanted to be an illustrator?
I knew that I wanted to be a graphic designer or illustrator. Today, I am an illustrator, not a graphic designer. But at the start, it wasn’t clear.
Your first famous portrait was of Saddam Hussein. Could you please share the story of how you created it as a teenager, while sitting in the shelter?
I was 17 during the First Gulf War, and I had a gas mask. Everything was kind of very blurry because of the steam and all the breathing in the shelter, and I read in a newspaper that Saddam Hussein was using chemical weapons on his own people, and the icon of the chemical weapon was there. And I drew around it, which looked like eyebrows and a mustache.
When I came to London, I recreated it as a postcard and sent it to magazines and newspapers, and so that was one of my portraits that I shared with the world in a way.
It opened some doors for you. Was the second breakthrough Shakespeare’s image?
Yes, Shakespeare was the first time that I worked with Time Out, which led to The Observer and The Guardian, and one led to the other. After six months, I left my day job as a designer, and since then, I have been working as a full-time artist and illustrator.
As an illustrator, you also work with writers. How does the collaboration work? Does a writer have an idea and tell you, or do you read the book and come up with the idea?
I read the book. The ideal scenario is that I have the whole book, but sometimes I have a summary because the book is not ready; it depends on who the writer is and what stage the book is at. Sometimes it’s a new cover for an existing book, so it depends.
Do you build relationships with the writers?
No, normally not. It’s going through my agent and their agent. I have a few days to read the book, and the courier is coming to collect it.
And where does the artist in you come in?
It’s always there when I wake up in the morning, and I go to the [Highgate] woods. Even with [books] of Atwood or Murakami, a lot happens in the middle [of a walk]. I look at things, I discover things, so I always have my sketchbook, and I’m writing and sketching, and it’s kind of in between; ideas are coming, and I’m not stopping it.
So I work on commission jobs, but at the same time I work on an exhibition with new prints or a new book. It’s an ongoing process.
Is the connection with the trees something that you brought from Afula, where your father worked as a forester for Keren Kayemeth LeIsrael-Jewish National Fund?
Yes, my father used to drop me off at 5 or 6 in the morning with a group of workers on Nazareth mountain, and I spent the day with them in the field.
How old were you then? Did you work with them?
From age eight to 17. I was cutting, mainly trimming trees, because trees need constant trimming; otherwise, they touch and pull each other. I spent a lot of time in the woods.
And this bond continues nowadays.
Yes, but I also knew that I didn’t want to be fully in the woods.
Was it also when you started noticing the negative space?
Yes, it’s those years as well that I discovered [other] things, if you look at my nine-year-old’s sketchbook.
It is on view at the exhibition. Already at that age, there was humor in your pictures. You drew, for example, your rich neighbor with a graph instead of teeth.
Like a financial graph.
And who was your favorite artist when you were a child?
Igael Tumarkin and Menashe Kadishman. And my aunt and another uncle; he worked in Haifa Port, and in the evening, he used to paint.
Who is your favorite artist now?
I think Mark Rothko. And I love [Alberto] Giacometti!
Interesting! By using very limited elements in your works and negative space, you create multiple perception effects. You show a mouse in a cat, a wolf in a sheep. When did you start thinking about those ideas?
Maybe 30 years ago. There isn’t any specific date, but I always had this kind of dialogue with the other side.
For example, when I worked in the news, on the morning shifts, I noticed that the napkins were left from pizza ordered in the evening. Someone who was tidying the room put the napkins in order. So I put the straws between the napkins, and then someone put spoons like that on the edge of the table, and [thus] I started a dialogue with someone I didn’t know. I added something every day, and he added something. I actually made it a project at Bezalel.
I didn’t know who it was, but eventually we met. I realized that he was the cleaner, an Arab from east Jerusalem. At some point he disappeared. So it’s kind of a bittersweet memory.
Which, by the way, was the title of your book. Why “Bittersweet”?
I did a book that used everything, kind of all the bitterness in the world: from wars, crime, and drugs. It’s a bit like writing a song where the lyrics are very sad, but the melody is a bit happier.
I think that a lot of my work has this kind of bitterness in the subject, but the sweetness in the rap of it. It’s very simple; it looks very colorful and appealing, but when you go deeper, you can find the bitter pill.
In the Tel Aviv exhibition, some works address politics, and yet it’s not a political show.
No, it’s not. It’s there, but it’s not obvious. Many of my other exhibitions were very political, but there’s so much politics here.
And when you do your political things, is your intention to put your foot in? In your 2013 show in London, “Cut the Conflict,” one of the works there was gun/dove. Simple, yet powerful.
I have a big 750-kg “dog” [a dog-shaped industrial die-cutting machine]. Her name is Flora, and she’s cutting my work. She has a huge engine inside her body and produces 60 prints in a few seconds.
When I did “Cut the Conflict” at Rook & Raven gallery in London, I asked people from all over the world to send me materials. People from Iran, the US, Israel and Palestine, Lebanon, and Syria. And I started to cut things together with a machine. It’s a machine that cuts both positive and negative, cuts my shirt, and [allows me to] create prints mixed with materials. This was a very political work, but one that brings two sides together.
So is it more of an act of activism?
It is activism by someone who wants to bring sides together. It started with cutting and showing the differences between them, and then I realized that they’re so similar. I ask people online to send me materials that represent their countries – maps, books, and papers – and suddenly I started to include all the countries: India, Pakistan, North Korea, South Korea. The materials showed how similar they are.
Could you explain the general process of your work?
It starts with drawing. Everything is hand-drawn, and then [I transfer it to the] computer. If it’s with a client, I will send [them] a rough, a few ideas, and then, if it all goes well, I move to the final. Sometimes this stage can be a week, and sometimes it can be a couple of hours.
And my sculptures are made with a 3D printer. There is a process for turning my drawings into 3D sculptures. I love to see the presence of the negative space. Not just to see it as flat, but to look at it from all sides.
In the times when AI is taking over our lives, what would you say to less experienced illustrators?
I would suggest that, if you want to create a personal language, stay away not just from AI; stay away from computers. Go out and experience the world, draw, and do your own thing. AI is a shortcut for people who don’t do that. The joy is in discovering things.
Speaking of discovery, I saw many children at the museum trying to figure out what they were seeing in the big, upside-down pink toy.
I’m showing them that there is another side to everything. Here’s the name of the exhibition, exactly. And I have a hidden philosophy: Behind everything that you see, there is another side to life. So don’t just look at the front and what they show you – that this is a monkey or a rabbit. Turn it, and you can discover a dog.
For me, that’s kind of the first lesson of coexistence for them, without saying they coexist, and I’m happy that kids relate to it and understand it. I wouldn’t create it if I hadn’t gone through that with my girls and become a father, when my house became more pink.
And “Tel Aviv Summer” is the installation created especially for this exhibition and this city.
I always look for one element, but make the most of it. “Matkot” was great, because it’s a very Tel Aviv thing in summer, and we were in August. They don’t play Matkot, but there is also a dialogue between the two sides.
I looked at your list of awards, and it’s endless!
Yes, I didn’t update it over the last few years.
Those are huge achievements, congratulations! What would you tell young you, the little boy from Afula back in time?
“Keep doing what you’re doing.” I was drawing all the time, and I had dreams. I wouldn’t change anything.

Nepalese and Indians account for more than half of nationals from 23 countries missing after devastating glacier collapse four days ago
