CARACAS – Venezuelan interim President Delcy Rodriguez said on Aug 29 that an energy agreement with the US would remain in force for 25 years, target an increase in crude output to 1.5 million barrels per day (bpd) and preserve the country’s sovereignty over its natural resources.
Rodriguez hailed the accord in a late-night address as a “historic” deal that would help revive the economy and boost government revenue, saying it would help shape the country’s future.
“This 25-year bilateral project envisages the development of 17 strategic oilfields with a production target of more than 1.5 million barrels per day,” Rodriguez said on state broadcaster VTV.
“That figure relates solely to the bilateral agreement between Venezuela and the United States.”
Rodriguez added that the agreement’s target of 1.5 million bpd was only an initial goal and that the broader plan also included the development of eight greenfield oil blocks as part of a wider expansion of the country’s energy sector.
US President Donald Trump on Aug 28 announced plans for the US to take partial control of Venezuela’s vast oil reserves, betting that American companies can help revive the South American nation’s battered energy industry while providing a new source of crude to help lower US fuel prices. Trump provided few details on the agreement, saying only that the US had secured majority control of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven oil reserves through a partnership with private business.
Venezuela has the world’s largest proven oil reserves, but it produces only about 1.25 million bpd – far below its potential – after years of underinvestment, mismanagement and sanctions.
Rodriguez said the agreement could generate about US$209 billion (S$267 billion) in revenue for the Venezuelan state, based on a benchmark oil price of US$65 per barrel, though she acknowledged that crude prices could fluctuate.
She said roughly US$19 from each barrel produced and sold under the arrangement would flow directly to Venezuela, providing a significant boost to government revenue. She said that the country retained “ownership of and sovereignty” over its natural resources, “while leveraging capital, technology and operational expertise to support the recovery of a strategic industry that has been severely affected by sanctions”.
Earlier on Aug 29, dozens of pro-government groups gathered in downtown Caracas to protest against the US presence in Venezuela.
Rodriguez welcomed the agreement following Trump’s announcement, saying it would bolster economic growth and increase government revenue.
Venezuelan officials are preparing to sign agreements next week granting new oil exploration and production rights to several companies, including US firms.
Two sources close to the negotiations said on Aug 28 that Chevron was among the companies expected to finalise talks to transition its Venezuelan joint ventures into the country’s new energy framework. REUTERS

====================================================================================================

Iceland EU referendum sees slim, early lead for 'yes' camp
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
02:48:00 UTC
11:48:00 KST

Iceland voters reject EU accession talks
Published August 30, 2026last updated August 30, 2026
Voters in Iceland have rejected a plan to restart accession talks with the European Union, final referendum results showed on Sunday.
The 'No' camp secured victory with 52.8% of the votes, while the 'Yes' camp garnered 47.2% support, the official count published by public broadcaster RUV showed.
The capital, Reykjavik, was the only area in the island nation of 400,000 people to support the referendum.
Some 270,000 Icelanders were eligible to vote, 82% of whom did so.
Iceland PM: 'Not a setback'
Icelandic Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir, who backed the "yes" campaign, said she did not see her fellow citizens' vote as a defeat but as a fair democratic result.
"I don't see this as a setback. I see this as a victory for democracy," she said. "We had over 80% of the country participate in a matter like this."
She confirmed that her government was "not going forward with the accession talks this term" but that it would continue to strengthen its relationship with the European Economic Area.
"I don’t feel that there is bitterness," she said. "I know tempers run high for some people, but I have now spent time with a large group of people from all over the country and people are quite open to different outcomes."
Meanwhile, EU chief Antonio Costa told Frostadottir the bloc "fully respects the democratic choice" of the island's voters not to resume EU membership talks, according to a spokesperson.
"Iceland remains one of the EU's closest and most trusted partners," said the spokesperson for the European Council president.
Iceland opposition: 'This isn't the time'
The count through the night had the island nation on edge as the "Yes" campaign took an early lead, attributable largely to votes in the capital, Reykjavik, before results swung in favor of the opposition.
By dawn, only a few hundred votes separated the two camps before the gap grew as more ballots were tallied in rural areas of the country where opposition was greater.
"This isn't the time to go," one "No" voter, Daniel Bjarkason, told the Associated Press.
"Maybe in 10, 15, 20 years or more, we can take another look. But, for now, we're too divided and that's not a good look. Because it should be 70-30 'Yes' if we're going to [join the EU]."
Neck-and-neck vote after long debate
Iceland has spent the better part of two decades wrestling with the question of becoming a member of the bloc.
The Nordic country originally applied to join the EU in 2009 following the global financial crisis, which hit the country particularly hard.
Accession talks were suspended in 2013 after a euroskeptic government took office.
Iceland's current left-leaning government, elected in 2024, originally vowed to hold a referendum next year but brought the vote forward because of rising geopolitical tension over Russia's war in Ukraine and Greenland.
Fishing industry pulled weight
The decision puts to bed concerns among many voters that joining the bloc would undermine Iceland's sovereignty, with fishing rights a major concern.
The fisheries sector has been fiercely opposed to joining the bloc, with 90% of industry players against the idea.
The result is a disappointment to Brussels, which had appeared willing to compromise on thorny issues, including fishing and farming, to facilitate Iceland's accession.

Israel pounds southern Lebanon as Iran vows to stand by Beirut
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
02:43:58 UTC
11:43:58 KST

Israel pounds southern Lebanon as Iran vows to stand by Beirut
Israel continued attacks across southern Lebanon on Saturday, carrying out airstrikes, artillery shelling and demolitions, while Tehran pledged continued support for the country amid stalled negotiations over an IDF withdrawal.
Most of the day’s attacks were concentrated in Nabatieh Province, RT’s Lebanon correspondent Steve Sweeney said. Two explosions were reported near Aita al-Jabal, while Israeli drones carried out two strikes on Nabatieh al-Fawqa on Saturday morning. Israeli forces separately set fire to homes in Beit Yahoun.
The latest strikes came two days after an Israeli attack on Arab Salim killed 28-year-old Saja Sharara just 48 hours after her wedding, according to Sweeney, who recently visited the southern Lebanese village. Six others were wounded, including a child, a woman, and two elderly people.
Israel, however, said Thursday’s strikes followed the launch of two Hezbollah drones toward Israeli troops.
The escalation comes as Tehran reaffirms its support for Lebanon. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi met Sheikh Ali al-Khatib, vice president of Lebanon’s Higher Shiite Islamic Council, in Tehran on Friday. According to Lebanese L’Orient Today, Khatib described a deteriorating situation in the south, saying many displaced residents had exhausted their savings and had been left without homes or work. He appealed in particular for financial assistance for affected communities.
Araghchi said Tehran was working to revive the US-Iran memorandum of understanding signed in June, the first clause of which called for an end to Israeli attacks on Lebanon. He argued that implementing the agreement remained the way to resolve the crisis, while acknowledging that “the circumstances are difficult,” as cited by L’Orient Today.
The memorandum followed a renewed escalation between Israel and Hezbollah after the latter resumed attacks two days after the US-Iran war began on February 28. Hezbollah said its operation was retaliation for the killing of former Iranian Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei.
Hezbollah says it has observed the ceasefire reached under the subsequent US-Iran agreement. Israel, however, has continued strikes and demolitions in southern Lebanon and currently occupies more than 600 square kilometers of Lebanese territory.
Beirut and Israel have meanwhile been holding direct negotiations aimed at securing an Israeli withdrawal and ending the hostilities. Another round is reportedly expected in Rome in September, but progress has been limited.

Killing of Palestinian children and teens by Israel surges in West Bank
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
02:43:00 UTC
11:43:00 KST

Killing of Palestinian children and teens by Israel surges in West Bank
- The killing of Palestinian children and teenagers by Israeli forces in the West Bank has surged since October 2023, with an average of seven deaths per month compared to one per month previously.
- Many teenagers are killed during clashes when Israeli troops shoot youths accused of throwing stones, while younger children are often victims of indiscriminate fire.
- Families suffer deep grief and struggle for justice, with investigations by the Israeli military often disputed and Palestinians expressing that they rarely receive accountability for such deaths.
AI generated
RAMALLAH, Palestinian Territories - Alia al-Hallaq’s son Mohammed was nine when he was killed by an Israeli army bullet last October, but the Palestinian homemaker still speaks of herself as a mother of five, not four.
“I still haven’t accepted the idea of the loss. I often sit in the courtyard of the house and look at Mohammed’s grave below, and I cry while making sure that my children don’t see me,” she told AFP.
She said Mohammed was killed after running away from soldiers patrolling their village of Al-Rihiya, in the south of the occupied West Bank.
Hallaq’s uncle, also named Mohammed Hallaq, told AFP that his nephew was killed by a stray bullet during a confrontation between the army patrol and a group of older youths.
The bullet travelled through Mohammed’s abdomen, according to emergency services.
“Mohammed’s killing was the end,” his mother said.
The Israeli military, contacted by AFP for comment on Mohammed’s death, said at the time that soldiers opened fire during an altercation while deployed in Al-Rihaya.
“Soldiers responded with fire toward the suspects in the rock-hurling. Hits were identified,” it said, using language it generally employs to say troops shot and hit someone.
The killing of Palestinian children and teenagers by Israel has become increasingly common since the start of the war in Gaza.
B’Tselem, an Israeli rights group, reported 235 children and teenagers killed by Israeli forces in the West Bank since Oct 7, 2023 – when Hamas launched a massive attack on Israel from the Gaza Strip – through June 2026, including five killed by Israeli settlers.
The Palestinian Authority’s Colonisation and Wall Resistance Commission, a Palestinian government institution, reported 250 such deaths over the same time period.
In the 17 years between 2005 and 2021, an average of roughly one Palestinian child or teenager was killed by Israeli forces every month, according to B’Tselem, a frequent but much lower rate.
For the period since the Oct 7 attack, the average using B’Tselem figures is around seven killed per month.
Bullets for stones
AFP spoke to 12 women who lost children since Oct 7, 2023.
Although the details of each case differ, all spoke of family life stopped in its tracks and a lack of accountability.
In 2025, of the 54 Palestinian children or teenagers killed according to B’Tselem, the youngest was just two years old, while the majority were aged between 14 and 17.
Teenagers are often killed when Israeli forces engage with Palestinian youths throwing rocks, whom they routinely label terrorists, and shoot them.
The Israeli military commander for the West Bank, Major-General Avi Bluth, said in early 2026 that the army had killed 42 Palestinians for throwing stones in 2025, not specifying how many were minors.
In several other cases, usually involving younger children such as Mohammed, witnesses said the army had fired indiscriminately at Palestinians and killed children who were present.
One such casualty was seven-month-old Sam Abu Haikal, shot in the face by Israeli troops in the West Bank city of Hebron in June 2026.
‘Palestinians don’t get justice’
His mother, Dania Abu Haikal, 28, told AFP she was also wounded when the troops fired at their car while Sam was on her lap, with a bullet entering through her cheek and exiting through her ear.
She bore a large scar on her face when she met with AFP at her home in Bethlehem, holding a stuffed fox that had belonged to her son.
“Why would anyone shoot an infant? What did a little baby, a seven-month-old infant, do to harm the soldiers?”Abu Haikal, a university lecturer, said.
After a preliminary investigation, the army said one of its soldiers had opened fire on “uninvolved civilians” after their vehicle accelerated in the direction of the troops.
Abu Haikal disputes this, and said her husband had brought their car to a stop before the soldiers started shooting.
She carries the agony of losing her only child on top of the physical pain from the shooting.
“I cry every day; now my life is empty without him,” she said.
Like others whom AFP spoke to, Abu Haikal consulted a lawyer to push the army to investigate the incident fully.
“Palestinians don’t get justice for being killed by Israelis. But we hope that we get justice.” AFP

Tests loom for popular British PM Andy Burnham as Parliament returns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
02:41:00 UTC

Tests loom for popular British PM Andy Burnham as Parliament returns
- Andy Burnham has had a positive first month as British Prime Minister, gaining popularity with cost-of-living measures and a relaxed public image.
- Parliament returns on Sept 1, bringing challenges like prison reform decisions and Burnham’s first Prime Minister’s Questions session.
- Key issues ahead include funding his budget without tax rises, North Sea oil drilling debates, and managing relations with the EU and possibly Donald Trump.
AI generated
LONDON – Andy Burnham has enjoyed a honeymoon first month as Britain’s prime minister, but the hard trade-offs involved in governing are about to get real as Parliament returns from its summer break in the coming days.
Since succeeding Keir Starmer on July 20, Burnham has pleased voters with several low-cost sweeteners, including cutting electricity bills and bus fares, while burnishing his casual man-of-the-people vibes.
He has poured pints of beer with his finance minister, played guitar in Ukraine, and kept up a prolific output of slick social media videos during a self-styled “listening tour” of Britain.
Projecting a sunnier outlook than the straitlaced Starmer, and benefiting from the woes besetting hard-right rival Nigel Farage, Burnham has sparked a poll bounce for his ruling Labour Party.
A YouGov survey published on Aug 18 found that 46 per cent of Britons view him favourably, up 12 percentage points from when he first arrived at Downing Street.
With lawmakers on holiday, the new Prime Minister has largely been able to avoid thornier issues during his first weeks in office.
“He’s benefited enormously from Parliament not being there,” former senior civil servant Jill Rutter told AFP, adding that it had allowed the 56-year-old Burnham to “control the narrative” so far.
MPs return to Westminster on Sept 1, when Burnham is expected to deliver his first speech to Parliament as prime minister.
His government will detail a watering down of contentious plans to release thousands of prisoners early to ease chronic overcrowding in jails.
Burnham said on Aug 30 that hundreds of more serious offenders will remain behind bars, but conceded he was pushing the prison system to “the very limits of what’s possible without risking... (it)... collapsing within months”.
Then on Sept 2, MPs and the public will learn whether Burnham is any good at facing down the weekly grilling by the leader of the opposition when he takes part in his first Prime Minister’s Questions session.
Looming on the horizon is his government’s first budget on Oct 28, when Burnham must demonstrate that he can fund his pledges regarding cost-of-living support and ending rough sleeping, all while plugging a huge gap in defence spending.
He must do so against a backdrop of strained public finances and with limited levers to pull due to his commitment not to raise income tax, employee payroll contributions, or a value-added tax on consumer goods.
“That might be when reality starts to hit,” former minister Tony McNulty, who served alongside Burnham in Labour governments of the early 2000s, told AFP.
McNulty, now a politics lecturer at Queen Mary University of London, insists Burnham is capable of taking tough decisions and “sticking” to them, despite opponents labelling him a “people pleaser”.
Trump meeting?
Plenty of sensitive issues lie ahead, including welfare reform, how to fund social care, and whether to proceed with the scrapping of jury trials for many offences.
Whether to extract oil and gas at the controversial Jackdaw and Rosebank fields in the North Sea could be one of the most divisive questions.
“You either alienate the unions by saying no and get noises off from (US President) Donald Trump in a very unhelpful way,” explained Rutter.
Or Burnham gives drilling a green light and “you alienate the Labour net zero (supporters) who say we’re going to lose more support to the Greens”.
Burnham will host his first European leader since taking office when French President Emmanuel Macron visits London this week.
It comes as he must decide how to proceed with a “reset” with the European bloc that was championed by Starmer ahead of a bilateral summit expected in 2026.
Burnham has said Britain must be “bolder” in getting closer to the bloc, but has ruled out rejoining the single market, customs union or allowing freedom of movement.
“The EU isn’t handing out sweets just because we’ve got a sort of fun prime minister who likes (1980s English rock band) The Smiths,” added Rutter.
A likely first meeting with Trump, possibly at the United Nations General Assembly in September, will be tricky for Burnham who once described the US President’s policies as “poisonous”.
Labour lawmaker Jess Phillips said on a Sky News podcast last week that Burnham must “show what his actual priorities are” but in doing so runs the risk of disappointing many MPs.
MP Luke Akehurst told AFP that Burnham’s positive start “gives him a significant bank of political capital” among Labour colleagues “who will need to trust his judgement in addressing the range of complex policy issues that the government faces”. AFP

NEW YORK, August 30. /TASS/. NASA has postponed the planned mid-September launch of the Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station (ISS), which includes Roscosmos cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov, the US space agency said.
"NASA and SpaceX are adjusting the launch date for the agency’s Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station to address an oxidizer leak on Dragon’s propulsion system which was detected during standard prelaunch spacecraft processing. Joint NASA and SpaceX teams are performing additional tests and data review and will complete any necessary rework prior to launch. A new target date will be announced once available," NASA said on its website.
Earlier, Dana Weigel, who oversees NASA's low-Earth orbit programs, said Crew-13 was scheduled to launch no earlier than September 12. Teteryatnikov and Kutryk will serve as mission specialists, Watkins as commander and Delaney as pilot.

TOKYO, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- Japan's weather agency on Sunday issued its highest-level emergency warning for heavy rain for some areas in Fukui Prefecture, central Japan, amid reports of mudslides and vehicles stranded on flooded roads.

The ministry may take the emergency step of discharging water from a dam in Sakai to secure more room as water levels are rising, it added. ■

261 foreign nationals unaccounted for after mudslide hits border port in China's Xizang
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
10:39:09 CST
11:39:09 KST

GYIRONG, Xizang, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- A total of 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries have been identified as unaccounted for after a mudslide struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Aug. 26, local authorities said Sunday.
The figure was announced at a press conference held by the information office of the regional government, following a joint search and cross-checking of information by foreign affairs, public security, culture and tourism, and emergency management authorities.
Those unaccounted for include 104 people from Nepal, 49 from India, 33 from Latvia, 18 from the United States, 15 from Britain, six from Canada, six from Australia, four from South Africa, three from Malaysia, three from Germany, three from Russia, two from Ireland, two from Estonia, two from France, two from the Netherlands, two from New Zealand, and one each from Kazakhstan, Finland, Lithuania, Portugal, Ukraine, Spain and Hungary.
Chinese authorities have notified the countries' embassies and consulates in China, according to the press conference.
Following multiple rounds of searches, site inspections and checks of individuals at the port, no foreign tourists are currently stranded in Gyirong County, the authorities said.

China's Chang wins first ranking event title at snooker's Wuhan Open (updated)
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
10:39:07 CST
11:39:07 KST

Chang Bingyu poses for photos during the awarding ceremony after the final match between Zhao Xintong of China and Chang Bingyu of China at Wuhan Open 2026 snooker tournament in Wuhan, central China's Hubei Province, Aug. 29, 2026. (Xinhua/Wu Zhizun)
WUHAN, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- China's Chang Bingyu won his first ranking event title at the World Snooker Wuhan Open, beating new world No.1 Zhao Xintong 10-7 in an all-Chinese final here on Saturday.
Chang, 24, held his nerve in a dramatic deciding frame. With the final black remaining and Zhao already ahead on points, Chang used a snooker to force a foul before clearing four colors close to the cushion. He then potted the final black to win the frame by two points and seal the title.
After shaking hands with Zhao, Chang covered his face with a towel and struggled to contain his emotions.
"This title means a lot to me," Chang said. "There was a period when I couldn't participate in matches, then I came back and regained my professional status. Last year I reached a final, and now I finally won the title. I have really put in a lot over these years, that's why I'm so emotional."
Chang reached his first ranking final at the Scottish Open in December 2025, where he led Chris Wakelin 2-1 before losing eight consecutive frames.
"After that loss, I reminded myself every day that if I reached another final, I had to seize the opportunity," Chang said.
His path to the Wuhan title included victories over fellow Chinese player Liu Hongyu, Ali Carter, former world No. 1 Judd Trump and his idol, seven-time world champion Ronnie O'Sullivan.
"I never thought I could beat Zhao," Chang said after the final. "I came into the match with the mentality of learning from him. I've watched most of his matches in recent years. His game is both attractive and practical, and I have imitated many aspects of his style."
Zhao, who had won all seven of his previous ranking finals, praised Chang despite the loss.
"Although it's a little disappointing, Chang Bingyu deserved to win," Zhao said. "Many young players, including him, have already reached a very high level. I believe they will continue to get better."
The Wuhan Open has now been won by Chinese players for three consecutive editions. This year's semifinals also featured three generations of Chinese players, with Xiao Guodong (born in the 1980s), Zhao (born in the 1990s) and Chang (born in the 2000s) all reaching the last four.
Chang said he still has plenty to improve despite the breakthrough.
"The gap between me and the world's top 16 is still big," he said. "There were a lot of ups and downs emotionally in this match. I still need to work on my mentality and make myself more composed." ■

PM Modi received by Uzbek President Mirziyoyev in Tashkent, leaders share car ride

PM Narendra Modi with Uzbekistan Shavkat President Mirziyoyev
Prime Minister Narendra Modi received a warm and personal welcome from Uzbekistan President Shavkat Mirziyoyev after arriving in capital Tashkent on Saturday for a two-day state visit.From the airport, the two leaders travelled together by car to the presidential palace, marking the latest instance of PM Modi sharing a car ride with a world leader. They held a dinner meeting at the presidential palace.During the visit, the first leg of the prime minister’s two-nation tour, PM Modi will hold delegation-level talks with the Uzbek president to further strengthen the strategic partnership between the two countries.The discussions will cover cooperation in trade and investment, defence, digital connectivity, energy, education and people-to-people ties, while also setting the agenda for future bilateral engagement.
In his departure statement, PM Modi noted that the India-Uzbekistan Strategic Partnership had witnessed “significant advancement” in recent years.“I look forward to my discussions with President Mirziyoyev on further deepening our cooperation in trade and investment, digital connectivity, defence, energy, and on advancing our shared visions of Viksit Bharat and Yangi Uzbekistan,” he wrote on X.The visit marks his fourth trip to Uzbekistan since taking office.
He previously visited the country in 2015, 2016 and 2022.From Tashkent, PM Modi will travel to Bishkek at the invitation of Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov to attend the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit, which will mark 25 years of the organisation.
PM Modi first “carpooled” with a world leader during his 2014 visit to the United States, when he shared a car ride with then-US President Barack Obama.However, since last year, car rides with world leaders have become a recurring feature of what has been described as the prime minister's "informal diplomacy."In September last year, during his visit to China for the SCO Summit, PM Modi travelled in the same car as Vladimir Putin, reciprocating the gesture months later when the Russian president visited New Delhi in December.Since then, he has shared car rides with world leaders including French President Emmanuel Macron, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Three more unknown Ukrainian soldiers buried at National Military Cemetery
The press service of the National Military Memorial Cemetery reported this on Facebook, according to Ukrinform.
"They gave their lives fighting for the freedom of our land, and although their names have yet to be established, the state welcomed its heroes with the highest honors. Each soldier was buried with dignity and appropriate military honors," the statement said.
Among those who attended the burial ceremony were Head of the Office of the President Lieutenant General Kyrylo Budanov, Deputy Head of the Office of the President Iryna Vereshchuk, Minister for Veterans Affairs Vitalii Kim, Minister of Social Policy, Family and Unity Denys Uliutin, Minister of Internal Affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi, Deputy Head of the Kyiv Regional Military Administration Ivan Dobrovolskyi, and Deputy Head of the Poltava Regional Military Administration Yevhen Konchakovskyi.
Members of Ukraine's Defense Forces, veterans, families of fallen defenders, representatives of the public, clergy and other visitors to the memorial also took part in the ceremony.
The fallen soldiers were carried along the Alley of Remembrance through a guard of honor. Following the burial ceremony, military chaplains from various denominations offered prayers for all fallen defenders. Each chaplain prayed according to their own religious tradition.
The state emphasized that work to restore the names of each of these soldiers will continue even after their burial. "Regardless of whether their name has been established, each of them is a Defender of Ukraine," the National Military Memorial Cemetery emphasized.
A "Table of Remembrance" was also installed at the cemetery today at the initiative of the Grabar Foundation. Relatives and friends of fallen soldiers, fellow service members and other visitors wrote the names of the soldiers they remember on special cards.
As part of an initiative by the "Honor" public organization, relatives of fallen defenders, service members and other participants also took part in the communal weaving of remembrance wreaths, an ancient Ukrainian tradition of honoring the fallen. The wreaths and fresh flowers were placed on the soldiers' graves as symbols of love and remembrance.
As reported, on August 29, Ukraine honors the memory of fallen defenders.

High-level review meet held over proposed 'ARISE' project for coastal projection and climate resilience in Odisha
Edited by: Ayush Pandey / TIMESOFINDIA.COM / Updated: Aug 30, 2026, 08:16 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
High-level review meet held over proposed 'ARISE' project for coastal projection and climate resilience in Odisha
A high-level meeting on the proposed Adaptive Resilience Investment in Coastal Systems on Economics (ARISE) Project was held on Saturday at Lok Seva Bhawan to deliberate on a comprehensive and long-term strategy for protecting Odisha's coastline, enhancing climate resilience and promoting sustainable economic development in coastal areas.Odisha Minister of Revenue & Disaster Management, Suresh Pujari, who chaired the meeting, emphasised the need for a comprehensive approach to coastal management that combines coastal protection, environmental conservation, livelihood security, biodiversity protection and economic sustainability. He stressed that the ARISE Project should contribute towards strengthening the resilience of coastal communities and ecosystems against the growing impacts of climate change.A preliminary assessment of Odisha's 573-km coastline has been undertaken jointly by the Asian Development Bank (ADB) and the Odisha State Disaster Management Authority (OSDMA). Consultations have also been held with ADB and the Departments of Water Resources, Forest, Fisheries & Animal Resources Development & Revenue & Disaster Management on key issues relating to coastal erosion, sediment management, protection of coastal villages and safeguarding the lives and livelihoods of coastal communities.
Based on these consultations, ADB and OSDMA have prepared a preliminary report, which was discussed in detail during the meeting.It was informed that ADB (Asian Development Bank) has also been working with the State Governments of Kerala, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu on coastal protection initiatives. The first phase of the coastal protection project in Karnataka has already been completed. The Minister informed that after completion of the final assessment and report for Odisha, the ARISE Project would be taken up in a phased manner, with appropriate interventions to strengthen coastal protection across the State.The meeting discussed integrated measures to address coastal erosion along Odisha's coastline. Emphasis was placed on scientific & technology-driven interventions to reduce erosion, protect vulnerable coastal stretches and strengthen long-term coastal resilience.The development of Odisha's Blue Economy was also deliberated upon, with emphasis on harnessing the State's vast marine resources and economic potential in a sustainable and responsible manner. The approach would seek to generate greater livelihood and economic opportunities for coastal communities while contributing to the State's overall economic growth, a release said.The meeting also focused on promoting Climate-Resilient Coastal Tourism in view of the increasing impacts of climate change and natural hazards. Discussions centred on developing sustainable tourism models that balance economic opportunities with environmental conservation and strengthen the resilience of coastal tourism infrastructure and communities.Coastal Protection and Sediment Management were identified as key components of the proposed interventions. The meeting emphasised the need to understand the natural dynamics of Odisha's coastline and adopt scientifically informed approaches for managing sediment movement and deposition. Strengthening natural coastal defence systems and undertaking suitable protective measures at vulnerable locations were also discussed.For effective implementation of the ARISE Project, special emphasis was laid on Institutional Strengthening, Capacity Building and Advanced Technological Systems. The meeting discussed strengthening the institutional capacity of departments and agencies involved in coastal management, enhancing the technical skills of officials and personnel, and promoting knowledge and experience sharing among stakeholders.The use of modern technology, real-time data and digital platforms for effective coastal management was also emphasised. An integrated technological monitoring system for tracking coastal erosion, improving hazard forecasting, supporting data-driven decision-making and strengthening preparedness and response mechanisms was identified as an important component of the long-term strategy, a release further said.
The meeting emphasised that the ARISE Project should adopt a long-term, scientific, integrated and sustainable approach to enhance climate resilience along Odisha's extensive coastline while simultaneously strengthening environmental protection, disaster resilience, coastal livelihoods and economic development.Special Relief Commissioner and Managing Director, OSDMA, Rajesh Prabhakar Patil, senior officials of OSDMA and senior officials of the Asian Development Bank attended the meeting, a release added.

A total of 261 foreign nationals from 23 countries have been identified as unaccounted for after a mudslide struck Gyirong Port on the China-Nepal border in southwest China's Xizang Autonomous Region on Aug. 26, local authorities said Sunday.
The figure was announced at a press conference held by the information office of the regional government, following a joint search and cross-checking of information by foreign affairs, public security, culture and tourism, and emergency management authorities.
Those unaccounted for include 104 people from Nepal, 49 from India, 33 from Latvia, 18 from the United States, 15 from Britain, six from Canada, six from Australia, four from South Africa, three from Malaysia, three from Germany, three from Russia, two from Ireland, two from Estonia, two from France, two from the Netherlands, two from New Zealand, and one each from Kazakhstan, Finland, Lithuania, Portugal, Ukraine, Spain and Hungary.
Chinese authorities have notified the countries' embassies and consulates in China, according to the press conference.
Following multiple rounds of searches, site inspections and checks of individuals at the port, no foreign tourists are currently stranded in Gyirong County, the authorities said. China has also opened two 24-hour English-language hotlines for the families of the unaccounted-for foreign nationals: 0086-891-6817165 and 0086-18308026705. (Xinhua)

"If Ukraine loses, we will lose too": Finland's president stressed the importance of supporting Kyiv
Kyiv • UNN
The president of Finland believes that Ukraine has a military, political, and financial advantage over the Russian Federation. He called it a guarantee of Europe's security.
Finnish President Alexander Stubb believes that Ukraine is currently in a stronger position than at any time since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion and has an advantage over the russian federation, but the fate of European countries depends precisely on Ukraine and its victory over the russian federation. Details
Today, Ukraine is in a stronger and better position than at any time in this war—in military, political and financial terms

If you survive, if you remain independent, if you remain a sovereign state—then that is victory
"If Ukraine loses, then so do we"
Stubb emphasized that supporting Kyiv is directly linked to the security of European countries. He called Ukraine the best security guarantee Europe has against russia.
We must understand—you in Germany and we in Finland—that Ukraine is the best security guarantee we have against russia. If Ukraine loses, we lose

Plibersek indicates support for ban on choking in pornography
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
02:03:00 UTC
11:03:00 KST

Tanya Plibersek says Labor should consider UK-style ban on strangulation in pornography
In short:
Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek has indicated support for banning the depiction of strangulation and suffocation in pornography, with some pointing to a similar ban in the UK.
Advocates' calls have intensified following the death of a 16-year-old Sydney girl, linked to to a suspected sexual choking act, earlier this week.
What's next?
The government is still consulting on its digital duty of care bill, which could force social media giants to proactively prevent foreseeable harm on their services.
Australia should be "very seriously" looking at banning depictions of strangulation or suffocation in pornography, says a senior Labor minister who has indicated her support.
Advocates' calls for the ban have intensified following the death of a 16-year-old Sydney girl, understood to be treated as a suspected sexual choking act.
Social Services Minister Tanya Plibersek highlighted the prevalence of the act during sexual encounters among young people after a 2024 study found that 57 per cent of 18 to 35 year olds have experienced strangulation in the bedroom.
Last year, the UK made it a criminal offence to possess or publish pornography showing strangulation or suffocation.
Ms Plibersek said Australia should "very seriously" consider following the UK's decision to outlaw depictions of choking in pornography.
"There is something wrong with a situation where 60 per cent of young people say they've experienced strangulation," she told Insiders on Sunday morning.
"This is not sex education. It's not real life," she added.
Pointing to risks of long-term brain damage or aneurysms in the case of a non-fatal strangulation, Ms Plibersek said there was "no safe way to strangle someone".
NSW Liberal leader Kellie Sloane added to the calls on Sunday, writing to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese to ask him to urgently introduce the ban.
"When pornography depicts an act capable of causing brain injury, unconsciousness or death, it should not be treated as just another form of adult entertainment," she wrote.
Ms Sloane said young people were being exposed to sexual violence online without understanding the danger of the behaviour.
"We cannot wait until another family is living through a tragedy before we take seriously what our children are being taught by pornography."
It is an issue found in other online content, with a 2024 study demonstrating that on average young boys are served extremely misogynistic content within 23 minutes of downloading social platforms, such as TikTok and YouTube shorts.
Ms Plibersek acknowledged the role that social media algorithms played in perpetuating harmful narratives online, following a push by advocates for the government to introduce laws that make algorithms opt-in only.
Among them is Teach Us Consent founder Chanel Contos, who urged the government to take the issue more seriously.
"I think it's quite obvious the harm that algorithms are doing to everyone, but particularly young people, and women are largely on the receiving end of that," Ms Contos told the ABC.
"And I think that something that has 71 per cent of Australians supporting it should be taken as a serious policy proposition."
Ms Plibersek said there were ongoing discussions about how that would look in practice, but remained open to an opt-in model as the government continued to consult on its upcoming digital duty of care bill.
The issue was also front and centre earlier in the week, when national cabinet acknowledged rates of intimate-partner homicide and sexual violence remained "unacceptably high", agreeing on priorities for the next five-year plan to tackle the issues.
Smart glasses moratorium considered
The federal government is also closely considering a moratorium on the import of smart glasses, which can be used to discreetly film people without their consent.
The devices look like ordinary glasses and yet allow the wearer to record images, video and audio, mostly surreptitiously, with the press of a button.
The Greens, with the support of some crossbenchers, have called on the government to halt the import of such glasses as well as as other wearable recording devices for at least 12 months, until tougher privacy protections are passed into law.
Ms Plibersek revealed the attorney-general was due to deliver an update on the government's position shortly, as she labelled any use of the glasses "really troubling".
"If they're going to be used, there should be safeguards around how they can be used," she said.
"I mean, it's already possible, I believe, to buy glasses where you can disable the filming light, so it's not apparent that they're filming as they're being used. That is really, really troubling".

‘Green miracle’: US teacher returns to China after 26 years to find donation grew into forest

Unknown Publisher

‘Green miracle’: US teacher returns to China after 26 years to find donation grew into forest
‘You gave the trees life and watched them grow, just as parents take pride in their children,’ says Sakolsky
A retired American teacher has reunited with a Chinese farmer 26 years after their initial encounter, returning to the once-barren sandy landscape transformed by his generous donation into a lush green environment.
In 1999, Ronald Sakolsky, now 67, was teaching English in Luoyang, Henan province, central-eastern China, when he discovered Inner Mongolian farmer Yin Yuzhen’s efforts to combat desertification. Inspired by her dedication, he donated US$5,000 to support her mission.
The pair first met during a donation ceremony in the Mu Us Desert in 2000. Afterwards, Sakolsky returned to the US, while Yin used the funds to plant over 50,000 trees.
Today, vegetation covers more than 80 per cent of the Mu Us Desert, which is one of China’s four major sandy regions.
In May, Yin, now 60, reconnected with Sakolsky via video call and invited him back to China to witness the “green miracle” that his contribution had helped foster.

In Brief
- A social media trend known as "sardinemaxxing" has seen sardines cleared from supermarket shelves after hot demand.
- Experts say the social media trend could be dangerous for other fish.
Walk down the canned fish aisle at your local supermarket right now, and there's a good chance you'll find a gap where the tinned sardines used to be, as a viral TikTok trend sends a wave of new fans in search of the small, oily fish.
The trend, dubbed "sardinemaxxing", has seen influencers push sardines as a beauty and wellness must-have, with some calling them "Botox on a fork" for their purported skin, hair, and anti-ageing benefits.
But experts say the trend raises real questions about where those sardines are coming from — and what happens if the hype spreads to other seafood.
Why groceries are going viral
Sardines are just the latest grocery item swept up in a social media-driven buying frenzy.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Cottage cheese and Greek yoghurt both had their moment in the past year, part of a broader "proteinmaxxing" wave prizing high-protein foods.
Lisa Asher, a retail and supermarket expert at the University of Sydney Business School, said the pattern is driven by a mix of influencer culture and wellness trends.
"What bothers me isn't that the kids are eating sardines … it's that they're taking advice now from people who are probably not people you should be listening to," Asher said.
"It's a new form of advertising with a lot of unknowns — we don't really know who's paying who and how much they're making out of it. That is a problem.
"In magazines, we used to look at celebrities, but celebrities have been replaced by influencers."
She said the trends all follow a similar pattern: demand increases, the product goes out of stock, prices sometimes rise, and eventually, when the hype cools down, it comes back in stock.
"But this is a product that is made from fish in the sea," she adds. "We don't want to overfish because suddenly, then we have none."
The big catch
That's where the environmental risks come in.
Adrian Meder, sustainable seafood program manager at the Australian Marine Conservation Society, says history shows a sudden cultural appetite for a particular seafood can do serious damage — pointing to shark fin soup, sea cucumber and some tuna fisheries as species pushed towards collapse by surging demand.
"We've yet to see online popularity as a driver of major declines in our oceans, but a cultural surge in popularity of a seafood has time and time again decimated populations of species from tunas, to sharks, to abalone, to sea cucumbers," Meder told SBS News.
"Online popularity is clearly capable of producing massive changes in consumer demand."
There's also a traceability problem: much of the tinned sardines on Australian shelves is imported, and it can be difficult to know where a can came from or how sustainably it was caught.
Jonathan Smart, an affiliate senior research scientist at James Cook University, agrees that origin matters.
He co-authored a study, released last week, that found Australia ranked just 52nd in seafood production, despite having about eight million square kilometres of fishing waters.
"The fisheries that a lot of our imported seafood comes from are actually quite unsustainable — and Australia imports a lot of seafood when perhaps it shouldn't," Smart told SBS News.
"By importing so much seafood, we're essentially exporting our environmental footprint to other countries that don't have the same level of management that we do."
He worries a viral trend like this one could make that problem worse.
"If a trend like this is popping up and all of a sudden you've got greater consumption of a species, the fear I would have is that then is going to lead to, again, a greater surge in that imported seafood.
"We just don't know if that's going to have the same sustainability levels as if you were actually consuming something locally."
A resilient little fish
But of all the species to go viral, sardines might be one of the best placed to handle their 15 minutes of fame.
Smart says sardines are a fast-growing, short-lived species with rapid turnover, making them naturally resilient to heavy fishing.
Because changes in biomass are driven more by environmental conditions — like ocean upwellings — rather than fishing activity, sardine and anchovy fisheries are some of the biggest in the world, he said.
"They can actually provide a really, really big harvest from them normally under sustainable conditions, depending on the fishery that they're coming from."
Locally, there's also a genuine opportunity: Australia's biggest fishery is a sardine fishery in South Australia — a fact Smart says is little known because much of the catch goes to aquaculture feed.
"Very little of it actually goes to human consumption," he said. "That's why I often recommend to people that we should be eating more sardines because that is a really sustainable fishery.
"We catch a lot of fish from it, and there's a lot of opportunity."
Meder agrees that there's room for Australians to put more sardines on their plate.
"Some cultures, including many Australian communities, actually used to eat a lot more sardines than they do now," he said, pointing to a shift in seafood consumption to more environmentally vulnerable, less abundant, and expensive fish species — of which trends like these could help reverse.
But that only holds if the sardines on the shelf are actually Australian — which means consumers may need to check labels and do a bit of Googling before putting them in their shopping basket.
So while sardines may be getting the limelight for just a brief period before scrollers move on to the next trend, if there's anything we can take from it, it's that the humble little sardine is actually built for this moment.

Human-wildlife clashes on the rise in China’s Giant Panda National Park
Farmers on the giant nature reserve report rising concerns over damage to crops and livestock as well as attacks from wild animals
Friction between humans and wild animals at China’s Giant Panda National Park intensified significantly over the past decade as conservation efforts expanded, a new study has found.
Farmers reported increasing losses between 2015 and 2024, stemming from damage to property and crops as well as attacks on humans and livestock.
The team behind the study said the issue had become the most prominent challenge facing the park’s administrators.
The Giant Panda National Park covers 22,000 sq km (8,500 sq miles), 2½ times the size of Yellowstone in the United States, and officially opened in 2021.
Spanning the provinces of Sichuan, Shaanxi and Gansu, the park is now home to more than 1,300 wild giant pandas, 70 per cent of their total population.

The embankment dissolves into a chain of gentle mounds—undulating along the river's grain, as if wind-swept ripples were spreading across the water, wave after wave washing up the bank, swelling into mounds, spilling into the city's edge. Pacific leader heads home before PIF to face no-confidence motion

Solomon Islands PM returns home before PIF meeting to face no-confidence motion
In short:
Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale, who was due to attend the Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) meeting in Palau this week, has instead headed home to deal with a no-confidence motion.
In the no-confidence motion, Solomon Islands Home Affairs Minister Manasseh Maelanga accused Mr Wale of "repeatedly making decisions of matters of national importance" without properly consulting and gaining the approval of cabinet.
This year's PIF meeting was already facing a large number of absent leaders.
Solomon Islands Prime Minister and outgoing Pacific Islands Forum (PIF) chair Matthew Wale has made a shock departure from the PIF leaders meeting, flying out of Palau just hours after arriving, in order to deal with a looming leadership challenge back home.
Mr Wale's political coalition was shaken yesterday after Solomon Islands Home Affairs Minister Manasseh Maelanga announced he had filed a no-confidence motion to topple Mr Wale, who has only been in the top job for three months.
In his motion, Mr Maelanga accused Mr Wale of "repeatedly making decisions of matters of national importance without proper consultation with, or the approval of, cabinet, thereby undermining the principles of collective cabinet responsibility, representative democracy and good governance".
Mr Maelanga was one of Mr Wale's main challengers for the top job this year, and has held a senior position in his cabinet since then.
"Whatever the outcome, I am confident that our country will move forward peacefully, government services will continue, and members will work together in the national interest," Mr Maelanga said in statement released this afternoon.
But his arguments echo many of those made by the Solomon Islands opposition, whose leader, former prime minister Manasseh Sogavare, has accused Mr Wale of bulldozing through major changes without consulting properly with parliament or the electorate.
Mr Wale appeared to be shaken by the news on arrival in Palau on Saturday night, and declined to comment on the challenge when asked about it by reporters.
The ABC understands Mr Wale left Palau early on Sunday morning and is due to arrive back in Solomon Islands on Monday.
Two of Mr Wale's key lieutenants in his coalition — Foreign Minister Rick Hou and Minister of National Planning and Development Peter Kenilorea Jr — will now represent Solomon Islands at the meeting.
Mr Kenilorea Jr said in Palau late yesterday that he "had no idea as to why" the challenge was launched.
"[I'm] looking forward to finding out more,"
The news is a blow to the PIF, which is already facing a large number of absent leaders at this year's gathering.
Kiribati President Taneti Maamau announced yesterday he would not attend, and that his nation would be represented instead by its ambassador to China.
Organisers say Mr Maamau could not get flights to Palau to attend PIF while also attending a parliamentary sitting, but New Zealand Foreign Minister Winston Peters said his decision was "hugely disappointing" and suggested the president should have found a way to travel.
"The question at hand is that flights weren't available [for Mr Maamau] in a parliamentary sitting," he said.
"We've all got to organise ourselves around these matters to get here.
"The centrality of the Pacific Islands Forum is not going to be compromised … but it's not going to help."
When asked if there had been any evidence that foreign interference had contributed to the absence of leaders, Mr Peters made no direct allegation — and didn't name any countries — but said, "You'd be defying gravity and logic if you said [it] wasn't a big problem."
Mr Peters has previously suggested that China had worked to stop PIF from issuing a clear condemnation of Beijing's recent ballistic missile test in the region.
The ABC has approached Mr Maamau's office for comment.
Samoa's Prime Minister, Laʻauli Leuatea Schmidt, and Vanuatu's Prime Minister, Jotham Napat, are also not attending, while it is unclear whether Fiji's Prime Minister, Sitiveni Rabuka, will fly to Palau for the meeting.
The challenge will also unsettle Australia, which sees Mr Wale as far more sympathetic than his predecessors, Jeremiah Manale and Manasseh Sogavare.
Mr Wale fiercely criticised China's recent ballistic missile launch and has made it clear he is uneasy with China's security role in Solomon Islands, although he has not tried to tear up the 2022 agreement the Pacific nation signed with Beijing.
He also announced not long after taking power that he had agreed to kick off negotiations with Australia on a new treaty, with officials racing to complete the discussions by the end of this year.
Wale's departure 'unfortunate'
The incoming PIF chair, Surangel Whipps Jr, said while it was "unfortunate" Mr Wale had to leave, he understood the prime minister's decision.
"We're so grateful that he made it, but he has a few things back home that he has to take care of,"
He also played down the significance of looming absences, saying that up to 14 leaders were still set to make it to Palau, and that the forum was still much more united than in the era of the so-called PIF split.
"One of the things we want to focus on is … crises come up, but how can we find a way to make sure that we make — within everybody's schedule — to maximise the amount of leaders," he said.
"Because there's no question that when the leaders are all assembled we can get partners to deliver.
"More leader participation is now happening than in previous years … and we want that to continue."

NASA’s Roman telescope set to launch on cosmic mapping mission
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
01:50:00 UTC
10:50:00 KST

NASA’s Roman telescope set to launch on cosmic mapping mission
WASHINGTON – NASA is preparing to launch its new flagship space telescope on Aug 30, embarking on a multi-year mission to create an unprecedented map of the cosmos and shed light on some of the biggest mysteries in physics.
Designed to take a panoramic view of the vast reaches of space, the Roman Space Telescope “will help unlock the secrets of the universe”, US President Donald Trump said on Aug 28 during a ceremony at NASA headquarters in Houston, Texas.
Standing over 12m tall, the state-of-the-art observatory is scheduled to launch from Florida at 7.26am (7.26pm Singapore time) aboard a SpaceX Falcon Heavy rocket.
Developed over more than a decade at a cost topping US$4 billion (S$5.09 billion), the telescope is named after pioneering US astronomer Nancy Grace Roman, who became known as the “Mother of Hubble”, another of NASA’s flagship telescopes.
While Hubble revealed that the universe is expanding faster than previously thought, Roman will seek to answer some of the other unsolved mysteries, including those of dark matter and dark energy.
“Roman will give the Earth a new atlas of the universe,” NASA administrator Jared Isaacman said in April when he unveiled the project to the press.
With a field of view more than 100 times larger than Hubble’s – and significantly wider than James Webb’s – Roman will survey vast swaths of the sky from a vantage point 1.5 million km from Earth, which it will take about 100 days to reach.
Designed to work in tandem with other observatories such as Webb, which offers greater power and precision, Roman aims to discover thousands of exoplanets as well as tens of thousands of supernovae, the explosive deaths of massive stars.
“It will be the biggest catalogue of astronomical objects anybody’s ever produced, and it will help us understand how common are solar systems like our own,” Dave Content, Roman’s technical manager, told AFP.
The new telescope will also shed light on two of the biggest mysteries in physics: dark matter and dark energy.
Their origins remain unknown, but together they are believed to make up about 95 per cent of the universe.
Dark matter is thought to act as a kind of gravitational glue, while dark energy is believed to be a repulsive force driving the universe’s expansion.
With its infrared vision, Roman will be able to detect light emitted by celestial objects billions of years ago, effectively looking back in time and offering scientists a glimpse into the universe’s distant past and helping them better understand these two mysterious phenomena.
Surprise
Roman’s observations will complement the work of the Rubin Observatory in Chile and the European Space Agency’s (ESA) Euclid probe, and are highly anticipated because they could challenge scientists’ understanding of the universe’s structure.
Julie McEnery, Roman’s senior project scientist, said recent research suggests the way scientists have been thinking about the universe’s early expansion, based on the predictions of existing models, may be wrong.
“Recent observations hint that our standard model of the universe is incorrect,” she told a press conference on Aug 29, adding that Roman will help clear that up.
“It will definitively say, ‘Yeah, the model works, or it doesn’t’. And if it doesn’t, it’s going to provide us with the precision and quality of data that will allow us to start to distinguish between those options.”
Scientists and the general public will have access to all of Roman’s data.
But the sheer volume will be daunting, Content warned.
The telescope will be generating about 1.3 terabytes of data a day, “which means you basically can’t download the data to anybody’s laptop”, he said.
For McEnery, the more data, the better.
“I very much hope, and in fact expect, that the most exciting science from Roman will be a surprise, something we couldn’t predict, and that will set the stage for the next deeper set of questions for future missions to address.” AFP

The Australian government is considering allowing users to opt in or opt out of social media algorithms, and is looking at a recent UK ban on depictions of strangulation and suffocation in pornography.
The social services minister, Tanya Plibersek, said social media was “playing a huge role” in the increase in sexual violence among teenagers and choking, and confirmed the options were being considered as the government develops its second action plan to end family and domestic violence against women and children.
It follows the death of a 16-year-old girl in Sydney after a suspected sexual strangulation act. Guardian Australia reported on Thursday that a source informed about the case said the teenager was believed to have become unconscious as a result of asphyxiation during sexual intercourse, often referred to as “choking”. No arrests have been made.
Plibersek told the ABC’s Insiders program on Sunday that social media algorithms are deliberately feeding boys and men violent content and normalising strangulation during sex.
“If you set up a social media account as a young boy in Australia today, it takes an average of 23 minutes for you to be fed misogynistic, violent misogynistic content online. That is a deliberate decision of the social media companies that is wrecking our young boys, giving them all of the wrong ideas about what healthy relationships look like,” Plibersek said.
“It is no coincidence that 60% of young people now report that they’ve experienced strangulation during a sexual encounter … It is pervasive and widespread and deadly, and it’s being fed to our young people and normalised.”
Chanel Contos’s Teach Us Consent has campaigned for algorithms to be opt-in only on social media.
Plibersek said the government was working with the group and considering how to potentially design an opt-in or opt-out system for algorithms.
“We’re absolutely up for work on algorithms. Opting in to those recommender algorithms that are causing so much harm, opting in or opting out,” she said.
“We’re also, of course, looking very closely at the recent Meta case in the US [and] the moves that the UK government have introduced to prevent the depiction of strangulation and suffocation in pornography. These are all really important considerations as we develop our next action plan on family domestic and sexual violence, so that work’s going on right now.”
The government legislated a ban on social media for under-16s which took effect in December, and has also introduced age-verification for pornography. But Plibersek has previously conceded children were easily able to dodge the new rules.
Labor will also soon begin consultation on a digital duty of care bill that will put the onus on tech companies, including AI companies, to make online spaces safer for all users.
Plibersek said the digital duty of care legislation, as well as a second round of privacy reforms, could also help tackle camera-equipped smartglasses, which she said she had serious concerns about.
“Tech companies should know that their products are safe and make them safe before they release them on to an unsuspecting public. I know the Attorney-General has asked the privacy commissioner to look specifically at these glasses,” Plibersek said.
“We’ve got a second tranche of privacy legislation coming up soon as well … things like this that can be used to furtively film, including during sexual encounters, for that filming then to be made public or used against someone who is being filmed as a way of blackmailing them, I am very concerned about the potential uses of these glasses.”

Dortmund's pressure brought a second goal in first-half stoppage time when Maximilian Beier fed Konstantelias, whose effort took a decisive deflection off Sebastiaan Bornauw's knee.
The visitors returned with greater purpose and Patson Daka went close twice, most notably when his effort struck the outside of the post in the 67th minute.
Dortmund had already suffered a setback when Konstantelias was forced off in the 54th minute after twisting his left knee in a challenge.
Their task became harder when substitute Samuele Inacio was shown a straight red card in the 77th minute, only moments after entering the field, for a challenge on Albert Gronbaek.
Hamburg pressed against the 10 men, but goalkeeper Gregor Kobel denied Gronbaek and the hosts held on for the victory.
Dortmund next face fifth-tier HEBC Hamburg in their rescheduled German Cup first-round tie, while Hamburg host Mainz in the Bundesliga.
"We were pushed too deep in the first half and once Dortmund get into their rhythm, you are always chasing them. Going into halftime only 1-0 down would have been better, but after the second goal it became difficult. If you want to get something here, you have to be ready from the first minute. We made it too easy for Dortmund," said Hamburg captain Nicolai Remberg.
"The first half was excellent. We implemented everything we had planned. We came out of halftime reasonably well and wanted to put the game to bed, but we struggled to do that," said Dortmund defender Waldemar Anton.
Elsewhere on Saturday, newly promoted Elversberg produced the biggest shock of the day, stunning Bayer Leverkusen 3-2 after racing into a two-goal halftime lead. RB Leipzig opened with a convincing 3-0 victory over Borussia Monchengladbach, while Cologne edged Hoffenheim 3-2. Union Berlin and Eintracht Frankfurt shared the points in a 3-3 draw, while Mainz and Paderborn played out a goalless stalemate. ■

Xinhua Commentary: How the SCO is raising the bar for better global governance
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-30
09:45:59 CST
10:45:59 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 30 (Xinhua) -- The world is facing a growing crisis of global governance. Protectionism, unilateralism and power politics are throttling international cooperation just as mounting global challenges demand it most.
Against this backdrop, Chinese President Xi Jinping proposed the Global Governance Initiative (GGI) at last year's "Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Plus" Meeting, calling for a more just and equitable system of global governance.
The SCO offers a practical answer. Over the past 25 years, it has demonstrated how countries with different political systems, development paths and civilizations can work together.
Guided by the Shanghai Spirit of mutual trust, mutual benefit, equality, consultation, respect for diversity of civilizations and pursuit of common development, the SCO's 25-year practice offers a vivid illustration of the five principles of the Global Governance Initiative -- adhering to sovereign equality, abiding by international rule of law, practicing multilateralism, advocating the people-centered approach, and focusing on taking real actions.
These principles are reflected in the SCO's increasingly institutionalized cooperation across a wide range of sectors. With regional security and stability at the heart of its original mission, SCO countries have committed themselves to long-term good neighborliness, friendship and cooperation based on equality, consultation and respect for diversity.
The establishment of four new security-focused centers demonstrated the SCO's emphasis on translating multilateral consensus into concrete action. Cooperation among SCO countries has helped thwart more than 1,400 terrorism- and extremism-related incidents in the past 25 years, while the organization has conducted over 40 joint counter-terrorism exercises and operations.
The SCO's approach to security also reflects a broader understanding among SCO countries that lasting security cannot be separated from political trust, economic development and people-to-people exchanges.
The launch of seven China-SCO cooperation platforms covering green industry, digital economy, scientific and technological innovation, energy, higher education, vocational and technical education, and artificial intelligence further underscores the emphasis on shared development with people-centered outcomes.
Through high-quality Belt and Road cooperation and closer alignment of development strategies, SCO members have seen positive momentum in both foreign trade and intra-SCO commerce. Calculations based on World Trade Organization data showed the total volume of goods imports and exports of the ten members reached about 8.88 trillion U.S. dollars in 2025.
Projects such as the China-Kyrgyzstan-Uzbekistan railway, the Silk Road e-commerce service hub and the SCO university network are further turning connectivity into tangible benefits, making it easier for people across SCO countries to travel, trade, study and access broader economic opportunities.
People-to-people exchange activities have also become an important pillar of SCO cooperation. Through institutionalized dialogue and expanded interaction, differences in history, culture and civilization can be turned into sources of mutual understanding and cooperation.
Beyond the region, the SCO has played an active role in upholding the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and international law, contributing to the settlement of regional and international issues and promoting coordination among multilateral mechanisms.
The SCO Plus format has further broadened the space for dialogue among the Global South, facilitating exchanges in governance experience and practical cooperation.
Over the past decades, the SCO has shown that diversity need not lead to division, and that countries with different political systems, development paths, and civilizations can cooperate on equal footing without butting heads.
Looking ahead, the SCO is well positioned to bolster high-quality regional development and contribute more wisdom to building a more just and equitable global governance system. ■
